identification.summary: APT.3102 is a name for the actor behind a variant of the '9002' Trojan called '3102', which Palo Alto Networks Unit 42 reported in September 2015 after two spear-phishing attacks that used the same lure document [S1]. The name comes from the string '3102', which the payload uses as the first four bytes of its network communications [S1]. Malpedia lists the group as APT.3102 and cites the Unit 42 report as its reference [S3].
identification.firstObserved: Unit 42 observed the two spear-phishing attacks on 2015-05-06 and 2015-05-11 [S1]. Unit 42 also cites a Cylance article on a May 2014 targeted attack against a Chinese national that delivered the 3102 variant of 9002 [S1].
identification.notes: Unit 42 says the 3102 payload appears related to the Evilgrab payload used in a May 2015 watering-hole attack on the Myanmar president's website [S1][S2]. That is a payload relationship reported by one vendor, not a confirmed merge of actor clusters. No Microsoft name or MITRE group ID was found for this actor.

attribution.confidence: Unit 42 assessed that the C2 infrastructure ties to individuals in China who are active on hacking forums and claim to develop Trojans [S1]. No source reviewed attributes the activity to a specific government organization.
attribution.basis: Unit 42 infrastructure analysis linking C2 to individuals in China, and the payload similarity to Evilgrab [S1][S2]. The encyclopedia country field (CN) is carried from the imported record.

targeting.notes: Unit 42 observed one spear-phishing attack on a US government target and one on a European media company, using the same lure document [S1]. The related Evilgrab watering hole targeted the Myanmar president's website [S2].

capabilities.summary: Spear-phishing with a weaponized delivery document that installs the 3102 variant of the 9002 Trojan, which relies heavily on plugins [S1]. The payload uses the string '3102' as the first four bytes of its C2 communications [S1]. A related Evilgrab payload was delivered in the May 2015 Myanmar watering hole, in which an IFRAME was injected into a Drupal theme JavaScript file [S2].

campaigns.name: Spear-phishing of a US government target
campaigns.summary: Unit 42 observed a spear-phishing attack on a US government target using a weaponized document that installed the 3102 payload [S1].

campaigns.name: Spear-phishing of a European media company
campaigns.summary: Unit 42 observed a second attack, using the same lure document, against a European media company [S1].

campaigns.name: Evilgrab watering hole on the Myanmar president's website (related payload)
campaigns.summary: Unit 42 reported a watering hole that delivered an Evilgrab variant. Unit 42 said it had evidence of access to the site since November 2014 or earlier. The 3102 payload appears related to Evilgrab [S1][S2].

diamond.adversary: Unit 42 tied the C2 infrastructure to individuals in China active on hacking forums [S1].
diamond.capability: Spear-phishing documents; the 3102 variant of 9002, which is plugin-based; a related Evilgrab payload [S1][S2].
diamond.infrastructure: C2 infrastructure that Unit 42 linked to individuals in China [S1]. Further details were not accessible.
diamond.victim: A US government target and a European media company [S1].

gaps: I could not open the primary Unit 42 reports. WebFetch failed with a DNS error, so the content above comes from WebSearch result summaries only. Re-verify against the Unit 42 articles before use [S1][S2].
The exploit and CVE used in the lure document, the C2 domains and the indicators were not obtained.
No sponsor, no government attribution and no stated objective were found. The 'individuals in China' language does not establish state sponsorship.
Whether APT.3102 is the same cluster as the Evilgrab actor, or maps to groups in other vendors' naming, is unresolved.
No activity after 2015 was found in the results. The Cylance 2014 article was not reviewed.
Malpedia lists no malware families for this actor [S3]. The Malpedia page itself could not be fetched.

identification.summary: APT1 is the China-based cyber-espionage group that Mandiant exposed in February 2013 and tied to PLA Unit 61398, the 2nd Bureau of the PLA General Staff Department's 3rd Department, based in Pudong, Shanghai [S1][S2][S8]. Mandiant reported that APT1 stole hundreds of terabytes of data from at least 141 organizations across 20 major industries since 2006. It said 87% of those victims were headquartered in English-speaking countries [S1][S2]. In May 2014 the US Justice Department charged five Unit 61398 officers with economic espionage against US nuclear, solar, steel and metals companies and a labor union [S4].
identification.firstObserved: Mandiant: tracked since 2006 [S1][S2]. The 2014 US indictment describes intrusions from 2006 into 2014 [S4].
identification.notes: Also tracked as Comment Crew, Comment Panda, GIF89a and Byzantine Candor [S8]. Microsoft's public naming map has no Typhoon name for APT1, Comment Crew, Comment Panda or Unit 61398 (checked 2026-10-14) [S10]. Later activity reusing APT1 tooling (Siesta in 2014, Oceansalt in 2018) was not firmly attributed to APT1 by the reporting vendors; see campaigns and gaps [S5][S6].

attribution.sponsor: People's Republic of China, People's Liberation Army: Unit 61398, 3rd Department of the General Staff Department (per Mandiant and the 2014 US indictment) [S1][S4].
attribution.confidence: Mandiant stated that the scale and duration of the attacks from a single group based in China 'leaves little doubt about the organization behind APT1' [S2]. The US government formally charged five named Unit 61398 officers in May 2014, which Attorney General Eric Holder called the first charges of their kind against a state actor [S4]. China's Defense Ministry denied the accusations and called the report 'unprofessional' [S9]. Some independent commentators, such as Jeffrey Carr, argued that Mandiant did not prove APT1 is Unit 61398 [S8].
attribution.basis: Mandiant traced APT1 activity to four large networks in Shanghai and linked it to Unit 61398 using infrastructure and persona analysis [S1][S2]. DOJ indictment allegations, which name Wang Dong, Sun Kailiang and Wen Xinyu as hackers and Huang Zhenyu and Gu Chunhui as managers of supporting infrastructure [S4].

actors.objectives: Long-term, large-scale theft of intellectual property and confidential business information from foreign organizations, chiefly in English-speaking countries [S1][S2]. The 2014 indictment alleges the stolen information benefited Chinese state-owned competitors. Several victims had filed trade complaints against Chinese rivals [S4].

sectors: Steel and specialty metals (U.S. Steel, Allegheny Technologies) [S4]
regions: United States (115 of the victims Mandiant counted, per press coverage) [S11]
15 countries in total, per press coverage of the Mandiant report [S11]
targeting.notes: Mandiant counted 141 victim organizations across 20 major industries [S1][S2] and said its visibility was probably only a small fraction of APT1's total activity [S2]. Sectors from the possibly related Siesta (energy, defense, telecom) [S5] and Shady RAT [S7] campaigns are left out of this list because attribution to APT1 is unconfirmed.

capabilities.summary: Mandiant described a mature, high-volume operation. Average dwell time in victim networks was 356 days and the longest was 1,764 days [S2][S3]. In one case APT1 took 6.5 TB of compressed data from a single organization over ten months [S2]. Its infrastructure included at least 937 command-and-control servers on 849 IP addresses in 13 countries, mostly registered in China (709) and the US (109) [S2]. The 2014 indictment separates hands-on-keyboard intrusion operators from personnel who managed domain accounts and other infrastructure [S4]. Its custom malware (for example Seasalt, circa 2010) was later partly reused in Oceansalt [S6]. The tool and technique list comes from MITRE ATT&CK G0006 separately.

The Oceansalt implant reused part of APT1's Seasalt code, but McAfee said APT1 was unlikely to have conducted it.

diamond.adversary: PLA Unit 61398 (GSD 3rd Department, 2nd Bureau), Shanghai, per Mandiant [S1][S2]. Five officers were named in the 2014 US indictment [S4].
diamond.capability: Spear-phishing-led intrusions, custom backdoors such as Seasalt, and long-dwell data theft at terabyte scale [S2][S5][S6].
diamond.infrastructure: At least 937 C2 servers on 849 IPs in 13 countries, mostly China-registered. Activity was traced to four large Shanghai networks. Dedicated personnel managed domain accounts [S1][S2][S4].
diamond.victim: 141+ organizations in 20 industries, 87% in English-speaking countries. US industrial firms in nuclear, solar, steel and aluminum, plus a labor union [S2][S4][S11].
diamond.socioPolitical: Economic espionage that allegedly benefited Chinese state-owned enterprises, including firms in trade disputes with victims [S4]. Exposure drove the first US criminal charges against state military hackers [S4].
diamond.technology: Corporate Windows enterprise networks and email holding IP and negotiation data, which can be accessed for long periods without detection [S2][S4].

gaps: The original Mandiant APT1 PDF was not fetched directly (fetches to mandiant/fireeye/lawfare hosts failed). Figures come from a course-site mirror listing and Lawfare and press reproductions [S1][S2][S3].
The DOJ indictment and press release (justice.gov) were not opened. Indictment details come from press coverage [S4].
The APT1 link to Operation Shady RAT rests on a secondary (Wikipedia) citation of Dell SecureWorks. The original Secureworks analysis was not reviewed [S8].

Siesta (2014) and Oceansalt (2018) are tooling overlaps only: FireEye allowed for a copycat, and McAfee judged APT1 unlikely to be responsible. Do not count them as confirmed APT1 operations [S5][S6].
No authoritative public reporting was found on APT1/Unit 61398 activity after 2014, or on how the unit was reorganized after the 2015-2016 PLA reforms.
Microsoft has no public name for this actor [S10]. Overlaps with other PRC clusters are not established in the sources gathered.
Exact publication dates for some secondary sources are given to the month only.

implications.jipoe: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. STEP 1 (operational environment): For DoD, key terrain is the defense industrial base and industrial-supply-chain enterprise networks (aerospace, metals, energy engineering), which hold technical IP and negotiation data [S4][S11]. STEP 2 (effects): Average dwell times of nearly a year and terabyte-scale exfiltration mean an undetected intrusion can compromise whole program data holdings [S2]. STEP 3 (threat model): The template is spear-phishing, a custom backdoor beaconing to China-registered C2, long-term persistence, then bulk archive-and-exfiltrate. Separate personnel manage infrastructure [S2][S4][S5]. STEP 4 (COAs): MLCOA is sustained economic and technical espionage against firms tied to PRC industrial or trade interests [S4]. MDCOA is a successor PLA unit or a tool-reusing actor using APT1-style long-dwell access against DIB partners supporting Air Force programs. Old APT1 code may be reused under false-flag ambiguity [S6]. Candidate indicators: long-lived low-volume beacons to China-registered IPs, large compressed archives leaving the network, and spear-phishing lures tied to current business or infrastructure projects [S2][S6].
implications.jcc2: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. (1) Situational awareness: APT1 shows that dwell time is measured in months to years [S2]. Treat historical log retention and retrospective hunting as mission requirements. (2) Authorities: The 2014 indictment shows how law enforcement responds to state-military intrusions against private firms [S4]. Coordinate DIB-victim intrusions with DOJ/FBI and DC3 rather than handling them as purely military events. (3) Mission assurance: Theft of contractor IP and program data erodes technological advantage without degrading operations, so include contractor networks in mission-relevant terrain analysis [S4]. (4) Coordination: Code reuse across actors complicates attribution [S5][S6]. Pair technical indicators with multi-source intelligence before naming an actor in operational reporting.

identification.summary: CrowdStrike published its profile of PLA Navy-linked 'Anchor Panda' on 2013-03-22. It said it had tracked the adversary for about a year, targeting civilian and military maritime operations in green/brown water regions, mainly the area of operations of the PLA Navy South Sea Fleet [S1]. Beyond maritime targets it said the actor heavily targeted Western companies in the US, Germany, Sweden, the UK and Australia, plus other countries involved in maritime satellite systems, aerospace and defense contracting [S1]. CFR's cyber operations tracker lists the activity as espionage with China as suspected sponsor [S2].
identification.firstObserved: CrowdStrike said in March 2013 that it had tracked the actor for roughly the previous year (about 2012) [S1].
identification.notes: Vendor naming varies by source. This record's aliases (ALUMINUM, QAZTeam, ANCHOR PANDA) came from MISP Galaxy; a search-result summary of the Malpedia APT14 page also lists Anchor Panda, ALUMINUM and QAZTeam under APT14. An earlier note that Malpedia places these under APT15 was not supported by this check and was removed. Do not merge activity across APT14/APT15 without a primary report. No Microsoft Typhoon/Storm name was confirmed for this actor. No MITRE group ID is recorded.

attribution.sponsor: CrowdStrike's own title calls the actor 'PLA Navy Anchor Panda' and ties its focus to the PLA Navy South Sea Fleet area of operations [S1]. CFR lists China as suspected state sponsor [S2].
attribution.confidence: No confidence level is stated in the sources I could read. CFR labels the sponsor as 'suspected' [S2]. This is vendor-level attribution; no government attribution was found.
attribution.basis: CrowdStrike cites target selection aligned with PLA Navy South Sea Fleet interests; its detailed technical basis was withheld in the post [S1].

actors.objectives: Collection of maritime, satellite, aerospace and defense-contractor information and political/diplomatic intelligence, inferred by CrowdStrike from victim selection around the South Sea Fleet area and space-related industries [S1].

regions: South Sea Fleet area of operations (green/brown water) [S1]
United States, Germany, Sweden, United Kingdom, Australia [S1]
targeting.notes: Targeting described by CrowdStrike in 2013 [S1]. No later targeting reporting was found.

capabilities.summary: CrowdStrike's post said it would withhold most technical detail but included detection signatures; secondary summaries say these covered Adobe Gh0st and Poison Ivy beacons, and one secondary source also mentions Torn RAT and spear-phishing (not verified against the primary text) [S1].

campaigns.name: CrowdStrike 'Who is Anchor Panda' disclosure
campaigns.summary: CrowdStrike publicly profiled the actor, describing about a year of tracked maritime, satellite, aerospace and defense-contractor targeting across several Western countries and the South China Sea region.

diamond.adversary: Suspected PRC actor with apparent PLA Navy tasking alignment, per CrowdStrike [S1][S2].
diamond.capability: Remote access tools (Poison Ivy, Gh0st variants) per signatures in the CrowdStrike post, as summarized by secondary sources [S1].
diamond.victim: Maritime operators, satellite/aerospace firms, defense contractors, embassies, intelligence services and space-program governments [S1].
diamond.socioPolitical: Naval and maritime interests in the South China Sea region and space-related technology acquisition [S1].
diamond.technology: Maritime satellite systems and aerospace/defense industrial networks [S1].

gaps: No reporting after March 2013 was found; current activity status is unknown.
Could not open the primary CrowdStrike post (host unreachable from tooling); capability details rely on search-result summaries of it.
No Microsoft actor name, MITRE group, malware list, infrastructure, or CVEs confirmed.
Mandiant APT-groups page listed in the record was not reviewed.
Alias mapping (APT14 vs APT15) not verified against a primary report; Malpedia, MISP Galaxy and Red Sky Alliance pages were seen only as search results and are not cited as sources.

implications.jipoe: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. STEP 1: Maritime satellite ground and communications nodes, shipping and port-related networks, and aerospace/defense contractor networks supporting naval and space programs are candidate key terrain [S1]. STEP 2: The actor aligns with the PLA Navy South Sea Fleet area of operations, so collection interest likely rises around South China Sea activity [S1]. STEP 3: Template is RAT-based intrusion (Gh0st/Poison Ivy-type per secondary summaries) against contractors and maritime operators [S1]. STEP 4: MLCOA is continued collection against maritime, satellite and defense-industrial targets. MDCOA is use of access to defense contractors or satellite providers to learn US/allied maritime posture during a crisis. Candidate indicators: Poison Ivy/Gh0st-style beacons from maritime or satellite-sector hosts. Evidence is dated 2013 and thin.
implications.jcc2: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. (1) Situational awareness: treat as low-confidence legacy reporting; confirm current activity before tasking. (2) Authorities: contractor and commercial maritime/satellite networks fall outside DoDIN; coordinate through DC3/DIB CS and sector partners. (3) Mission assurance: prioritize protection of satellite communications and maritime logistics dependencies in the Indo-Pacific. (4) Coordination: confirm actor naming with intelligence partners before sharing indicators.

provenance.importedSummary: PLA Navy Anchor Panda is an adversary that CrowdStrike has tracked extensively over the last year targeting both civilian and military maritime operations in the green/brown water regions primarily in the area of operations of the South Sea Fleet of the PLA Navy. In addition to maritime operations in this region, Anchor Panda also heavily targeted western companies in the US, Germany, Sweden, the UK, and Australia, and other countries involved in maritime satellite systems, aerospace companies, and defense contractors. Not surprisingly, embassies and diplomatic missions in the region, foreign intelligence services, and foreign governments with space programs were also targeted.

identification.summary: APT16 is a China-based threat group that has run spear-phishing campaigns against Japanese and Taiwanese organizations [S2]. FireEye reported that between 26 November and 1 December 2015 known and suspected China-based APT groups, including APT16, sent spear-phishing emails to Japanese and Taiwanese organizations in the high-tech, government services, media and financial services sectors [S1][S4]. The lure documents exploited an Encapsulated PostScript (EPS) dict copy use-after-free flaw together with the Windows privilege escalation flaw CVE-2015-1701, and delivered either the IRONHALO downloader or the ELMER backdoor [S1][S4]. Press coverage of FireEye's research said Taiwanese news organizations and the opposition Democratic Progressive Party (DPP) were targeted ahead of Taiwan's January 2016 elections [S6][S7].
identification.firstObserved: FireEye's public reporting covers activity from 26 November to 1 December 2015 [S1][S4]. Earlier start dates that appear on secondary sites are not supported by the sources gathered.
identification.notes: Microsoft name: none found. APT16 and SVCMONDR do not appear in Microsoft's public threat-actor naming map (checked 2026-10-15) [S8]. Malpedia lists the aliases G0023 and SVCMONDR [S4]. APT16 is FireEye/Mandiant's designation, and MITRE tracks it as G0023 [S2]. Malpedia's Danti entry also lists ELMER as an associated malware family, so the tooling is not unique to this cluster [S4].

attribution.sponsor: China, a suspected state sponsor according to the CFR Cyber Operations Tracker [S5].
attribution.confidence: MITRE describes APT16 as 'China-based' [S2]. CFR lists China as the 'suspected state sponsor' [S5]. Press coverage reports that FireEye attributed the Taiwan activity to Chinese hackers [S6][S7]. No government attribution or indictment specific to APT16 was found.
attribution.basis: FireEye's December 2015 technical reporting on the EPS/CVE-2015-1701 spear-phishing campaigns [S1], which MITRE, Malpedia and CFR reuse [S2][S4][S5].

actors.objectives: Espionage, classified as such by CFR [S5]. In the Taiwan campaign the reported aim was to obtain information on opposition (DPP) policies and speeches ahead of the January 2016 presidential and legislative elections [S6][S7].

targeting.notes: CFR files the target category as private sector [S5]. The 2015 reporting describes several China-based groups in the same window, so not every targeted sector necessarily belongs to APT16 alone [S1][S4].

capabilities.summary: Spear-phishing with malicious Microsoft Word documents that chain an EPS use-after-free exploit with CVE-2015-1701 for local privilege escalation [S1][S4]. The documents dropped IRONHALO, a downloader, or ELMER, a backdoor [S1][S4]. MITRE describes ELMER as a non-persistent, proxy-aware HTTP backdoor written in Delphi that can list directories and running processes [S3]. APT16 has compromised otherwise legitimate sites and used them as staging servers for second-stage payloads [S2]. In the Taiwan activity, emails reportedly used the lure subject 'DPP's Contact Information Update' [S6][S7].

campaigns.name: EPS / CVE-2015-1701 spear-phishing against Japan and Taiwan
campaigns.summary: From 26 November to 1 December 2015, spear-phishing emails carrying Word documents with the EPS exploit and CVE-2015-1701 hit Japanese and Taiwanese high-tech, government-services, media and financial organizations, delivering IRONHALO or ELMER.

campaigns.name: Targeting of Taiwanese media and the DPP before the 2016 election
campaigns.summary: Coverage of FireEye's research reports phishing of Taiwanese news organizations with a 'DPP's Contact Information Update' lure, seeking information on opposition policies and speeches before the January 2016 elections.

diamond.adversary: China-based group; China is the suspected state sponsor (CFR) [S2][S5].
diamond.capability: Weaponized Word documents (an EPS use-after-free exploit plus CVE-2015-1701), the IRONHALO downloader and the ELMER Delphi HTTP backdoor [S1][S3][S4].
diamond.infrastructure: Compromised legitimate websites used as staging servers for second-stage payloads; HTTP command and control for ELMER [S2][S3].
diamond.victim: Japanese and Taiwanese government-services, financial, media and high-tech organizations; Taiwan's DPP and news outlets [S1][S5][S6].
diamond.socioPolitical: Intelligence collection on Taiwanese domestic politics ahead of the January 2016 presidential and legislative elections [S6][S7].
diamond.technology: Unpatched Microsoft Office EPS handling and Windows privilege escalation (CVE-2015-1701) on victim endpoints [S1][S4].

gaps: FireEye's primary report 'The EPS Awakens' (2015-12-16) could not be opened (host unreachable). Details come from search excerpts and from Malpedia/MITRE quotations of it. 'The EPS Awakens Part 2', which MITRE also cites, was not reviewed.

The MITRE ATT&CK, Malpedia, CFR, SCMP and Security Affairs pages could not be fetched directly. Their content and dates come from search-result excerpts. The CFR entry date (2016-12) and the press dates (2015-12) need checking.
No Microsoft designation exists for APT16 in Microsoft's public naming map, so it may be untracked or merged without public disclosure.

The FireEye 2015 reporting covers several China-based groups in the same window. Which victims and sectors belong specifically to APT16 rather than other groups is not clear from the sources gathered.
A reported compromise of DPP staff email accounts appears only in secondary press excerpts. Whether it was APT16 activity is unverified.
Kaspersky's 2016 'CVE-2015-2545: overview of current threats' is an existing record reference that may mention SVCMONDR. It could not be retrieved or checked.
No public reporting on APT16 activity after 2015 was found, so its current status is unknown.
Malpedia associates ELMER with the Danti actor as well. Shared tooling between these clusters has not been resolved.
Secondary blogs claiming activity since 2012, an 'OpTaiwan' link, or DOORJAMB use were not corroborated and were excluded.

implications.jipoe: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. STEP 1 (operational environment): The relevant environment is the Taiwan and Japan government, media, financial and high-tech information space, plus the political-party networks around Taiwanese elections [S1][S6]. STEP 2 (effects): Office documents arriving by email and unpatched Windows endpoints are the main avenue of approach. Compromised legitimate websites hide second-stage delivery [S2][S4]. STEP 3 (adversary model): Political or contact-update themed spear-phish, then Word EPS exploit plus CVE-2015-1701, then IRONHALO download or ELMER HTTP backdoor, then directory and process discovery [S1][S3][S6]. STEP 4 (COAs): MLCOA is spear-phishing for espionage against Taiwanese and Japanese political, media and government organizations around significant political events such as elections [S6][S7]. MDCOA is use of the resulting access to US, allied or partner organizations in the region for sustained collection on regional policy during a crisis; this is not observed in sources. Candidate indicators: Word documents carrying embedded EPS content, privilege escalation via CVE-2015-1701 on endpoints, Delphi-compiled HTTP beacons that honor proxy settings, and second-stage downloads from legitimate but compromised websites [S2][S3][S4].
implications.jcc2: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. (1) Situational awareness: Track regional political events, such as Taiwanese elections, as triggers for heightened spear-phishing against partner and media organizations [S6]. (2) Authorities: Partner-nation victims (Taiwanese and Japanese organizations) fall outside DoD networks, so information sharing goes through appropriate partner and interagency channels. (3) Mission assurance: Exploitation relied on known Office and Windows vulnerabilities, so patch compliance for document-handling components is a key mitigation [S1][S4]. (4) Coordination: Reporting is old (2015) and vendor-specific. Coordinate with intelligence partners for current activity before assigning APT16 as a named threat in planning.

provenance.importedSummary: Between November 26, 2015, and December 1, 2015, known and suspected China-based APT groups launched several spear-phishing attacks targeting Japanese and Taiwanese organizations in the high-tech, government services, media and financial services industries. Each campaign delivered a malicious Microsoft Word document exploiting the aforementioned EPS dict copy use-after-free vulnerability, and the local Windows privilege escalation vulnerability CVE-2015-1701. The successful exploitation of both vulnerabilities led to the delivery of either a downloader that we refer to as IRONHALO, or a backdoor that we refer to as ELMER.

identification.summary: APT20 is a China-linked cyber espionage actor. Fox-IT (NCC Group) published Operation Wocao in December 2019, assessing with high confidence that the actor behind that activity is a Chinese group likely supporting Chinese government interests, and with medium confidence that its tools, techniques and procedures are those industry partners call APT20 [S2]. Earlier, in September 2014, Palo Alto Networks Unit 42 attributed a series of watering-hole attacks using Poison Ivy to a group it called 'th3bug' [S1]. The imported record lists TH3Bug, Crawling Taurus (Unit 42) and VIOLIN PANDA (CrowdStrike) as APT20 aliases; those vendor mappings were not verified from a primary source.
identification.firstObserved: 2014-07 (earliest th3bug Poison Ivy sample Unit 42 saw, dated 14 July 2014) [S1]. MITRE dates Operation Wocao activity from December 2017 to December 2019 [S4].
identification.notes: Two distinct bodies of reporting are tied to the APT20 name: the 2014 th3bug watering holes (Unit 42) [S1] and the 2017-2019 Operation Wocao intrusions (Fox-IT) [S2][S4]. Fox-IT rates the Wocao-to-APT20 link only medium confidence, so facts from the two should not be merged without checking [S2]. Microsoft has no mapped name for APT20 in this encyclopedia record. Not a Microsoft-named cluster.

attribution.sponsor: Fox-IT judges the Operation Wocao actor to be a Chinese group likely working in support of Chinese government interests; this is Fox-IT's assessment, not a government attribution [S2][S6].
attribution.confidence: Fox-IT: high confidence in Chinese nationality and motive; medium confidence that the observed TTPs correspond to APT20 [S2]. Unit 42's 2014 report attributes the watering holes to the th3bug group based on shared Poison Ivy password and C2 infrastructure; the excerpts reviewed do not state a state-sponsor conclusion [S1].
attribution.basis: Fox-IT basis: the name Wocao comes from a Chinese expletive typed by an operator after losing access [S2][S6]. Unit 42 basis: Poison Ivy samples sharing a password and the same command-and-control server [S1].

actors.objectives: Fox-IT assesses the Wocao actor is likely tasked with espionage supporting the interests of the Chinese government [S2]. The 2014 th3bug targeting of Uyghur sympathizers, a US university, a US computer maker office and an international telecom provider is consistent with intelligence collection, though Unit 42 excerpts reviewed do not state objectives [S1].

regions: Brazil, China, France, Germany, Italy, Mexico, Portugal, Spain, United Kingdom and United States (MITRE list for Operation Wocao) [S4]
targeting.notes: Fox-IT says victims were government entities, managed service providers and a wide variety of industries including energy, health care and high-tech [S2]. Press adds aviation, finance and insurance [S5]. The 2014 victims come from Unit 42 [S1].

capabilities.summary: 2014: compromise of legitimate websites as watering holes delivering Poison Ivy RAT variants; Unit 42 could not recover the initial exploit and said it was possibly the CVE-2014-0515 Adobe Flash exploit [S1]. 2017-2019 (Operation Wocao): initial access commonly through vulnerable web servers, often JBoss, sometimes already carrying web shells from other attackers; web shells for reconnaissance and lateral movement; credential dumping and capture of a password manager master password via keylogging; lateral tool transfer over SMB; deletion of tools and files to hide traces; and use of stolen VPN credentials as backdoors, in some cases despite two-factor authentication, which Fox-IT speculated was done with a stolen RSA SecurID software token [S4][S5].

campaigns.name: th3bug watering-hole attacks
campaigns.summary: Unit 42 (19 September 2014) reported that over the summer the group compromised several legitimate websites, including a well-known Uyghur-language site, and delivered Poison Ivy variants using the same C2. Victims included Uyghur sympathizers, an East Asian office of a major US computer maker, a major US university and an international telecom provider. Earliest sample dated 14 July 2014. Actors changed their Poison Ivy password, possibly after FireEye publicity [S1].

campaigns.name: Operation Wocao
campaigns.summary: Fox-IT named intrusions across more than 10 countries Operation Wocao. MITRE lists activity first seen December 2017 and last seen December 2019. Actors exploited web servers (often JBoss), used web shells, harvested credentials, moved laterally, bypassed 2FA on VPN accounts and deleted tools [S2][S4][S5].

campaigns.name: Public disclosure of Operation Wocao
campaigns.summary: Fox-IT published 'Operation Wocao: Shining a light on one of China's hidden hacking groups' dated 19 December 2019, rating the actor Chinese with high confidence and APT20 with medium confidence [S2][S6].

diamond.adversary: China-based group assessed by Fox-IT as working for Chinese government interests; linked to APT20 at medium confidence [S2].
diamond.capability: Poison Ivy RAT via watering holes (2014); web shells, JBoss exploitation, credential theft, SMB lateral movement, VPN and 2FA bypass, anti-forensic deletion (2017-2019) [S1][S4][S5].
diamond.infrastructure: Compromised legitimate websites and shared C2 for Poison Ivy (2014) [S1]; compromised web servers and stolen VPN accounts as persistent access (2019) [S5]. Specific IOCs not captured.
diamond.victim: Uyghur-interest sites and sympathizers, US technology and academic organizations, a telecom provider (2014); government, managed service providers and multiple industries in about ten countries (2017-2019) [S1][S2][S4].
diamond.socioPolitical: Espionage consistent with Chinese government interests per Fox-IT; the 2014 Uyghur focus indicates monitoring of a minority community [S1][S2].
diamond.technology: Internet-facing application servers such as JBoss, VPN gateways with software-token 2FA, password managers, and frequently visited websites [S1][S4].

gaps: WebFetch failed (host resolution errors) for all pages, so no primary document was opened. The Fox-IT Operation Wocao report, the Unit 42 th3bug report, MITRE C0014 and the Unit 42 Crawling Taurus page were read only through search-result excerpts.
Whether the 2014 th3bug cluster and the 2017-2019 Wocao cluster are the same operators rests on Fox-IT's medium-confidence TTP link and vendor naming; not independently verified.
Alias status of 'Twivy' and 'APT 8' appeared only in aggregator results (strobes.co, Malpedia excerpts) and was not confirmed in a vendor primary source, so not added.
No CrowdStrike VIOLIN PANDA report and no Mandiant APT20 profile were retrieved; the existing record's Mandiant and Unit 42 atoms URLs are unverified.
No public APT20 reporting after 2019 was found; current status of the actor is unknown.
Exact 2FA bypass method is unconfirmed; RSA SecurID token theft is Fox-IT's hypothesis [S5].
Specific malware families and indicators for Wocao were not retrieved.

Dark Reading and SecurityLab.ru sources were removed because their URLs could not be confirmed in search results; claims resting only on them (activity since 2009/2011, working-hours basis, construction and gambling targeting) were deleted.

implications.jipoe: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. STEP 1: Key terrain includes internet-facing application servers (JBoss), VPN gateways, managed service provider access paths, and frequently visited community websites [S1][S4]. STEP 2: The actor reuses web servers already holding web shells and uses stolen VPN credentials as durable backdoors, which blurs initial access ownership and survives patching [S5]. STEP 3: Observed template is vulnerable web server or watering hole, then web shell or RAT, then credential theft, SMB lateral movement, VPN access and tool deletion [S1][S4][S5]. STEP 4: MLCOA is quiet, long-duration collection against government, MSP and industry networks. MDCOA is use of a compromised MSP or stolen VPN/software token to reach defense-sector customers while bypassing 2FA. Candidate indicators: unexpected web shells on JBoss hosts, VPN logins from new locations that satisfy 2FA, token-generator files accessed on workstations, password-manager keylogging, SMB tool transfers and bulk deletion of tools [S4][S5]. Evidence is from 2014 and 2017-2019; current applicability is unverified.
implications.jcc2: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. (1) Situational awareness: track legacy JBoss and similar application servers and VPN authentication anomalies on mission networks. (2) Authorities: MSP and contractor compromise requires coordination with the owning organization and DIB reporting channels rather than direct action. (3) Mission assurance: treat software-token 2FA as bypassable if endpoint token seeds can be stolen, and prefer hardware-bound factors for privileged access. (4) Coordination: share indicators with the DIB cyber program and allied partners given the multinational victim set [S2][S4].

provenance.importedSummary: We’ve uncovered some new data and likely attribution regarding a series of APT watering hole attacks this past summer. Watering hole attacks are an increasingly popular component of APT campaigns, as many people are more aware of spear phishing and are less likely to open documents or click on links in unsolicited emails. Watering hole attacks offer a much better chance of success because they involve compromising legitimate websites and installing malware intended to compromise website visitors. These are often popular websites frequented by people who work in specific industries or have political sympathies to which the actors want to gain access. In contrast to many other APT campaigns, which tend to rely heavily on spear phishing to gain victims, “th3bug” is known for compromising legitimate websites their intended visitors are likely to frequent. Over the summer they compromised several sites, including a well-known Uyghur website written in that native language.

identification.summary: China-linked espionage actor tracked by Google Threat Intelligence/Mandiant as APT21 (alias TEMP.Zhenbao) and publicly associated with the NetTraveler malware family and campaign first disclosed by Kaspersky in June 2013 [S1][S6]. Kaspersky reported more than 350 high-profile victims in 40 countries, including government institutions, embassies, oil and gas, research centers, military contractors and activists [S1]. Google's APT group page describes APT21 as a suspected China-origin actor against government targets that uses Russian-language national-security decoy documents and targets groups seeking autonomy or independence such as Tibet and Xinjiang [S6].
identification.firstObserved: Kaspersky: earliest known NetTraveler samples date to 2005, with indications that the first version may date to 2004 [S1][S3]. Recent-activity reporting covers 2015-2016 [S4][S5].
identification.notes: Aliases per the imported record: HAMMER PANDA (CrowdStrike), NetTraveler, TEMP.Zhenbao (Mandiant). NetTraveler is both a malware family and a Kaspersky campaign name, and the mapping of the whole campaign to a single vendor-defined group (APT21/Zhenbao) is a vendor-cluster judgment; keep malware names and actor names distinct. Google lists SOGU, TEMPFUN, Gh0st and TRAVELNET as associated malware, and says APT21 frequently uses TRAVELNET and TEMPFUN [S6]. Proofpoint's 2016 activity used NetTraveler after the same operators earlier used PlugX [S5]. No Microsoft Threat Actor naming entry is recorded for APT21 in this record.

attribution.sponsor: Google Threat Intelligence lists APT21 as suspected China-origin [S6]. No government attribution found in sources gathered.
attribution.confidence: Kaspersky estimated the NetTraveler group at roughly 50 people, mostly native Chinese speakers with working English [S2]. Proofpoint assessed the operator as based in China, but its director of threat intelligence said there was no indication that the activity was state-sponsored [S5]. Google labels the origin 'suspected' [S6].
attribution.basis: Language and operator-profile assessment by Kaspersky [S2]; targeting patterns (Tibetan and Uyghur activists, diplomatic and government targets) [S1][S3]; vendor assessments by Proofpoint and Google [S5][S6]. Vendor assessments are not government attribution.

actors.objectives: Collection of information from government, diplomatic, research, energy, defense-industry and activist targets, with sustained interest in Tibetan and Uyghur communities and, in 2015-2016, Russia and neighboring states [S1][S3][S5][S6]. Whether the operation serves a state customer is disputed in vendor reporting [S5][S6].

Military contractors and defense / weapons manufacturing
Activists and civil society (Tibetan, Uyghur, pro-democracy and human rights)
regions: Mongolia, India and Russia had the most infections in 2013; also China, Germany, the UK and Spain [S2]
Russia, Mongolia, Belarus and other European countries (2016) [S5]
targeting.notes: Kaspersky reported in 2014 that diplomatic targets made up 32% and government 19% of recent victims [S3]. Tibetan and Uyghur activist targeting continued in Kaspersky's later reporting [S2][S3].

capabilities.summary: Spear-phishing with Microsoft Office documents exploiting old, patched vulnerabilities CVE-2012-0158 and CVE-2010-3333 to install the NetTraveler spyware [S2]; a Java exploit patched in June 2013 was used against Uyghur activists in Q3 2013 [S2]. In 2014 Kaspersky described an updated backdoor with a new encryption scheme and a new configuration-file format designed to hide settings, with C2 servers in Hong Kong and the USA [S3]. In 2015-2016 lures were built with the MNKit document builder, installed NetTraveler via DLL side-loading, and used spoofed Russian Foreign Ministry themes [S4]. Proofpoint also reported RAR-packed executables and Word attachments, and lookalike news and military sites for C2 and payload hosting [S5]. After the 2013 disclosure the operators moved C2 to servers in China, Hong Kong and Taiwan [S2].

diamond.adversary: Suspected China-based operators, estimated by Kaspersky at about 50 people, mostly Chinese speakers [S2][S6]; state sponsorship disputed in vendor statements [S5].

gaps: Primary vendor pages (Securelist, Kaspersky, Proofpoint, Unit 42, CFR, Mandiant) could not be fetched in this run (host resolution failed); details rely on search-result summaries and should be re-verified against the originals.

Kaspersky links NetTraveler to Travle/PYLOT as a possible successor and to Enfal and Microcin; RedAlpha infrastructure overlap with NetTraveler was reported by Recorded Future. Neither was verified from primary documents or dated, so they are not stated as fact here.
Possible overlap with Ke3chang was mentioned by one secondary source but no direct tie to APT21 was found; keep clusters separate.
Relationship between the Kaspersky NetTraveler campaign and Mandiant's APT21 / CrowdStrike's HAMMER PANDA clusters is a vendor mapping, not confirmed boundary equivalence.

implications.jipoe: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. STEP 1: Key terrain is diplomatic, foreign-ministry and defense-contractor email and the endpoints of personnel who open Office attachments [S3][S4][S5]. STEP 2: The actor reuses old patched exploits (CVE-2012-0158, CVE-2010-3333) and public builders, so unpatched Office is the exploitable condition [S2][S4]. STEP 3: Observed template is a themed spear-phish (e.g., SCO or ministry lures), an exploit document, DLL side-loaded NetTraveler, then C2 to China/Hong Kong/Taiwan/USA servers or lookalike sites [S2][S3][S4][S5]. STEP 4: MLCOA is continued email-borne collection against regional diplomatic, defense-industry and activist targets, with Russia and Central Asia emphasis in 2015-2016 [S4][S5]. MDCOA (analyst judgment) is the same tooling pointed at partner-nation ministries or defense suppliers in a regional crisis. Candidate indicators: Office documents spawning DLL side-loading, lookalike news or military domains, and spoofed foreign-ministry senders [S4][S5].
implications.jcc2: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. (1) Situational awareness: the sourced activity is old and recent status is unknown, so treat as a legacy-TTP hunt baseline rather than current tasking. (2) Authorities: DoD-network detection of these TTPs falls under standard DODIN defensive operations; partner-nation or contractor victims need information sharing via DC3/DIB programs. (3) Mission assurance: enforce Office patching and attachment controls for personnel handling diplomatic or coalition correspondence. (4) Coordination: Vendor attribution is contested on state sponsorship [S5], so coordinate with intelligence elements before characterizing the actor in reporting.

identification.summary: North Korean cyber espionage actor that Mandiant (then FireEye) named APT37 (Reaper) in February 2018. Mandiant says it is likely active since at least 2012 and focuses on public and private sectors primarily in South Korea, with 2017 expansion to Japan, Vietnam and the Middle East [S1]. The group has exploited zero-days in Adobe Flash and Internet Explorer [S1][S2][S4]. Recent reporting describes RokRAT delivered through LNK lures with cloud-service C2 [S6][S7], tools that reach air-gapped networks [S8], and a supply-chain compromise of a gaming platform used by ethnic Koreans in China [S9].
identification.firstObserved: Mandiant: likely active since at least 2012 [S1]. Kaspersky's Operation Daybreak, the earliest dated campaign in these sources, began in March 2016 [S2].
identification.notes: Mandiant believes APT37 aligns with activity publicly reported as ScarCruft (Kaspersky) and Group123 (Cisco Talos) [S1]. Volexity tracks it as InkySquid [S3] and AhnLab as RedEyes [S5]. Microsoft's public naming map (retrieved 2026-10-15) lists no Microsoft name with APT37, ScarCruft, Reaper or InkySquid as an alias, so no Microsoft name is assigned here [S11]. Zscaler coverage lists 'Ruby Sleet' as an APT37 alias, but Microsoft's map ties Ruby Sleet to CERIUM / VELVET CHOLLIMA; see gaps [S8][S11].

attribution.sponsor: Democratic People's Republic of Korea (North Korea) [S1][S4].
attribution.confidence: Mandiant: high confidence that the activity is carried out on behalf of the North Korean government [S1]. Google TAG describes APT37 as North Korean government-backed [S4]. Zscaler calls APT37 DPRK-backed [S8]. ESET calls ScarCruft North Korea-aligned [S9]. No US government attribution was found in the sources gathered.
attribution.basis: Malware development artifacts and targeting aligned with North Korean state interests (Mandiant) [S1]. Consistent tooling (RokRAT, BLUELIGHT) and a victim set of North Korea experts, defectors and North Korea-focused media across vendor reporting [S3][S5][S6][S7][S9].

actors.objectives: Strategic intelligence collection on behalf of the North Korean state [S1]. Collection centers on South Korean policy circles, North Korea experts, defectors, journalists and human-rights activists; AhnLab describes the task as monitoring the lives of specific individuals [S5][S6][S7]. ESET assesses that refugees or defectors from the Yanbian region were the likely targets of the 2024-2026 supply-chain campaign [S9]. SentinelLabs assessed the group may seek threat research to learn whether defenders have detected its techniques [S6]. Mandiant notes access to wiper malware [S1].

sectors: Cybersecurity and threat intelligence professionals (assessed future target)
regions: Japan, Vietnam and the Middle East (2017) [S1]
Russia, Nepal, China, India, Kuwait and Romania (Operation Daybreak victims) [S2]
China: Yanbian region ethnic Korean community [S9]
targeting.notes: Industry sectors and the 2017 regional expansion come from Mandiant [S1]. Individual targeting comes from AhnLab, SentinelLabs, Seqrite and ESET [S5][S6][S7][S9]. The cybersecurity-professional target is SentinelLabs' forecast based on a Kimsuky report used as a decoy, not an observed campaign [S6].

capabilities.summary: Mandiant describes an expanding toolset including zero-day access and wiper malware [S1]. Kaspersky tied Flash zero-day CVE-2016-4171 to ScarCruft and reported that its Operation Erebus used CVE-2016-4117 and watering holes [S2]. In 2021 the group used Internet Explorer exploits (CVE-2020-1380, CVE-2021-26411) in a watering hole on Daily NK, delivering Cobalt Strike and the BLUELIGHT backdoor [S3]. In 2022 it exploited IE JScript zero-day CVE-2022-41128 through an Office document that loaded a remote RTF template [S4]. In 2023 AhnLab found FadeStealer (keylogging, screenshots, removable-media theft, audio wiretapping) delivered via CHM files, with a Go backdoor using the Ably platform for C2 [S5]. RokRAT is the recurring backdoor; recent chains use LNK files, fileless XOR-decoded payloads and C2 via Dropbox, pCloud and Yandex [S6][S7]. The 2025-26 Ruby Jumper toolset included RESTLEAF (Zoho WorkDrive C2), SNAKEDROPPER (installs a Ruby runtime), THUMBSBD and VIRUSTASK (removable-media relay and infection to reach air-gapped systems), plus FOOTWINE and BLUELIGHT [S8]. BirdCall, described as an evolution of RokRAT, has Windows and Android versions; the Android version collects contacts, SMS, call logs, documents, media and private keys and records audio [S9].

diamond.adversary: North Korean state-backed espionage operators [S1][S4].
diamond.capability: Zero-day and n-day exploits (Flash, IE), RokRAT, BLUELIGHT, FadeStealer, BirdCall (Windows and Android), and air-gap tooling (THUMBSBD, VIRUSTASK) [S1][S2][S3][S4][S5][S8][S9].
diamond.infrastructure: Compromised news sites as watering holes [S3]; commercial cloud and messaging services for C2, including Ably, Dropbox, pCloud, Yandex and Zoho WorkDrive [S5][S7][S8]; a legitimate software-update channel for supply-chain delivery [S9].
diamond.victim: South Korean academics, former officials and North Korea-focused media; defectors, activists and professors; ethnic Koreans in Yanbian, China; 2017 industrial targets in Japan, Vietnam and the Middle East [S1][S5][S6][S7][S9].
diamond.socioPolitical: Regime-security intelligence on defectors, critics and South Korean policy toward North Korea [S5][S6][S9].
diamond.technology: Windows endpoints with legacy IE components invoked through Office, LNK and CHM handling, removable media crossing air gaps, and Android devices [S4][S5][S8][S9].

gaps: No Microsoft name confirmed. Microsoft's public mapping has no APT37/ScarCruft alias; Zscaler and other third-party alias lists cite 'Ruby Sleet' (and one list 'Opal Sleet'), which Microsoft maps to CERIUM and to APT43/Konni respectively. Treat these as unverified [S8][S11].
No US government (CISA/FBI/DOJ) attribution document specific to APT37 was located.
Primary reports from Volexity, Seqrite, Zscaler and SentinelLabs were read only through search summaries or secondary coverage. The full Mandiant PDF was not reviewed.

Kaspersky's 2019 Bluetooth device-harvester report (securelist.com/scarcruft-continues-to-evolve-introduces-bluetooth-harvester/90729/, in the imported references) was not reviewed in this pass and is excluded from the timeline.
Overlap with Kimsuky (APT43) is not assessed here; the clusters are tracked separately.
Victim counts for the Daily NK watering hole and the Yanbian supply-chain campaign are not public in the sources gathered [S3][S9].

Imported aliases 'Venus 121', 'APT-C-28', 'ATK4', 'Operation Erebus' as an alias, and 'Moldy Pisces' were not confirmed by a cited source in this pass; Operation Erebus is a Kaspersky campaign name, not a group alias [S2].

implications.jipoe: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. STEP 1 (environment): Key terrain includes email of Korea-policy staff, academics and liaison personnel, South Korean partner endpoints, and removable media used to move data across air gaps [S1][S7][S8]. STEP 2 (effects): C2 over commercial cloud services (Dropbox, pCloud, Yandex, Zoho WorkDrive, Ably) blends with legitimate traffic and weakens perimeter detection [S5][S7][S8]. STEP 3 (adversary model): Topical lure (news event, think-tank newsletter, official statement) then LNK, CHM or weaponized document, then fileless RokRAT or similar with cloud C2, then collection including keystrokes and audio [S4][S5][S6][S7][S8]. STEP 4 (COAs): MLCOA is continued spear-phishing of South Korean and allied Korea specialists timed to peninsula news events [S4][S7]. MDCOA is use of removable-media tooling to reach air-gapped partner or mission networks, or a trusted update channel for supply-chain access, as already shown against civilian targets [S8][S9]. Candidate indicators: LNK or CHM attachments with Korean-language decoys; Office documents fetching remote RTF templates; non-browser processes calling cloud-storage APIs; unexpected Ruby runtime installs; LNK files replacing documents on USB drives [S4][S5][S7][S8].
implications.jcc2: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. (1) Situational awareness: track lure themes tied to Korean peninsula events and warn Korea-focused staff, since APT37 used the Itaewon disaster as a lure within days [S4]. (2) Authorities: activity largely targets ROK persons and networks; response affecting partner networks requires coordination through USFK and ROK channels rather than unilateral DODIN actions. (3) Mission assurance: removable-media controls on air-gapped enclaves directly counter THUMBSBD and VIRUSTASK-style tooling [S8]. (4) Coordination: share cloud-service C2 indicators with providers and with DC3 and the DIB CS program, since the infrastructure is commercial [S7][S8].

identification.summary: Iranian state-sponsored cyber espionage group that Mandiant publicly named in September 2022. Mandiant reported more than 30 confirmed targeted operations since early 2015 and said the true total is likely much higher [S1]. The group relies mainly on trust-building social engineering and credential harvesting against personal and corporate email and cloud accounts. It also uses Android surveillance malware and lightweight Windows backdoors (NICECURL, TAMECAT) [S1][S2]. Google TAG reported in August 2024 that the US and Israel made up about 60% of APT42's known geographic targeting over the prior six months [S3].
identification.firstObserved: At least 2015 per Mandiant; Android-malware C2 infrastructure in use since at least late 2015 [S1].
identification.notes: Mandiant formerly tracked the activity as UNC788 [S1]. Google TAG tracks it as CALANQUE [S2]. Mandiant says the following public names partially coincide with APT42: TA453 (Proofpoint), Yellow Garuda (PwC), ITG18 (IBM X-Force), Phosphorus/Mint Sandstorm (Microsoft) and Charming Kitten (ClearSky, CERTFA) [S1][S2]. Volexity documented the NICECURL infection chain as CharmingCypress [S2]. Check Point tracks related activity as Educated Manticore [S4][S5]. Mandiant notes historical connections with APT35 [S1]. Microsoft's name: none confirmed. Mandiant lists Mint Sandstorm as a partial overlap, but this encyclopedia keeps Mint Sandstorm as a separate record because Microsoft's own mapping does not place APT42 under it.

attribution.sponsor: Islamic Republic of Iran; assessed by Mandiant to operate on behalf of the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps Intelligence Organization (IRGC-IO) [S1][S2]. Google TAG describes APT42 as IRGC-linked [S3]. Check Point and Israel's National Digital Agency also associate it with the IRGC [S4][S5].
attribution.confidence: Mandiant: moderate confidence that APT42 operates on behalf of the IRGC-IO (2022) [S1]. These are vendor and foreign-government assessments. No US government attribution naming 'APT42' was found in the sources gathered.
attribution.basis: Targeting patterns that align with IRGC-IO mandates and priorities [S1][S2]. For the cloud intrusions, Mandiant cited overlapping credential-harvesting domains and the Iran-focused nature of the stolen data [S2].

actors.objectives: Strategic intelligence collection and surveillance for the Iranian state. Targets include foreign policy officials, think tanks, journalists and academics working on Iran, plus monitoring of dissidents, activists and the Iranian diaspora [S1][S2]. Since 2024 the group has also targeted US political campaign affiliates and Israeli defense, government and academic figures [S3][S4][S5]. Mandiant notes that, unlike other IRGC-affiliated groups, APT42 does not focus mainly on the defense industrial base or on large-scale PII collection [S1].

sectors: Academia, including Israeli computer science and nuclear physics faculty [S2][S4]
NGOs, human rights and women's rights activists [S2]
Government officials, diplomats and military personnel [S1][S3][S5]
targeting.notes: APT42 has used stolen credentials to reach the employers, colleagues and relatives of an initial victim [S1]. Israel's National Digital Agency reported targeting of family members of defense and government officials to widen the attack surface and pressure primary targets [S5].

capabilities.summary: Primary tradecraft is long-running social engineering. Operators pose as journalists, event organizers, NGOs or researchers, build trust over days or weeks, then deliver credential-harvesting links [S1][S2][S5]. Lures use typosquatted news and think-tank domains (for example Washington Post, Aspen Institute), fake Google Meet, Drive and Gmail pages, Microsoft 365 look-alikes, URL shorteners and Google Sites [S2][S3]. MFA bypass includes fraudulent push prompts, SMS-token phishing, cloned DUO pages and real-time relay of 2FA codes [S2][S4]. In 2022-2023 Microsoft 365 intrusions, APT42 abused Keep-Me-Signed-In, created app passwords and used Thunderbird, Citrix and RDP. It ran reconnaissance with native commands and PowerShell, staged data in password-protected 7-Zip archives, cleared browser history and exfiltrated to a OneDrive account. It hid behind ExpressVPN, Cloudflare-hosted domains and short-lived VPSs [S2]. Malware: NICECURL, a VBScript backdoor delivered by LNK and PDF decoys that downloads modules such as a datamining module [S2]; TAMECAT, a PowerShell toehold that runs arbitrary PowerShell or C# and checks for antivirus via WMI [S2]. In 2025 TAMECAT was used for reconnaissance, file theft, Chrome and Edge browser data theft, Outlook mailbox theft and continuous screenshots [S5]. APT42 has run Android surveillance malware for location tracking and communications monitoring since at least late 2015 [S1]. It contacts targets over WhatsApp as well as email [S4][S5]. Google reported that APT42 accounted for over 30% of Iranian threat-actor use of Gemini, mainly for crafting phishing content including lures aimed at US defense organizations [S6]. Google later reported it attempted to build an AI 'data processing agent' to query personal data, such as linking phone numbers to owners and tracking travel [S7].

campaigns.name: Microsoft 365 intrusions at US/UK legal and NGO organizations (2022-2023)
campaigns.summary: Credential theft with MFA push fatigue and KMSI abuse. Iran-relevant files were exfiltrated to OneDrive using built-in features and open-source tools.

campaigns.name: Cluster C: phishing of an Israeli nuclear physics professor
campaigns.summary: Microsoft 365-themed phishing against US and Israeli defense, foreign-affairs and academic personnel; this example dates to November 2023.

campaigns.name: Mandiant NICECURL / TAMECAT reporting
campaigns.summary: Mandiant details three credential-harvesting clusters and two backdoors used against NGOs, media, academia, legal and activist targets.

campaigns.name: Phishing of 2024 US presidential campaign affiliates (May-June 2024)
campaigns.summary: Google TAG observed APT42 targeting about a dozen people affiliated with the Biden and Trump campaigns. It blocked numerous login attempts and confirmed one political consultant's Gmail account was accessed; Google reported this to the FBI in July 2024.

campaigns.name: Gemini misuse reported by Google
campaigns.summary: Google reports APT42 was the heaviest Iranian user of Gemini, using it for phishing content, reconnaissance and research.

campaigns.name: Israeli academics, journalists and cyber experts (Educated Manticore)
campaigns.summary: During the Iran-Israel escalation, operators posing as cybersecurity staff used email and WhatsApp to steer targets to fake Gmail and Google Meet pages that captured passwords and 2FA codes.

campaigns.name: SpearSpecter (Israel National Digital Agency)
campaigns.summary: Ongoing campaign detected in early September 2025 against senior defense and government officials and their families. It used conference and meeting lures, WhatsApp impersonation, malicious LNK files and the TAMECAT backdoor.

campaigns.name: AI 'data processing agent' attempt
campaigns.summary: Google reports APT42 tried to use Gemini to build an agent turning natural-language requests into SQL queries over personal data. Google disabled the accounts.

diamond.adversary: APT42, assessed by Mandiant with moderate confidence to act for the IRGC-IO [S1][S2].
diamond.capability: Trust-building spear-phishing and credential harvesting with MFA bypass; cloud (M365) living-off-the-land; NICECURL and TAMECAT backdoors; Android surveillance malware; AI-assisted lure crafting [S1][S2][S5][S6].
diamond.infrastructure: Typosquatted media, think-tank and NGO domains; fake Google and Microsoft login pages; URL shorteners; Google Sites; glitch[.]me and drive-file-share[.]site hosting; ExpressVPN, Cloudflare-fronted domains and short-lived VPSs; WhatsApp contact [S2][S3][S4][S5].
diamond.victim: Think tanks, journalists, academics, NGOs and activists, legal firms, government and defense officials and their relatives, and US political campaign affiliates, chiefly in the US, Israel, UK and Middle East [S1][S2][S3][S5].
diamond.socioPolitical: Collection on Iran's foreign-policy adversaries and monitoring of regime opponents. Activity rises around elections and the Israel-Hamas and Iran-Israel conflicts [S1][S2][S3][S4].
diamond.technology: Personal webmail and Microsoft 365/Google cloud accounts protected by push or SMS MFA; Windows endpoints via LNK/VBScript/PowerShell; Android phones; messaging apps [S1][S2][S4][S5].

gaps: Microsoft naming: Mandiant lists Mint Sandstorm/Phosphorus as a partial overlap, but Microsoft's mapping does not list APT42 under Mint Sandstorm. Microsoft attributed the June 2024 spear-phishing of a presidential campaign official to Mint Sandstorm [S8], while Google attributed 2024 campaign targeting to APT42 [S3]. These may describe overlapping but not identical activity; they are not merged here.

The September 2024 DOJ indictment of three IRGC employees (Jalili, Aghamiri, Balaghi) for hacking the Trump campaign was reviewed only through press coverage [S9]. The indictment text was not opened, and no source found states it names APT42.

Primary documents not opened: Google TAG's August 2024 blog (summarized via search result) [S3], Check Point Research's June 2025 report (host unreachable) [S4], Israel National Digital Agency SpearSpecter report (reported via The Hacker News) [S5], Google GTIG 'Adversarial Misuse of Generative AI' (reported via TechTarget) [S6], Volexity's CharmingCypress reporting.
Press coverage says SpearSpecter and the June 2025 Check Point activity were run by different APT42 sub-groups [S5]; the internal structure of APT42 is not documented in sources gathered.
Mandiant did not observe technical overlap between APT42 and the ransomware-linked UNC2448 (Najee Technology/Afkar System) [S1]; any APT42 role in disruptive operations is unverified.
Android malware family names, current mobile tooling and the full victim count are not detailed in sources gathered.
Activity after November 2025 was not researched.

implications.jipoe: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. STEP 1 (operational environment): the key terrain is people and their accounts more than networks. That includes personal webmail, Microsoft 365 and Google cloud tenants, messaging apps and the families of senior officials [S2][S3][S5]. STEP 2 (effects): MFA based on push or SMS approval and trust in impersonated media, think-tank and conference brands weaken defenses. Credential theft can grant cloud access without malware on any DoD endpoint [S2][S4]. STEP 3 (threat model): weeks-long rapport building by a fake journalist, researcher or security staffer leads to a fake Google/Microsoft login page or LNK/macro lure. MFA relay or push approval follows, then mailbox and cloud data collection via built-in features, with TAMECAT or NICECURL as a fallback [S2][S4][S5]. STEP 4 (COAs): MLCOA is continued credential phishing of officials, staff, advisors and academics on Iran, Israel and Middle East policy, rising during regional crises [S3][S4]. MDCOA is compromise of senior officers' or relatives' personal accounts and phones, giving location, travel and communications data for targeting or coercion; reporting on family targeting and AI-assisted analysis of travel data points this way [S5][S7]. Candidate indicators: unsolicited interview or conference invitations that move to WhatsApp; typosquatted news or think-tank domains; unexpected MFA push prompts; new app passwords or KMSI sessions; mail-client access from VPN or VPS IPs; LNK files spawning VBScript/PowerShell; and OneDrive exfiltration to look-alike outlook.com accounts [S2][S5].
implications.jcc2: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. (1) Situational awareness: identity telemetry (sign-in logs, MFA prompts, app-password creation) and personal-account reporting are the main sensors, because much APT42 activity sits outside DODIN endpoints [S2][S3]. (2) Authorities: personal and family accounts, plus contractor and think-tank accounts, fall outside DoD network authorities. Response depends on user reporting, provider takedowns (Google and Microsoft) and FBI coordination; Google referred a 2024 compromise to the FBI [S3]. (3) Mission assurance: enforce phishing-resistant MFA and protect senior leaders and their families during Middle East contingencies, when APT42 tempo rises [S4][S5]. (4) Coordination: reconcile vendor names (APT42, CALANQUE, Educated Manticore, Mint Sandstorm) in intelligence sharing with coalition partners, especially Israel, to avoid duplicate or mismatched tracking [S2][S4][S5][S8].

identification.summary: Mandiant describes APT9 as a cyber espionage actor whose goal is data theft, usually focused on the data and projects that make an organization competitive in its field, and historically very active in pharmaceuticals and biotechnology [S1]. Mandiant has observed spearphishing, valid accounts and remote services for initial access, and a wide range of backdoors, including public ones and ones believed custom but shared by multiple APT groups [S1]. Aliases listed by Malpedia are Group 27, NIGHTSHADE PANDA and Red Pegasus [S1].
identification.notes: Not mapped to a Microsoft name in this record. Alias boundaries are unstable: Cisco Talos used the name Group 27 for the cluster behind the Trochilus/Seven Pointed Dagger toolset, which Arbor ASERT attributed to that group [S2][S4]; one aggregator also lists FlowerLady and FlowerShow as synonyms [S6]; another profile in search results lists Red Pegasus under APT19/Deep Panda, so that alias is disputed [S6]. Do not confuse APT9/Group 27 with APT27 (Emissary Panda/Threat Group-3390), a separate group. Whether Mandiant's APT9 and the Talos/Arbor Group 27 are the same cluster is asserted by alias lists only, not by a primary report seen.

attribution.basis: No source gathered attributes APT9 to a government. Coverage of the Trochilus campaign said it was unclear who was behind it and that either China or North Korea could feasibly be responsible [S2]. The imported record lists country as CN (MISP Galaxy tags the group as China-based per aggregator) [S6]; this is a third-party tag, not a sourced vendor attribution statement.

actors.objectives: Data theft focused on competitively valuable data and projects, historically in pharmaceuticals and biotechnology [S1]. For the Group 27 cluster, ASERT said capabilities could be used against other entities including non-government organizations [S2].

sectors: Government websites and election-related sites in Myanmar (Group 27 / Seven Pointed Dagger) [S2][S3]
Thai utility organizations (Trochilus/MoonWind campaign; actor not named in the Unit 42 text seen) [S5]
targeting.notes: Mandiant observed APT9 at two biotechnology companies and suspects initial access to one may have come via a trusted relationship between them [S6]. The Asia-focused activity comes from Group 27 reporting and cannot be firmly tied to Mandiant's APT9 [S2][S3].

capabilities.summary: Mandiant: spearphishing, valid accounts and remote services for initial access; a wide range of backdoors, both public and believed custom but used by multiple APT groups [S1]. Group 27 toolset 'Seven Pointed Dagger' comprised seven malware items including PlugX, EvilGrab, a 3102 variant of the 9002 RAT and the newly described Trochilus RAT, which had minimal antimalware detection and offered file manager, download/execute and upload/execute functions [S2][S3][S4]. Malpedia links APT9 to the win.9002 family [S6]. Unit 42 reported Trochilus and a new RAT, MoonWind, hosted on compromised legitimate Thai websites, separate C2 per family, and Mimikatz found alongside [S5].

campaigns.name: Seven Pointed Dagger / Trochilus (Group 27)
campaigns.summary: Watering-hole compromise of Myanmar government and election-related sites, including the Union Election Commission site, delivering PlugX, EvilGrab and 9002 variants; Arbor ASERT attributed the cluster to Cisco Talos's Group 27; January 2016 reporting.

campaigns.name: Trochilus and MoonWind against Thai organizations
campaigns.summary: From September to late November 2016 an unnamed actor used Trochilus and the new MoonWind RAT against a Thai utility organization, hosting malware on two compromised Thai websites. Unit 42 published 2017-03-30; it did not name Group 27 in the text surfaced.

diamond.adversary: Unattributed cluster; PRC origin is a third-party tag only [S6]. Group 27 label from Talos via ASERT reporting [S2].
diamond.capability: Spearphishing, valid accounts, remote services, public and shared backdoors [S1]; PlugX, EvilGrab, 9002 variant, Trochilus [S2][S4].
diamond.infrastructure: Compromised legitimate websites used as watering holes and malware hosts [S2][S5]; separate C2 per malware family in the Thai campaign [S5].
diamond.victim: Pharmaceutical and biotechnology firms [S1]; Myanmar government and election sites [S2][S3].
diamond.technology: Trusted relationships between partner firms [S6]; public-facing government websites trusted by visitors [S2].

gaps: Mandiant's primary APT9 page (cloud.google.com/security/resources/insights/apt-groups) could not be fetched; its text was seen only through Malpedia [S1].
Search tooling returned no dated Mandiant, CrowdStrike or Talos primary report on APT9/NIGHTSHADE PANDA/Group 27; first/last activity dates and the date of the Mandiant profile are unknown.
No sourced government attribution or sponsor; confidence unassessed.
Whether APT9 (Mandiant), Group 27 (Talos) and NIGHTSHADE PANDA (CrowdStrike) are one cluster is unverified; Red Pegasus mapping is disputed [S6].
Unit 42's Thai-utility report does not name Group 27 in the text seen; linkage unverified [S5].
Original Unit 42, Arbor ASERT and Talos pages could not be opened (host resolution failures); reporting by secondary outlets used.
Recent activity (post-2017) not found; the biotechnology victims and timeframe are unspecified.
Removed unverified claims: EvilGrab watering hole on the Myanmar president's site (May 2015) and Trochilus first appearing in October 2015; neither was confirmed in search results.

implications.jipoe: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. STEP 1: Biotechnology and pharmaceutical R&D networks, partner-company trust links and government-affiliated public websites are the relevant terrain [S1][S2][S6]. STEP 2: Data-theft focus on competitive projects points to commercial and research collection rather than disruption [S1]. STEP 3: Observed pattern is spearphishing, valid accounts or remote services, or a watering hole, followed by public or shared RATs such as PlugX or Trochilus, with credential theft tools [S1][S2][S5]. STEP 4: MLCOA is continued quiet collection against biotech/pharma and Southeast Asian government targets. MDCOA is use of a trusted partner relationship to reach a defense-health supplier. Candidate indicators: new PlugX/9002-family implants, visitors' traffic to compromised government sites, Mimikatz use, and remote-service logons with valid credentials [S1][S4][S5]. Confidence is low because the cluster mapping is unresolved.
implications.jcc2: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. (1) Situational awareness: treat reporting as low-confidence and cluster boundaries as unsettled; track by tooling and TTP rather than alias. (2) Authorities: DIB/defense-health contractors and partner networks fall to DC3/DIB CS coordination. (3) Mission assurance: valid-account and remote-service abuse argues for monitoring of third-party and partner access. (4) Coordination: share indicators for PlugX/9002-family and Trochilus with allied partners in Southeast Asia.
