provenance.importedSummary: APT9 engages in cyber operations where the goal is data theft, usually focusing on the data and projects that make a particular organization competitive within its field. APT9 was historically very active in the pharmaceuticals and biotechnology industry. We have observed this actor use spearphishing, valid accounts, as well as remote services for Initial Access. On at least one occasion, Mandiant observed APT9 at two companies in the biotechnology industry and suspect that APT9 actors may have gained initial access to one of the companies by using a trusted relationship between the two companies. APT9 use a wide range of backdoors, including publicly available backdoors, as well as backdoors that are believed to be custom, but are used by multiple APT groups.

identification.summary: APTIran (also written APT IRAN) is a pro-Iran hacktivist persona that Sophos says has posted claimed compromises of Israeli critical infrastructure and organizations on Telegram since 28 February 2026, including an unverified claim about water control systems [S1]. A threat-intel profile says it claimed to have leaked over 350,000 Israeli government credentials and about 300 internal databases and threatened a 'zombie' network of infected devices; that profile also says ALPHV and LockBit ransomware were 'reportedly' used. These are the group's claims and are unverified [S4].
identification.firstObserved: Sophos reports APTIran Telegram posting since 2026-02-28, the date of the US and Israeli strikes on Iran [S1]. Earlier activity is not established in the sources gathered.
identification.notes: Sophos describes pro-Iran hacktivist attacks as historically low-sophistication with limited success [S1]. Sophos separately tracks Handala Hack Team (COBALT MYSTIQUE); this is a different persona and its facts are not merged here [S1]. No MITRE group or Microsoft name was found for APTIran.

attribution.confidence: Jordan's National Cybersecurity Center said the March 2026 attempt against the grain silo management system was traced back to Iran [S2]. That statement concerns the incident, and the sources gathered do not give a government attribution of the APTIran persona to a specific Iranian state entity.
attribution.basis: Self-identification as pro-Iran on Telegram [S1][S3]; Jordanian government statement tracing the silo attempt to Iran [S2]. No technical attribution evidence was available in the sources.

actors.objectives: Retaliation and propaganda in support of Iran after the 28 February 2026 strikes, via claimed intrusions and leaks against Israel and its neighbors, and encouraging other pro-Iran hackers to retaliate [S1][S4].

sectors: Food security and agriculture (Jordan grain silos)
targeting.notes: Sectors for Israel come from the group's own claims relayed by a threat-intel profile and Sophos, and are unverified [S1][S4]. The Jordan silo operator is the one target for which a government account exists, and that account says the attempt was stopped with no impact [S2].

capabilities.summary: The group claimed phishing as the initial access vector for the Jordan Silos intrusion [S3]. A Jordan News report headline attributes the breach to a weak password, and an account says the intruder reached the power system before being contained; the body text was not retrieved [S5]. A threat-intel profile says ransomware (ALPHV, LockBit) was reportedly used and attributes no exploited CVEs to the group; the ransomware claim is unverified [S4]. Sophos judges Iranian hacktivist activity generally to be website defacement, DDoS and doxxing of low sophistication [S1].

campaigns.name: Telegram claims against Israeli infrastructure
campaigns.summary: Sophos reports APTIran began sharing leaks and compromises allegedly from Israeli critical infrastructure and organizations on Telegram, including an unverified water control system claim, after the US and Israeli strikes on Iran [S1].

campaigns.name: Claimed Israeli government credential and database leak
campaigns.summary: A threat-intel profile says the group claimed over 350,000 Israeli government logins and about 300 databases leaked, and threatened a zombie network. Unverified; no victim confirmation found [S4].

campaigns.name: Jordan grain silo intrusion attempt
campaigns.summary: Jordan's National Cybersecurity Center said it thwarted an attempted attack on the grain silo management system, traced to Iran, with no impact [S2]. A Telegram post attributed to APT IRAN claimed a phishing breach of Jordan Silos and Supply General Co and manipulation of silo temperatures and weighing software; Jordan disputes damage [S3]. FDD dates the incident to 3 March 2026 [S6].

diamond.adversary: Pro-Iran hacktivist persona operating on Telegram; sponsor and operators not established [S1].
diamond.capability: Claimed phishing, credential theft, data leaks and ransomware use; mostly unverified [S3][S4].
diamond.infrastructure: Telegram channel used for claims and recruitment of other pro-Iran hackers [S1]. Technical infrastructure unknown.
diamond.victim: Claimed Israeli government, health, education and finance bodies; Jordan Silos and Supply General Co [S3][S4].
diamond.socioPolitical: Conflict following the 28 February 2026 US and Israeli strikes on Iran; retaliation messaging [S1].
diamond.technology: Weak credentials and phishing exposure at the victim, and operational technology (silo management, power) reachable from IT networks [S3][S5].

gaps: Sophos and Cisco Talos primary posts listed as leads in the record could not be opened (fetch blocked); Sophos content here is from search-result summaries. Talos coverage of APTIran was not found.

Claims of 350,000 credentials, 300 databases, ALPHV/LockBit use and Israeli water system access have no independent victim or vendor confirmation. The only source for the credential figure is an aggregator profile [S4].
Whether APTIran is state-directed, state-aligned or independent is unknown; no government attribution of the persona was found.
Overlap with Handala, Malek Team and other Iran-linked personas that claimed Israeli hospital leaks was not established; those claims are not attributed to APTIran.
Jordan News and Threatbeat article bodies were not fully read; the weak-password and phishing details rest on summaries.
No technical indicators, malware or infrastructure were found.

implications.jipoe: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. STEP 1: Key terrain is internet-facing credentials and IT networks bridging to OT (the silo incident reached a power system) [S5]. STEP 2: Adversary is a low-to-moderate sophistication persona whose claims likely exceed demonstrated impact [S1][S2]. STEP 3: Template is phishing or weak-password access, then claim and leak via Telegram [S3][S5]. STEP 4: MLCOA is continued claim-heavy hack-and-leak and nuisance activity against Israel and regional partners tied to kinetic events. MDCOA is disruptive OT manipulation at a partner food, water or power operator whose controls are weakly protected. Candidate indicators: Telegram claims naming partner-nation entities, spikes in phishing to regional operators, and anomalous logins to OT-adjacent systems [S1][S3].
implications.jcc2: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. (1) Situational awareness: monitor persona claims but treat them as unverified until the victim or a government confirms [S2][S4]. (2) Authorities: partner-nation incidents like Jordan's are handled by host-nation agencies; coordinate through established channels. (3) Mission assurance: verify MFA and password hygiene on remote access to OT-adjacent systems at installations and partner facilities [S5]. (4) Coordination: share indicators through intelligence and DC3-style channels; avoid amplifying unverified claims.

provenance.importedSummary: APTIran has claimed responsibility for a large-scale campaign targeting Israeli critical infrastructure, asserting infiltration of government ministries, hospitals, universities, and financial institutions as retaliation for Israeli military operations. The group has leaked over 350,000 Israeli government login credentials and approximately 300 internal databases, while also threatening to create a 'zombie' network from infected devices. They have reportedly deployed ransomware strains such as ALPHV and LockBit as part of their offensive toolkit. Additionally, APTIran has made unverified claims of compromising Israeli water control systems and the state-owned food security agency Jordan Silos and Supply General Co.

identification.summary: Aqua Blizzard (formerly ACTINIUM, earlier DEV-0157) is what Microsoft calls the Russia-based actor that other vendors track as Gamaredon [S1][S2]. Microsoft describes it as an espionage and data-theft actor that mainly targets Ukrainian government, military, judiciary, law enforcement and non-profit organizations [S1][S2]. Its hallmarks are high-volume spearphishing, heavily obfuscated VBScript and PowerShell, self-extracting archives and LNK files, and fast-changing infrastructure [S1][S2]. Unit 42 named the group in 2017 and reported a shift from off-the-shelf tools to custom malware [S10]. ESET reports that the group was still very active in 2024 and 2025, running many spearphishing waves against Ukrainian government and military institutions [S8][S9].
identification.firstObserved: Active since at least mid-2013, per LookingGlass 'Operation Armageddon' [S11] and Unit 42 [S10]. Microsoft said in February 2022 that the group had been operating for 'almost a decade' [S1].
identification.notes: Microsoft name: Aqua Blizzard. It was ACTINIUM until April 2023 and DEV-0157 before that [S1]. Microsoft's profile lists Primitive Bear, ACTINIUM, SectorC08, Shuckworm, Gamaredon, UNC530 and Armageddon as other names [S2]. Unit 42 uses Trident Ursa [S5], and Symantec uses Shuckworm [S6]. The name 'Gamaredon' is an anagram of 'Armageddon', taken from LookingGlass's 2015 report [S10][S11]. Microsoft notes that Aqua Blizzard is distinct from DEV-0586 (Cadet Blizzard) [S1]. MITRE tracks the group as Gamaredon Group (G0047) [S12].

attribution.sponsor: Russian Federation, Federal Security Service (FSB). The Security Service of Ukraine (SSU) says the group consists of officers of the FSB in Crimea, operates from Sevastopol and takes orders from the FSB Center for Information Security (Center 18) in Moscow [S3][S9].
attribution.confidence: The attribution to the FSB is a Ukrainian government attribution (SSU, November 2021) [S3]. Microsoft repeats the Ukrainian attribution and says it observed ACTINIUM 'operating out of Crimea'; it does not give its own confidence level [S1][S2]. ESET says it believes with high confidence that Gamaredon collaborates with Turla [S7]. LookingGlass said in 2015 that it was 'highly confident' that the SBU's claims of FSB involvement were accurate [S11].
attribution.basis: The SSU named five individuals and cited intercepted communications, including published recordings of phone calls between members [S3]. Microsoft's telemetry places operations in Crimea [S1]. Vendor technical reporting from Unit 42, Symantec and ESET describes consistent tooling and targeting [S5][S6][S8][S9]. In 2025 ESET found technical links to Turla, another FSB-linked actor, with Gamaredon tools used to restart or deploy Turla's Kazuar backdoor [S7].

actors.objectives: Microsoft describes the objectives as espionage: exfiltrating sensitive information, maintaining access, and moving laterally into related organizations [S1][S2]. Since October 2021 Microsoft has seen a focus on organizations critical to emergency response, territorial security, and the coordination of international and humanitarian aid to Ukraine [S1]. Secondary coverage of Symantec's 2023 reporting says the material stolen from Ukrainian security, military and government bodies included casualty, engagement, air-strike, arsenal-inventory and training reports [S6]. ESET says the group probably gives Turla initial access to selected high-value machines [S7].

sectors: Emergency response, territorial security and humanitarian-aid coordination organizations [S1]
Energy: an attempted intrusion at a petroleum refining company in a NATO member state [S5]
Western government entity operating in Ukraine [S4]
regions: Ukraine, the primary and in 2024-2025 almost exclusive target [S1][S2][S8][S9]
NATO member states, occasionally: the August 2022 refinery attempt [S5] and the NATO-country targeting ESET describes in 2022-2023 [S13]
targeting.notes: ESET reports that in 2024 the group refocused exclusively on Ukrainian government institutions [S8], and that throughout 2025 it targeted only Ukrainian governmental and military institutions [S9]. Targeting outside Ukraine appears opportunistic or tied to Ukraine support, but this is inferred from limited cases [S4][S5].

capabilities.summary: The tradecraft is high-volume rather than sophisticated. Initial access comes through spearphishing with macro documents that use remote template injection, web bugs that track email opens, and lures impersonating legitimate bodies such as the WHO [S1]. Later waves used archives and XHTML files with HTML smuggling to deliver HTA downloaders [S9]. From late September 2025 the group exploited the WinRAR flaw CVE-2025-8088 to plant downloaders in the Startup folder [S9]. Execution relies on multi-stage, heavily obfuscated VBScript and PowerShell, self-extracting archives and LNK files, with scheduled tasks for persistence [S1][S2]. Malware includes the Pterodo family, QuietSieve, PowerPunch, DinoTrain, DesertDown, DilongTrash, ObfuBerry and ObfuMerry, plus UltraVNC for interactive access [S1][S2]. ESET documented an expanding set of Ptero-series PowerShell tools, including PteroSand, PteroPaste, PteroOdd, PteroGraphin and PteroSetup, with six new tools in 2025 [S7][S9]. The group spreads through USB and removable drives, which can reach air-gapped machines [S6][S7]. Its infrastructure churns quickly: Microsoft saw more than 25 new domains and more than 80 IPs in a 30-day window, with DNS records changing about daily and mostly hosted on REG.RU [S1]. Unit 42 counted more than 500 new domains over 10 months [S5]. The group has used Telegram and Telegraph dead drops to find C2 addresses [S6]. It has hidden almost all of its C2 behind Cloudflare tunnels (2024) and Cloudflare Workers (from May 2025), and has also used devtunnels.ms, Loophole, No-IP, Clever Cloud, Supabase, Dropbox and S3-compatible storage for exfiltration [S8][S9].

campaigns.name: Microsoft ACTINIUM disclosure
campaigns.summary: Microsoft describes campaigns since October 2021 against Ukrainian government, military, NGO, judicial, law-enforcement and aid-coordination organizations, using remote-template phishing and the Pterodo and QuietSieve families, among others.

campaigns.name: NATO-state petroleum refinery attempt
campaigns.summary: Unit 42 reports an unsuccessful attempt to compromise a large petroleum refining company in a NATO member state, as part of a period in which it tracked more than 500 new domains and 200 samples.

campaigns.name: Shuckworm intrusions on Ukrainian security and military bodies
campaigns.summary: Symantec, as reported by The Hacker News, describes intrusions beginning in February/March 2023 that lasted up to three months, used USB propagation of Pterodo, located C2 through Telegram and Telegraph, and stole battlefield-related reports.

campaigns.name: Intensified spearphishing against Ukrainian government
campaigns.summary: ESET reports that the group focused exclusively on Ukrainian government institutions, sharply increased spearphishing in the second half of 2024, and hid almost all of its C2 behind Cloudflare tunnels.

campaigns.name: Gamaredon-Turla collaboration
campaigns.summary: ESET observes PteroGraphin restarting Turla's Kazuar on a Ukrainian machine, followed in April and June 2025 by Kazuar v2 deployed through PteroOdd and PteroPaste. ESET detected Turla on seven machines in Ukraine.

campaigns.name: WinRAR CVE-2025-8088 exploitation
campaigns.summary: ESET reports exploitation of CVE-2025-8088 to drop HTA downloaders into the Startup folder. This was part of 35 distinct spearphishing campaigns in 2025 against Ukrainian government and military institutions.

diamond.adversary: Officers of the Russian FSB in Crimea (Center 18), according to the SSU attribution, which Microsoft repeats [S1][S2][S3].
diamond.capability: High-volume spearphishing with remote template injection, HTML smuggling, HTA, VBScript and PowerShell chains; Pterodo/Ptero-series tools, QuietSieve, PowerPunch and UltraVNC; USB propagation; and WinRAR CVE-2025-8088 [S1][S6][S9].
diamond.infrastructure: Rapidly rotating domains and IPs, largely on REG.RU [S1][S5]; Telegram and Telegraph dead drops [S6]; Cloudflare tunnels and Workers, devtunnels.ms, Loophole, No-IP, Clever Cloud, Supabase, Dropbox and S3-compatible storage [S8][S9].
diamond.victim: Ukrainian government, military, security-service, judicial, law-enforcement and NGO organizations [S1][S6][S9]. Occasionally Western or NATO-state entities: a Western government body in Ukraine and a NATO-state refinery [S4][S5].
diamond.socioPolitical: Intelligence collection supporting Russia's war against Ukraine, including information on aid coordination, territorial security and battlefield reporting [S1][S6]. The group may also act as an access broker for Turla [S7].
diamond.technology: Windows endpoints with Office, WinRAR and scripting hosts (mshta, wscript, PowerShell); removable media; and trusted cloud and tunnelling services used to blend in with normal traffic [S1][S6][S9].

gaps: Primary vendor reports could not be fetched (Unit 42, ESET WeLiveSecurity and ESET white papers, Symantec, The Record). Details for S4-S9 rely on search-result and press coverage of those reports.
The SSU's original 2021 announcement and its claims (names, more than 5,000 attacks, Center 18 tasking) were not opened directly and are not independently verified [S3].
Microsoft has not published its own confidence level for the FSB attribution; it repeats the Ukrainian government attribution [S1][S2].
The exact date of ESET's 2022-2023 toolset white paper (reported as September 2024) and its NATO-country targeting details were not verified from the primary document [S13].
The full scope and the victims of Gamaredon's non-Ukrainian targeting are unclear. The public cases are few and unnamed [S4][S5].
The division of labour between Gamaredon and Turla is not public beyond ESET's technical observations (for example, whether Gamaredon brokers access as tasked or opportunistically) [S7].
No public reporting was found on Aqua Blizzard targeting US DoD networks directly.

implications.jipoe: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. STEP 1 (OE): The key terrain is Ukrainian government and military networks, and the networks of partners who coordinate aid to Ukraine [S1]. Western government and NATO-state entities operating in or supporting Ukraine are secondary terrain [S4][S5]. Removable media can bridge to air-gapped segments [S6]. STEP 2 (effects): Constant domain churn and abuse of trusted cloud and tunnel services such as Cloudflare, Telegram and Dropbox weaken static blocklists and reputation-based filtering [S1][S8][S9]. STEP 3 (adversary template): The chain runs from a spearphish (remote template, HTML smuggling, archive or WinRAR exploit) to an HTA, VBS or PowerShell downloader, then a Ptero-series implant with scheduled-task persistence, then USB spread and document theft. Selected hosts may be handed off to Turla's Kazuar [S1][S6][S7][S9]. STEP 4: The MLCOA is continued mass spearphishing for intelligence on Ukrainian military and government operations [S8][S9]. The MDCOA is access to a coalition or NATO-partner network supporting Ukraine, brokered to a more capable FSB actor (Turla) for long-term espionage [S5][S7]. Candidate indicators: mshta, wscript or PowerShell spawned from Office or WinRAR; new scheduled tasks with wordlist-style names; LNK files appearing on USB drives; and outbound traffic to trycloudflare, workers.dev, devtunnels.ms, Telegraph or Telegram from non-browser processes [S1][S6][S9].
implications.jcc2: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. (1) Situational awareness: the actor's tempo (35 campaigns in 2025) and infrastructure churn mean behaviour-based detections must feed JCC2 common operating picture tools, not just IOC feeds [S1][S9]. (2) Authorities: the attribution to the FSB comes from the Ukrainian government and vendors. Microsoft has not given a confidence level, so planners should not present it as a US government attribution without a separate basis [S1][S3]. (3) Mission assurance: units and contractors supporting aid or security cooperation with Ukraine should enforce controls on removable media and Office and WinRAR patching, given the USB propagation and CVE-2025-8088 exploitation [S6][S9]. (4) Coordination: because Gamaredon may hand access to Turla, any Gamaredon detection on partner or coalition networks should trigger a hunt for Kazuar-class follow-on implants and be shared with coalition CERTs [S7].

provenance.importedSummary: Unit 42 threat researchers have recently observed a threat group distributing new, custom developed malware. We have labelled this threat group the Gamaredon Group and our research shows that the Gamaredon Group has been active since at least 2013. In the past, the Gamaredon Group has relied heavily on off-the-shelf tools. Our new research shows the Gamaredon Group have made a shift to custom-developed malware. We believe this shift indicates the Gamaredon Group have improved their technical capabilities.

identification.summary: AVIVORE is a threat group named by Context Information Security in October 2019 after it investigated attacks on multinational enterprises that compromised smaller engineering and consultancy suppliers in their supply chains [S2][S3]. Context described the activity as 'horizontal' island hopping through connectivity between supply-chain partners [S3].
identification.firstObserved: Publicly named in 2019-10 [S2][S3]. Earlier start dates (summer 2018) could not be verified and were removed.
identification.notes: Context's name only. No Microsoft name, MITRE group ID or other vendor aliases were found in the sources reviewed. Initial press reporting on Airbus suppliers had floated APT10 or the Jiangsu State Security Department (JSSD); Context disputed this and treated AVIVORE as a separate group that shares some similarities with APT10/JSSD [S3]. Keep AVIVORE separate from APT10 unless a source merges them.

attribution.confidence: Context assessed with moderate confidence that the campaign's objective is intellectual property theft [S3]. Context stopped short of blaming China, but said the group operates in the same time zone and shares some similarities with APT10/JSSD [S3]. ETDA's threat card lists the actor as China-linked [S6]; this is a secondary catalogue entry, not a vendor or government attribution.
attribution.basis: Context's own investigation of multiple intrusions, with similarities to APT10/JSSD and a matching time zone of activity [S3]. No government attribution found.
attribution.note: Country 'CN' in the record is inherited from the import and is supported only by secondary reporting [S6].

actors.objectives: Context assessed with moderate confidence that the aim is intellectual property theft [S3].

targeting.notes: Context described incidents against UK and European aerospace and defence in which both large primes and smaller engineering or consultancy secondary firms were victims [S3]. Context also saw AVIVORE target assets in automotive, consultancy, energy/nuclear and space and satellite technology [S3]. Press reporting linked the Airbus supplier attacks to Rolls-Royce and Expleo; this link rests on press reporting, not on Context naming victims.

capabilities.summary: Context said the group abuses legitimate remote connectivity and collaboration tools (including commercial VPNs) shared between large firms and their suppliers to bypass well-defended perimeters [S3]. ETDA lists PlugX, Mimikatz and living-off-the-land techniques [S6]; this rests on a secondary catalogue, not a primary Context statement I could open.

campaigns.name: Context names AVIVORE
campaigns.summary: Context publicly identified AVIVORE as the group behind a multi-vertical campaign, disputed the APT10 attribution, assessed IP theft as the objective with moderate confidence, and noted targeting beyond aerospace [S2][S3].

diamond.adversary: AVIVORE, a group named by Context with no stated sponsor; similarities to APT10/JSSD and same time zone noted [S3].
diamond.capability: Abuse of legitimate remote connectivity and collaboration tools; PlugX reported by secondary sources [S3][S6].
diamond.infrastructure: Abuse of commercial VPNs and collaboration platforms as trust paths between organizations [S3]. Adversary-owned infrastructure not described in sources reviewed.
diamond.victim: Aerospace and defence primes and smaller engineering/consultancy suppliers, plus automotive, energy/nuclear and space/satellite assets in the UK and Europe [S3].
diamond.socioPolitical: Intellectual property theft assessed with moderate confidence by Context; sponsor not named [S3].
diamond.technology: Inter-company VPNs, remote access and collaboration tools [S3].

gaps: No state sponsor is stated by any source reviewed; China link is inferred from similarity to APT10/JSSD and time zone [S3].
Context's primary post/press release and Computer Weekly article could not be confirmed in search results; sources removed.
Exact publication dates of several sources are unverified beyond month.
Link between AVIVORE and the named Airbus suppliers comes from press reporting.
No malware, IOC or infrastructure details from a primary source; PlugX association unverified.
Start of activity unverified (summer 2018 claim removed; one search summary suggested possibly as early as 2015).
No activity reporting after 2019-10 found; current status unknown.

implications.jipoe: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. The relevant terrain is the trusted inter-company connectivity (VPNs, collaboration tools) between defence primes and small suppliers [S3]. Threat: an actor abusing legitimate remote access, with moderate-confidence IP-theft intent [S3]. Candidate indicators: anomalous supplier VPN logins and PlugX-style activity (secondary source) [S3][S6].
implications.jcc2: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. Defence industrial base suppliers, including small engineering firms, are likely entry points, so supplier incident reporting should feed the common operating picture [S3]. Segment and monitor partner VPN links; share indicators with suppliers and allied counterparts since victims span nations [S3].

identification.summary: Axiom is the name Novetta gave to a China-linked cyberespionage group in its October 2014 'Operation SMN' report, produced by an industry coalition that cleaned Axiom tooling from about 43,000 installations, including 180 top-tier Hikit implants [S2][S3][S6]. Novetta described Axiom as a 'well resourced, disciplined, and sophisticated subgroup of a larger cyberespionage group' [S1]. Cisco Talos tracks the same activity as Group 72 and called it well funded and sophisticated, with a defined software development process [S5]. MITRE ATT&CK lists Axiom as G0001, a suspected Chinese state-linked espionage group active since at least 2008 against aerospace, defense, government, manufacturing and media targets [S11].
identification.firstObserved: MITRE: active since at least 2008 [S11]. Press coverage of the Novetta report describes activity spanning more than six years before October 2014 [S3].
identification.notes: Microsoft has no single name for Axiom. Microsoft tracks Brass Typhoon (APT41), Heart Typhoon (APT17, Hidden Lynx, DeputyDog) and Leopard Typhoon (Winnti Group) as separate actors that overlap with this umbrella record [S12]. MITRE says Axiom and Winnti Group both use Winnti for Windows but treats them as distinct because their reported TTPs and targeting differ [S11]. Talos observed the same email address in Group 72 activity and in two other actor groups, which may indicate shared staff or infrastructure [S5].

attribution.sponsor: People's Republic of China (vendor assessment). Novetta assessed with 'moderate to high confidence' that the organization tasking Axiom is part of the Chinese intelligence apparatus [S1][S2].
attribution.confidence: Moderate to high (Novetta's assessment, not a government attribution) [S2]. Novetta cited an FBI flash to InfraGard, which said the actors are affiliated with the Chinese government, as partial support [S2]. MITRE describes the group as suspected Chinese state-linked [S11].
attribution.basis: Shared tooling (Hikit, Derusbi, Hydraq, ZxShell and others) and infrastructure found by the Novetta-led coalition [S3][S4][S6]; targeting of groups the Chinese state could see as a threat to its stability [S2]; Talos analysis of Group 72 [S5]; and the FBI flash Novetta cited [S2].

actors.objectives: Long-term espionage. Victims include organizations of strategic economic interest, groups that influence environmental and energy policy, and developers of cutting-edge information technology [S2]. Axiom also targeted pro-democracy NGOs and other groups and individuals that the Chinese state could see as a threat to its stability [S2]. Novetta treated the presence of Hikit as a sign that attackers had held long-term access to a network [S1].

sectors: NGOs focused on human rights, pro-democracy, international politics and environmental policy [S1][S2]
regions: Hikit infections were found mostly in the United States, South Korea, Taiwan, Japan and the European Union [S1]
Worldwide deployment of Hikit on targeted organizations' machines [S1]
targeting.notes: Novetta reported that attacks on NGOs covering international politics, environmental policy, pro-democracy or human rights tend to be multistaged [S2]. Sector lists come from press coverage of the Novetta report and from MITRE. The primary report was not retrieved.

capabilities.summary: Axiom used a tiered toolset. Commodity or shared RATs (PlugX, Gh0st RAT, Poison Ivy) sat at the lower tiers, and the custom Hikit backdoor was kept for high-value long-term persistence and data theft [S1][S3]. The coalition found Derusbi, DeputyDog, Hydraq, ZxShell, Fexel and DarkMoon tooling as well, and Microsoft's October 2014 MSRT update and coalition products targeted those families [S4][S6][S7]. Axiom used these tools to get into environments and re-infect them [S4]. Axiom set up separate command-and-control infrastructure for almost every Hikit target [S3]. Hikit samples were signed with a code-signing certificate stolen from Bit9 in 2012, and Novetta believes Axiom carried out that breach [S3]. Talos noted a mature software development process [S5].

campaigns.name: Operation Aurora (overlap only)
campaigns.summary: Coverage of the Novetta report says Axiom's tools and infrastructure overlap with Operation Aurora, which hit Google, and with other campaigns. This is an overlap finding, not direct attribution.

campaigns.name: Bit9 code-signing certificate theft
campaigns.summary: A certificate stolen from Bit9 was used to sign Hikit. Novetta believes Axiom was behind the breach. Symantec separately attributed the Bit9 compromise to Hidden Lynx.

campaigns.name: Operation DeputyDog
campaigns.summary: FireEye reported that watering holes on Japanese media sites delivered an IE zero-day (CVE-2013-3893) to Japanese organizations from as early as 19 August 2013, and tied the C2 to the Bit9 attackers. Novetta later listed DeputyDog among Axiom's tools.

campaigns.name: Operation SMN coalition disruption
campaigns.summary: A Novetta-led coalition (Cisco, Microsoft, FireEye, F-Secure, iSIGHT, Symantec, Tenable, ThreatConnect, ThreatTrack, Volexity and others) removed about 43,000 Axiom tool installations, including 180 Hikit implants, through Microsoft's MSRT and vendor products. Novetta then published its Axiom report.

campaigns.name: Anthem breach (possible link)
campaigns.summary: Coverage of ThreatConnect research tied infrastructure behind the Anthem intrusion to a Chinese group that press called Deep Panda, Axiom, Group 72 or Shell_Crew. The link was described as possible, not confirmed.

diamond.adversary: A disciplined, well-resourced subgroup of a larger PRC cyberespionage group. Novetta assessed with moderate to high confidence that its tasking organization is part of the Chinese intelligence apparatus [S1][S2].
diamond.capability: Tiered malware: PlugX, Gh0st RAT and Poison Ivy, then Hikit for long-term persistence. Also Derusbi, Hydraq, ZxShell and DeputyDog tooling, plus malware signed with a stolen Bit9 certificate [S1][S3][S4][S7].
diamond.infrastructure: Command-and-control infrastructure built for almost every Hikit target [S3]. In the related DeputyDog activity, watering holes on legitimate Japanese media sites and staging and C2 hosts in Hong Kong and South Korea [S8].
diamond.victim: Asian and Western government agencies, human-rights and environmental NGOs, energy, pharmaceutical, telecommunications and IT or electronics firms, and academia. Concentrated in the US, South Korea, Taiwan, Japan and the EU [S1].
diamond.socioPolitical: Collection on organizations of strategic economic interest and on groups seen as threats to the stability of the Chinese state [S2].
diamond.technology: Windows enterprise endpoints. Trust in code-signing certificates and application allow-listing, which the stolen Bit9 certificate undermined. Browser exploitation through watering holes [S3][S8].

gaps: Novetta's primary 'Operation SMN: Axiom Threat Actor Group Report' (47 pages, October 2014) was not retrieved. Figures and quotes come from press coverage [S1][S2][S3][S4].

Web fetching failed for every host tried (MITRE, Help Net Security, Dark Reading, Lawfare, Infosecurity Magazine), so all content comes from search-result summaries. Exact wording should be checked against the originals.

Cluster boundaries are disputed. Microsoft splits the activity across Brass Typhoon, Heart Typhoon and Leopard Typhoon [S12], and MITRE separates Axiom from Winnti Group [S11]. Hidden Lynx and DeputyDog map to Heart Typhoon (APT17) under Microsoft, so the Bit9 and DeputyDog campaigns may belong to that cluster rather than to Axiom as Novetta defined it [S3][S8][S9][S12].
Press coverage of the Anthem breach treats Deep Panda, Axiom, Group 72 and Shell_Crew as one group [S10]. CrowdStrike tracks Deep Panda separately, and that equivalence is not established here.
Accounts of the activity window differ (MITRE's 'since at least 2008' versus 'more than six years' before 2014), as do accounts of the Aurora linkage (overlap versus attribution) [S3][S4][S11].
No sourced activity under the Axiom name after 2015 was found. Whether the cluster still operates, or now exists only under successor names, is unknown.
The FBI flash to InfraGard that Novetta cited is not public and was not reviewed [S2].

Many imported aliases (for example Earth Baku, TA415, Wicked Spider, BRONZE ATLAS/EXPORT, Grayfly, Red Kelpie) look like APT41 or Winnti-family names from umbrella mappings. No source gathered here equates them with Axiom as Novetta defined it.

implications.jipoe: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. STEP 1 (operational environment): Key terrain is Windows enterprise endpoints, code-signing and allow-listing trust chains, and frequently visited third-party websites that can be turned into watering holes [S3][S8]. STEP 2 (effects): Signed malware can defeat allow-listing. Tiered implants mean that removing commodity RATs does not end access while Hikit-class implants stay in place [S1][S3][S4]. STEP 3 (threat model): The template is initial access through watering holes or exploits, then commodity RATs, then a custom backdoor with per-victim C2 for long-term collection [S1][S3][S8]. STEP 4 (COAs): MLCOA is persistent, low-noise espionage against government, defense-industrial, technology and policy NGO networks [S1][S11]. MDCOA is a supply-chain or certificate compromise of a security vendor that lets signed implants run widely inside DoD or DIB enclaves [S3][S9]. Candidate indicators: binaries signed with unexpected or revoked vendor certificates; Hikit, Derusbi, ZxShell, PlugX or Gh0st detections [S7]; and unique per-host C2 domains [S3].
implications.jcc2: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. (1) Situational awareness: Operation SMN shows how coordinated industry and vendor action (MSRT, AV signatures) can remove a toolset at scale. JCC2 should track vendor and Microsoft disruption actions as events that can trigger re-infection attempts [S4][S6][S7]. (2) Authorities: The 2014 action was led by private industry, independent of law enforcement [S3]. Coordinating with similar private disruptions needs clear legal and policy lanes. (3) Mission assurance: Trust in code signing and allow-listing tools is a single point of failure, so certificate revocation monitoring belongs in mission-assurance checks [S3]. (4) Coordination: Overlapping vendor names (Axiom, Group 72, APT17, Winnti, APT41) make cross-organization reporting harder. Exchange IOCs and behaviors, not names alone [S5][S11][S12].

identification.summary: Berry Sandstorm is a Microsoft threat actor name. Microsoft's public naming mapping lists its origin as Iran and its other name as Storm-0852 [S1]. In Microsoft's taxonomy, 'Sandstorm' is the family name for Iran-attributed actors, and 'Storm-' plus four digits marks a cluster still in development before it gets a full name [S2]. No public Microsoft or third-party report describing Berry Sandstorm's operations was found.
identification.notes: Microsoft name: Berry Sandstorm (in-development designation Storm-0852) [S1]. No MITRE ATT&CK group and no third-party vendor cluster mapping was found. Do not confuse it with Storm-0842 (Void Manticore/Red Sandstorm) or Storm-0558; search engines tend to return those for this query. One search-engine summary claimed Storm-0852 was an alternate name for 'Blue Tsunami'. Microsoft's mapping file contradicts this: it lists Blue Tsunami as an Israel-based private-sector offensive actor with no other names, and maps Storm-0852 to Berry Sandstorm [S1].

attribution.confidence: Microsoft classifies Berry Sandstorm with origin 'Iran' [S1]. Microsoft gives no public confidence statement, sponsoring organization (for example MOIS or IRGC) or rationale for this actor.
attribution.basis: Microsoft's threat actor naming mapping only [S1], read through Microsoft's naming-taxonomy rules [S2]. No government attribution was found.

targeting.notes: No public targeting information was found for Berry Sandstorm or Storm-0852.

diamond.adversary: Iran-origin actor tracked by Microsoft as Berry Sandstorm, previously the in-development cluster Storm-0852 [S1][S2].

gaps: No public Microsoft blog post, Security Insider profile or Digital Defense Report passage describing Berry Sandstorm or Storm-0852 was found in 9 searches across microsoft.com and the open web.

Microsoft's 'How Microsoft names threat actors' page on learn.microsoft.com, the record's original reference, could not be fetched (DNS/proxy block). Its Berry Sandstorm row was checked against the equivalent Microsoft MSTIC GitHub mapping file instead [S1].
Microsoft's February 2024 report on Iranian cyber-enabled influence operations supporting Hamas was checked and does not mention Berry Sandstorm or Storm-0852.
Sponsoring organization, first-observed date, objectives, targeting, tooling, infrastructure and campaigns are all unknown from open sources.
Whether Berry Sandstorm overlaps with any other vendor's cluster (Mandiant UNC/APT, CrowdStrike Kitten, Check Point Manticore, etc.) is unknown. No cited source states any overlap.

When Microsoft promoted Storm-0852 to a full name, and on what basis, is not publicly documented. Microsoft says it promotes a Storm cluster to a named actor once it reaches high confidence [S2], but gives no criteria specific to this actor.

identification.summary: BLACKGEAR (also Topgear and Comnie) is a cyberespionage campaign that Trend Micro describes as active since at least 2008, mainly targeting entities in Taiwan, South Korea and Japan [S1][S3]. Its operators use the Elirks backdoor and, in later reporting, the Protux backdoor and the Marade downloader [S1][S2]. It is known for hiding command-and-control (C&C) configuration in blog, microblog and social media posts so the real C&C server can be swapped quickly [S1][S2].
identification.firstObserved: Trend Micro dates the campaign to 2008, based on the Protux backdoor its operators used [S1][S3]. Elirks was reported in 2012 as used against Taiwan [S6].
identification.notes: Trend Micro uses the name BLACKGEAR and lists Topgear and Comnie as other names [S1][S3]. Microsoft has no mapped name for this record. Unit 42 reported Elirks use in Japan in June 2016 and earlier linked an Elirks variant to the Scarlet Mimic campaign [S5]; that is a separate vendor cluster and is not merged here. Unit 42 later published related Elirks reporting under the name MILE TEA [S5].

attribution.confidence: Trend Micro stated that some limited evidence suggests the attacks may be conducted by Chinese state-sponsored actors [S2][S4]. This is a vendor assessment with limited confidence, not a government attribution.
attribution.basis: Limited evidence cited by Trend Micro; the specific indicators were not reviewed because the primary report could not be fetched [S2][S4].

actors.objectives: Cyberespionage against public sector agencies and telecommunications and other high-technology organizations [S1][S6]. Specific collection requirements are not stated in the sources reviewed.

targeting.notes: Taiwan was the original focus, including government agencies [S6]. Trend Micro's October 2016 report said Japanese-language decoy documents and Japan-based blogging and microblogging services indicated an added focus on Japan [S1]. Later reporting describes Taiwan, South Korea and Japan as the main targets [S2][S3].

capabilities.summary: Delivery by spear-phishing email or compromised websites used for watering-hole attacks, ending in a binder that drops the malware [S1][S6]. Elirks backdoor used since at least 2012 reporting [S1][S6]. In 2018 Trend Micro described a new Protux backdoor version and the Marade downloader, delivered through spam with decoy documents or fake installers such as Adobe Flash Player; the Marade file was padded past 50 MB to evade sandboxes [S2][S4]. Encrypted C&C configurations were stored in blog and social media posts, including a Facebook post, with strings disguised as a magnet link [S2][S4]. Unit 42 observed Elirks variants using Japanese blog services across the preceding couple of years [S5].

campaigns.name: Earliest activity (Protux)
campaigns.summary: Trend Micro dates the campaign to 2008 based on the Protux backdoor used by its operators.

campaigns.name: Elirks used against Taiwan
campaigns.summary: Elirks was reported as used to target Taiwan, including government agencies.

campaigns.name: Elirks variants in Japan (Unit 42)

campaigns.name: Resurgence with Protux, Marade and social media C&C

diamond.adversary: Unattributed operators; Trend Micro cites limited evidence of possible Chinese state sponsorship [S2][S4].
diamond.capability: Elirks, Protux and Marade; binder-based droppers; spear-phishing, watering holes and fake installers; oversized files to evade sandboxes [S1][S2][S4].
diamond.infrastructure: C&C addresses held in encrypted form in blog, microblog and social media posts (including Japan-based services and Facebook), letting operators change servers by editing a post [S1][S2][S4].
diamond.victim: Public sector, telecommunications and other high-technology organizations in Taiwan, Japan and South Korea [S1][S3].
diamond.socioPolitical: Regional intelligence collection in East Asia; the sources reviewed do not state requirements beyond espionage [S1][S2].
diamond.technology: Email and web browsing by government and technology staff, and reliance on commodity blogging and social media services that defenders usually allow, which hides C&C lookups [S2][S4].

gaps: The primary Trend Micro reports (October 2016 and July 2018) could not be fetched; facts come from search excerpts and secondary coverage and should be verified against the originals [S1][S2].
Basis for the limited Chinese state-sponsorship assessment is not available; no government attribution was found.
Relationship to the Scarlet Mimic and MILE TEA clusters named by Unit 42 (shared Elirks malware and infrastructure) is unresolved and not merged here [S5].
Publication dates for S3, S4 and S6 are approximate (month taken from search results).
No victim counts, named victims or activity after 2018 were found.
No MITRE ATT&CK group, no Microsoft name and no US government reporting were identified.

implications.jipoe: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. STEP 1: Government and telecom or high-technology networks in Taiwan, Japan and South Korea, with email gateways and web proxies as key terrain [S1][S3]. STEP 2: Commodity blog and social media platforms are allowed by default on most networks, giving the actor a hard-to-block C&C channel [S2]. STEP 3: Spear-phishing or watering hole, then binder, then Elirks, Protux or Marade, then C&C fetched from a social media post [S1][S2][S4]. STEP 4: MLCOA is continued low-volume espionage against regional government and telecom targets with rotating C&C posts. MDCOA is use of telecom or government footholds in an allied partner nation for collection during a regional crisis. Candidate indicators: unusually large (50 MB+) executables from email, hosts querying blog or social media pages with encoded strings (including magnet-link style text), and fake software installers [S2][S4].
implications.jcc2: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. (1) Situational awareness: track regional partner-nation compromise reporting, since Taiwan, Japan and South Korea are named targets [S3]. (2) Authorities: partner-network defense typically needs host-nation consent or sharing channels; plan indicator sharing through established agreements. (3) Mission assurance: restrict personal social media and blog access from mission systems or log it, and sandbox large email attachments [S2][S4]. (4) Coordination: confidence in sponsorship is low, so share indicators without asserting attribution [S2].

provenance.importedSummary: BLACKGEAR is an espionage campaign which has targeted users in Taiwan for many years. Multiple papers and talks have been released covering this campaign, which used the ELIRKS backdoor when it was first discovered in 2012. It is known for using blogs and microblogging services to hide the location of its actual command-and-control (C&C) servers. This allows an attacker to change the C&C server used quickly by changing the information in these posts. Like most campaigns, BLACKGEAR has evolved over time. Our research indicates that it has started targeting Japanese users. Two things led us to this conclusion: first, the fake documents that are used as part of its infection routines are now in Japanese. Secondly, it is now using blogging sites and microblogging services based in Japan for its C&C activity.

identification.summary: Blackwood is a China-aligned APT group named by ESET, which says it has operated since at least 2018 and conducts cyberespionage against individuals and companies in China, Japan and the United Kingdom [S1][S2]. ESET documented the group's multistage NSPX30 implant, delivered through adversary-in-the-middle (AitM) hijacking of unencrypted HTTP software update requests [S1][S3]. ESET traces NSPX30 back to a 2005 backdoor it calls Project Wood [S1][S3].
identification.firstObserved: ESET: operating since at least 2018; earliest known NSPX30 sample dated 2018; implant lineage traced to Project Wood (2005) [S1][S3][S4]. First publicized 2024-01-24 [S1].
identification.notes: The name Blackwood comes from a recurring theme in a mutex name [S1]. This is an ESET-coined name; no Microsoft name or MITRE ATT&CK group entry was found in the searches run. ESET observed one victim also hit by toolkits tied to Evasive Panda, LuoYu and LittleBear and suggests Blackwood may share access with other Chinese APT groups; it does not name these as aliases [S4]. SonicWall separately reports a Blackwood DLL loader sample; whether it is an NSPX30 component was not confirmed [S5].

attribution.confidence: ESET describes Blackwood as China-aligned and believes its activities align with Chinese state interests [S1][S4]. No government attribution to a specific PRC agency was found in the sources reviewed.
attribution.basis: ESET research and telemetry on NSPX30 and its victims [S1][S3]. This is a vendor assessment only.

actors.objectives: Cyberespionage against individuals and companies; ESET describes the activity as espionage and the backdoor and plugins as supporting communications monitoring and data collection [S1][S5]. Specific collection requirements are not stated in the sources reviewed.

sectors: Engineering (China office of a Japanese company)
Academia (individual tied to a UK public research university network)
targeting.notes: Victims include unidentified individuals in China and Japan, a Chinese manufacturing and trading company, the China office of a Japanese engineering company, and a Chinese-speaking individual tied to a UK public research university's network [S2][S4]. SonicWall reports the DLL loader targeting companies and individuals in Japan and China [S5].

capabilities.summary: NSPX30 is a multistage implant with a dropper, installer, loaders, an orchestrator and a backdoor; the orchestrator and backdoor each load plugins [S1][S3]. It is delivered when software such as Tencent QQ, WPS Office and Sogou Pinyin fetches updates over unencrypted HTTP and the request is intercepted AitM [S1][S4]. ESET speculates a network implant on vulnerable appliances such as routers or gateways may perform the interception, but this is unconfirmed, and it saw no DNS-based redirection [S4]. Interception of traffic also helps hide the location of command-and-control servers [S1][S2]. Operators attempt to re-compromise systems if access is lost [S2]. SonicWall describes a Blackwood DLL loader that attempts privilege escalation via the CMSTPLUA interface, includes anti-analysis and locale checks, and tries to install a backdoor for communications monitoring and diversion [S5].

campaigns.name: Project Wood origin
campaigns.summary: ESET traces NSPX30 to a small backdoor it names Project Wood, whose oldest sample it found was compiled in 2005; it believes NSPX30 evolved from DCM, a Project Wood descendant (2008) [S1][S3][S4].

campaigns.name: Earliest NSPX30 activity
campaigns.summary: ESET dates the earliest known NSPX30 sample and the group's operation to at least 2018 [S1][S3].

campaigns.name: ESET publishes Blackwood and NSPX30 research
campaigns.summary: ESET publicly named Blackwood and described AitM delivery of NSPX30 via Tencent QQ, WPS Office and Sogou Pinyin updates against targets in China, Japan and the UK [S1][S2][S3].

campaigns.name: SonicWall reports new DLL loader
campaigns.summary: SonicWall Capture Labs analyzed a Blackwood DLL loader sample targeting companies and individuals in Japan and China and released a MalAgent.Blackwood signature [S5].

diamond.adversary: Blackwood, a China-aligned cluster named by ESET; sponsor not publicly established [S1][S4].
diamond.capability: NSPX30 multistage implant with plugin architecture, AitM update hijacking, and a DLL loader reported by SonicWall [S1][S3][S5].
diamond.infrastructure: Command-and-control location is concealed by traffic interception; the AitM position is unconfirmed, with possible network implants on routers or gateways speculated by ESET [S1][S2][S4].
diamond.victim: Individuals and companies in China, Japan and the UK, including a manufacturer/trader, a Japanese engineering firm's China office and a UK university-linked individual [S2][S4].
diamond.socioPolitical: ESET assesses alignment with Chinese state interests; the sources reviewed give no more detailed political context [S4].
diamond.technology: Windows endpoints using Tencent QQ, WPS Office and Sogou Pinyin that fetch updates over unencrypted HTTP [S1][S4].

gaps: Could not open the ESET WeLiveSecurity report, SonicWall blog, BleepingComputer or The Hacker News pages (fetch failed with DNS errors); findings rely on search-result summaries of them, so technical details, IOCs and plugin capabilities are not captured.
Actual AitM mechanism (router, gateway or other on-path device) is unknown; ESET's router hypothesis is unconfirmed [S4].
No government attribution or named sponsoring organization found.
No MITRE ATT&CK group ID or Microsoft naming identified; overlaps with Evasive Panda, LuoYu and LittleBear are shared-access indications only and should not be merged.
Relationship between the SonicWall DLL loader and NSPX30 components is not confirmed [S5].
No activity reporting after January 2024 was found in the searches run.

implications.jipoe: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. Step 1-2: the operational environment is endpoint and network paths used by individuals and firms in China, Japan and the UK; relevant terrain includes software update channels for Tencent QQ, WPS Office and Sogou Pinyin over unencrypted HTTP, and possibly edge network devices [S1][S4]. Step 3-4: MLCOA is continued espionage-oriented AitM delivery of NSPX30 to China/Japan/UK-linked users and organizations [S1][S2]; MDCOA is adoption of additional update channels or edge-device compromise to reach other targets, which the sources do not show. Candidate indicators: software updates fetched over HTTP followed by unexpected DLL loading, CMSTPLUA privilege escalation behavior, and use of the MalAgent.Blackwood signature [S5].
implications.jcc2: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. Situational awareness: track vendor reporting on Blackwood and NSPX30 and share indicators through established channels, noting that evidence is vendor-sourced [S1]. Authorities: monitoring of partner or personal devices and networks requires the appropriate legal authority; this is a planning consideration, not a finding. Mission assurance: personnel or partners using the affected Chinese software, or operating in China and Japan, face exposure through update hijacking; enforce encrypted, verified update channels and remove unneeded software [S1][S4]. Coordination: coordinate with allied and commercial threat-intelligence partners given Japan and UK victimology [S2].

provenance.importedSummary: Blackwood is a China-aligned APT group that has been active since at least 2018. They primarily engage in cyberespionage operations targeting individuals and companies in China, Japan, and the United Kingdom. Blackwood utilizes sophisticated techniques such as adversary-in-the-middle attacks to deliver their custom implant, NSPX30, through updates of legitimate software. They also have the capability to hide the location of their command and control servers by intercepting traffic generated by the implant.

identification.summary: BladedFeline is an Iran-aligned APT group that has been active since at least 2017, targeting Iraqi and Kurdish government officials for cyberespionage. The group employs a variety of tools, including the Shahmaran backdoor, Whisper, and PrimeCache, which is a malicious IIS module. BladedFeline utilizes techniques such as spearphishing (T1566), exploiting public-facing applications (T1190), and timestomping to maintain access and exfiltrate data. The group is assessed with medium confidence to be a subgroup of OilRig, focusing on strategic access to high-ranking officials in the region.
Blue Termite is a group of suspected Chinese origin active in Japan.

identification.summary: First observed activity in December 2013.

China-based actor that combines state-sponsored espionage with financially motivated intrusions. US charges describe members working through a Chengdu company and compromising more than 100 victims worldwide, stealing source code, code-signing certificates, customer data and business information [S1]. Mandiant documented a deliberate 2021–2022 campaign that compromised at least six US state government networks [S2]. Google disrupted a 2025 campaign that used Google Calendar for command and control [S3].
identification.firstObserved: MITRE: active since at least 2012 [S4]. US indictments were returned in August 2019 and August 2020 [S1].
identification.notes: Microsoft name: Brass Typhoon (formerly BARIUM). Microsoft maps WICKED PANDA and APT41 to it [S5]. Microsoft tracks Leopard Typhoon (LEAD / Winnti Group) separately, though both share the CrowdStrike label WICKED PANDA; public 'Winnti' reporting often blurs the two.

attribution.sponsor: People's Republic of China. Indicted members include employees of Chengdu 404 Network Technology [S1].
attribution.confidence: Formal US charges against five PRC nationals (announced 16 Sep 2020) [S1]. Mandiant describes APT41 as state-sponsored with a history of moonlighting for personal financial gain [S2].
attribution.basis: DOJ indictments and domain/server seizures [S1]; Mandiant incident response [S2]; Google Threat Intelligence [S3].

actors.objectives: Dual-purpose: espionage aligned with PRC state priorities and theft for profit. Mandiant could not determine the motive of the state-government campaign, given the group's history of financially motivated activity [S2]. Theft of source code and code-signing certificates enables later supply-chain operations [S1].

sectors: Software and video-game companies (source code, signing certificates)
Healthcare, higher education and technology (broad victim set in indictment)
regions: Global: more than 100 victims across multiple countries
targeting.notes: Victims from the 2020 indictment coverage [S1], Mandiant [S2] and GTIG [S3].

capabilities.summary: Exploitation of internet-facing web applications, including .NET deserialization, SQL injection, directory traversal and a zero-day in the USAHerds livestock-tracking application (CVE-2021-44207) [S2]. Supply-chain compromise using stolen code-signing certificates [S1]. Abuse of cloud services for C2: TOUGHPROGRESS used hidden Google Calendar events for commands and exfiltration [S3]. MITRE lists 82 techniques and 32 software entries, including ShadowPad, Winnti for Linux, KEYPLUG, DUSTPAN, DUSTTRAP and MESSAGETAP [S4].

campaigns.name: TOUGHPROGRESS / Google Calendar C2
campaigns.summary: Spear-phishing with archives hosted on a compromised government website; malware used Google Calendar events for C2. Google terminated the attacker's Workspace accounts. Reported 28–29 May 2025.

diamond.adversary: PRC-based operators including Chengdu 404 employees charged by the DOJ [S1].
diamond.capability: Web-application exploitation and zero-days; stolen code-signing certificates; ShadowPad, KEYPLUG, DUSTTRAP, TOUGHPROGRESS [S1][S2][S3][S4].
diamond.infrastructure: Actor-controlled domains and servers (seized in 2020) [S1]; abuse of legitimate cloud services (Google Calendar, free web hosting) and compromised government websites [S3].
diamond.victim: Software and gaming firms, telecoms, US state governments and government entities worldwide [S1][S2][S3].
diamond.socioPolitical: PRC intelligence priorities, alongside personal financial gain by the operators [S1][S2].
diamond.technology: Vulnerable custom and commercial web applications and trust in legitimate cloud platforms [S2][S3].

gaps: Boundary between Brass Typhoon (APT41/BARIUM) and Leopard Typhoon (Winnti Group/LEAD): vendor reporting often merges them.
APT41 activity after May 2025 was not found in this research pass.
DOJ press release and indictment text not fetched (government sites blocked); details come from coverage.
Whether the 2021–2022 state-government campaign was espionage or financially motivated remains open per Mandiant [S2].

implications.jipoe: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. STEP 1: Include state and local government systems and commercial software suppliers in the OE. They support National Guard, emergency management and DoD-adjacent functions and are soft entry points. STEP 2: Abuse of legitimate cloud services for C2 blends with normal business traffic. STEP 3: The template is web-application exploitation or spear-phishing, then web shells and custom backdoors, then credential theft and lateral movement, plus theft of code-signing material for later supply-chain use. Re-compromise after eviction is likely. STEP 4: MLCOA is continued espionage against government and technology targets mixed with profit-driven theft. MDCOA is a supply-chain operation using stolen signing certificates to reach DoD or DIB networks during a crisis. Candidate indicators: .NET deserialization exploit attempts, newly signed binaries with unexpected certificates, and calendar or cloud-API traffic from servers [S1][S2][S3].
implications.jcc2: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. (1) Expect re-entry after eviction: JCC2 tracking should keep cases open with heightened monitoring after remediation. (2) Coordinate with state partners (National Guard cyber units, state CISOs, CISA) because state networks are in the target set. (3) Monitor code-signing certificate revocations and abuse reports as part of supply-chain situational awareness. (4) Cloud-service C2 requires provider cooperation (e.g. Google, Microsoft) for disruption, which should be built into response playbooks.

provenance.importedSummary: APT41 is a threat group that researchers have assessed as Chinese state-sponsored espionage group that also conducts financially-motivated operations. Active since at least 2012, APT41 has been observed targeting various industries, including but not limited to healthcare, telecom, technology, finance, education, retail and video game industries in 14 countries. Notable behaviors include using a wide range of malware and tools to complete mission objectives. APT41 overlaps at least partially with public reporting on groups including BARIUM and Winnti Group.

identification.summary: BrazenBamboo is a Chinese state-affiliated threat actor known for developing the LIGHTSPY, DEEPDATA, and DEEPPOST malware families. Their infrastructure includes capabilities for zero-day exploitation, specifically targeting vulnerabilities like FortiClient, and employs a command-and-control architecture that supports multi-platform operations. Volexity's analysis indicates that BrazenBamboo is a well-resourced entity with a focus on domestic targets, utilizing custom analyst software to manage data collected from their malware. The ongoing development of their malware families is evidenced by the timestamps associated with their latest payloads.

China-based cyberespionage group that Microsoft tracks as Brocade Typhoon (formerly BORON) and that other vendors call APT3, Gothic Panda, UPS, Buckeye and TG-0110 [S1][S4]. FireEye/Mandiant tied it to browser and Flash zero-day campaigns in 2014-2015 (Operation Clandestine Fox, Operation Clandestine Wolf) [S2][S9]. Symantec reported a targeting shift from the US to Hong Kong political entities starting in June 2015 [S4]. Security researchers linked the group to the Guangzhou firm Boyusec, three of whose personnel were indicted by the US in November 2017 [S6][S7]. Symantec reported that known Buckeye tool activity ceased in mid-2017 [S5].
identification.firstObserved: Symantec (2016) assessed the group had been operating for 'well over half a decade' [S4]; the 2017 US indictment alleges intrusions from 2011 to May 2017 (reporting DOJ indictment) [S7]. Earliest named public campaign: Operation Clandestine Fox, April 2014 [S9].
identification.notes: Microsoft name: Brocade Typhoon. Microsoft's public mapping lists BORON, GOTHIC PANDA, UPS, APT3, OLDCARP, TG-0110, Red Sylvan and CYBRAN as other names [S1]. Symantec calls it Buckeye and equates it with APT3, Gothic Panda, UPS Team and TG-0110 [S4]. Palo Alto Unit 42 tracks the same activity as UPS and associates it with the Pirpi backdoor [S10]. MITRE ATT&CK tracks the group as APT3 (G0022) [S11]. Boyusec is a company the researchers link to the group; whether Boyusec is all of APT3 or only one component was unresolved in 2017 reporting [S8].

attribution.sponsor: People's Republic of China, Ministry of State Security (MSS), per Recorded Future's assessment that Boyusec worked on behalf of the MSS [S6]. The US indictment does not name the Chinese government [S7][S8].
attribution.confidence: Recorded Future assessed with high confidence (May 2017) that APT3 is attributable to the MSS through the contractor Boyusec [S6]. FireEye's Ben Read said FireEye believed the indicted individuals and Boyusec are linked to APT3 [S7]. The November 2017 US indictment charged three Boyusec personnel (Wu Yingzhuo, Dong Hao, Xia Lei) but, per press reporting, made no reference to Chinese state links [S7][S8]. Microsoft's mapping lists the origin as China [S1].
attribution.basis: Domain-registration analysis by the anonymous 'intrusiontruth' blog tied Pirpi C2 domains to Boyusec shareholders, which Recorded Future corroborated and linked to Guangdong ITSEC, which it describes as subordinate to the MSS-run CNITSEC [S6][S8]. Charges against Boyusec personnel cited use of 'UPS'/'exeproxy' malware (reporting DOJ indictment) [S7]. Vendor malware and campaign reporting from FireEye/Mandiant, Symantec and Unit 42 [S2][S3][S4][S5][S10].

actors.objectives: Espionage and theft of commercial and technical intellectual property: the indictment alleges theft of Siemens energy, technology and transportation business data, Trimble satellite-navigation (GNSS) development data and Moody's Analytics economist email (reporting DOJ indictment) [S7]. From 2015 it also collected against political entities in Hong Kong [S4].

sectors: Industrial and engineering (Siemens energy, technology, transportation businesses) [S7]
regions: Vietnam and the Philippines (later use of the Bemstour/DoublePulsar package; Symantec did not tie that later use to Buckeye's known tools) [S12]
targeting.notes: Symantec counted 13 Hong Kong, 3 US and 1 UK victim organizations in its 2016 reporting, and said US and UK targeting stopped from March 2016 (reported by SecurityWeek) [S4]. The Vietnam and Philippines intrusions used the Bemstour exploit tool with different malware after Buckeye's known tools went quiet in mid-2017, so they may not belong to this cluster [S5][S12].

capabilities.summary: Early access to browser and plugin zero-days: Internet Explorer CVE-2014-1776 (Clandestine Fox, April 2014) [S9] and Adobe Flash CVE-2015-3113 delivered by phishing links to compromised servers, followed by the SHOTPUT backdoor (Clandestine Wolf, June 2015) [S2]. Rapid use of newly disclosed exploits such as CVE-2014-6332 and CVE-2014-4113 within days of disclosure (Operation Double Tap, November 2014), with PlugX/Kaba C2 noted [S3]. Custom backdoors including Pirpi/UPS [S10] and 'exeproxy' [S7]. From March 2016 the group used a DoublePulsar variant, newer than the Shadow Brokers version, delivered by the custom Bemstour exploit tool, which chained Windows vulnerabilities including the zero-day CVE-2019-0703 for remote kernel code execution; this was over a year before the Shadow Brokers leak [S5]. Spearphishing with malicious attachments or links is alleged in the indictment [S7]. MITRE lists software including PlugX, SHOTPUT, OSInfo, RemoteCMD and LaZagne [S11].

diamond.adversary: PRC-based operators linked by researchers to Guangzhou Boyu Information Technology (Boyusec), assessed by Recorded Future as working for the MSS; three Boyusec personnel indicted by the US [S6][S7].
diamond.capability: Browser and Flash zero-days (CVE-2014-1776, CVE-2015-3113), fast use of new n-days, SHOTPUT, Pirpi/UPS, exeproxy, PlugX, and a pre-leak DoublePulsar variant with Bemstour (CVE-2019-0703) [S2][S3][S5][S7][S9][S10].
diamond.infrastructure: Phishing links to compromised servers hosting exploits [S2]; actor-registered C2 domains, including Pirpi domains registered to a Boyusec shareholder [S6][S8]; domains such as securitywap.com and walterclean.com in Double Tap [S3]; email forwarding rules on a victim mail server [S7].
diamond.victim: US aerospace, defense and industrial firms (Siemens, Trimble, Moody's Analytics); Hong Kong political entities; targets in the UK and Belgium [S2][S4][S7][S12].
diamond.socioPolitical: Commercial and technical IP theft benefiting PRC industrial priorities, plus political intelligence on Hong Kong from 2015 [S4][S7].
diamond.technology: Windows endpoints running Internet Explorer and Adobe Flash; Windows SMB and kernel vulnerabilities exploited by Bemstour; enterprise email servers [S5][S7][S9].

gaps: No Microsoft Threat Intelligence report specific to Brocade Typhoon/BORON was found; Microsoft coverage is limited to its naming map [S1].
The DOJ press release and indictment (justice.gov) could not be opened; indictment details come from Security Affairs and Foreign Policy coverage [S7][S8].

The original FireEye/Mandiant, Symantec, Recorded Future, Unit 42 and Secureworks (BRONZE MAYFAIR) pages could not be fetched (network blocks); details come from search-result summaries and press coverage.
MITRE ATT&CK G0022 could not be fetched in this session; the software list is taken from the imported actor record [S11].

Activity after mid-2017 is not publicly attributed to this cluster. Bemstour/DoublePulsar use into late 2018 (Vietnam, Philippines) was with different malware, and Symantec did not attribute it to Buckeye [S5][S12].
It is unresolved whether Boyusec is the whole of APT3 or one part of it, and how Buckeye obtained Equation Group tools [S5][S8].
Aliases Boyusec, Group 6, Pirpi, Threat Group-0110 and UPS Team in the imported record come from MISP/other mappings; only those in cited sources are added below.

implications.jipoe: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. STEP 1 (OE): Key terrain is user endpoints running browsers and plugins, enterprise mail servers and Windows SMB-exposed hosts at defense, aerospace, industrial and navigation-technology firms, including DIB contractors whose engineering data has value (Siemens, Trimble precedent) [S2][S5][S7]. STEP 2 (effects): Zero-day and fast n-day use (exploits within about a week of disclosure) shortens the defender's patch window; stealthy mail-forwarding rules allow long-term, low-noise collection [S3][S7]. STEP 3 (adversary template): phishing link or attachment, then browser/Flash exploit, then SHOTPUT/Pirpi/PlugX backdoor, then credential theft and lateral movement, possibly with a kernel-level implant such as DoublePulsar, then data staging and exfiltration [S2][S3][S5][S7]. STEP 4: MLCOA is quiet theft of engineering and program data (for example GNSS and energy technology) from DIB and partner networks. MDCOA is use of an unpublished exploit chain that gives kernel-level implants across many hosts. Candidate indicators: unexpected mailbox forwarding rules to external accounts, anomalous SMB traffic consistent with DoublePulsar, browser processes spawning shells, and connections to newly registered domains [S5][S7]. Note: no public activity has been attributed since mid-2017 [S5].
implications.jcc2: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. (1) Situational awareness: track emergency browser, plugin and Windows patches alongside exposure of mission-relevant enclaves, since this actor used exploits within days of disclosure [S3]. (2) Authorities: activity against contractors such as Siemens and Trimble falls under law enforcement and DIB channels; the US addressed it by indictment, not military response [S7]. (3) Mission assurance: PNT-related development data (Trimble GNSS) was a target, so protect PNT program and supplier data as mission-critical [S7]. (4) Coordination: share indicators with DC3/DIB CS partners and commercial vendors, since public attribution came from vendor and researcher reporting (Recorded Future, Symantec, FireEye) [S5][S6][S7].
