diamond.adversary: DPRK state-sponsored operators, reportedly linked to RGB Bureau 121 [S1]. Clustered by vendors as Citrine Sleet, UNC4736, Gleaming Pisces and Labyrinth Chollima [S1][S2][S3].
diamond.capability: AppleJeus trojanized apps [S4]; Chromium and Windows kernel zero-days with the FudModule rootkit [S1]; supply-chain implants (VEILEDSIGNAL, TAXHAUL, POOLRAT) [S2]; PondRAT [S3]; INLETDRIFT [S5].
diamond.infrastructure: Fake cryptocurrency trading and wallet websites [S1][S4]. Exploit delivery domain voyagorclub[.]space and weinsteinfrog[.]com [S1]. A compromised legitimate vendor site (tradingtechnologies[.]com) and GitHub-hosted icon files used for C2 resolution [S2]. PyPI packages and C2 domains jdkgradle[.]com and rebelthumb[.]net [S3]. A spoofed contractor website and Telegram accounts [S5].

diamond.socioPolitical: Sanctions evasion and revenue generation for the DPRK regime through theft of digital assets [S1][S4].
diamond.technology: Exploits trust in signed software and software update channels [S2], open-source package ecosystems [S3], browser and kernel vulnerabilities [S1], and multisignature wallet-signing workflows on developer endpoints [S5].

gaps: Microsoft's own attribution of the 3CX compromise was not found. The 3CX link to Citrine Sleet rests on Mandiant's UNC4736 cluster (moderate-confidence AppleJeus link) and on Microsoft listing UNC4736 as an alias [S1][S2].
Unit 42's Gleaming Pisces report could not be opened (DNS failure). Its content comes from search-result summaries [S3].
CISA AA21-048A could not be opened (government site blocked). Details come from search-result coverage, including McGuireWoods and other secondary reporting [S4].
Mandiant's Radiant Capital findings are known only through the victim's statement as reported in press. SecurityWeek could not be fetched, and the article's exact date is approximate [S5].
No cited source explicitly confirms that Microsoft's DEV-0139 (December 2022) is Citrine Sleet. The Microsoft blog itself was not opened [S6][S8].
Boundary with Diamond Sleet and Sapphire Sleet: the clusters share FudModule and infrastructure, and some victims overlap. Tool attribution may span actors [S1].
AppleJeus reporting in the 2021 US advisory refers broadly to the 'Lazarus Group'. Its victim-sector list may cover activity beyond the Citrine Sleet cluster [S4].
No public reporting on Citrine Sleet activity in 2025 or 2026 was found in this research pass.
The meaning and scope of Microsoft's Storm-1222 designation are not described in the cited sources [S8].

implications.jipoe: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. STEP 1 (OE): Key terrain includes developer endpoints, software build environments, update and code-signing chains, open-source package dependencies (PyPI), and the browser and kernel attack surface of Windows workstations [S1][S2][S3]. Personnel reached through Telegram and LinkedIn-style job lures are part of the human terrain [S5][S6]. STEP 2 (effects): One trojanized vendor installer can cascade into downstream supply-chain compromise of widely deployed enterprise software such as VoIP clients [S2]. Zero-day chains can bypass browser sandboxes and kernel defenses [S1]. STEP 3 (adversary template): social-engineering lure (fake job, trusted-contact impersonation, fake trading site) or zero-day watering hole, then cross-platform backdoor (AppleJeus, POOLRAT/PondRAT, INLETDRIFT, VEILEDSIGNAL), then credential and wallet access or build-system tampering [S1][S2][S3][S5]. STEP 4: The MLCOA is continued financially motivated theft from crypto and fintech entities, with no direct targeting of DoD. The MDCOA is a supply-chain implant in software also used by DoD or defense industrial base networks, giving incidental access that could be passed to espionage-focused DPRK units, as in the 3CX case where victims were downstream customers [S2]. Candidate indicators: unexpected child processes or DLL side-loading from signed vendor installers [S2]; installs of newly published or typosquatted PyPI packages on developer hosts [S3]; Chromium renderer crashes followed by kernel-mode tampering of security callbacks [S1]; connections to known C2 such as voyagorclub[.]space, jdkgradle[.]com and rebelthumb[.]net [S1][S3]; and macOS .app files posing as PDFs delivered over Telegram [S5].
implications.jcc2: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. (1) Situational awareness: track software bill-of-materials and vendor-compromise alerts, such as trojanized 3CX builds, across DODIN and mission partner networks, because this actor's supply-chain operations can reach DoD users incidentally [S2]. Monitor emergency Chromium and Windows kernel patches, since the 2024 chain was patched within days of discovery [S1]. (2) Authorities: activity is primarily financial theft by a state actor. Coordinate with FBI and Treasury, which have issued joint guidance on AppleJeus, and with law enforcement for any DIB victim [S4]. (3) Mission assurance: harden developer and build environments, enforce package allow-listing for PyPI, and verify code-signing provenance of third-party installers [S2][S3]. (4) Coordination: share indicators with DC3/DIB CS and commercial vendors. Note that vendor clusters (Citrine Sleet, UNC4736, Gleaming Pisces, Labyrinth Chollima) overlap but are not identical, and tools such as FudModule are shared with Diamond Sleet, so prioritize containment over precise attribution [S1][S2][S3].

provenance.importedSummary: AppleJeus is a North Korean state-sponsored threat group attributed to the Reconnaissance General Bureau. Associated with the broader Lazarus Group umbrella of actors, AppleJeus has been active since at least 2018 and is closely aligned in resources with TEMP.hermit, another DPRK-affiliated group under the same umbrella. The group’s primary mission is to generate and launder revenue to provide financial support to the government. AppleJeus primarily targets the cryptocurrency industry and is most notably responsible for the 3CX Supply Chain Attack. The group traditionally deploys malicious cryptocurrency software in combination with Phishing. From these compromised environments, it selectively deploys additional backdoors to enable extended operations against high-value financial targets.

identification.summary: CL-STA-0043 is a Chinese state-nexus cyber-espionage actor tracked by Palo Alto Networks Unit 42, which promoted the activity cluster to the named threat actor Phantom Taurus in September 2025, having previously designated it TGR-STA-0043 and linked it to the Operation Diplomatic Specter campaign. The group targets government and telecommunications organizations, including ministries of foreign affairs, embassies and diplomatic missions, across Africa, the Middle East and Asia, with a focus on geopolitical and military intelligence collection. It typically gains access by exploiting internet-facing Internet Information Services (IIS) and Microsoft Exchange servers, then performs reconnaissance and privilege escalation using native Windows tooling. In more recent operations the actor deployed NET-STAR, a fileless .NET malware suite targeting IIS web servers that comprises the IIServerCore backdoor and the AssemblyExecuter V1 and V2 loaders.

CL-STA-0048 is a Chinese state-backed APT that targets strategic sectors in South Asia, particularly government and telecommunications entities, with a focus on espionage. The group has been linked to SAP NetWeaver intrusions and employs techniques such as DNS beaconing using ping commands and exploiting unpatched vulnerabilities in services like IIS, Apache Tomcat, and MSSQL. Analysts have observed its use of reverse shell commands and command-and-control traffic directed to specific IP addresses. The actor adapts its methods to evade detection and maintain persistent access to high-value networks.

CL-STA-1087 is a suspected state-sponsored espionage campaign operating out of China, targeting military organizations in Southeast Asia. The actor has demonstrated operational patience, maintaining dormant access for extended periods while focusing on precision intelligence collection and employing robust operational security measures. Their infrastructure includes the use of a legitimate cloud service for C2 operations, indicating a cloud-native approach. File timestamps and other indicators trace the campaign's activity back to 2020, suggesting a long-running operation.

CL-UNK-1068 is a Chinese threat actor that has targeted critical infrastructure in Asia, primarily focusing on cyberespionage. They utilize cross-platform tools, including the Xnote Linux backdoor and the GodZilla web shell, to maintain a persistent presence and execute credential theft. Their TTPs involve DLL side-loading, the use of custom malware, and batch scripts to bypass security measures. The group has demonstrated a capability for data exfiltration from SQL servers and has employed tools like DumpIt and Volatility for memory analysis.

Clay Typhoon is a Microsoft designation for a China-nexus actor; public reporting found here describes it only through vendor crosswalks rather than a Microsoft write-up [S1][S2]. Volexity's June 2026 reporting links Clay Typhoon (Microsoft) with its own VerdantBamboo cluster, Google's UNC5221 and CrowdStrike's Warp Panda, all associated with the BRICKSTORM backdoor used for long-term espionage access to VMware, storage and network appliances that typically lack EDR [S1][S2][S5].
identification.firstObserved: No Microsoft first-observed date located. CrowdStrike says Warp Panda has been active since at least 2022 [S4]; the CISA-investigated BRICKSTORM intrusion began in April 2024 [S6]; Volexity's VerdantBamboo intrusion lasted at least 18 months before discovery in September 2025 [S1].
identification.notes: Storm-2416 is the Microsoft in-development name already held in this record (from Microsoft's naming table, which could not be opened in this pass). Overlaps: Volexity states VerdantBamboo is tracked by Microsoft as Clay Typhoon, by Google as UNC5221 and by CrowdStrike as Warp Panda [S1][S2]. These are overlapping vendor clusters, not proven identical sets; facts below are attributed to the vendor that reported them. GTIG says UNC5221 is often reported as Silk Typhoon but GTIG does not consider the two the same cluster [S5].

attribution.confidence: Microsoft's own confidence statement for Clay Typhoon was not located. CrowdStrike describes Warp Panda as a China-nexus adversary whose access likely supports intelligence collection aligned with China's strategic interests [S3][S4]. Google GTIG tracks UNC5221 as a suspected China-nexus cluster [S5]. CISA, NSA and the Canadian Centre for Cyber Security attribute BRICKSTORM use to PRC state-sponsored actors, without using the Clay Typhoon name [S6]. The Clay Typhoon to VerdantBamboo/UNC5221/Warp Panda mapping rests on Volexity's reporting as relayed by secondary coverage [S1][S2].

capabilities.summary: BRICKSTORM is a Go-based ELF backdoor aimed at VMware vCenter and ESXi that blends C2 into HTTPS/WebSocket traffic and uses DNS-over-HTTPS; operators stole cloned VM snapshots for credential extraction, created hidden rogue VMs, and in one CISA case compromised ADFS and exported cryptographic keys [S6]. Google reports deployment on appliances without EDR (network storage, vCenter, remote access appliances), average dwell time of 393 days, and at least one case of Ivanti Connect Secure zero-day exploitation for access [S5]. CrowdStrike reports Warp Panda used Golang implants Junction (ESXi) and GuestConduit (guest VM tunneling), pivoted from internet-facing edge devices into vCenter with valid credentials or vCenter CVEs (e.g., CVE-2024-38812, CVE-2023-34048, CVE-2021-22005), and abused Ivanti (CVE-2024-21887, CVE-2023-46805) and F5 BIG-IP (CVE-2023-46747) flaws [S3][S4]. Volexity reports a FreeBSD BRICKSTORM variant on a pfSense firewall, the .NET Core backdoor PLENET (aka GRIMBOLT) and the Python reverse shell AGENTPSD, plus local privilege escalation on an Egnyte Storage Sync appliance [S1][S2].

diamond.capability: BRICKSTORM (Linux/ESXi and FreeBSD variants), Junction, GuestConduit, PLENET/GRIMBOLT, AGENTPSD; edge-device and vCenter exploitation; VM snapshot theft and rogue VMs [S1][S3][S6].

implications.jipoe: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. Step 1 (operational environment): key terrain is the virtualization and appliance layer (vCenter/ESXi, VPN/edge devices, firewalls, storage sync, backup appliances) where EDR is absent [S5][S6], plus MSP trust relationships [S1]. Step 2 (effects): compromise of vCenter permits snapshot theft, credential extraction and hidden VMs, and ADFS key theft enables identity forgery across federated services [S6]. Step 3 (adversary model): patient espionage operator with average dwell above a year, multiple BRICKSTORM variants and fallback implants, and re-entry via stolen credentials after remediation [S1][S5]. Step 4: MLCOA - exploit or reuse credentials on an internet-facing edge device, pivot to vCenter, install BRICKSTORM and quietly collect from DIB-adjacent legal, technology and IT service providers [S3][S5][S6]. MDCOA - leverage MSP or SaaS provider access to reach downstream mission partners, or use ADFS key theft for broad identity compromise [S1][S5][S6]. Candidate indicators: unexpected DNS-over-HTTPS from appliances, new or unregistered VMs, VM clone/snapshot operations outside change windows, vpxuser SSH/SFTP activity, unknown ELF binaries on vCenter/ESXi or FreeBSD firewalls [S3][S6].
implications.jcc2: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. Situational awareness: hypervisor and appliance telemetry is a blind spot that standard endpoint reporting will not cover, so DODIN and partner visibility requests should name vCenter/ESXi, edge, firewall and backup systems explicitly [S5][S6]. Authorities: much exposure lies in contractor, MSP and SaaS environments outside DoD networks, implying coordination through DC3/DIB channels and CISA rather than direct action [S1][S5]. Mission assurance: ADFS key export and vCenter control threaten identity and hosting for mission systems; prioritize key rotation and hypervisor integrity checks after any finding [S6]. Coordination: align with CISA/NSA/Canadian Centre AR25-338A indicators and vendor reporting, recognizing vendors name the activity differently (Clay Typhoon, UNC5221, Warp Panda, VerdantBamboo) [S1][S6].

provenance.importedSummary: Microsoft threat actor profile. Origin or category: China.

identification.summary: China-linked espionage actor that Microsoft tracks as Copper Typhoon and maps to Tonto Team, Earth Akhlut and Sharp-R [S1]. MITRE describes Tonto Team as a suspected Chinese state-sponsored espionage group that has mainly targeted South Korea, Japan, Taiwan and the United States since at least 2009, and that expanded to other Asian and Eastern European countries by 2020 [S2]. Its signature tooling is the long-lived Bisonal backdoor, delivered through spear-phishing documents, including documents built with the Royal Road weaponizer [S3][S4][S7][S8]. In 2020 Kaspersky reported that the group had also moved to more advanced tools such as ShadowPad [S4].
identification.firstObserved: MITRE: active since at least 2009, and linked to the Heartbeat Campaign (2009-2012) [S2]. Kaspersky describes CactusPete as active since at least 2012 [S4].
identification.notes: Microsoft name: Copper Typhoon. Microsoft's public mapping lists only Tonto Team, Earth Akhlut and Sharp-R as other names [S1]. MITRE G0131 (Tonto Team) lists Earth Akhlut, BRONZE HUNTLEY, CactusPete and Karma Panda as associated names [S2]. Recorded Future tracks TAG-74 as a separate cluster that overlaps with Tonto Team/COPPER/CactusPete/Earth Akhlut/Karma Panda/Bronze Huntley; it is not a confirmed one-to-one match [S3]. Recorded Future also judges that a custom ReVBShell variant is likely shared with Tick Group, which is a different actor [S3].

attribution.sponsor: People's Republic of China, People's Liberation Army (per vendor reporting). Recorded Future notes that Tonto Team has been publicly linked to the former Shenyang Military Region Technical Reconnaissance Bureau of the PLA Strategic Support Force, now part of the Northern Theater Command [S3]. In 2017 FireEye described Tonto Team as tied to China's military and based in Shenyang [S5].
attribution.confidence: Recorded Future assesses with moderate confidence that TAG-74 is aligned with the PLA Northern Theater Command, based on targeting patterns [S3]. MITRE calls Tonto Team a 'suspected' Chinese state-sponsored group [S2]. In the sources gathered, Microsoft gives no public confidence statement beyond assigning the Typhoon (China) name [S1]. No US government indictment or advisory naming this actor was found.
attribution.basis: Targeting pattern consistent with the Northern Theater Command's area of responsibility [S3]; FireEye statements reported in the press [S5]; exclusive use of Bisonal by Chinese APTs and Simplified Chinese document metadata [S7][S8]; Microsoft naming taxonomy [S1]. China's Ministry of Defense denied that the PLA supports hacking [S5].

actors.objectives: Long-term intelligence collection against military, government, defense-industrial and political targets in states bordering China's northeast, including South Korea, Japan and Russia [S2][S3]. Kaspersky judged that the 2019-2020 Eastern Europe campaign most likely sought confidential information from military and financial organizations [S4]. In 2017 the group targeted South Korean entities connected to the THAAD missile-defense deployment [S5].

targeting.notes: South Korea is the most consistent focus, from Heartbeat (2009-2012) through TAG-74 (2023) [S2][S3]. Russian targeting rose in 2022, though SentinelLabs' attribution of that activity to Tonto Team is tentative [S7]. Group-IB, a security vendor, was targeted in March 2021 and June 2022 [S8].

capabilities.summary: The primary tool is the Bisonal backdoor. Kaspersky linked more than 300 samples to the group from March 2019 to April 2020, about 20 new samples a month. Bisonal can run programs, terminate processes, manage files and support lateral movement [S4]. Group-IB documents the Bisonal.DoubleT variant and a new TontoTeam.Downloader (QuickMute) [S8]. For initial access the group uses spear-phishing with weaponized Office/RTF documents built with Royal Road [S7][S8], and in TAG-74 activity it used .chm files that launch a DLL search-order-hijacking chain to load a customized ReVBShell VBScript backdoor before Bisonal [S3]. In March 2021 ESET observed the group exploiting Exchange ProxyLogon vulnerabilities [S6]. Kaspersky reported a move to ShadowPad in 2020 [S4]. MITRE lists Mimikatz, gsecdump, LaZagne, NBTscan, Bisonal and ShadowPad as associated software [S2].

diamond.adversary: PRC-linked operators publicly associated with the PLA's former Shenyang Military Region technical reconnaissance bureau, now under the Northern Theater Command; Microsoft names the cluster Copper Typhoon [S1][S3][S5].
diamond.capability: Bisonal family (including DoubleT), ReVBShell, TontoTeam.Downloader, ShadowPad, Royal Road documents, CHM/DLL hijacking chains, ProxyLogon exploitation, and credential tools such as Mimikatz and LaZagne [S2][S3][S4][S6][S8].
diamond.infrastructure: Actor-controlled C2 for Bisonal and ReVBShell [S3][S4], and free webmail (GMX) sender accounts posing as legitimate firms [S8]. Detailed infrastructure patterns are not covered in the sources gathered.
diamond.victim: Government, military, defense-industrial, political and academic organizations in South Korea, Japan, Russia and Eastern Europe, plus security vendors [S2][S3][S4][S8].
diamond.socioPolitical: Regional security intelligence on the Korean Peninsula (e.g., THAAD), Japan and Russia, consistent with a Northern Theater Command focus [S3][S5].
diamond.technology: Microsoft Office and Equation Editor exploitation through Royal Road, Windows CHM handling and DLL search order, and on-premises Exchange servers [S3][S6][S8].

gaps: No Microsoft Threat Intelligence report on Copper Typhoon activity was found; Microsoft's public mapping gives only the name and its alias links [S1].
The MITRE and Microsoft naming pages could not be fetched directly (network blocked); MITRE details come from search-result summaries [S2].
Primary reports by Kaspersky (Securelist), Recorded Future (TAG-74 PDF), SentinelLabs, Trend Micro and ESET could not be fetched; this file relies on search-result coverage of them.

The 2022 Pakistan E-Office supply-chain attack that delivered ShadowPad (Trend Micro) appears in the imported references, but coverage found states that Trend Micro made no firm attribution; do not credit it to Copper Typhoon without the primary paper [S9].
The Cybereason PortDoor attack (2021) on Russia's Rubin Design Bureau used Royal Road, which Tonto Team and other groups share; it was not attributed to Tonto Team, so it is excluded.
TAG-74 (Recorded Future) overlaps with Tonto Team but is not confirmed as identical, and it likely shares tooling with Tick Group [S3].
No US government indictment, sanction or joint advisory naming Tonto Team/Copper Typhoon was found.
Operation Bitter Biscuit (2017) and the original Trend Micro HeartBeat paper were not reviewed.
Activity after 2023 attributable to this actor was not found.

implications.jipoe: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. STEP 1 (OE): Key terrain is user endpoints and email at government, military, defense-industrial and academic organizations in Northeast Asia, especially South Korea and Japan, along with exposed on-premises Exchange servers [S2][S3][S6]. STEP 2 (effects): Spear-phishing with Office/RTF exploits and CHM files depends on unpatched Office components and user execution, so patch status and attachment filtering shape the attack surface [S3][S8]. STEP 3 (adversary template): Royal Road document or CHM lure; DLL search-order hijack; ReVBShell or downloader; Bisonal backdoor; credential dumping and lateral movement [S2][S3][S4][S8]. STEP 4: MLCOA is sustained espionage against Korean Peninsula defense and policy entities, including those tied to US-ROK missile-defense cooperation such as THAAD [S3][S5]. MDCOA is opportunistic mass exploitation of a newly disclosed server vulnerability, as with ProxyLogon in 2021, to reach DoD-adjacent or coalition networks [S6]. Candidate indicators: CHM attachments spawning signed executables that side-load DLLs; RTF documents exploiting Equation Editor; Bisonal C2 beacons; Simplified Chinese metadata in lure documents; new web shells on Exchange [S3][S6][S8].
implications.jcc2: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. (1) Situational awareness: track Copper Typhoon/Tonto Team, TAG-74 and CactusPete as overlapping clusters with distinct confidence levels, not as a single fused entity [S1][S3]. (2) Authorities: reporting is vendor-sourced; no US government attribution was found, so attribution-dependent responses need IC validation [S2][S3]. (3) Mission assurance: USFK and coalition partners in South Korea and Japan, plus defense contractors supporting missile defense, are high-likelihood targets for phishing and should get priority for email and endpoint hardening against Office and CHM execution chains [S3][S5]. (4) Coordination: share indicators with ROK and Japanese partners and with DIB CS participants, because Tonto activity spans academic, political and defense-industrial targets outside DoD networks [S3][S4].

provenance.importedSummary: Tonto Team is a Chinese-speaking APT group that has been active since at least 2013. They primarily target military, diplomatic, and infrastructure organizations in Asia and Eastern Europe. The group has been observed using various malware, including the Bisonal RAT and ShadowPad. They employ spear-phishing emails with malicious attachments as their preferred method of distribution.

identification.summary: Iran-linked cyber espionage group first publicly exposed by ClearSky and Minerva Labs in November 2015 for attacks on Israeli targets, including diplomats at Israel's Ministry of Foreign Affairs and Israeli academics who study the Middle East [S1][S2]. ClearSky and Trend Micro's July 2017 'Operation Wilted Tulip' report described a broad espionage apparatus targeting government, defense and academic organizations in Israel, Saudi Arabia, Turkey, the United States, Jordan and Germany [S4][S5]. Researchers describe the group as persistent and successful at exfiltrating data but lacking technical sophistication and operational discipline [S6][S8].
identification.firstObserved: ClearSky/Minerva (2015): attacks on Israeli targets since at least August 2014 [S1]. ClearSky/Trend Micro (2017): active since at least 2013 [S4][S5].
identification.notes: No Microsoft threat-actor name was found mapped to CopyKittens in the searches run; the actor record's msName is empty. MITRE ATT&CK tracks the group as CopyKittens (G0052) [S10]. The Hacker News and Security Affairs coverage of Wilted Tulip call the group 'also known as Rocket Kittens' [S5][S7], while VOA reporting distinguishes CopyKittens from the separate Iran-based group Rocket Kitten; this alias is not adopted here (see gaps). The existing alias 'Slayer Kitten' (CrowdStrike) could not be confirmed in a cited source.

attribution.sponsor: Iran (suspected). The CFR Cyber Operations Tracker lists Iran as the suspected state sponsor [S9]; ClearSky labels CopyKittens an 'Iranian threat agent' [S3].
attribution.confidence: Vendor assessment only. ClearSky and Minerva Labs estimated in 2015 that the group is a state actor or endorsed by one, based on targets, delivery methods and malware [S1]. No government attribution to CopyKittens was found; Germany's BSI described the Jerusalem Post manipulation tied to Bundestag targeting without naming a group, and the link to CopyKittens is ClearSky's assessment [S3].
attribution.basis: Targeting pattern (Israel, Saudi Arabia, Turkey, US and others hostile to Iranian interests) and malware analysis by ClearSky, Minerva Labs and Trend Micro [S1][S4][S5]; tracker listing by CFR [S9].

actors.objectives: Long-running espionage and data theft against government ministries (including foreign affairs), defense companies, large IT companies and academic institutions in states that are regional adversaries of Iran or their partners [S1][S4][S5]. Researchers note the group exfiltrated large volumes of data despite inferior tools [S8].

sectors: Academic institutions and Middle East researchers [S1][S4]
News media websites used as watering holes [S3]
Legislators (German Bundestag offices, per ClearSky's assessment) [S3]
targeting.notes: Israeli targets dominate the early reporting [S1][S3]; the 2017 Wilted Tulip report widened the observed victim set to multiple countries [S4][S5]. Compromised Israeli news and other websites served as watering holes rather than end targets [S3].

capabilities.summary: Delivery via spear-phishing emails with weaponized documents or links, watering-hole attacks that insert a single line of JavaScript into existing libraries on compromised sites, and fake Facebook profiles used to build trust and spread malicious links [S1][S3][S4]. Malicious Office documents exploiting CVE-2017-0199 were reported in 2017 [S6]. The group also exploited web servers using SQL injection tools [S8]. Tooling includes the Matryoshka RAT (v1 from 2015, v2 in 2017), a multi-stage framework assembled from public code snippets that uses DNS for command and control and exfiltration [S1][S4]; TDTESS backdoor, Vminst lateral-movement tool, NetSrv Cobalt Strike loader and ZPP compression utility [S4][S5]; and frequent use of trial versions of Cobalt Strike, plus Metasploit and other commercially available tools [S4][S6]. MITRE lists Cobalt Strike, TDTESS, Matryoshka and Empire as associated software [S10].

campaigns.name: Early attacks on Israeli targets
campaigns.summary: ClearSky and Minerva Labs date CopyKittens attacks on Israeli targets to at least August 2014; victims included senior MFA diplomats and Israeli Middle East scholars, reached with spear-phishing documents delivering Matryoshka.

campaigns.name: First public exposure (ClearSky/Minerva report)
campaigns.summary: Joint report names the group CopyKittens and its Matryoshka malware; the vendors assess a state actor or state-endorsed group.

campaigns.name: Jerusalem Post and Israeli website watering holes (Oct 2016 - Jan 2017)
campaigns.summary: ClearSky reports the Jerusalem Post, multiple other Israeli sites and one Palestinian Authority site were compromised with injected JavaScript; ClearSky assesses with high certainty this is the incident Germany's BSI linked to targeting of the Bundestag, though BSI did not name a group.

campaigns.name: Operation Wilted Tulip
campaigns.summary: ClearSky and Trend Micro expose a wide espionage apparatus spanning the group's activity since 2013, including previously unreported tools (TDTESS, Vminst, NetSrv, ZPP), Matryoshka v2, Cobalt Strike use, and victims in six countries.

diamond.adversary: Iran-linked espionage group CopyKittens; assessed by vendors as a state or state-endorsed actor; described as persistent but noisy and lacking operational discipline [S1][S6][S8][S9].
diamond.capability: Matryoshka RAT v1/v2 with DNS C2, TDTESS backdoor, Vminst, NetSrv, ZPP, trial Cobalt Strike, Metasploit, CVE-2017-0199 documents, SQL injection tools [S1][S4][S5][S6][S8].
diamond.infrastructure: Compromised legitimate news and government-adjacent websites serving injected JavaScript from actor-controlled domains; fake Facebook profiles; DNS-based C2 channels [S1][S3][S4].
diamond.victim: Foreign ministries, defense firms, IT companies, academics, legislators and UN employees in Israel, Saudi Arabia, Turkey, the US, Jordan and Germany [S1][S3][S4][S5][S8].
diamond.socioPolitical: Intelligence collection against Israel and states contrary to Iranian interests, consistent with suspected Iranian state sponsorship [S1][S4][S9].
diamond.technology: Trust in frequently visited news websites, Microsoft Office document handling (CVE-2017-0199), vulnerable web applications (SQL injection) and DNS egress [S1][S3][S6][S8].

gaps: No public reporting of new CopyKittens campaigns after 2017 was found; whether the cluster remains active, was renamed, or was absorbed into another vendor cluster is unknown.
No Microsoft threat-actor name mapped to CopyKittens was found; Microsoft's naming table could not be checked directly.

Alias conflict: The Hacker News and Security Affairs say 'aka Rocket Kittens' [S5][S7], but VOA reporting says CopyKittens is distinct from Rocket Kitten; the VOA article could not be opened to cite, so the overlap is unresolved and Rocket Kitten facts must not be merged here.
The 'Slayer Kitten' (CrowdStrike) alias in the imported record was not confirmed by any source found; CrowdStrike's adversary page was not reached.
No government attribution: Germany's BSI did not name a group for the Jerusalem Post/Bundestag incident; the CopyKittens link is ClearSky's assessment [S3].

Primary PDFs (Minerva/ClearSky 2015 CopyKittens.pdf, ClearSky/Trend Micro Operation_Wilted_Tulip.pdf) and vendor pages could not be fetched; content is drawn from search-result summaries and secondary coverage.

The DomainTools 'Hunting Campaign Indicators on Privacy Protected Attack Infrastructure' case study (2017-03-21) is in the imported references, but the search result summary did not confirm it names CopyKittens; not cited.
Organizational identity (MOIS vs. IRGC vs. contractor) is not established in any source found.

implications.jipoe: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. STEP 1 (operational environment): Key terrain includes commonly visited regional news sites and partner-government web properties that can be turned into watering holes, plus email and social media channels used to reach foreign-affairs, defense and academic staff [S1][S3][S4]. STEP 2 (effects): Watering holes on trusted media sites can reach legislators and staff of partner nations (e.g., Bundestag offices per ClearSky) without direct targeting [S3]. STEP 3 (threat evaluation): Template is spear-phish or watering hole, then Matryoshka/TDTESS or Cobalt Strike implant, lateral movement with Vminst, compression with ZPP, and DNS or HTTP exfiltration; tradecraft is noisy and reuses commodity tooling [S1][S4][S5][S6]. STEP 4 (COAs): MLCOA is persistent collection against Israeli, Gulf, Turkish, US and German government, defense and academic targets for policy intelligence [S4][S5]. MDCOA is a watering-hole compromise of a regional news or partner-government site frequented by coalition personnel to gain footholds in DoD-adjacent or partner networks [S3]. Candidate indicators: unexpected single-line JavaScript additions to site libraries, Office documents exploiting CVE-2017-0199, anomalous DNS query volumes or encoded subdomains, and Cobalt Strike trial-version artifacts [S1][S3][S4][S6].
implications.jcc2: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. (1) Situational awareness: this cluster's latest public reporting is 2017; treat it as a historical case and correlate with current Iranian clusters before tasking [S4]. (2) Authorities: attribution rests on vendor assessments, not government statements, so products should label confidence accordingly [S1][S3]. (3) Mission assurance: DNS egress monitoring and Office patching address the documented C2 and delivery paths [S1][S6]. (4) Coordination: watering holes on partner-nation media and legislative targeting (Germany) argue for sharing indicators with partner CERTs such as BSI and Israeli counterparts [S3].

identification.summary: Coral Sleet (formerly Storm-1877) is Microsoft's name for a North Korean state actor. Microsoft groups it with Sapphire Sleet and Jasper Sleet as actors that often use financial-opportunity or job-interview lures to get initial access [S1]. Microsoft first described Storm-1877 in May 2024. It said the actor had used malicious npm packages since late 2023 to deliver JavaScript-based malware to software developers, and that Palo Alto Networks publicly reported this campaign as 'Contagious Interview' [S2]. Unit 42 first reported Contagious Interview in November 2023: fake employers persuade job seekers to install malware during online interviews, using the BeaverTail stealer/loader and the InvisibleFerret Python backdoor [S5]. In March 2026 Microsoft reported that Coral Sleet used AI coding tools to build and iterate malware components, including the OtterCookie malware, and used agentic AI for end-to-end lure development and infrastructure provisioning [S1]. In September 2026 Japanese, US, Australian and German agencies published a joint advisory on the same activity cluster (as 'WaterPlum' / Contagious Interview). The advisory, as reported, said the actors infected at least 30,000 devices in more than 100 countries and took funds or credentials from more than 7,000 cryptocurrency wallets [S11].
identification.firstObserved: Microsoft says the Contagious Interview campaign has been active since at least December 2022 [S4]. Microsoft says Storm-1877 used malicious npm packages since late 2023 [S2]. Unit 42's first public report was November 2023 [S5], and ESET says the overlapping DeceptiveDevelopment cluster has been active since at least November 2023 [S7].
identification.notes: Microsoft name: Coral Sleet. Microsoft explicitly gives 'Coral Sleet (formerly Storm-1877)' [S1]. Microsoft maps Storm-1877 to the npm campaign Palo Alto calls Contagious Interview [S2]. Unit 42 tracks Contagious Interview as CL-STA-0240 [S5][S6]. NTT Security tracks the cluster as WaterPlum and equates it with CL-STA-0240, DeceptiveDevelopment, DEV#POPPER, Famous Chollima, PurpleBravo and Tenacious Pungsan, as reported [S8]. ESET's DeceptiveDevelopment overlaps with Contagious Interview, DEV#POPPER, Famous Chollima, PurpleBravo and Tenacious Pungsan, as reported [S7][S13]. Trend Micro associates its Void Dokkaebi intrusion set, also known as Famous Chollima, with this campaign cluster [S10]. CLUSTER BOUNDARY: Microsoft tracks North Korean remote IT workers separately as Jasper Sleet (formerly Storm-0287). It says Storm-1877 is one of several other DPRK clusters that also pursue fraudulent employment [S3]. Unit 42 likewise separates the job-seeker IT-worker campaign Wagemole (CL-STA-0241) from Contagious Interview [S5]. CrowdStrike's Famous Chollima covers both the recruiter and IT-worker activity, so it is broader than Coral Sleet. The imported summary on this record describes WageMole (IT-worker fraud), which better matches Jasper Sleet than Coral Sleet. Microsoft's March 2026 Contagious Interview post describes the campaign but does not name Coral Sleet [S4].

attribution.sponsor: Democratic People's Republic of Korea. Microsoft describes Coral Sleet as a North Korean threat actor [S1]. The September 2026 multinational advisory, as reported, assesses (per Japan's National Police Agency and the FBI) that WaterPlum operators and some North Korean IT workers fall under the 313 General Bureau of the Munitions Industry Department of the Workers' Party of Korea Central Committee [S11][S12].
attribution.confidence: Microsoft names Coral Sleet as North Korean but gives no confidence level in the cited post [S1]. SentinelLABS attributes the CTI-platform activity it observed to North Korean Contagious Interview actors with high confidence [S9]. The 313 General Bureau assessment is from the NPA and FBI (government), as reported in press coverage. It was made against the WaterPlum / Contagious Interview cluster, not against Microsoft's Coral Sleet designation by name [S11][S12].
attribution.basis: Microsoft Threat Intelligence telemetry and reporting [S1][S2][S3]; Unit 42 telemetry and malware analysis [S5][S6]; ESET, NTT, SentinelLABS/Validin and Trend Micro vendor research [S7][S8][S9][S10]; joint government advisory from Japan, the US, Australia and Germany (reported via press) [S11][S12].

actors.objectives: Revenue generation for the DPRK through cryptocurrency theft. The 2026 joint advisory, as reported, says the actors took funds or credentials from more than 7,000 crypto wallets and moved about $10.7 million (about 1.7 billion yen) to North Korea [S11][S12]. Unit 42 assessed the goals as stealing cryptocurrency and using compromised targets as staging environments for future attacks [S5]. Microsoft notes the actors harvest API tokens, cloud credentials, signing keys, crypto wallets and password-manager artifacts. A compromised developer could therefore become a route into the employer's environment or software supply chain [S4][S11].

sectors: Software developers and job seekers in the technology sector [S2][S5]
Developers at enterprise solution providers and media and communications firms [S4]
regions: Global: at least 30,000 devices in more than 100 countries (December 2025 to July 2026, per the joint advisory as reported) [S11]
Japan, United States, Australia and Germany were the co-authoring governments [S11][S12]
targeting.notes: Targeting is individual-centric. The actors approach developers through fake recruiter personas, job postings on platforms such as LinkedIn and Upwork, and fake coding tests. Victim organizations are then exposed through the individual's device [S4][S7][S11]. SentinelLABS counted over 230 victims between January and March 2025 and said the true figure is likely higher [S9]. Recruiter lures have posed as cryptocurrency trading firms and AI solution providers [S4].

capabilities.summary: Social engineering through fake recruiters and technical interviews. Victims are asked to clone and run booby-trapped repositories (GitHub, GitLab, Bitbucket), install malicious npm packages, or follow 'quick fix' steps for supposed video-conferencing errors [S2][S4][S11]. Malware: the BeaverTail JavaScript stealer and loader, and the InvisibleFerret Python backdoor, which supports keylogging, file exfiltration and remote access via AnyDesk [S5][S6][S7]. Unit 42 reported Qt-compiled BeaverTail builds for Windows and macOS from July 2024 [S6]. Later families: the OtterCookie JavaScript backdoor (v3 and v4 in February and April 2025; v4 added VM detection and Chrome/MetaMask credential theft), a JavaScript beaconing agent, FlexibleFerret, and VS Code task-file abuse that runs code when a project is trusted [S4][S8]. The joint advisory coverage also lists OtterCandy and StoatWaffle [S11]. Microsoft says Coral Sleet uses AI coding tools to generate and revise malware, including OtterCookie, and uses agentic AI for lure websites and remote infrastructure provisioning [S1]. The operators watch threat intelligence platforms (Validin, VirusTotal) to spot their own exposed infrastructure and stand up replacements quickly [S9].

campaigns.name: Multinational WaterPlum advisory
campaigns.summary: Japan, the US, Australia and Germany report at least 30,000 infected devices in over 100 countries (December 2025 to July 2026), more than 7,000 affected crypto wallets and about $10.7M moved to the DPRK. They attribute the activity to the 313 General Bureau (reported via press).

diamond.adversary: North Korean state actor (Microsoft: Coral Sleet, formerly Storm-1877) [S1]. NPA and FBI assess the WaterPlum operators fall under the 313 General Bureau of the Munitions Industry Department, as reported [S12]. Operators work in coordinated teams [S9].
diamond.capability: Fake-recruiter social engineering. Malware includes BeaverTail, InvisibleFerret, OtterCookie, OtterCandy, StoatWaffle and FlexibleFerret, delivered through npm packages, trojanized repositories and VS Code tasks. Malware is developed with AI assistance [S1][S4][S5][S8][S11].
diamond.infrastructure: Public code hosting (GitHub, GitLab, Bitbucket) and the npm registry; fake interview and company websites built on development platforms; URL shorteners redirecting to vercel.app [S1][S4]. Russian IP ranges behind VPN, proxy and RDP layers [S10]. Infrastructure is replaced quickly after exposure [S9].
diamond.victim: Software developers, freelancers, and Web3/crypto professionals, and their employers [S4][S7][S9][S11]. At least 30,000 devices in more than 100 countries [S11].
diamond.socioPolitical: Sanctions-evasion revenue for the DPRK through crypto theft. The advisory links the activity to the same bureau as DPRK IT workers [S11][S12].
diamond.technology: Developer workstations holding credentials, signing keys, cloud tokens and wallets. Trust in code repositories, package managers, IDE automation (VS Code tasks) and remote hiring workflows [S4][S11].

gaps: Microsoft has not published a dedicated Coral Sleet profile in the sources gathered. The Coral Sleet = Storm-1877 equivalence rests on one sentence in the March 2026 AI-tradecraft post [S1]. Microsoft's March 2026 Contagious Interview post does not name the actor [S4].

Cluster boundaries: Microsoft says Storm-1877 also pursues fraudulent employment [S3], and its March 2026 post groups Coral Sleet with Jasper Sleet [S1]. It is unclear how much IT-worker (WageMole) activity Microsoft folds into Coral Sleet versus Jasper Sleet. The imported record summary (WageMole) may belong to Jasper Sleet.

The September 2026 joint advisory primary text (FBI IC3 / NPA) could not be opened. Figures and the 313 General Bureau attribution come from press coverage [S11][S12]. The advisory names the cluster WaterPlum, not Coral Sleet.
Unit 42, SentinelLABS, Trend Micro, ESET and NTT primary reports could not be fetched (host blocked). Their content is taken from search-result summaries and press coverage.
MITRE ATT&CK G1052 page could not be fetched to confirm its group name and associated-group list.
No Microsoft confidence level for the Coral Sleet North Korea attribution was found.

Aliases Gwisin Gang, Nickel Tapestry, TAG-121 and UNC5267 in the imported record were not confirmed against cited sources for this cluster. Some (for example UNC5267) are commonly used for IT-worker activity.
ContagiousDrop tooling and the face-swap/deepfake claims in some advisory coverage were not verified against primary sources.

implications.jipoe: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. STEP 1 (OE): Key terrain is people, not networks. Individual developers and Web3 personnel on LinkedIn and Upwork, their personal and work devices, and the code repositories, npm registry and IDE automation they trust [S4][S7][S11]. DoD-adjacent software contractors and personnel using personal devices for job searches fall in scope. STEP 2 (effects): A single compromised developer exposes cloud tokens, signing keys and credentials that can be pivoted into the employer and its software supply chain [S4][S11]. AI-assisted development shortens the actor's retooling cycle [S1]. STEP 3 (adversary template): Recruiter persona approach, then a fake coding test or 'fix your camera' instruction, then a malicious repo, npm package or VS Code task, then BeaverTail or OtterCookie, then InvisibleFerret or a beaconing agent, then credential and wallet theft [S4][S5][S6][S8]. Infrastructure is replaced when CTI platforms expose it [S9]. STEP 4: MLCOA is high-volume, opportunistic theft of cryptocurrency and credentials from developers worldwide [S11]. MDCOA is pivoting from a compromised contractor developer into a defense software supply chain via stolen signing keys or cloud credentials, or handing access to other DPRK units [S4][S5]. Candidate indicators: unsolicited recruiter contact leading to repo clone or npm install on a work device; node or python child processes spawned from VS Code tasks.json; outbound connections to vercel.app or short-link redirects from developer hosts; AnyDesk installed unexpectedly; bulk reads of browser credential and wallet extension stores [S4][S5][S8].
implications.jcc2: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. (1) Situational awareness: Fuse identity, endpoint and developer-tooling telemetry (IDE task execution, package installs) into the common operational picture. Network-centric sensors alone will miss an intrusion that starts on a personal or contractor device [S4]. (2) Authorities: The initial compromise usually occurs off the DODIN, on personal or contractor endpoints. Response depends on coordination with FBI, DC3 (a co-sealer of the 2026 advisory) and DIB CS partners rather than DoD-internal authorities alone [S11][S12]. (3) Mission assurance: Treat code-signing keys, CI/CD secrets and cloud tokens on developer workstations as mission-critical assets. Rotate them after any suspected Contagious Interview exposure [S4]. (4) Coordination: The cluster has many vendor names (Coral Sleet, Contagious Interview, WaterPlum, DeceptiveDevelopment, Famous Chollima), and some of these names also cover IT-worker activity. Normalize names on the Microsoft designation in reporting, and coordinate with allied partners (Japan, Australia, Germany) who co-authored the advisory [S1][S8][S11].

provenance.importedSummary: WageMole is a North Korean state-sponsored APT that employs social engineering and technology to secure remote job opportunities in Western countries, leveraging stolen personal data from the Contagious Interview campaign. Threat actors create fake identities, including passports and driver's licenses, and prepare study guides for interviews, often utilizing generative AI for well-structured responses. They target small to mid-sized businesses and utilize job platforms like Upwork and Indeed, while employing automation scripts for account creation. WageMole's activities include sharing code within their group and requesting payments through platforms like PayPal to conceal their identity.

identification.summary: Iranian state actor that Microsoft tracks as Cotton Sandstorm (formerly NEPTUNIUM), also known as Emennet Pasargad, which Microsoft says is run by the IRGC and calls Iran's most prolific influence actor [S1][S3]. It specializes in cyber-enabled influence operations, meaning intrusions paired with hack-and-leak, intimidation and amplification through false personas [S2][S3][S7]. US authorities sanctioned and indicted members over the 2020 US presidential election influence operation [S5][S6]. A 2024 joint FBI, Treasury and Israel National Cyber Directorate advisory says the group has operated since mid-2024 under the front company Aria Sepehr Ayandehsazan (ASA) [S8][S9][S12].
identification.firstObserved: Kaspersky reports ViceLeaker Android spyware activity against Israeli users since at least May 2018 [S11]; Microsoft maps Vice Leaker to Cotton Sandstorm [S1]. The FBI says Emennet targeted mainly Israeli entities since at least 2020 [S7].
identification.notes: Microsoft name: Cotton Sandstorm (formerly NEPTUNIUM); Microsoft maps NEPTUNIUM, HAYWIRE KITTEN (CrowdStrike) and Vice Leaker to it [S1]. Coverage of the 2024 joint advisory lists Cotton Sandstorm, Marnanbridge and Haywire Kitten as private-sector names for Emennet Pasargad / ASA [S9]. 'Holy Souls' is a persona Microsoft attributes to NEPTUNIUM, not a separate group [S2]. Earlier corporate names: Treasury coverage says Emennet's former name Net Peygard Samavat was sanctioned in 2019 for supporting the IRGC cyber unit [S5]. Personas reported by the FBI include Savior Pro (2020-2022) and Deus (2021) [S7]; Microsoft reports Al-Toufan, For Humanity and For Palestinians [S3].

attribution.sponsor: Islamic Republic of Iran, Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC). Microsoft says the group is run by the IRGC [S3][S4]. Treasury tied Emennet's predecessor company to support for the IRGC cyber unit [S5].
attribution.confidence: Microsoft's DTAC attributed the Charlie Hebdo operation to Iran/NEPTUNIUM using its attribution framework and intelligence it says it cannot fully disclose [S2]. US Government: OFAC designations and an SDNY indictment (November 2021) against the company and two employees [S5][S6]; coverage notes the indictment did not tie the two men directly to the Iranian government but said the company had done government work [S6]. FBI, Treasury and Israel's INCD jointly published the October 2024 advisory [S8][S9][S12].
attribution.basis: Microsoft telemetry and influence-operations analysis [S2][S3][S4]; US sanctions and indictment [S5][S6]; FBI Private Industry Notification [S7]; joint FBI/Treasury/INCD advisory (via coverage) [S8][S9]; Kaspersky malware research on ViceLeaker [S11].

actors.objectives: Advance Iranian government aims through cyber-enabled influence: embarrass and intimidate adversaries, undermine confidence in democratic processes, and punish perceived insults to Iran's leadership or Islam [S2][S3][S6][S7]. Microsoft assessed the Charlie Hebdo leak as a government response to cartoons ridiculing Khamenei [S2]. After 7 October 2023 it ran operations against Israel and its supporters, including the UAE and Bahrain [S3]. Mobile espionage (ViceLeaker) collected data from Israeli users [S11].

sectors: News media and media content management systems [S4][S5]
Individual citizens via bulk SMS and email [S3][S6]
regions: United Arab Emirates, Canada, United Kingdom (streaming hijack) [S3]
targeting.notes: Microsoft reported 2024 reconnaissance and limited probing of election-related websites in unnamed US battleground states and a May 2024 scan of a US news outlet [S4]. Sweden's Säpo attributed a 2023 SMS-provider breach to a group called Anzu acting for the IRGC; the cited coverage does not name Emennet, though coverage of the October 2024 advisory lists Sweden among the group's targets [S10][S12].

capabilities.summary: Hack-and-leak operations with false-flag hacktivist and cybercriminal personas, data theft, social-media amplification and sometimes destructive encryption malware [S7]. Bulk SMS and email intimidation in at least six operations from August 2023, at least once from a compromised account [S3]. Website and digital-display defacement [S2][S3]. Hijacking of streaming TV services to air a broadcast with an apparently AI-generated news anchor, and AI-generated images [S3]. Sockpuppet networks and impersonation of authority figures [S2][S3]. 2020 operations obtained voter information, sent threatening emails posing as the Proud Boys, attempted to hack state voting-related websites and produced a fake video [S5][S6]. FBI reported that it disrupted the group's attempt to use unauthorized access to US media content management accounts [S6]. 2024 advisory coverage describes compromise of a French dynamic display provider and attempts to harvest content from IP cameras [S9]. Mobile spyware (ViceLeaker) trojanized Android apps, delivered through Telegram and WhatsApp, collecting calls, texts, photos and location [S11].

diamond.adversary: IRGC-run Iranian operators working through Emennet Pasargad and the front company Aria Sepehr Ayandehsazan; two charged employees (Kazemi, Kashian) [S3][S6][S9].
diamond.capability: Hack-and-leak, false-flag personas, bulk SMS/email intimidation, defacement, streaming and display hijacking, AI-generated media, and Android spyware [S2][S3][S7][S11].
diamond.infrastructure: Compromised SMS and email services, at least one compromised account, sockpuppet social-media accounts, Telegram and hacker-forum leak channels, and compromised display and streaming providers [S2][S3][S9][S10].
diamond.victim: Israeli citizens and organizations, US voters, election websites and media, Charlie Hebdo subscribers, Gulf states normalizing with Israel, and Paris Olympics audiences [S2][S3][S4][S6][S9].
diamond.socioPolitical: Retaliation and coercion supporting Iranian regime narratives: the Israel-Hamas war, insults to the Supreme Leader, Quran burnings, and US elections [S2][S3][S10].
diamond.technology: Weakly secured media CMS, streaming, digital-display, SMS gateway and IoT camera platforms that give one intrusion a large public audience [S3][S6][S9][S10].

gaps: Primary documents not opened: the October 30, 2024 FBI/Treasury/INCD advisory (ic3.gov) [S12], the Treasury press release, the DOJ indictment and the FBI PIN; details come from secondary coverage [S5][S6][S7][S8][S9].
Microsoft's October 2024 MTAC election report was not opened; details come from Iran International coverage [S4].
The date of the Duo Decipher article [S7] is inferred from Microsoft's reference to an October 2022 FBI PIN [S2] and was not confirmed on the page.
The cited Swedish coverage does not name Emennet or Cotton Sandstorm; the Anzu-to-Emennet link depends on the unopened 2024 advisory [S10][S12].

ViceLeaker's link to Cotton Sandstorm comes from Microsoft's alias mapping [S1]; the Kaspersky report itself (securelist.com) could not be opened, and the cited coverage does not attribute ViceLeaker to Iran.
No MITRE ATT&CK group ID was found for this actor in the record.
Malware, infrastructure IOCs and initial-access vectors for the 2023-2024 operations are not public in the sources gathered.
Activity after October 2024, including any during the June 2025 Israel-Iran conflict, was not covered by the sources gathered.

implications.jipoe: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. STEP 1: Relevant terrain includes public-facing information platforms (news CMS, streaming/IPTV, digital displays, SMS gateways and IoT cameras) and personal data on servicemembers and citizens, because the actor turns access to these into influence effects [S3][S6][S9][S10]. STEP 2: The actor's goal is psychological and reputational effect, not long-term espionage; a modest intrusion paired with a persona claim and sockpuppet amplification creates outsized perceived impact [S2][S3][S7]. STEP 3: The pattern runs intrusion or data theft, then a persona claim (Holy Souls, Al-Toufan, Savior Pro), then a leak on Telegram or forums, bulk SMS/email intimidation and AI-enhanced media, then amplification [S2][S3][S7]. STEP 4: MLCOA is opportunistic hack-and-leak and intimidation messaging against Israel-aligned and Western audiences, timed to geopolitical triggers such as elections, insults to Iranian leadership or major events [S2][S3][S4][S9]. MDCOA is a compromise of media, display or SMS infrastructure used to deliver threatening messages to US personnel or families during a US-Iran crisis, possibly combined with destructive encryption malware as reported against a US organization [S3][S7]. Candidate indicators: new hacktivist personas claiming breaches of US or allied entities; bulk SMS or email threats referencing recipients' personal data; unauthorized content on displays or streams; and reconnaissance scans of election or media websites [S3][S4][S7].
implications.jcc2: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. (1) Situational awareness: fuse cyber intrusion reporting with information-environment monitoring, because this actor's effects appear first as persona claims and leaks [S2][S3]. (2) Authorities: activity mixes cyber intrusion with influence operations against civilians and elections, so response may cross DoD, FBI, CISA and DHS lanes; FBI has already acted against the group's media-CMS access [S6]. (3) Mission assurance: protect installation and family-facing communications channels (mass notification, base media, displays) against hijacking and spoofed threats [S3][S9]. (4) Coordination: partner with allies already engaged against the actor, including Israel's INCD (co-author of the 2024 advisory) and France and Sweden as victims, and with platform companies that suspend persona accounts [S2][S8][S10].

provenance.importedSummary: In May 2018, we discovered a campaign targeting dozens of mobile Android devices belonging to Israeli citizens. Kaspersky spyware sensors caught the signal of an attack from the device of one of the victims; and a hash of the APK involved (Android application) was tagged in our sample feed for inspection. Once we looked into the file, we quickly found out that the inner-workings of the APK included a malicious payload, embedded in the original code of the application. This was an original spyware program, designed to exfiltrate almost all accessible information. During the course of our research, we noticed that we were not the only ones to have found the operation. Researchers from Bitdefender also released an analysis of one of the samples in a blogpost. Although something had already been published, we decided to do something different with the data we acquired. The following month, we released a private report on our Threat Intelligence Portal to alert our clients about this newly discovered operation and began writing YARA rules in order to catch more samples. We decided to call the operation “ViceLeaker”, because of strings and variables in its code.

identification.summary: Crimson Sandstorm (formerly CURIUM) is an Iran-based espionage actor [S1][S2]. Microsoft says it uses a network of fictitious social media accounts to build trust with targets and then delivers malware to exfiltrate data [S1]. Microsoft says it has targeted the defense, maritime shipping, transportation, healthcare and technology sectors, often using watering-hole attacks and social engineering to deliver custom .NET malware. Microsoft also notes earlier research on its malware that used email for command and control [S2]. Microsoft's 2021 CyberWarCon presentation describes CURIUM spending months posing as an attractive woman on LinkedIn or Facebook before sending a malicious document [S3].
identification.firstObserved: Microsoft: active since at least 2017 [S2]. Symantec (as Tortoiseshell): active since at least July 2018 (summary of Symantec report via Malpedia) [S4].
identification.notes: Microsoft name: Crimson Sandstorm (formerly CURIUM) [S1][S3]. Microsoft states other researchers track it as Tortoiseshell, Imperial Kitten and Yellow Liderc [S2]. Microsoft's profile also lists Houseblend and Tortoise Shell [S1]. PwC tracks it as Yellow Liderc and lists Imperial Kitten, Tortoiseshell, TA456 and Crimson Sandstorm as overlapping names (reported via press) [S8]. Proofpoint tracks TA456 and says it overlaps with Tortoiseshell and Imperial Kitten (reported via press) [S7]. Press coverage of Meta's 2021 takedown says researchers linked much of the activity to Mandiant's UNC1833, with some infrastructure overlap with APT35 [S6]. This is a press claim and is not used to merge clusters. CrowdStrike's IMPERIAL KITTEN is also mapped by Microsoft to Cuboid Sandstorm and Smoke Sandstorm, which Microsoft tracks separately. Facts from CrowdStrike IMPERIAL KITTEN reporting [S9] should therefore be read as the CrowdStrike cluster, not Microsoft's boundary.

attribution.sponsor: Iran. Microsoft assesses Crimson Sandstorm to be connected to the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) [S2]. Meta (Facebook) said the malware used in the 2021 Tortoiseshell campaign was developed by Mahak Rayan Afraz, a Tehran IT company with ties to the IRGC (reported via press) [S6]. CrowdStrike assesses that IMPERIAL KITTEN likely fulfills Iranian strategic intelligence requirements associated with IRGC operations (reported via press) [S9].
attribution.confidence: Microsoft describes the actor as 'assessed to be connected to' the IRGC and gives no numeric confidence level [S2]. Its public profile names Iran as country of origin without naming a sponsor [S1]. CrowdStrike uses 'likely' [S9]. In 2019, Symantec and Cisco Talos declined to tie Tortoiseshell to a specific nation-state [S5]. No government attribution of this cluster was found in the sources gathered.
attribution.basis: Microsoft telemetry and its 2024 OpenAI collaboration, which disabled Crimson Sandstorm accounts and assets [S2]. Meta platform investigation and malware-developer attribution [S6]. Vendor victimology and malware analysis from PwC, Proofpoint and CrowdStrike [S7][S8][S9].

actors.objectives: Strategic intelligence collection in support of Iranian (IRGC-associated) requirements [S2][S9]. Targets include US military and defense contractors, IT services firms, and Middle Eastern governments [S1]. The actor uses supply-chain access through IT, engineering and contractor firms to reach their downstream defense and intelligence customers [S1][S4][S7]. Since 2023 it has collected against Israeli and Mediterranean maritime, logistics and technology entities [S8][S9].

sectors: US military personnel and defense contractors [S1][S6]
Aerospace and defense, including smaller subsidiaries of contractors [S6][S7]
IT services and engineering providers to US defense and intelligence agencies [S1]
IT providers in Saudi Arabia (supply chain) [S4]
targeting.notes: Microsoft says that in 2021 the actor spear-phished companies providing IT and engineering services to US defense and intelligence agencies, probably to reach their customers [S1]. Focus shifted from Middle East IT firms (2018-2019) to US military and defense personnel (2019-2021) [S4][S5][S6]. It shifted again to Israeli and Mediterranean shipping, logistics and technology targets (2022-2023) [S8][S9].

capabilities.summary: The actor's signature is long-duration social engineering through fictitious personas on LinkedIn, Facebook and other platforms. It builds trust over months, sends benign media, and then sends a look-alike malicious file [S1][S3][S6][S7]. Lures include fake recruiting and job sites: 'Hire Military Heroes' (2019) delivered a reconnaissance downloader [S5], and a site spoofing a US Labor Department job site was used in 2021 [S6]. The actor runs watering-hole (strategic web compromise) operations that use JavaScript to fingerprint visitors and selectively serve malware [S2][S8][S9]. It also uses macro-laced Excel phishing, credential theft for VPN access, and one-day vulnerability exploitation [S9]. Custom .NET malware includes IMAPLoader, which uses email as C2 and AppDomain Manager Injection [S8], and StandardKeyboard, which uses email C2 and installs as a Windows service [S9]. LEMPO (an updated Liderc) handles persistence, reconnaissance, exfiltration to actor email accounts and artifact deletion [S7]. A Python reverse shell has also been observed [S9]. In 2023 Microsoft observed the actor using LLMs for phishing content, scripting, and defense-evasion code [S2]. In the Symantec-reported Saudi supply-chain intrusions it gained domain-admin access in at least two organizations [S4].

diamond.adversary: Iran-based operators that Microsoft assesses to be IRGC-connected [S2]. Meta tied malware development to Mahak Rayan Afraz (reported) [S6].
diamond.capability: Fictitious social-media personas, fake job sites, watering holes with visitor fingerprinting, and macro Excel phishing. Custom .NET malware with email C2 (IMAPLoader, StandardKeyboard, LEMPO/Liderc) [S1][S5][S7][S8][S9].
diamond.infrastructure: Fake persona accounts on Facebook and LinkedIn [S3][S6]. Spoofed recruiting and job domains [S5][S6]. Compromised legitimate websites used as watering holes [S8][S9]. Actor-controlled email accounts used for C2 and exfiltration [S7][S8][S9].

diamond.socioPolitical: Iranian strategic intelligence requirements tied to the IRGC. Activity against Israel intensified after the October 2023 Israel-Hamas war [S2][S9].
diamond.technology: Trust in professional social networks and recruiting, the email protocols abused for C2, and third-party IT and contractor access into defense customers [S1][S7][S8].

Primary vendor reports (Symantec 2019, Cisco Talos 2019, Proofpoint 2021, Meta 2021, PwC 2023, CrowdStrike 2023) could not be fetched; content is from press coverage and search-result summaries.

Cluster boundary: CrowdStrike IMPERIAL KITTEN is mapped by Microsoft to Crimson, Cuboid and Smoke Sandstorm. Not every IMPERIAL KITTEN fact (e.g., October 2023 Israel activity) is confirmed by Microsoft as Crimson Sandstorm.

Nimbus Manticore (Check Point, 2025) appears in this record's aliases, but Check Point describes it as overlapping UNC1549/Smoke Sandstorm. Its 2025 European aerospace campaign was excluded pending Microsoft confirmation.
No government (CISA/FBI/DOJ/Treasury) attribution or indictment specific to this cluster was found.

Activity after February 2024 attributable by Microsoft to Crimson Sandstorm was not found in sources gathered.

implications.jipoe: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. STEP 1 (OE): The human and persona layer of cyberspace is key terrain. This includes LinkedIn and Facebook profiles of service members, recruiters and contractor staff, plus third-party IT and engineering providers with access into DoD and intelligence networks [S1][S3][S6]. STEP 2 (effects): Months-long trust building defeats one-time phishing awareness. Email-based C2 blends with normal mail traffic, and watering holes on sector websites let the actor select victims passively [S3][S7][S8][S9]. STEP 3 (adversary template): The template is a fake recruiter or attractive persona, or a compromised sector website with JavaScript fingerprinting. That leads to a lure file or fake job app, then a .NET implant with IMAP/SMTP C2, then reconnaissance and exfiltration to actor email [S5][S7][S8][S9]. STEP 4: MLCOA is continued espionage against US defense personnel, contractor subsidiaries, and Israeli and Mediterranean logistics targets through persona-driven social engineering. MDCOA is leveraging compromised IT and engineering providers for supply-chain access into defense or intelligence customer networks, as seen in 2018-2021 [S1][S4]. Candidate indicators: unsolicited recruiter or persona contacts with Airmen or contractors that move to off-platform chat or file sharing [S6][S7]; downloads of 'job' applications [S5]; outbound IMAP from non-mail hosts [S8][S9]; AppDomain Manager Injection artifacts [S8]; and a new 'Keyboard Service' Windows service [S9].
implications.jcc2: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. Situational awareness: fuse platform-takedown reporting (Meta, LinkedIn), vendor IOCs for IMAPLoader and StandardKeyboard, and DIB partner reporting into the common operational picture, since the actor's entry points sit outside DoDIN boundaries [S6][S8][S9]. Authorities: persona engagement with personnel on commercial platforms and compromises of contractor networks fall to counterintelligence, the DC3/DIB program and platform providers rather than DODIN defenders alone. Coordinate early [S1][S6]. Mission assurance: prioritize hunting for email-protocol C2 egress and macro and Excel execution on mission systems. Identify contractor and IT service accounts with privileged access as supply-chain risk [S1][S4][S8][S9]. Coordination: share persona and fake-job-site indicators with force protection and OPSEC offices for awareness training on long-duration social engineering [S3][S5][S6].

provenance.importedSummary: A previously undocumented attack group is using both custom and off-the-shelf malware to target IT providers in Saudi Arabia in what appear to be supply chain attacks with the end goal of compromising the IT providers’ customers. The group, which we are calling Tortoiseshell, has been active since at least July 2018. Symantec has identified a total of 11 organizations hit by the group, the majority of which are based in Saudi Arabia. In at least two organizations, evidence suggests that the attackers gained domain admin-level access.

identification.summary: Iran-based cyber-espionage cluster that Microsoft tracked as DEV-0228 and now calls Cuboid Sandstorm [S1][S2]. In July 2021 it compromised a single Israel-based IT company that provides business management software. It then used that company's credentials and access to reach downstream customers in Israel's defense, energy and legal sectors [S1][S3]. Microsoft says the group compromised at least a dozen other organizations and assesses that at least four were reached with the stolen IT-provider access [S1].
identification.firstObserved: Microsoft: July 2021 (credential dumping at the Israeli IT provider in early July 2021) [S1].
identification.notes: Microsoft name: Cuboid Sandstorm (formerly DEV-0228) [S2]. When Microsoft published its 2021 report, a DEV designation marked a cluster whose origin or identity was not yet established with high confidence [S1]. Microsoft's mapping also lists IMPERIAL KITTEN (CrowdStrike) for Cuboid Sandstorm, but the same file lists IMPERIAL KITTEN under Crimson Sandstorm and Smoke Sandstorm as well, so that alias is a many-to-one overlap rather than an equivalence [S2]. Cybereason's MalKamak / ShellClient reporting has tooling similarities but is a separate vendor cluster (see gaps) [S4][S8]. No MITRE ATT&CK group ID is recorded.

attribution.sponsor: Iran. Microsoft assesses the cluster as based in Iran and treats the activity as part of a broader Iranian espionage effort against organizations of interest to the Iranian regime [S1]. No specific Iranian organization is named for Cuboid Sandstorm in the sources gathered.
attribution.confidence: Microsoft (MSTIC) assessment: based in Iran [S1]. In 2021 the DEV label meant Microsoft had not yet reached high confidence on origin or identity. No government attribution was found for this cluster. Microsoft maps the CrowdStrike name IMPERIAL KITTEN to three Sandstorm actors [S2], so CrowdStrike assessments of that cluster should not be applied to Cuboid Sandstorm specifically.
attribution.basis: Microsoft incident telemetry, nation-state notifications and tool hashes [S1]; Microsoft naming mapping [S2].

actors.objectives: Espionage against Israeli organizations of interest to the Iranian regime, achieved by compromising a trusted IT service provider and pivoting to its customers [S1]. Microsoft frames the wider 2021 Iranian IT-sector targeting as an effort to gain indirect access to IT providers' clients and subsidiaries [S1].

sectors: IT services / business management software providers [S1]
targeting.notes: All victims named for DEV-0228 are in Israel [S1]. Microsoft's report also covers wider Iranian activity against IT companies in India and the UAE, and covers DEV-0056 in Bahrain. Those findings belong to the broader Iranian set or to DEV-0056 (now Smoke Sandstorm), not to Cuboid Sandstorm specifically [S1].

capabilities.summary: Microsoft describes a supply-chain style pivot. The group dumped credentials on the IT provider's on-premises network, then reused the provider's accounts to reach customers. It used PAExec for remote execution against a law firm, and an email account the IT provider had in a defense company's Office 365 tenant [S1]. Its custom .NET remote access trojan used Dropbox for command and control and was disguised as RuntimeBroker.exe or svchost.exe. Microsoft Defender detects it as Backdoor:MSIL/ShellClient.A [S1]. After gaining persistence, the operators dumped LSASS memory. They staged lsa.exe, PAExec (pa.exe), ProcDump (pc.exe) and Rar.exe in C:\Windows\TAPI. Mimikatz-related detections were also reported [S1]. Microsoft did not publish C2 IP addresses or domains [S1].

campaigns.name: Downstream customer intrusions
campaigns.summary: Using the provider's access, the group compromised at least a dozen other organizations. These included an Israeli law firm in August, reached via PAExec, and an Israeli defense company reached through the provider's Office 365 account. Defense, energy and legal sectors were affected.

campaigns.name: Microsoft public disclosure
campaigns.summary: Microsoft published DEV-0228 activity, tool hashes, Defender detections and hunting queries as part of its report on rising Iranian targeting of the IT sector.

diamond.adversary: An Iran-based espionage cluster (Microsoft assessment). No named organization or individuals are given [S1].
diamond.capability: Credential dumping (LSASS, ProcDump, a custom lsa.exe); PAExec lateral movement; a custom .NET RAT detected as ShellClient that uses Dropbox C2; RAR staging [S1].
diamond.infrastructure: The Dropbox cloud service used as C2; reused IT-provider accounts and an Office 365 tenant account as access paths. No dedicated C2 domains or IPs were published [S1].
diamond.victim: An Israeli business-management software/IT provider and its downstream customers in Israeli defense, energy and legal sectors [S1].
diamond.socioPolitical: Iranian regime intelligence interest in Israeli defense, energy and legal organizations, pursued through trusted third parties [S1].
diamond.technology: Trusted IT-provider relationships: shared credentials, provider-managed accounts, and provider accounts inside customer Office 365 tenants. Also abuse of legitimate cloud storage for C2 [S1].

gaps: Alias ambiguity: Microsoft's mapping lists IMPERIAL KITTEN under Cuboid, Crimson and Smoke Sandstorm, so CrowdStrike's IMPERIAL KITTEN reporting cannot be assigned to Cuboid Sandstorm from the sources gathered [S2].

Possible overlap with Cybereason's MalKamak (Operation GhostShell). Cybereason's ShellClient RAT also used Dropbox C2 and ran as svchost.exe with the internal name RuntimeBroker.exe. It was first found in a July 2021 incident, and reporting also mentions an lsa.exe credential dumper. Microsoft's DEV-0228 detection is named ShellClient. However, no source gathered explicitly equates DEV-0228/Cuboid Sandstorm with MalKamak. MalKamak victims were aerospace and telecom firms, mainly in the Middle East with others in the US, Russia and Europe [S1][S4][S8].
No public Cuboid Sandstorm activity after the November 2021 disclosure was found. Current operational status is unknown.
The sponsoring Iranian organization (MOIS, IRGC or a contractor) is not stated by Microsoft.
The identities of the Israeli IT provider and the downstream victims are not public.

Could not open Microsoft Learn's threat actor naming page, the Cybereason primary report, Malpedia or ETDA cards (fetch blocked or DNS failure); relied on the Microsoft blog, the Microsoft GitHub mapping and press coverage.

implications.jipoe: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. STEP 1 (operational environment): Key terrain includes IT and managed-service providers with standing credentials or tenant accounts in defense and energy customers [S1]. STEP 2 (effects): Trusted-provider access can bypass perimeter controls on the end target. Abuse of Dropbox C2 blends with sanctioned cloud traffic [S1]. STEP 3 (threat model): Compromise a provider, dump credentials (LSASS/ProcDump), reuse provider accounts, move laterally with PAExec, plant a Dropbox-C2 RAT disguised as svchost.exe or RuntimeBroker.exe, and stage data with RAR [S1]. STEP 4 (COAs): MLCOA is espionage against Israeli or partner defense and energy organizations through a shared IT vendor. MDCOA is the same pivot technique applied to a vendor that supports US or coalition defense contractors, giving broad covert access across multiple customers. Candidate indicators: files created in C:\Windows\TAPI; PAExec execution; Defender detections Backdoor:MSIL/ShellClient.A or Mimikatz; LSASS access by unusual processes; svchost.exe or RuntimeBroker.exe running from non-standard paths and calling Dropbox APIs; provider-provisioned O365 accounts logging in from anonymizing services [S1].
implications.jcc2: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. (1) Situational awareness: Track third-party and MSP accounts that hold access into DoD-adjacent and DIB tenants. Cuboid Sandstorm's documented path ran through a provider's O365 account in a defense company [S1]. (2) Authorities: Defending contractor and provider networks generally falls to the owners plus DC3 and DIB coordination rather than DoD cyber forces directly. Pre-coordinate information sharing. (3) Mission assurance: Enforce MFA and conditional access on vendor accounts, block ActiveSync bypass, and enable the ASR rule against LSASS credential theft, following Microsoft's mitigations [S1]. (4) Coordination: Share IOCs with coalition partners, especially Israel. Alias overlap (IMPERIAL KITTEN mapped to three Microsoft actors) means cross-vendor reporting must be deconflicted before it drives attribution-based decisions [S2].
