identification.summary: Curious Gorge, a group TAG attributes to China's PLA SSF, has conducted campaigns against government and military organizations in Ukraine, Russia, Kazakhstan, and Mongolia. The actor has remained active against government, military, logistics and manufacturing organizations in Ukraine, Russia and Central Asia. In Russia, long running campaigns against multiple government organizations have continued, including the Ministry of Foreign Affairs. Over the past week, TAG identified additional compromises impacting multiple Russian defense contractors and manufacturers and a Russian logistics company.

Curly COMrades is a threat actor identified by Amazon Threat Intelligence and Bitdefender, believed to operate in support of Russian interests. They employ techniques such as Hyper-V abuse for EDR evasion and utilize proxy tools like Resocks, SSH, and Stunnel to gain access to internal networks. Their activities include repeated attempts to extract the NTDS database from domain controllers and establishing covert access through virtualization features on compromised Windows 10 machines.

One of the threat actors responsible for the denial of service attacks against U.S in 2012–2013. Three individuals associated with the group—believed to be have been working on behalf of Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps—were indicted by the Justice Department in 2016.

Cyber Av3ngers is an Iranian IRGC Cyber-Electronic Command-affiliated threat actor that targets internet-exposed operational technology and industrial control systems. Public reporting documents disruptive targeting of Israeli-made Unitronics PLCs and HMIs, broader critical-infrastructure targeting, and use of the IOCONTROL malware against IoT and OT devices.

actors.primaryName: Cyber fighters of Izz Ad-Din Al Qassam

identification.summary: Cyber Islamic Resistance is a hacktivist collective ideologically aligned with Iran, engaging in operations such as website defacements, DDoS attacks, and data exfiltration targeting Israeli and Western entities. They have claimed breaches of Israeli cybersecurity firms and academic platforms, framing their actions as part of a broader narrative of retaliation. The group has also targeted critical infrastructure, asserting access to industrial control systems and operational technology environments. Their activities are often presented as part of a coordinated cyber mobilization campaign, emphasizing psychological and reputational impacts.

UAC-0255 is a threat actor that conducted a phishing campaign impersonating CERT-UA to distribute the AGEWHEEZE RAT, targeting organizations in Ukraine's public and private sectors. The campaign is part of a broader trend of using trusted identities to enhance victim engagement, as seen in previous activities like UAC-0190 and UAC-0252. CERT-UA identified UAC-0255 after discovering links to the CyberSerp Telegram channel, which claimed responsibility for the attack. The activity is documented under the identifier CERT-UA#21075, with detection rules available for cybersecurity analysts.

Cyber Toufan is a threat actor group that has gained prominence for its cyberattacks targeting Israeli organizations. The group's tactics suggest potential nation-state backing, possibly from Iran. They have been involved in hack-and-leak operations, data breaches, and data destruction, impacting over 100 organizations. Cyber Toufan's activities align with geopolitical tensions in the Middle East and their attacks are characterized by a combination of technical breaches and psychological warfare.

identification.summary: Operate since at least 2011, from several locations in China, with members in Korea and Japan as well. Possibly linked to Onion Dog. This threat actor targets government institutions, military contractors, maritime and shipbuilding groups, telecommunications operators, and others, primarily in Japan and South Korea.

Daggerfly is Symantec's name for a China-linked espionage group, also tracked as Evasive Panda and BRONZE HIGHLAND [S1][S5]. The group's signature tool is the modular MgBot framework, which Kaspersky says Evasive Panda has used for cyber espionage since at least 2012 [S9]. It has repeatedly delivered malware through hijacked or trojanized software updates, watering holes and supply-chain compromises [S3][S4][S7][S9]. Symantec judges the group 'capable of responding to exposure by quickly updating its toolset to continue its espionage activities with minimal disruption' [S5][S6].
identification.firstObserved: Kaspersky: MgBot in use by Evasive Panda since at least 2012 [S9]. Malwarebytes linked 2020 activity to earlier attacks in 2014 and 2018 that used MgBot variants [S2].
identification.notes: Vendor names: Daggerfly (Symantec), Evasive Panda (ESET, Kaspersky; also listed for CrowdStrike in the imported record), BRONZE HIGHLAND (Secureworks), StormBamboo (Volexity) [S3][S4][S5][S8]. MITRE lists Evasive Panda and BRONZE HIGHLAND as associated groups under Daggerfly G1034 [S10]. A check of Microsoft's public naming-mapping file (2026-10-15) found no Microsoft name for this actor, so none is assigned here. Volexity's StormBamboo reporting is treated as an overlapping vendor cluster [S8].

attribution.sponsor: China-linked per vendor reporting; no government attribution found in the sources gathered [S1][S4][S5].
attribution.confidence: ESET attributed its 2023-2024 Tibetan watering-hole and supply-chain campaign to Evasive Panda with high confidence [S4]. Malwarebytes attributed its 2020 India and Hong Kong campaign to a Chinese APT group with moderate confidence [S2]. The imported Secureworks profile assesses with moderate confidence that BRONZE HIGHLAND operates on behalf of China. That assessment comes from the encyclopedia's existing record and was not re-verified here.
attribution.basis: Symantec links its 2023 Africa telecom campaign to Daggerfly partly through a renamed Rundll32.exe and the loader DLL pMsrvd.dll, both seen in a 2020 Evasive Panda campaign [S1]. Symantec tied the macOS backdoor Macma to Daggerfly through code overlaps with MgBot and a shared C2 server [S5][S6]. ESET linked IPs in its Tencent QQ campaign to the earlier LuoYu APT campaign [S3].

actors.objectives: Espionage, including what Symantec calls internal espionage. Its 2024 targets included a US NGO operating in China [S5][S6]. The group has watched the Tibetan diaspora and Buddhist community [S4] and pro-democracy-linked Hong Kong website visitors [S6]. It has also collected intelligence on regional governments and telecoms around China's periphery and in Africa [S1][S2].

sectors: International NGOs operating in mainland China [S3][S5]
Academic networks (Georgia Tech network named among ESET targets) [S4]
Users of Chinese consumer software (Tencent QQ, iQIYI, SohuVA) [S3][S9]
regions: Australia and United States (watering-hole target networks) [S4]
targeting.notes: Targeting combines regional government and telecom espionage with surveillance of groups the PRC treats as domestic security concerns: NGOs in China, Tibetans and Hong Kong activists [S1][S2][S3][S4][S5]. The DNS-poisoning delivery Kaspersky reported was selective and aimed at specific victims [S9].

capabilities.summary: MgBot is the core of the toolkit. It is a modular Windows framework with plugins for keylogging, file theft, credential theft and command execution. Symantec documented previously unseen MgBot plugins in 2023 [S1][S9]. The group runs a cross-platform arsenal. Symantec says MgBot, Macma and other Daggerfly tools share code from one library used to build Windows, macOS, Linux and Android threats. Symantec also reports evidence that the group can trojanize Android APKs, intercept SMS and DNS requests, and target Solaris [S5][S6][S7]. Nightdoor (also tracked as Suzafk/NetMM) is a newer Windows backdoor that uses the Google Drive API for C2 [S4][S6]. Delivery methods: spear-phishing with template-injection documents carrying Cobalt Strike and MgBot [S2]; trojanized software updates [S3][S9]; watering holes on compromised sites; and trojanized installers from a compromised Indian software vendor [S4]. Volexity reports DNS poisoning at a compromised ISP that redirected insecure HTTP update requests to MACMA and POCOSTICK (MgBot) payloads [S8]. Kaspersky reports DNS poisoning that served encrypted payload parts, a new loader, and hybrid encryption that makes implants unique per victim [S9]. After intrusion, the group has used BITSAdmin and PowerShell to fetch AnyDesk. It has run GetCredManCreds to dump Windows Credential Manager, created local accounts for persistence, and used a PlugX loader [S1]. It also exploited an Apache HTTP server vulnerability for initial access [S5][S6]. Malwarebytes reported Android apps that collect call logs, contacts and SMS and record audio and the screen [S2].

campaigns.name: India and Hong Kong spear-phishing (MgBot/Cobalt Strike)
campaigns.summary: Malwarebytes reported spear-phishing against Indian and Hong Kong government targets from 2 July 2020. Lures included a fake gov.in security check. Payloads were Cobalt Strike and MgBot, alongside malicious Android apps. Timing coincided with Hong Kong's new security law and India's app ban [S2].

campaigns.name: Tencent QQ malicious updates against an NGO in China
campaigns.summary: ESET found MgBot delivered through Tencent QQ automatic updates to individuals in Gansu, Guangdong and Jiangsu, mostly members of an international NGO. ESET could not decide between supply-chain compromise and adversary-in-the-middle; reported in April 2023 [S3].

campaigns.name: African telecom operator intrusion
campaigns.summary: Symantec tracked activity against an African telecom from November 2022 using new MgBot plugins, a PlugX loader, AnyDesk and GetCredManCreds; reported April 2023 [S1][S7].

campaigns.name: Fake-update / DNS-poisoning MgBot campaign
campaigns.summary: Kaspersky reported lures posing as updates for SohuVA, iQIYI Video, IObit Smart Defrag and Tencent QQ, delivered with DNS poisoning, against systems in Türkiye, China and India; reported December 2025 [S9].

campaigns.name: ISP DNS poisoning of software updates (StormBamboo)
campaigns.summary: Volexity traced infections back to DNS poisoning at a compromised ISP. Update traffic for several software vendors was redirected to install MACMA and POCOSTICK (MgBot); reported August 2024 [S8].

campaigns.name: Monlam festival watering hole and Tibetan software supply chain
campaigns.summary: ESET found the Kagyu International Monlam Trust website compromised for watering-hole attacks. The actor also trojanized Tibetan-language software from an Indian developer, delivering MgBot and Nightdoor to networks in India, Taiwan, Hong Kong, Australia and the US; reported March 2024 [S4].

campaigns.name: Major toolset update (Taiwan and US NGO in China)
campaigns.summary: Symantec reported a new MgBot-based malware family, a new Macma version and Nightdoor. They were used against Taiwanese organizations and a US NGO in China, with an Apache HTTP server exploit used for access [S5][S6].

diamond.adversary: China-linked espionage group named by several vendors (Daggerfly, Evasive Panda, BRONZE HIGHLAND, StormBamboo). It has been active since at least 2012 and changes its tools quickly after exposure [S5][S8][S9].
diamond.capability: MgBot modular framework, Nightdoor, Macma (macOS) and Android implants; PlugX and Cobalt Strike; trojanized installers and updates; DNS poisoning; credential theft with GetCredManCreds [S1][S2][S4][S5][S8][S9].
diamond.infrastructure: Compromised legitimate websites used as watering holes; a compromised software vendor's distribution site [S4]; DNS poisoning at a compromised ISP [S8]; Google Drive API C2 for Nightdoor [S6]; multiple redundant MgBot C2 servers [S9]; and C2 shared between MgBot and Macma [S6].
diamond.victim: Tibetan communities, NGOs in China, Hong Kong and Indian government targets, Taiwanese organizations, an African telecom, and users in Türkiye, China and India [S1][S2][S3][S4][S5][S9].
diamond.socioPolitical: Surveillance of groups Beijing treats as internal security concerns (Tibetans, Hong Kong pro-democracy circles, foreign NGOs in China), plus regional and strategic intelligence collection [S2][S3][S4][S5][S6].
diamond.technology: Exploits insecure HTTP update mechanisms that do not verify installer signatures [S8], trust in software vendors' update channels [S3][S4][S9], and internet-facing Apache servers [S5].

gaps: Primary vendor reports (Symantec 2023 and 2024, Kaspersky Securelist 2025, Volexity 2024) could not be fetched (DNS failure); details come from search-result summaries and secondary coverage.
Microsoft has no public name for this actor in its naming-mapping file as of 2026-10-15.
No US or allied government attribution or indictment specific to Daggerfly/Evasive Panda was found.

Cluster boundaries are not settled. Volexity's StormBamboo is equated with Evasive Panda in press coverage [S8]. ESET noted IP overlap with LuoYu [S3]. Third-party alias lists (TAG-112, Digging Taurus, Storm Cloud) were not confirmed by primary vendors and were excluded.

Whether Tencent QQ updates were compromised at the vendor or in transit (AiTM) remains unresolved [S3]. Kaspersky's DNS-poisoning findings and Volexity's ISP finding may describe the same mechanism, but this is unconfirmed [S8][S9].
The role of KsRemote (Android RAT, from the imported Secureworks summary) was not confirmed in the sources gathered.
Symantec's Solaris and Linux capability claims come from secondhand coverage, without analyzed samples in the sources seen [S7].
The imported Secureworks moderate-confidence assessment was not re-verified against a live Secureworks page.

implications.jipoe: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. STEP 1 (operational environment): Software update channels, upstream ISP DNS resolution, and websites trusted by target communities are key cyber terrain. Theater networks in the Indo-Pacific, India, Taiwan and Africa that rely on regional ISPs and consumer software count as relevant terrain [S4][S8][S9]. STEP 2 (effects): Any application that updates over unauthenticated HTTP can be turned into a delivery vector, and the group retools quickly after public exposure, so signature-based defenses lose value fast [S5][S8]. STEP 3 (threat model): Typical chain is a hijacked update, watering hole or spear-phish; then the MgBot or Nightdoor loader; then plugin-based keylogging, file and credential theft; with C2 over actor servers or the Google Drive API [S1][S2][S4][S6][S9]. STEP 4 (COAs): MLCOA is continued selective surveillance of NGOs, diaspora and activist communities and regional government and telecom networks using poisoned updates and watering holes [S1][S3][S4][S9]. MDCOA is ISP-level DNS poisoning that pushes malicious updates to Windows and macOS hosts of personnel or partners in the region during a Taiwan-related crisis [S5][S8]. Candidate indicators: update binaries fetched over HTTP whose hashes do not match the vendor's; DNS answers for update domains that point to unexpected IPs; renamed Rundll32.exe or a pMsrvd.dll loader; GetCredManCreds; unexpected AnyDesk installs via BITSAdmin/PowerShell; new local accounts; Google Drive API traffic from non-browser processes [S1][S6][S8].
implications.jcc2: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. (1) Situational awareness: track software inventories with insecure update channels and DNS integrity alerts for forward-deployed and partner networks that rely on host-nation ISPs [S8]. (2) Authorities: the ISP and third-party software vendors sit outside DoD control, so remediation needs coordination with host-nation, vendor and interagency partners rather than unilateral action [S3][S8]. (3) Mission assurance: enforce signed-update verification and DNS over trusted resolvers for mission systems and mobile devices, given Macma and Android capabilities [S5][S6]. (4) Coordination: share indicators with DC3, CISA and allied CERTs, especially those of Taiwan and India, and keep in mind that vendors track overlapping clusters (StormBamboo, Evasive Panda, Daggerfly) under different names [S4][S5][S8].

Their targets of attack are usually Windows servers that are poorly managed or are not patched to the latest version. identification.summary: DEV-0147 is a China-based cyber espionage actor was observed compromising diplomatic targets in South America, a notable expansion of the group's data exfiltration operations that traditionally targeted gov't agencies and think tanks in Asia and Europe. DEV-0147 is known to use tools like ShadowPad, a remote access trojan associated with other China-based actors, to maintain persistent access, and QuasarLoader, a webpack loader, to deploy additional malware. DEV-0147's attacks in South America included post-exploitation activity involving the abuse of on-premises identity infrastructure for recon and lateral movement, and the use of Cobalt Strike for command and control and data exfiltration.

Microsoft threat intelligence teams have been tracking multiple ransomware campaigns and have tied these attacks to DEV-0270, also known as Nemesis Kitten, a sub-group of Iranian actor PHOSPHORUS. Microsoft assesses with moderate confidence that DEV-0270 conducts malicious network operations, including widespread vulnerability scanning, on behalf of the government of Iran.

North Korean state-sponsored actor that pursues espionage, data theft, financial gain and network destruction, typically targeting media, IT services and defense organizations worldwide [S1][S2]. Microsoft tracks it as one of several separate North Korean clusters that public reporting often groups as 'Lazarus Group'.

Destructive capability demonstrated in the 2014 Sony attack attributed to the Lazarus program [S3]. MITRE lists 93 techniques for Lazarus Group (G0032) [S5].

implications.jipoe: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. STEP 1: The OE includes software vendors and CI/CD infrastructure that supply DoD and DIB networks; supply-chain paths are key terrain. STEP 2: A validly signed installer defeats allow-listing based on signer trust, so terrain analysis must include update channels. STEP 3: The template is n-day exploitation of developer infrastructure or trojanized signed software, then credential theft (ForestTiger) and hijack-based persistence (RollSling), then espionage or destruction. STEP 4: MLCOA is espionage against defense and IT targets with opportunistic financial theft. MDCOA is a destructive attack, Sony-style, against a high-profile target during a Korean Peninsula crisis. Candidate indicators: unexpected child processes from vendor updaters, DLL search-order hijacks in IT tools, and newly exploited CI/CD CVEs [S1][S2].
implications.jcc2: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. (1) Supply-chain visibility: JCC2 data should flag vendor-signed binaries behaving abnormally, not just unsigned code. (2) Coordinate with INDOPACOM and USFK on Korean Peninsula crisis I&W, since DPRK cyber activity can precede or accompany provocations. (3) Revenue-focused operations (crypto theft) are a Treasury, FBI and law-enforcement lead, but they finance regime programs and so are relevant to campaign-level assessment. (4) Naming discipline: reporting chains should carry the specific cluster (Diamond, Onyx, Jade, Sapphire Sleet), because 'Lazarus' aggregates distinct actors with different targets.

provenance.importedSummary: CryptoCore is a North Korean APT known for targeting cryptocurrency exchanges and financial institutions, employing spear-phishing techniques that lead to LONEJOGGER malware infections. The group has leveraged social engineering tactics, including deepfake technology and hijacked YouTube accounts, to execute sophisticated giveaway scams that deceive victims into sending cryptocurrencies. Their operations have involved the misuse of platforms like Gemini for reconnaissance and the development of fraudulent content. Additionally, CryptoCore has been linked to a variety of campaigns, including Dangerous Password and SnatchCrypto, focusing on financial gain through cryptocurrency theft.

identification.summary: DiceyF is an advanced persistent threat group that has been targeting online casinos and other victims in Southeast Asia for an extended period. They have exhibited overlapping activity with LuckyStar PlugX and Earth Berberoka/GamblingPuppet, as reported by various cybersecurity vendors. While their motivations remain unclear, previous incidents suggest a combination of espionage and intellectual property theft rather than immediate financial gain. DiceyF continuously evolves their codebase and adds encryption capabilities to enhance their stealthy cyberespionage activities.

An extensive surveillance operation targets specific groups of individuals with malicious mobile apps that collect sensitive information on the device along with surrounding voice recordings. Researchers with CheckPoint discovered the attack and named it Domestic Kitten. The targets are Kurdish and Turkish natives, and ISIS supporters, all Iranian citizens.

DragonSpark is a threat actor that has been conducting attacks primarily targeting organizations in East Asia. They utilize the open-source tool SparkRAT, which is a multi-platform and frequently updated remote access Trojan. The threat actor is believed to be Chinese-speaking based on their use of Chinese language support and compromised infrastructure located in China and Taiwan. They employ various techniques to evade detection, including Golang source code interpretation and the use of the China Chopper webshell.

DriftingCloud is a persistent threat actor known for targeting various industries and locations. They are skilled at developing or acquiring zero-day exploits to gain unauthorized access to target networks. Compromising gateway devices is a common tactic used by DriftingCloud, making network monitoring solutions crucial for detecting their attacks.

Earth Alux is a China-linked APT group known for conducting cyberespionage attacks across various sectors, including government, technology, and telecommunications. They primarily exploit vulnerable services in exposed servers to gain initial access, implanting web shells like GODZILLA and deploying backdoors such as VARGEIT and COBEACON. The group employs tools like RSBINJECT and MASQLOADER for lateral movement and network discovery, while also utilizing RAILSETTER for persistence through mspaint injection. Their operations have predominantly targeted the APAC region and have extended to Latin America, with a focus on exfiltrating sensitive information to attacker-controlled cloud storage.

Earth Baxia is a threat actor opearting out of China, targeting government organizations in Taiwan and potentially across the APAC region, using spear-phishing emails and exploiting the GeoServer vulnerability CVE-2024-36401 for remote code execution, deploying customized Cobalt Strike components with altered signatures, leveraging GrimResource and AppDomainManager injection techniques to deliver additional payloads, and utilizing a new backdoor named EAGLEDOOR for multi-protocol communication and payload delivery.

According to TrendMicro, Earth Berberoka is a threat group originating from China that mainly focuses on targeting gambling websites. This group's campaign uses multiple malware families that target the Windows, Linux, and macOS platforms that have been attributed to Chinese-speaking actors. Aside from using tried-and-tested malware families that have been upgraded, such as PlugX and Gh0st RAT, Earth Berberoka has also developed a brand-new complex, multistage malware family, which has been dubbed PuppetLoader.

Earth Freybug, identified as a subset of APT41, is a cyberthreat group active since at least 2012, engaging in espionage and financially motivated activities across various sectors worldwide. The tactics, techniques, and procedures (TTPs) used in this campaign are similar to the ones from a campaign (Operation CuckooBees) described in an article published by Cybereason. They employ a diverse toolkit, including LOLBins and custom malware, to execute sophisticated cyberespionage attacks. The group's recent tactics involve DLL hijacking and API unhooking through a newly discovered malware named UNAPIMON, which prevents child processes from being monitored. This technique was observed in a vmtoolsd.exe process creating remote tasks to deploy malicious batch files for reconnaissance and backdoor access. UNAPIMON's simplicity and use of Microsoft Detours for defense evasion highlight the group's evolving methods and the need for vigilant security measures, such as restricting admin privileges and adhering to the principle of least privilege. Earth Freybug's persistence and creativity in refining their techniques underscore the ongoing threat they pose and the importance of proactive cybersecurity practices.

Earth Krahang is an APT group targeting government organizations worldwide. They use spear-phishing emails, weak internet-facing servers, and custom backdoors like Cobalt Strike, RESHELL, and XDealer to conduct cyber espionage. The group creates VPN servers on infected systems, employs brute force attacks on email accounts, and exploits compromised government infrastructure to attack other governments. Earth Krahang has been linked to another China-linked actor, Earth Lusca, and is believed to be part of a specialized task force for cyber espionage against government institutions.

Earth Lamia is a China-nexus APT that targets organizations across multiple sectors, including finance, logistics, and government, primarily in Latin America, the Middle East, and Southeast Asia. The actor exploits web application vulnerabilities, such as CVE-2025-55182, and employs techniques like SQL injection, DLL sideloading, and the deployment of custom backdoors like PULSEPACK and BypassBoss. Earth Lamia conducts reconnaissance, file operations, and credential theft, often utilizing tools like Cobalt Strike and VShell.

Earth Naga is an APT group that has persistently targeted high-value organizations, including government agencies, telecommunications, and military-related manufacturers, primarily in Taiwan and the broader APAC region. They have been linked to the use of Draculoader and ShadowPad C&C infrastructure, demonstrating sophisticated TTPs such as establishing SSH connections through compromised mail servers. Earth Naga has collaborated with Earth Estries, sharing access to facilitate continued exploitation, complicating detection and attribution efforts. Their operations reflect a growing interest in global intelligence collection, extending to NATO member countries and Latin America.

Earth Wendigo is a threat actor from China that has been targeting several organizations — including government organizations, research institutions, and universities in Taiwan — since May 2019, aiming to exfiltrate emails from targeted organizations via the injection of JavaScript backdoors to a webmail system that is widely used in Taiwan. The threat actor also sent spear-phishing emails embedded with malicious links to multiple individuals, including politicians and activists, who support movements in Tibet, the Uyghur region, or Hong Kong.

Edalat-e Ali is a hacktivist group known for disrupting Iranian state-run TV and radio transmissions during significant events, such as the Revolution Day ceremonies. They have also targeted government facilities, releasing security camera footage to expose abuses and draw attention to human rights violations. The group has used their hacks to call for protests against the Iranian regime and have displayed anti-government messages during their disruptions. Edalat-e Ali has been active in releasing sensitive information and footage to embarrass Iranian officials and highlight injustices within the country.

Educated Manticore is an Iranian APT group aligned with the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps, primarily engaged in espionage targeting government, military, and academic sectors. The group employs spear-phishing tactics, utilizing custom backdoors like POWERLESS and phishing kits designed as SPAs to harvest credentials. Their operations have included impersonating credible figures to lure victims and using ISO images to initiate infection chains. Educated Manticore's activities are characterized by rapid domain setup and aggressive spear-phishing campaigns, particularly against Israeli individuals.

Elderwood is the name Symantec gave in September 2012 to a systematic espionage group that reused components of an infrastructure it called the 'Elderwood platform' and that Symantec tracked back to the 2009 Operation Aurora attacks on Google and other companies [S1][S2]. Symantec reported the group had exploited at least eight zero-day vulnerabilities since late 2010, all in Internet Explorer or Adobe Flash Player, and that it was moving from spear-phishing toward watering-hole attacks against defense supply chain targets [S2][S6]. Symantec tied a December 2012 Internet Explorer zero-day (CVE-2012-4792) served from the Council on Foreign Relations website to the same group [S6][S7]. MITRE ATT&CK tracks it as G0066, a suspected Chinese cyber espionage group reportedly responsible for Operation Aurora [S8].
identification.firstObserved: 2009: Symantec tracks the group back to the 2009 Operation Aurora attacks [S2].
identification.notes: Symantec says the name comes from a source-code variable used by the attackers [S2]. Malpedia lists Elderwood, Elderwood Gang, G0066, SIG22 and SNEAKY PANDA; MITRE lists Elderwood Gang, Beijing Group and Sneaky Panda [S8]. No Microsoft Typhoon/Storm name was found for this cluster in the sources gathered. Symantec separately named 'Hidden Lynx' in 2013 and linked it to Aurora through shared malware; CrowdStrike tracked that group as 'Aurora Panda'. These are distinct vendor clusters from Elderwood/Sneaky Panda and should not be merged without primary evidence [S9].

attribution.sponsor: Suspected People's Republic of China. Google stated the Aurora attacks originated in China [S2]; MITRE describes Elderwood as a suspected Chinese cyber espionage group [S8].
attribution.confidence: Symantec's 2012 report did not name China or a geographic origin and said only that the group's sophistication probably indicated support from organized crime or a nation state [S2]. MITRE's characterization is 'suspected' [S8]. No US government attribution of the Elderwood cluster by name was found in the sources gathered; 2013 press reporting citing unnamed US officials described the Google breach as by Chinese hackers [S5].
attribution.basis: Symantec analysis of shared infrastructure, packer license and code artifacts (for example a misspelled 'HeapSpary' function) linking successive zero-day campaigns [S2][S6]; MITRE ATT&CK group entry [S8].

actors.objectives: Strategic espionage. Google initially pointed to Gmail accounts of Chinese human rights activists and intellectual property [S5]; US officials later told the Washington Post the Google intrusion reached a database of law-enforcement and FISA surveillance orders, apparently to identify Chinese intelligence operatives under US surveillance [S5]. Symantec reported that the group's primary targets were usually members of the defense supply chain [S2].

sectors: Defense industrial base and defense supply chain manufacturers [S2]
Think tanks / foreign policy organizations (Council on Foreign Relations website) [S6][S7]
regions: United States (Council on Foreign Relations watering hole) [S7]

capabilities.summary: Repeated use of zero-day exploits in Internet Explorer and Adobe Flash Player, at least eight from 2010 to fall 2012 and a ninth (CVE-2012-4792) in December 2012 [S2][S6]. Aurora used an Internet Explorer zero-day (CVE-2010-0249) delivered via spear-phishing links in email and instant messages to drop the Hydraq remote access trojan [S1][S2]. From 2012 the group increasingly used watering-hole (strategic web compromise) attacks, [S2][S7]. Symantec described shared tooling ('Elderwood platform'), a common commercial packer license, and reuse of exploit components across campaigns [S2][S6]. MITRE lists associated software including PoisonIvy, Hydraq, Briba, Naid, Wiarp, Vasport, Pasam, Nerex and Linfo [S8].

campaigns.name: Operation Aurora
campaigns.summary: Intrusions against Google and other companies using the IE zero-day CVE-2010-0249 to install a remote access trojan, described by McAfee in January 2010; Symantec later tied the Elderwood group to these attacks.

campaigns.name: Aurora surveillance-database disclosure
campaigns.summary: Washington Post reporting, citing unnamed US officials, said the Google intruders accessed a database of surveillance orders including FISA orders.

campaigns.name: Elderwood zero-day series
campaigns.summary: Symantec counted at least eight zero-days in IE and Flash Player exploited since late 2010, four in about 16 weeks in spring and summer 2012, mainly against defense supply chain targets.

campaigns.name: CVE-2012-1889 watering hole
campaigns.summary: Symantec linked a June 2012 site serving CVE-2012-1889 with a movie.swf file to the Elderwood Project.

campaigns.name: Symantec 'The Elderwood Project' report

campaigns.summary: The CFR website was compromised to serve an IE 6-8 zero-day; Symantec assessed it as a continuation of the Elderwood Project; Microsoft later issued out-of-band fix MS13-008.

diamond.adversary: Suspected PRC espionage group (Symantec: likely nation-state or organized-crime backed; MITRE: suspected Chinese) [S2][S8].
diamond.capability: Serial IE and Flash zero-days, Hydraq and related backdoors, commercial packer, shared 'Elderwood platform' exploit components [S1][S2][S6][S8].
diamond.infrastructure: Compromised legitimate websites used as watering holes (e.g., CFR), spear-phishing links via email and instant message [S1][S7].
diamond.victim: Defense supply chain manufacturers, technology and internet firms (Google), human rights activists and NGOs, think tanks [S2][S5][S7][S8].
diamond.socioPolitical: Collection on PRC dissidents, US technology and defense IP, and US counterintelligence activity (surveillance orders) [S5].
diamond.technology: Unpatched Internet Explorer 6-8 and Adobe Flash Player on Windows endpoints; trust in frequently visited policy and industry websites [S1][S6][S7].

gaps: Original Symantec 'The Elderwood Project' PDF and Symantec Connect blog could not be opened; details come from search summaries and press coverage of them [S2][S6].
The Washington Post article was not opened directly; reliance is on secondary coverage [S5].
MITRE ATT&CK G0066 page and CFR Cyber Operations Tracker 'Sneaky Panda' entry could not be fetched; alias and description data are from search-result summaries.
No Microsoft threat actor name identified for Elderwood; Microsoft mapping not checked.
Relationship between Elderwood/Sneaky Panda and Symantec's Hidden Lynx / CrowdStrike's Aurora Panda is unresolved; shared Aurora malware does not establish identity [S9].
No public activity explicitly attributed to Elderwood after early 2013 was found; current status is unknown.
No US government attribution naming Elderwood or a specific PRC organization was found.

implications.jipoe: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. STEP 1: Key terrain includes user endpoints running browsers and plug-ins, and the third-party websites (policy, industry, supplier) that DoD and DIB personnel routinely visit [S7]. STEP 2: Historic reliance on browser and Flash zero-days means patch status alone does not bound the threat; defense supply chain firms are an indirect path to defense programs [S2][S6]. STEP 3: Doctrinal template is strategic web compromise or spear-phishing link, browser exploit, RAT such as Hydraq, then collection of IP and sensitive databases [S1][S2][S5]. STEP 4: MLCOA is persistent IP theft from DIB suppliers via watering holes. MDCOA is access to counterintelligence or sensitive legal-process data, as reported for the Google surveillance-order database [S5]. Candidate indicators: unexpected script injection on frequently visited partner sites, heap-spray exploit pages targeting legacy browsers, and Hydraq-family beacons [S1][S6].
implications.jcc2: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. (1) Situational awareness should track compromise of external websites frequented by the force, not only DoDIN assets [S7]. (2) Zero-day use means mitigation (browser isolation, plug-in removal) must be pre-authorized rather than waiting on vendor patches [S6]. (3) Mission assurance depends on DIB supplier hygiene; coordinate with DC3 and the DIB CS program when supplier compromise is suspected [S2]. (4) Coordinate with law enforcement and counterintelligence, since the reported Aurora objective included surveillance-order data [S5].

identification.summary: ELUSIVE COMET is a threat actor responsible for significant cryptocurrency theft through sophisticated social engineering attacks, particularly leveraging Zoom's remote control feature. Their attack methodology involves manipulating legitimate workflows and exploiting human-centric vulnerabilities rather than technical flaws. The actor employs tactics such as social proof, time pressure, and interface manipulation to deceive targets. Organizations can mitigate risks by implementing technical controls to disable the remote control feature and deploying email boundary protections like DMARC, SPF, and DKIM.

Emerald Sleet (formerly THALLIUM) is a North Korean threat actor that Microsoft says stayed highly active through 2023. It spear-phishes prominent individuals with North Korea expertise and often impersonates academic institutions and NGOs [S1]. Microsoft says it targets diplomats and Korean Peninsula experts in government, think tanks and NGOs, media and education, and assesses the motive as intelligence collection [S2]. Since January 2025 Microsoft has seen the actor trick targets into running PowerShell as administrator and pasting code the actor supplies [S3]. Microsoft and OpenAI also observed it using large language models (LLMs) for reconnaissance, vulnerability research and phishing content [S1][S11].
identification.firstObserved: Kaspersky's 2013 'Kimsuky' report dates the earliest signs of activity to 2013-04-03 and the first Kimsuky Trojan samples to 2013-05-05 [S8]. Microsoft was tracking the group as THALLIUM by 2019 [S4].
identification.notes: Microsoft name: Emerald Sleet (formerly THALLIUM). Microsoft says Emerald Sleet overlaps with the actors other researchers call Kimsuky and Velvet Chollima [S1]. Microsoft's naming map lists THALLIUM, VELVET CHOLLIMA, RGB-D5, Black Banshee, Kimsuky and Greendinosa as other names. It lists APT43 and Konni separately, under Opal Sleet [S5]. Material that vendors publish under Kimsuky, Springtail [S10] or TA427 [S9] is mapped to this record by alias, and boundaries may not match Microsoft's exactly. Mandiant's APT43 reporting is not merged here because Microsoft maps APT43 to Opal Sleet [S5]. MITRE tracks the group as Kimsuky (G0094) [S14].

attribution.sponsor: Democratic People's Republic of Korea. US Treasury describes Kimsuky as subordinate to the Reconnaissance General Bureau (RGB), the DPRK's primary foreign intelligence service [S7]. A May 2024 FBI, State Department and NSA advisory says Kimsuky is administratively subordinate to the 63rd Research Center, an element of the RGB [S6].
attribution.confidence: Microsoft calls Emerald Sleet a 'North Korean state actor' [S3]. In 2019 Microsoft said THALLIUM is 'believed to operate from North Korea' [S4]. US Treasury sanctioned Kimsuky as an RGB-subordinate entity on 2023-11-30 [S7]. These government statements name Kimsuky, which Microsoft maps to Emerald Sleet [S5]. Kaspersky's 2013 report only surmised North Korean origin from target profiles, Korean-language compile paths and registrant names [S8].
attribution.basis: Microsoft telemetry and actor tracking, joint Microsoft and OpenAI LLM-abuse research, and a 2019 civil court action [S1][S2][S3][S4]. US Treasury designation [S7]. Joint FBI, State Department and NSA advisory [S6]. Vendor technical reporting from Kaspersky, Proofpoint and Symantec [S8][S9][S10].

actors.objectives: Microsoft assesses the motive as intelligence collection on North Korea-related policy, gathered from diplomats and Korean Peninsula experts [S2]. Through LLM-informed reconnaissance, the actor sought out think tanks, government organizations and experts focused on North Korean defense issues or its nuclear weapons program [S1]. Its 2022 impersonation campaign asked North Korea experts for their views on security issues and offered payment to review a document on the North Korean nuclear program [S12]. The 2024 joint US advisory describes Kimsuky posing as journalists, academics and East Asia experts to collect information for the regime [S6].

sectors: Government agencies and services, including diplomats [S2][S3]
Individuals working in international affairs, especially Northeast Asia [S3]
Nuclear non-proliferation, world-peace and human-rights organizations and experts [S4]
regions: North America, South America, Europe and East Asia (2025 PowerShell campaign) [S3]
United States, Japan and South Korea (2019 THALLIUM targets) [S4]
South Korea (2013 Kimsuky campaign; 2024 Gomir and GoBear activity) [S8][S10]
targeting.notes: Microsoft's victim set centers on people with North Korea or Northeast Asia expertise rather than on infrastructure [S1][S2][S3]. Treasury describes the group's targets as government, research and media figures, mainly in South Korea, Japan and the US [S7].

capabilities.summary: Social engineering is the core capability. The actor builds rapport over time while posing as officials, journalists, academics or think-tank staff, then sends spear-phishing emails [S1][S3][S6][S9][S12]. In 2019, THALLIUM's spoofed Microsoft-themed credential phishing led to mailbox access and forwarding rules that sent new mail to actor-controlled accounts [S4]. From December 2023 the group abused lax DMARC policies to spoof personas, and from February 2024 it added web beacons to profile targets [S6][S9]. In 2025 it ran ClickFix-style lures: victims were told to paste PowerShell as administrator, which installed a browser-based remote desktop tool and registered the device for actor access [S3]. Proofpoint saw similar lures deliver QuasarRAT [S13]. Its malware includes Linux (Gomir) and Windows (GoBear) backdoors spread through trojanized South Korean software installers [S10]. The 2013 Kimsuky malware included a module for stealing HWP documents [S8]. LLM use covers vulnerability research (CVE-2022-30190), basic scripting, phishing content and reconnaissance [S1][S11].

diamond.socioPolitical: Intelligence collection on foreign policy toward the DPRK, nuclear issues and Korean Peninsula security in support of the regime [S1][S2][S6].
diamond.technology: Email trust (DMARC misconfiguration, sender spoofing), cloud mailbox rules, Windows PowerShell with administrator rights, and South Korean security and PKI software installers [S3][S4][S6][S10].

gaps: Cluster boundary: Microsoft maps APT43 and Konni to Opal Sleet, not Emerald Sleet, while many vendors treat APT43 and Kimsuky as one actor. Mandiant APT43 reporting, including cybercrime self-funding, is excluded until reconciled [S5].
Proofpoint TA427 and Symantec Springtail findings are mapped here by alias; neither source confirms the boundary matches Microsoft's Emerald Sleet [S9][S10].

The primary documents could not be opened: the IC3/FBI May 2024 advisory and the Treasury press release (blocked), plus the Microsoft On the Issues 2019 post, the Proofpoint blog and Kaspersky Securelist (DNS failures). Content is taken from search snippets and press coverage.
The full Microsoft write-up of the 2025 PowerShell tactic was seen only as an X thread summary. Victim counts and outcomes are not public.
No public reporting gathered here shows Emerald Sleet targeting US military networks or conducting disruptive operations.
An unverified search summary claims QR-code credential phishing by Emerald Sleet in May 2025; no primary source was found, so it is excluded.

implications.jipoe: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. STEP 1 (OE): The key terrain is people, not networks: personal and work email of policy, diplomatic, academic and think-tank staff working on Korean Peninsula issues, plus organizational email domains with weak DMARC policies [S2][S3][S6]. STEP 2 (effects): Spoofed trusted personas undermine email-based trust. Compromised mailboxes with forwarding rules give persistent collection without implants [S4][S9]. STEP 3 (adversary template): Benign rapport-building email from a spoofed expert or official, then a lure (PDF, 'secure document', or 'device registration'), then credential capture or PowerShell paste-and-run, then remote desktop or RAT, then mail and document collection [S3][S4][S13]. STEP 4: MLCOA is continued collection against DPRK-policy, nuclear and alliance-planning experts through impersonation and paste-and-run lures [S1][S3]. MDCOA is the compromise of a planner or liaison mailbox that gives sustained access to exercise, alliance or nuclear-policy correspondence [S4][S6]. Candidate indicators include unsolicited expert or official outreach that escalates to document review requests, instructions to run PowerShell as administrator, new inbox forwarding rules, spoofed domains failing DMARC alignment, and web-beacon tracking pixels in first-contact emails [S3][S4][S6][S9].
implications.jcc2: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. Situational awareness: Track Emerald Sleet lure themes and personas, such as South Korean officials, Japanese diplomats and think-tank staff. Monitor for PowerShell-as-admin and remote-desktop registration events and mailbox-rule changes [S3][S4][S9][S13]. Authorities: Most victims are civilian think tanks, academics and personal accounts outside the DODIN. Response relies on FBI and partner notification and on private-sector actions such as Microsoft's 2019 civil domain seizure and its account disablement with OpenAI [S1][S4][S6]. Mission assurance: Enforce DMARC quarantine or reject on mission-partner domains, restrict PowerShell for standard users, and train staff who handle Korean Peninsula topics to verify unsolicited expert contact out of band [S3][S6]. Coordination: Share indicators with USFK and INDOPACOM stakeholders and with ROK and Japanese partners, which mirrored the 2023 sanctions, and with industry reporters such as Microsoft and Proofpoint [S7][S9].

provenance.importedSummary: • APT43 is a prolific cyber operator that supports the interests of the North Korean regime. The group combines moderately-sophisticated technical capabilities with aggressive social engineering tactics, especially against South Korean and U.S.-based government organizations, academics, and think tanks focused on Korean peninsula geopolitical issues. • In addition to its espionage campaigns, we believe APT43 funds itself through cybercrime operations to support its primary mission of collecting strategic intelligence. • The group creates numerous spoofed and fraudulent personas for use in social engineering, as well as cover identities for purchasing operational tooling and infrastructure. • APT43 has collaborated with other North Korean espionage operators on multiple operations, underscoring the major role APT43 plays in the regime’s cyber apparatus.

identification.summary: EvilWeb is a pro-Russian hacktivist group created in March 2024 that targets American and European entities using a hack-and-leak method alongside DDoS attacks. The group claims to have obtained data from various high-profile American organizations. EvilWeb announced its participation in the #FreeDurov operation on August 25, 2024, and began executing DDoS and hacking attacks. As of September 3, 2024, their Telegram channel has 1,146 members.

identification.summary: Femwar02 is a previously unknown pro-Russian ransomware threat actor that emerged in early 2026, linked to a major cyberattack on Italy's Sapienza University of Rome in February 2026, which caused a full network shutdown and operational disruptions. The group deploys Bablock (also known as Rorschach), a next-generation ransomware strain first identified in 2023 that features fast hybrid encryption (curve25519 and hc-128), partial file encryption for speed, direct system calls to evade detection, and domain-wide propagation via Group Policy on Windows Domain Controllers. Bablock shares code similarities with LockBit 2.0 but incorporates elements from other families like Babuk and DarkSide, often delivered via encrypted payloads, DLL sideloading with tools like DarkLoader, and exploits such as those in Zimbra or phishing. Notably, the malware skips encrypting files written in Russian, reinforcing its pro-Russian alignment, with no prior attributions or campaigns documented before the Sapienza incident.

Ferocious Kitten is the name Kaspersky gave to an Iran-based espionage actor. Kaspersky says it has run surveillance against Persian-speaking individuals inside Iran since at least 2015 [S1][S2]. The group uses Persian-language Office decoy documents with malicious macros to install a custom Windows implant, MarkiRAT [S1][S2][S3]. MarkiRAT records keystrokes and clipboard content, uploads and downloads files, and runs arbitrary commands. Some variants hijack the Telegram and Chrome applications to stay persistent [S2][S4]. In July 2026 Recorded Future linked a new cluster, TAG-182, to MarkiRAT distribution through fake VPN and media-player apps. It cited tradecraft overlaps with Ferocious Kitten but did not assess an organizational link [S6].
identification.firstObserved: Kaspersky traced MarkiRAT activity back to at least 2015 [S1][S2]. The actor became publicly known in June 2021 after a lure document uploaded to VirusTotal in March 2021 was highlighted on Twitter [S2][S3].
identification.notes: Microsoft has no name for this actor: 'Ferocious Kitten' does not appear in Microsoft's public naming map as retrieved on 2026-10-15 [S8]. MITRE tracks the group as G0137 and lists BITSAdmin and MarkiRAT as its software [S7]. Kaspersky says some TTPs resemble those of Domestic Kitten (C2 domains reused for years) and Rampant Kitten (Telegram execution hijacking and KeePass data theft). These are TTP similarities, not shared attribution [S1][S4]. Recorded Future's TAG-182 is a separate cluster with overlapping tooling. Keep it distinct from Ferocious Kitten [S6].

attribution.sponsor: Iran (vendor assessment). Kaspersky describes the actor as appearing to be based in Iran and conducting domestic surveillance [S1][S4]. Recorded Future assesses that the related TAG-182 cluster is almost certainly an element of Iran's state surveillance apparatus [S6].
attribution.confidence: Kaspersky's assessment rests on victimology and on similarity to other Iran-focused surveillance actors, and its reporting names no sponsoring Iranian organization [S1][S2]. Recorded Future says its TAG-182/Ferocious Kitten overlaps support an operational connection, but more evidence is needed to judge whether the two clusters are organizationally linked [S6]. No government attribution was found.
attribution.basis: Persian-language lures that depict anti-regime protests or resistance camps [S2]; payloads built for software popular in Iran (Telegram, Psiphon) [S2][S3]; long-term C2 reuse and Telegram hijacking similar to Domestic Kitten and Rampant Kitten [S1][S4]; overlapping BITS job strings, file-naming patterns and C2 configurations between TAG-182 and historical MarkiRAT activity [S6].

actors.objectives: Domestic surveillance of Persian speakers, especially people tied to opposition or anti-regime activity, including theft of credentials, keystrokes, clipboard content and files [S1][S2][S3]. Recorded Future assesses that TAG-182 also targets Iranians abroad [S6].

sectors: Users of censorship-circumvention tools (Psiphon, VPN apps) and Telegram
regions: Iranian diaspora / anti-government movements abroad (TAG-182, per Recorded Future) [S6]
targeting.notes: Kaspersky's victim set is Persian-speaking individuals who appear to be in Iran [S1]. Lures pose as images or videos of protests or resistance camps against the Iranian government [S2]. TAG-182 promotes its malicious downloads through Instagram posts and staged websites [S6]. No government, military or DIB victims are reported in the cited sources.

capabilities.summary: Initial access through spearphishing Office documents with malicious macros, disguised as images or videos [S2][S7]. MarkiRAT records keystrokes and clipboard content, transfers files and runs commands [S2]. Picus also lists screenshots, file-system searches for target file types and credential stores, and staged exfiltration over HTTP(S) [S9]. Some MarkiRAT variants hijack the Telegram and Chrome launchers to stay persistent [S2][S4]. One variant is a backdoored build of the Psiphon circumvention VPN [S3][S4]. The group uses Windows BITS (BITSAdmin) for downloads [S7][S6] and file masquerading such as right-to-left override [S7]. Kaspersky saw signs of Android implants (APK/DEX files hosted on C2) but obtained no samples [S4]. In 2026 TAG-182 spread MarkiRAT through fake Android apps posing as VPNs and media players, such as 'Pis2ray VPN', 'YEPlayer' and 'YEMPlayer', promoted mainly on Instagram [S6]. Secondary vendor write-ups say the group exploited MSHTML CVE-2021-40444 to deliver a PowerShell stealer [S9]. That claim is not confirmed in SafeBreach's primary reporting (see gaps) [S5].

Victim counts for the Kaspersky campaign are not available in the sources gathered.

implications.jipoe: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. STEP 1 (environment): The operational environment is personal Windows and Android devices of Persian-speaking users and the tools they rely on: Telegram, Chrome, Psiphon and sideloaded VPN or media apps [S2][S4][S6]. For DoD this matters mainly for personnel, partners, linguists or sources with Iranian ties, and for information-environment monitoring of Iranian domestic and diaspora populations. STEP 2 (effects): Iranian internet restrictions push targets toward circumvention tools, which the actor then trojanizes. Expect campaigns to follow censorship and connectivity events [S3][S6]. STEP 3 (threat model): The template is a Persian-language lure (protest imagery or a fake VPN or media app), then macro or sideload execution, then MarkiRAT with BITS downloads, then persistence through Telegram or Chrome launcher hijacking, then collection of keystrokes, clipboard and files [S2][S6][S7]. STEP 4 (COAs): MLCOA is continued surveillance of dissidents and diaspora through fake circumvention apps during unrest or after connectivity is restored [S6]. MDCOA is the same tooling turned against US-affiliated persons of Iranian heritage or partner-force personnel to collect contacts and credentials for counterintelligence targeting. That extension is an analytic inference not reported in the sources. Candidate indicators: BITS jobs pulling executables to user-writable paths; Telegram or Chrome shortcuts pointing to non-standard executables; Psiphon or 'Pis2ray'/'YEPlayer'/'YEMPlayer' binaries from unofficial sources; RTLO characters in attachment names; and macro-enabled Persian-language documents [S2][S6][S7].
implications.jcc2: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. (1) Situational awareness: This actor targets individuals, not networks, so DODIN telemetry is unlikely to see it. Awareness depends on vendor reporting (Kaspersky, Recorded Future) and on Force Protection and counterintelligence channels [S1][S6]. (2) Authorities: Activity against foreign nationals and diaspora falls mostly outside DoD cyber authorities. Coordinate with counterintelligence (AFOSI, DCSA) and with interagency partners for any US-person victims. (3) Mission assurance: Restrict sideloaded VPN and media apps on mobile devices used by linguists, partner liaisons and influence-operations personnel. Hunt for BITS abuse and Telegram/Chrome launcher tampering on any managed Windows endpoints [S6][S7]. (4) Coordination: Share indicators of fake circumvention apps with partners supporting Iranian information-environment operations, and track the unresolved TAG-182/Ferocious Kitten relationship rather than merging the clusters [S6].

provenance.importedSummary: Ferocious Kitten is an APT group that has been active against Persian-speaking individuals since 2015 and appears to be based in Iran. Although it has been active over a large timespan, the group has mostly operated under the radar until a lure document was uploaded to VirusTotal and was brought to public knowledge by researchers on Twitter. Subsequently, one of its implants was analyzed by a Chinese intelligence firm. Kaspersky then expanded some of the findings on the group and provided insights on additional variants. The malware dropped from the aforementioned document is dubbed MarkiRAT and is used to record keystrokes and clipboard content, provide file download and upload capabilities as well as the ability to execute arbitrary commands on the victims machine. Kaspersky were able to trace the implant back to at least 2015, along with variants intended to hijack the execution of the Telegram and Chrome applications as a persistence method. Interestingly, some of the TTPs used by this threat actor are reminiscent of other groups operating in the domain of dissident surveillance. For example, it used the same C2 domains across its implants for years, which was witnessed in the activity of Domestic Kitten. In the same vein, the Telegram execution hijacking technique observed in this campaign by Ferocious Kitten was also observed being used by Rampant Kitten, as covered by Check Point.

identification.summary: FireEye first identified this activity during a recent investigation at an organization in the financial industry. They identified the presence of a financially motivated threat group that they track as FIN1, whose activity at the organization dated back several years. The threat group deployed numerous malicious files and utilities, all of which were part of a malware ecosystem referred to as ‘Nemesis’ by the malware developer(s), and used this malware to access the victim environment and steal cardholder data. FIN1, which may be located in Russia or a Russian-speaking country based on language settings in many of their custom tools, is known for stealing data that is easily monetized from financial services organizations such as banks, credit unions, ATM operations, and financial transaction processing and financial business services companies.

FIN13 is a financially motivated threat actor that Mandiant has tracked since 2017. Mandiant describes it conducting long-term intrusions against organizations in Mexico to gather information and carry out fraudulent money transfers, rather than smash-and-grab ransomware [S1]. Mandiant reports that the group relies heavily on custom passive backdoors, web shells and tunnelers rather than frameworks such as Cobalt Strike, with a median dwell time of about 2.5 years [S1]. Sygnia separately tracks an overlapping cluster as Elephant Beetle (TG2003), which it says steals millions of dollars from finance and commerce organizations, mainly in Latin America [S2][S3].
identification.firstObserved: Mandiant: tracked since 2017, with activity going back as early as 2016 [S1]. Sygnia: had tracked Elephant Beetle for about two years when it published in January 2022 [S2][S3].
identification.notes: Mandiant name: FIN13 [S1]. Sygnia name: Elephant Beetle, also tracked as TG2003 [S2][S3]. Secondary reporting on Sygnia's research states that Sygnia noted similarities or overlaps with Mandiant's FIN13 [S3]; MITRE ATT&CK tracks the group as FIN13 (G1016) and the imported record lists Elephant Beetle and TG2003 as associated names [S7]. No Microsoft name for this actor was found in the sources gathered.

attribution.sponsor: None. Mandiant and Sygnia describe a financially motivated criminal actor; neither source makes a nation-state attribution [S1][S2].
attribution.confidence: Mandiant makes no nation-state or geographic attribution; it notes Spanish-language strings in the SHELLSWEEP web shell, the GASCAN fraud tool and targeted database artifacts [S1]. The FIN13 to Elephant Beetle linkage is stated by Sygnia as an overlap, not as an identity [S3].
attribution.basis: Mandiant incident-response data covering more than five years of intrusions [S1]; Sygnia incident-response engagements [S2][S3].

actors.objectives: Financial theft: long, quiet reconnaissance of victim finance systems followed by fraudulent transactions, including point-of-sale and ATM-related fraud [S1]. Sygnia reports the group hides many small fraudulent transactions among legitimate activity to avoid detection [S2][S3].

regions: Mexico (Mandiant observed FIN13 operating exclusively against Mexico-based organizations over five years of data) [S1]
United States (secondary reporting says US-based firms were also affected) [S3]
targeting.notes: Mandiant says victims were large organizations, several with annual revenue in the millions to billions of USD, and that targeting a single country is rare: only 2.6% of financially motivated actors it tracks do so [S1]. Mandiant data is Mexico-only, while Sygnia's Elephant Beetle reporting extends to wider Latin America and some US firms; these cluster boundaries are not identical [S1][S3].

capabilities.summary: Initial access is primarily through exploitation of internet-facing servers. Mandiant saw indications of WebLogic and Apache Tomcat exploitation, though it could not confirm the specific vulnerabilities [S1]. Secondary reporting on Sygnia's research lists four exploited flaws: CVE-2017-1000486 (PrimeFaces), CVE-2015-7450 (WebSphere), CVE-2010-5326 and EDB-ID-24963 (both SAP NetWeaver). It also describes a focus on legacy Java applications on Linux, especially WebSphere and WebLogic, and obfuscated WAR archives [S4]. Mandiant documents a large custom toolset: BLUEAGAVE (a PowerShell/Perl passive backdoor), SIXPACK (ASPX tunneler), SWEARJAR (Java backdoor using DNS TXT), MAILSLOT (email-based C2), HOTLANE, BUSTEDPIPE, PORTHOLE, CLOSEWATCH, SPINOFF, DRAWSTRING, NIGHTJAR, LATCHKEY and a trojanized KeePass. Its fraud tool GASCAN sends ISO 8583 payment messages [S1]. The group also uses public tools such as Mimikatz, ProcDump, Invoke-WMIExec/SMBExec, NMAP and GOBOT2, and operates on both Windows and Linux [S1]. Sygnia reports more than 80 unique tools and scripts [S2][S3]. At publication, Mandiant had not seen FIN13 deploy ransomware [S1].

implications.jipoe: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. STEP 1 (environment): Key terrain is internet-facing legacy Java application servers (WebLogic, WebSphere, Tomcat, SAP NetWeaver) and the internal finance systems behind them: payment switches, POS, ATM and treasury applications [S1][S4]. STEP 2 (effects): Unpatched, years-old CVEs remain viable entry points, and multi-year dwell (median about 2.5 years) means compromise may predate current baselines [S1][S4]. STEP 3 (threat model): Exploit a public-facing server, drop a web shell or passive backdoor, tunnel inward, steal credentials, run reconnaissance on finance applications, then inject fraudulent transactions hidden among legitimate ones [S1][S2]. STEP 4 (COAs): MLCOA is continued quiet financial fraud against large Latin American organizations, including their US-linked subsidiaries [S1][S3]. MDCOA is long-term access to a financial institution or payment processor that serves DoD personnel or partner-nation forces in the region, enabling large-scale fraud or data theft. Candidate indicators: new JSP, ASPX or PHP files on Java or IIS servers; processes listening on high ephemeral ports (for example 65510-65512); unencrypted HTTP POST beacons to paths like /cpl/api.php; DNS TXT C2; anomalous ISO 8583 traffic or bursts of small transactions [S1].
implications.jcc2: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. (1) Situational awareness: FIN13 targets commercial and financial entities rather than DoD networks, so relevance is mainly to mission partners, contractors and financial services supporting operations in the USSOUTHCOM and USNORTHCOM areas; track legacy Java-server exposure on DODIN-adjacent systems [S1][S4]. (2) Authorities: this is criminal activity, so response falls primarily to law enforcement and partner-nation authorities, not military cyber forces; DoD's role is defensive hardening and information sharing. (3) Mission assurance: multi-year dwell argues for compromise-assessment hunts on legacy application servers, not just patching [S1]. (4) Coordination: share indicators with DC3, the DIB CS program and partner-nation CERTs in Mexico and Latin America.

provenance.importedSummary: Since 2017, Mandiant has been tracking FIN13, an industrious and versatile financially motivated threat actor conducting long-term intrusions in Mexico with an activity timeframe stretching back as early as 2016. Although their operations continue through the present day, in many ways FIN13's intrusions are like a time capsule of traditional financial cybercrime from days past. Instead of today's prevalent smash-and-grab ransomware groups, FIN13 takes their time to gather information to perform fraudulent money transfers. Rather than relying heavily on attack frameworks such as Cobalt Strike, the majority of FIN13 intrusions involve heavy use of custom passive backdoors and tools to lurk in environments for the long haul.

identification.summary: China-based, PRC-linked actor that gains and holds long-term access to networks with minimal malware, relying on built-in OS tools and legitimate software such as a SoftEther VPN bridge. Microsoft first exposed it for targeting Taiwanese organizations [S1]. US agencies later tied it to Integrity Technology Group, a Beijing company that ran a botnet of over 260,000 compromised SOHO, IoT and network devices [S2][S3].
identification.firstObserved: Active since mid-2021 per Microsoft [S1]. The associated Raptor Train botnet dates to May 2020 per Lumen [S4]. The FBI-attributed botnet has operated since mid-2021 [S2].
identification.notes: Microsoft name: Flax Typhoon. Microsoft maps Storm-0919 and ETHEREAL PANDA to it [S6]. Lumen also lists RedJuliett (Recorded Future) as overlapping [S4]; this encyclopedia holds a separate RedJuliett record from your import. Flax Typhoon has no MITRE ATT&CK group page as of the 2026-09-23 data [S7].

attribution.sponsor: People's Republic of China. Integrity Technology Group (Yongxin Zhicheng), a publicly traded Beijing company, controlled the botnet infrastructure [S2]. OFAC sanctioned it for supporting Flax Typhoon computer network exploitation, citing use of Integrity Tech-linked infrastructure against multiple victims from summer 2022 to fall 2023 [S3].
attribution.confidence: Formal US government attribution through the FBI/CNMF/NSA joint advisory (Sep 2024) [S2] and OFAC designation (Jan 2025) [S3]. Microsoft attributes the 2023 Taiwan campaign to Flax Typhoon and describes the actor as China-based [S1].
attribution.basis: Microsoft telemetry [S1]; FBI court-authorized operation and analysis of botnet management infrastructure [S2]; Lumen Black Lotus Labs infrastructure analysis, including Tier 3 management activity during Chinese working hours [S4]; Treasury findings [S3].

actors.objectives: Espionage through long-term, low-noise access. Microsoft assesses that observed behavior suggests intent to perform espionage and maintain access across sectors, though it had not observed the actor act on final objectives in the 2023 campaign [S1]. The botnet gave the actor a proxy layer to hide its operations and a DDoS capability [S2].

regions: Southeast Asia, North America and Africa (smaller numbers of victims, per Microsoft)
United States (botnet-enabled targeting; thousands of US devices in the botnet)
targeting.notes: Sector and region data from Microsoft [S1]; US and military/DIB targeting from FBI statements and the joint advisory as reported [S2][S5]. Botnet devices were spread across North America, South America, Europe, Africa, Southeast Asia and Australia [S2].

capabilities.summary: Exploitation of known vulnerabilities in public-facing servers, then web shells such as China Chopper [S1]. Privilege escalation with Juicy Potato; credential theft with Mimikatz [S1]. Persistence by enabling RDP and replacing the Sticky Keys accessibility binary to launch Task Manager with SYSTEM privileges, plus a SoftEther VPN bridge renamed to mimic Windows components and installed as a service [S1]. Infrastructure: Raptor Train, a tiered botnet built on the Mirai-variant 'Nosedive' implant across SOHO routers, IP cameras, NAS and IoT devices [S2][S4].

implications.jipoe: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. STEP 1: In a Taiwan contingency, the cyberspace OE includes Taiwanese government and industrial networks and the global pool of compromised consumer and SOHO devices used as proxy terrain. STEP 2: A botnet of this scale lets adversary traffic appear to come from domestic residential and small-business addresses, which degrades geolocation-based attribution and blocklisting. STEP 3: The template is web shell, then privilege escalation, then RDP plus Sticky Keys, then a SoftEther VPN tunnel, then quiet access with no observed final action. STEP 4: MLCOA is persistent espionage access in Taiwanese and allied networks. MDCOA is using the botnet for DDoS against Taiwanese or US targets during a crisis while maintaining espionage footholds. Candidate indicators: new outbound SoftEther or VPN services masquerading as Windows binaries, changes to accessibility executables, and spikes in SOHO-sourced authentication attempts against DIB portals [S1][S2].
implications.jcc2: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. (1) Shared situational awareness should include botnet infrastructure intelligence, such as FBI and partner-shared C2 and node lists, so that defensive cyber forces can recognize proxy-sourced traffic. (2) Coordinate with allied partners, Taiwan especially, through established channels. Flax Typhoon victims are predominantly non-US, so DoD visibility depends on partner sharing. (3) Disruption precedents: the 2024 court-authorized FBI operation shows that domestic botnet takedown is a law-enforcement lead. DoD options against foreign-hosted tiers fall under separate authorities and require deconfliction. (4) DDoS readiness: JCC2 planning should include upstream mitigation coordination for public-facing DoD and DIB services.

provenance.importedSummary: Flax Typhoon is a Chinese state-sponsored threat actor that primarily targets organizations in Taiwan. They conduct espionage campaigns and focus on gaining and maintaining long-term access to networks using minimal malware. implications.jipoe: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. STEP 1: The cyberspace OE includes commercial logistics providers, rail and port operators, and the IoT cameras along supply routes into Ukraine and NATO's eastern flank. These are intelligence collection points for the adversary. STEP 2: Compromised cameras turn the physical terrain itself into adversary ISR, which affects OPSEC for movements. STEP 3: The template is password spraying or phishing against mail accounts, then mailbox permission changes for persistence, then collection on shipments and schedules. In parallel, mass compromise of exposed cameras. STEP 4: MLCOA is continued collection on aid logistics to inform Russian targeting and diplomacy. MDCOA is using collected movement data to cue sabotage or strikes on aid shipments or nodes. implications.jcc2: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. (1) Treat commercial partners' camera and mail exposure as part of force-protection planning for movements. (2) JCC2 situational awareness should take in partner and industry reporting on logistics-sector intrusions, since the victims are mostly private. (3) Authorities: hardening of commercial and allied camera networks is a partner-nation and owner responsibility. DoD influence is through contracts, requirements and liaison. (4) OPSEC: plan movement security assuming adversary visibility through compromised cameras on routes.

provenance.importedSummary: A 2015 report by F-Secure describe APT29 as: 'The Dukes are a well-resourced, highly dedicated and organized cyberespionage group that we believe has been working for the Russian Federation since at least 2008 to collect intelligence in support of foreign and security policy decision-making. The Dukes show unusual confidence in their ability to continue successfully compromising their targets, as well as in their ability to operate with impunity. The Dukes primarily target Western governments and related organizations, such as government ministries and agencies, political think tanks, and governmental subcontractors. Their targets have also included the governments of members of the Commonwealth of Independent States;Asian, African, and Middle Eastern governments;organizations associated with Chechen extremism;and Russian speakers engaged in the illicit trade of controlled substances and drugs. The Dukes are known to employ a vast arsenal of malware toolsets, which we identify as MiniDuke, CosmicDuke, OnionDuke, CozyDuke, CloudDuke, SeaDuke, HammerDuke, PinchDuke, and GeminiDuke. In recent years, the Dukes have engaged in apparently biannual large - scale spear - phishing campaigns against hundreds or even thousands of recipients associated with governmental institutions and affiliated organizations. These campaigns utilize a smash - and - grab approach involving a fast but noisy breakin followed by the rapid collection and exfiltration of as much data as possible.If the compromised target is discovered to be of value, the Dukes will quickly switch the toolset used and move to using stealthier tactics focused on persistent compromise and long - term intelligence gathering. This threat actor targets government ministries and agencies in the West, Central Asia, East Africa, and the Middle East; Chechen extremist groups; Russian organized crime; and think tanks. It is suspected to be behind the 2015 compromise of unclassified networks at the White House, Department of State, Pentagon, and the Joint Chiefs of Staff. The threat actor includes all of the Dukes tool sets, including MiniDuke, CosmicDuke, OnionDuke, CozyDuke, SeaDuke, CloudDuke (aka MiniDionis), and HammerDuke (aka Hammertoss). '

Frontier Blizzard is Microsoft's name for a Russia-origin actor. Microsoft maps it to Google/Mandiant's UNC5792 [S1]. Google Threat Intelligence Group (GTIG) describes UNC5792 as a suspected Russian espionage cluster. It hijacks Signal accounts by altering legitimate Signal group-invite pages so that a victim who scans the code links their account to a device the actor controls [S2][S3]. In 2026, US government reporting linked UNC5792 to a broader campaign against Signal and WhatsApp accounts of officials. Press accounts say the campaign has compromised thousands of messaging accounts [S5][S6][S7].
identification.firstObserved: Publicly reported by GTIG on 2025-02-19, which describes activity in the preceding 'recent months' without giving specific start dates [S2].
identification.notes: Microsoft name: Frontier Blizzard (origin Russia); the only other name Microsoft lists is UNC5792 [S1]. GTIG says UNC5792 partially overlaps with CERT-UA's UAC-0195 [S2][S4]. A partial overlap is not the same as identity, so do not merge UAC-0195 reporting wholesale. UNC4221 (CERT-UA UAC-0185) is a separate Russia-linked cluster. GTIG reported it together with UNC5792, and the 2026 US announcements also named it alongside UNC5792 [S2][S5][S6]; this profile does not merge its facts into Frontier Blizzard. No Microsoft narrative profile or blog post naming Frontier Blizzard was found.

attribution.sponsor: Russian Federation. Press coverage of the June 2026 US announcements says UNC5792 is associated with officers of the Russian Federal Security Service (FSB) Border Guards [S5][S6][S7].
attribution.confidence: GTIG (February 2025) called UNC5792 a 'suspected' Russian espionage cluster and gave no further confidence level [S2]. In June 2026 the FBI (in a public service announcement) and the State Department Rewards for Justice program tied UNC5792 to FSB Border Guards officers. This summary comes from press coverage; the primary US documents were not opened [S5][S6][S7]. Microsoft lists Frontier Blizzard's origin as Russia without public sponsor detail [S1].
attribution.basis: GTIG technical reporting on altered Signal invite pages and actor infrastructure [S2]. FBI PSA I-062626-PSA (2026-06-26), as reported by the press [S7]. State Department Rewards for Justice offer of up to $10 million, as reported by the press [S5][S6]. Microsoft naming mapping [S1].

actors.objectives: Espionage collection from secure messaging. Device linking gives the actor real-time copies of a victim's Signal messages [S2]. GTIG frames the wider Russian Signal campaign around wartime demand for Ukrainian military and government communications [S2][S3]. 2026 reporting describes collection against US and NATO government, diplomatic, defense and media targets [S5][S6].

targeting.notes: The 2025 reporting focuses on Ukrainian military users of Signal [S2][S3]. GTIG did not list UNC5792 victims individually. It described the general target pool for these Russian Signal operations as military personnel, politicians, journalists, activists and other at-risk groups, and assessed that the tactics would likely spread beyond Ukraine [S2][S3]. The 2026 target list (US officials, diplomats, NATO member-state officials, defense staff and journalists) comes from US government announcements as reported by the press [S5][S6].

capabilities.summary: UNC5792 does not exploit flaws in Signal's encryption. It abuses Signal's legitimate linked-devices feature: phishing delivers altered Signal group-invite pages, and the page's JavaScript redirect is replaced with an sgnl://linkdevice URI. A victim who scans the code links an actor-controlled device, which then receives the victim's messages in real time [S2][S3]. GTIG notes that device linking is a low-signature form of access: few detections exist for newly linked devices, so access can persist unnoticed [S2]. The actor's lookalike domains imitate Signal group and security pages (for example signal-group[.]site and signal-security[.]online) [S2]. In 2026 the FBI reported a tactic shift, as reported by the press. Operators now persuade targets to reveal their Signal Backup Recovery Key, which lets them restore a backup and read the full message history, in addition to verification codes and 2FA credentials [S7].

campaigns.name: Signal device-linking via altered group invites
campaigns.summary: GTIG reports that UNC5792 altered Signal group-invite pages to link victims' accounts to actor devices, chiefly targeting Ukrainian military users. Signal added device-linking warnings in response.

campaigns.name: FBI/CISA warning on messaging-app account takeover
