provenance.importedSummary: OilRig is an Iranian threat group operating primarily in the Middle East by targeting organizations in this region that are in a variety of different industries; however, this group has occasionally targeted organizations outside of the Middle East as well. It also appears OilRig carries out supply chain attacks, where the threat group leverages the trust relationship between organizations to attack their primary targets. OilRig is an active and organized threat group, which is evident based on their systematic targeting of specific organizations that appear to be carefully chosen for strategic purposes. Attacks attributed to this group primarily rely on social engineering to exploit the human rather than software vulnerabilities; however, on occasion this group has used recently patched vulnerabilities in the delivery phase of their attacks. The lack of software vulnerability exploitation does not necessarily suggest a lack of sophistication, as OilRig has shown maturity in other aspects of their operations. Such maturities involve: -Organized evasion testing used the during development of their tools. -Use of custom DNS Tunneling protocols for command and control (C2) and data exfiltration. -Custom web-shells and backdoors used to persistently access servers. OilRig relies on stolen account credentials for lateral movement. After OilRig gains access to a system, they use credential dumping tools, such as Mimikatz, to steal credentials to accounts logged into the compromised system. The group uses these credentials to access and to move laterally to other systems on the network. After obtaining credentials from a system, operators in this group prefer to use tools other than their backdoors to access the compromised systems, such as remote desktop and putty. OilRig also uses phishing sites to harvest credentials to individuals at targeted organizations to gain access to internet accessible resources, such as Outlook Web Access. Since at least 2014, an Iranian threat group tracked by FireEye as APT34 has conducted reconnaissance aligned with the strategic interests of Iran. The group conducts operations primarily in the Middle East, targeting financial, government, energy, chemical, telecommunications and other industries. Repeated targeting of Middle Eastern financial, energy and government organizations leads FireEye to assess that those sectors are a primary concern of APT34. The use of infrastructure tied to Iranian operations, timing and alignment with the national interests of Iran also lead FireEye to assess that APT34 acts on behalf of the Iranian government.

identification.summary: China-based espionage actor that Microsoft tracks as Heart Typhoon and that Mandiant/Google tracks as APT17 [S1][S2]. FireEye reported that APT17 had conducted network intrusions against the U.S. government, international law firms and information technology companies, and that it had used the BLACKCOFFEE malware since 2013 [S3]. In 2014-2015 the group hid encoded command-and-control (C2) addresses in Microsoft TechNet forum profiles and posts [S3]. In 2024 Italian firm TG Soft attributed spear-phishing campaigns against Italian companies and government entities, using a 9002 RAT variant, to APT17 [S9].
identification.firstObserved: The Hacker News says Mandiant (then FireEye) first documented APT17 in 2013 [S9]. FireEye says APT17 had used BLACKCOFFEE since 2013 [S3]. Symantec dates the related Hidden Lynx cluster to 2009 and links it to Operation Aurora (2009-2010) [S5][S6].
identification.notes: Microsoft lists HELIUM, AURORA PANDA, APT17, Hidden Lynx, ATG3, Red Typhoon, KAOS, TG-8153, SportsFans, DeputyDog and Tailgater as other names for Heart Typhoon [S1]. MITRE tracks the group as APT17 (G0025) [S2]. FireEye states that APT17 is also known as Deputy Dog [S3]. Symantec's Hidden Lynx is a broader cluster (an estimated 50-100 operators in two teams) that Symantec did not equate with APT17 in the sources reviewed here, so Hidden Lynx facts are kept separate below [S5][S6].

attribution.sponsor: People's Republic of China (assessed). FireEye calls APT17 a China-based threat group [S3]. In July 2019 the anonymous research group Intrusion Truth alleged that APT17 is run by the Jinan bureau of the Ministry of State Security (MSS) through contractors managed by alleged MSS officer Guo Lin [S7][S8].
attribution.confidence: FireEye 'assesses' that APT17 was behind the TechNet activity but gives no formal confidence level [S3]. The MSS Jinan link rests on Intrusion Truth's allegations, which press coverage and CERT-EU treat as unverified claims [S7][S8]. No U.S. government indictment or advisory naming APT17 was found in this research.
attribution.basis: Vendor technical reporting (FireEye/Microsoft joint TechNet investigation) [S3]; Intrusion Truth open-source identity research covering Guo Lin, Wang Qingwei and Zeng Xiaoyong, and Jinan front companies, plus code similarities to the ZoxRPC malware [S7][S8]; Microsoft and MITRE name mappings [S1][S2].

actors.objectives: Cyber-espionage against government, defense, legal and technology targets [S2][S3]. CFR reports that APT17 also targeted Chinese citizens for financial gain [S10]. Symantec assessed the related Hidden Lynx cluster as a hacker-for-hire operation that collects information for clients, while CrowdStrike's Dmitri Alperovitch argued it was closely tied to the Chinese government [S5].

sectors: Security vendors (Bit9, via the Hidden Lynx cluster)
regions: Global; 52 percent of Hidden Lynx targets were in the U.S. [S5]
targeting.notes: U.S. government, defense, law, IT, mining and NGO targeting is from MITRE [S2] and FireEye [S3]. Japanese media, manufacturing and government targeting is from FireEye's 2013 DeputyDog reporting, as covered by the press [S4]. Italian corporate and government targeting is from TG Soft, as covered by the press [S9]. Hidden Lynx figures apply to Symantec's broader cluster [S5].

capabilities.summary: Uses legitimate public sites as dead-drop resolvers: BLACKCOFFEE retrieved encoded C2 IPs that had been posted to TechNet profiles and forums [S3]. Used strategic web compromise (watering holes) with an Internet Explorer zero-day (CVE-2013-3893) in the 2013 DeputyDog campaign [S4]. In 2024 used spear-phishing with Office documents and links to a fake Skype for Business MSI hosted on a domain that imitated an Italian government site; the chain ran a VBS script and a Java archive that decrypted 9002 RAT shellcode [S9]. TG Soft describes 9002 RAT as modular, with traffic monitoring, screenshots, file enumeration, process management, command execution and diskless variants [S9]. In the related Hidden Lynx cluster, Symantec describes code-signing abuse after the Bit9 breach, plus the Moudoor and Naid trojans [S5][S6]. MITRE lists BLACKCOFFEE as APT17 software [S2].

campaigns.name: Operation Aurora (Hidden Lynx linkage)
campaigns.summary: Symantec links the Hidden Lynx cluster to Operation Aurora: the Naid trojan was used there, and Symantec says the group either carried out the attack or worked with the attackers [S5][S6]. The Hacker News notes that 9002 RAT (Hydraq/McRAT) was the tool used in Aurora [S9].

campaigns.name: VOHO watering hole / Bit9 compromise (Hidden Lynx)
campaigns.summary: According to Symantec as reported by the press, Hidden Lynx breached security firm Bit9 and signed malware with Bit9 keys after Bit9 software blocked attacks on U.S. defense contractors; Bit9 disclosed the breach in February 2013. The VOHO watering-hole campaign compromised about 4,000 machines [S5][S6].

campaigns.name: Operation DeputyDog
campaigns.summary: Starting 19 August 2013, watering-hole attacks compromised at least three major Japanese media sites and served an IE zero-day (CVE-2013-3893) against manufacturing, government and media targets. FireEye linked the actor to the Bit9 compromise through a shared IP address [S4].

campaigns.name: TechNet C2 obfuscation
campaigns.summary: FireEye and Microsoft found that a BLACKCOFFEE variant retrieved encoded C2 IPs from TechNet profiles and forum posts. They sinkholed the activity by encoding a sinkhole IP into the posts, and released IOCs and signatures in May 2015 [S3][S10].

campaigns.name: Intrusion Truth exposure
campaigns.summary: Intrusion Truth alleged that APT17 is run by the MSS Jinan bureau and named Guo Lin, Wang Qingwei and Zeng Xiaoyong [S7][S8].

campaigns.summary: On 24 June and 2 July 2024, spear-phishing delivered a fake Skype for Business package that dropped a 9002 RAT variant on Italian companies and government entities; TG Soft attributed the activity to APT17 [S9].

diamond.adversary: PRC-based operators tracked as Heart Typhoon/APT17 [S1][S3]. Intrusion Truth alleges MSS Jinan bureau management through Jinan front companies [S7][S8].
diamond.capability: BLACKCOFFEE [S2][S3]; 9002 RAT variant [S9]; IE zero-day CVE-2013-3893 [S4]; Moudoor/Naid and stolen code-signing keys in the related Hidden Lynx cluster [S5][S6].
diamond.infrastructure: Legitimate public sites (TechNet) used as dead-drop resolvers for C2 [S3]; compromised Japanese media sites as watering holes and a Hong Kong payload host [S4]; a look-alike Italian government domain [S9].
diamond.victim: U.S. government, defense, law and IT organizations [S2][S3]; Japanese media, manufacturing and government organizations [S4]; Italian companies and government entities [S9].
diamond.socioPolitical: Intelligence collection that serves PRC interests; Intrusion Truth alleges MSS tasking [S7][S8]. Symantec's hacker-for-hire framing of Hidden Lynx is disputed [S5].
diamond.technology: Windows endpoints and Internet Explorer [S4]; user trust in collaboration software (Skype for Business) [S9]; web forums used for C2 resolution [S3].

gaps: No Microsoft Threat Intelligence publication describing activity under the Heart Typhoon name was found; the Microsoft name rests on Microsoft's naming mapping [S1]. learn.microsoft.com could not be fetched.
The Hidden Lynx/APT17 relationship is asserted by Microsoft's alias list [S1] but is not detailed in the sources reviewed; Symantec's cluster is broader and may include other actors.
Intrusion Truth's MSS Jinan attribution is unverified, and no U.S. government indictment, sanction or advisory naming APT17 was found.
The primary reports could not be opened: TG Soft (2024), Symantec's Hidden Lynx white paper, FireEye's DeputyDog blog, and Intrusion Truth's posts. Their details rely on secondary coverage.
Activity after 2024 and current infrastructure are unknown.

implications.jipoe: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. STEP 1: Key terrain includes widely visited public websites (news, forum and government look-alike domains) that can serve as watering holes or dead-drop resolvers, and user endpoints at government, defense, legal and IT organizations [S2][S3][S4][S9]. STEP 2: C2 hidden in legitimate sites blends with normal traffic and weakens IP blocklists [S3]. STEP 3: Observed templates are a watering hole with a browser zero-day leading to a RAT [S4], and spear-phishing with a fake software installer leading to MSI, VBS, JAR and in-memory 9002 RAT [S9]. STEP 4: MLCOA is spear-phishing with trusted-software lures against government and defense-adjacent organizations to deploy modular RATs for espionage [S9]. MDCOA is a supply-chain or code-signing compromise of a security or IT vendor, as in the Hidden Lynx Bit9 case, to deliver trusted-signed malware into defense networks [S5][S6]. Candidate indicators: endpoints fetching forum or profile pages and then contacting unrelated IPs; MSI installers that spawn wscript and java; unsigned 'Skype for Business' packages from non-Microsoft domains [S3][S9].
implications.jcc2: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. Situational awareness: correlate dead-drop-resolver patterns and look-alike government domains across DODIN and partner feeds [S3][S9]. Authorities: the TechNet sinkhole was a private-sector (FireEye/Microsoft) action [S3], so disruption of public-platform abuse likely depends on coordination with platform owners rather than military action alone. Mission assurance: prioritize monitoring and patch speed on defense-contractor and legal-support enclaves that hold program data [S2][S3]. Coordination: the actor's victims span allied nations (Japan, Italy) [S4][S9], which supports sharing indicators with partner CERTs; attribution to the MSS remains unofficial [S7].

This threat actor targets Uighurs—a minority ethnic group located primarily in northwestern China—and devices from Chinese mobile phone manufacturer Xiaomi, for espionage purposes.

China-based cyber-espionage actor that Microsoft tracks as Hexagon Typhoon and maps to APT12, NUMBERED PANDA, Calc Team, DNS-Calc, HYDROGEN, Red Anubis and HORDE [S1]. MITRE ATT&CK describes APT12 as a group attributed to China that has targeted media outlets, high-tech companies and multiple governments [S4]. Mandiant reported that APT12 compromised the New York Times in October 2012 and in August 2014 ran spear-phishing campaigns against Taiwanese government organizations, with possibly related activity against technology firms in Taiwan and Japan [S2]. Mandiant also documented a repeated pattern: after public exposure, the group paused briefly and then retooled [S2]. FireEye observed renewed, retooled activity in May 2013 [S10], and Zscaler reported a suspected IXESHE-linked watering-hole campaign against Taiwanese government networks in late 2016, while stopping short of confirming APT12 [S11].
identification.firstObserved: Trend Micro reported the IXESHE campaign active since at least July 2009 against East Asian targets [S6]; MITRE associates Ixeshe malware with APT12 [S4]. Arbor Networks (as reported by Mandiant) dated RIPTIDE/Etumbot campaigns to March 2011 [S2].
identification.notes: Microsoft name: Hexagon Typhoon. Microsoft lists HYDROGEN, NUMBERED PANDA, Calc Team, Red Anubis, APT12, DNS-Calc and HORDE as other names [S1]. MITRE tracks the group as APT12 (G0005) with associated names IXESHE, DynCalc, Numbered Panda and DNSCALC [S4]. Mandiant uses APT12 and lists 'Calc Team' as an alias [S3]. MISP Galaxy lists BRONZE GLOBE (Secureworks), BeeBus, Group 22 and Crimson Iron as synonyms [S8]. Do not confuse this actor with APT5 / Mulberry Typhoon (MANGANESE). The imported summary text in this record described APT5 and has been replaced.

attribution.sponsor: People's Republic of China. Mandiant says APT12 is 'believed to be a cyber espionage group thought to have links to the Chinese People's Liberation Army' [S2][S3]. MITRE records the group as attributed to China [S4], and Microsoft lists its origin as China [S1].
attribution.confidence: Mandiant's PLA link is hedged ('believed to be', 'thought to have links') and does not name a specific unit [S2][S3]. FireEye's Ned Moran said the company was 'almost certain' the 2013 retooled activity came from the same group that attacked the New York Times [S10]. Zscaler explicitly did not confirm APT12 for the 2016 CNACOM campaign, citing only 'strong reasons for suspicion' [S11]. MISP Galaxy, citing CFR data, records China as the suspected state sponsor with an attribution-confidence value of 50 [S8]. No government indictment or formal government attribution naming APT12 or Hexagon Typhoon was found in the sources gathered.
attribution.basis: Vendor technical reporting from Mandiant/FireEye on malware families, delivery documents and Taiwan-focused targeting [S2][S3][S10]; Trend Micro IXESHE research [S6]; CrowdStrike and FireEye reporting cited by MITRE [S4][S5][S7]; Zscaler malware-similarity analysis for 2016 activity [S11]; Microsoft's naming map [S1].

actors.objectives: Cyber espionage consistent with broader PRC goals, especially PRC self-interest regarding Taiwan, according to Mandiant [S2][S3]. The New York Times intrusion coincided with the paper's reporting on the wealth of Premier Wen Jiabao's relatives, pointing to intelligence collection on media coverage of the PRC leadership [S9][S2]. 2013 targeting of an organization that shapes international finance and economic policy suggests economic-policy collection as well [S10].

sectors: Government (including Taiwanese government ministries and networks) [S2][S6][S11]
regions: East Asia (IXESHE targeting since at least July 2009) [S6]
targeting.notes: The August 2014 HIGHTIDE campaign targeted multiple Taiwanese government organizations between 22 and 28 August 2014, with lures sent from apparently valid but compromised Taiwanese government accounts [S2]. Related THREEBYTE and WATERSPOUT activity hit a Taiwanese technology company and a Japanese high-technology company, but Mandiant did not firmly attribute those two campaigns to APT12 [S2]. The 2016 CNACOM watering hole used a compromised Taiwanese public-service website to deliver an IXESHE variant to Taiwanese government targets; Zscaler's attribution to APT12 is suspected only [S11].

capabilities.summary: Spear-phishing with weaponized Word and PDF attachments exploiting Office, Adobe Reader and Flash vulnerabilities (Trend Micro lists CVE-2009-4324, CVE-2009-0927, CVE-2011-0609 and CVE-2011-0611; Mandiant lists CVE-2012-0158 for 2014) [S2][S4][S6]. The group sends lures from compromised but legitimate accounts [S2][S3]. Trend Micro reported IXESHE C2 using dynamic DNS and previously compromised servers [S6]. Custom HTTP backdoors include RIPTIDE (Etumbot to Arbor), a proxy-aware backdoor with RC4-encrypted C2; its modified successor HIGHTIDE; and THREEBYTE and WATERSPOUT, which Mandiant says are possibly related [S2][S3]. It also used Ixeshe, Aumlib and the HTRAN connection-proxy tool [S4][S6][S10]. Per CrowdStrike reporting cited by MITRE, it derived C2 ports from IP octets ('DNS calculation') and used blogs and WordPress for C2 [S4][S5]. The group retools rapidly after disclosure: network-protocol changes to Aumlib and Ixeshe in 2013 to evade IDS signatures [S10], and RIPTIDE protocol and string changes after the June 2014 Arbor report [S2]. Suspected 2016 activity added strategic web compromise with a CVE-2016-0189 Internet Explorer exploit [S11].

campaigns.name: IXESHE campaign begins

campaigns.name: CNACOM strategic web compromise (suspected)
campaigns.summary: From 7 Nov 2016 an iframe injected into a major Taiwanese public-service website's registration page served a CVE-2016-0189 exploit delivering an IXESHE variant to Taiwanese government targets; Zscaler suspects but does not confirm APT12.

diamond.adversary: PRC-based espionage operators that Mandiant believes have links to the PLA; Microsoft calls the group Hexagon Typhoon and MITRE tracks it as APT12 [S1][S2][S4].
diamond.capability: Exploit documents (CVE-2012-0158 and Adobe/Flash CVEs); IE exploit CVE-2016-0189 in suspected 2016 activity; RIPTIDE, HIGHTIDE, THREEBYTE, WATERSPOUT, Ixeshe and Aumlib backdoors; HTRAN proxying; rapid retooling after disclosure [S2][S4][S6][S10][S11].
diamond.infrastructure: Hard-coded HTTP C2 servers, including direct-IP C2 and dynamic-DNS domains [S2][S6]; previously compromised servers used as C2 [S6]; compromised legitimate email accounts used to send lures [S2]; blogs and WordPress used for C2, with ports derived by DNS calculation [S4][S5]; a compromised Taiwanese public-service website used as a watering hole in suspected 2016 activity [S11].
diamond.victim: Taiwanese government ministries and networks, journalists and media (New York Times), defense contractors, finance/economic-policy organizations, telecommunications, and high-tech and electronics firms in Taiwan and Japan [S2][S3][S6][S9][S10][S11].
diamond.socioPolitical: Collection that supports PRC strategic goals, especially regarding Taiwan, and intelligence on foreign media coverage of PRC leadership [S2][S3][S9].
diamond.technology: Unpatched Microsoft Office and Adobe client software on Windows endpoints, plus trust in email from known colleagues [S2][S4].

gaps: No vendor or government reporting naming APT12/Hexagon Typhoon after the suspected December 2016 Zscaler CNACOM report was found in the searches run; current activity level, tooling and any re-designation are unknown [S11].
Microsoft has published no actor profile or blog content for Hexagon Typhoon that was found; only the naming map supports the Microsoft name [S1].

Primary documents not opened (hosts unreachable from this environment): CrowdStrike 'Whois Numbered Panda' [S5], Trend Micro IXESHE white paper [S6], FireEye 'Survival of the Fittest' [S7], Zscaler CNACOM blog [S11], TechCrunch and PCWorld articles [S9][S10], CFR APT12 entry, Secureworks BRONZE GLOBE profile and Arbor 'Illuminating the Etumbot APT Backdoor'. Claims from these rely on search-result excerpts or MITRE/Mandiant citations.

2013 press coverage of the New York Times breach attributed it to 'Chinese hackers' generally; the APT12 label comes from Mandiant's later 2014 reporting [S2][S9]. The original NYT article and Mandiant engagement details were not reviewed.
PLA link is a hedged vendor assessment (Mandiant). No specific PLA unit or MSS/contractor tie is public in the sources gathered, and no government attribution was found.
2016 CNACOM attribution to APT12 is suspicion based on targeting and malware similarity only [S11]; secondary coverage gives the sandbox-escape CVE inconsistently (CVE-2015-0116 vs CVE-2015-0016).

Alias boundary issue: MISP Galaxy's APT12 entry lists TG-2754 with the same identifier as BRONZE GLOBE [S8], but this encyclopedia maps TG-2754 to Mulberry Typhoon (APT5). Needs reconciling against Secureworks' own profiles.
THREEBYTE and WATERSPOUT campaigns were not positively attributed to APT12 by Mandiant [S2].
Aliases BeeBus, Group 22, Crimson Iron, Poisoned Flight and IXESHE-as-actor come from aggregator data (MISP) [S8], not from vendor reports reviewed here.

implications.jipoe: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. STEP 1 (OE): Key terrain is user endpoints running Office and PDF readers, and the email trust relationships between government personnel, especially in Taiwan and Japan and partner organizations that work with them [S2]. STEP 2 (effects): Because email arrives from compromised colleague accounts, sender-reputation filtering is weakened. The group's quick retooling after disclosure shortens the shelf life of published signatures [S2]. STEP 3 (adversary template): Spear-phish (or, in suspected 2016 activity, a watering hole on a government-used website filtering for target IP ranges [S11]) with an exploit document from a compromised trusted account, then an HTTP backdoor (RIPTIDE/HIGHTIDE-class) with RC4-encrypted C2 or DNS-calculated ports, then document collection; HTRAN can be used to hide C2 origin [S2][S4][S6]. STEP 4: MLCOA is continued spear-phishing espionage against Taiwan-focused government, defense-industrial and media targets [S2][S3]. MDCOA is a renewed or rebranded campaign against US and partner organizations that support Taiwan, using new tooling released immediately after any public exposure [S2]. Candidate indicators: injected iframes on government-used websites serving IE exploits [S11]; Word documents exploiting CVE-2012-0158 or newer Office flaws; executables dropped as word.exe or winword.exe in user Temp directories; HTTP beacons with anomalous User-Agent/URI patterns to direct IPs or dynamic-DNS domains; C2 ports that look computed from IP octets [S2][S4][S5].
implications.jcc2: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. (1) Situational awareness: public reporting on this actor stops in 2016 (suspected only) in the sources gathered [S11], so treat any detection as a prompt to check current vendor reporting rather than to rely on 2014 IOCs [S2]. (2) Authorities: activity traced to commercial media or partner-nation government networks lies outside DoD defensive authorities and needs interagency and partner coordination [S2]. (3) Mission assurance: phishing from compromised partner accounts threatens DODIN users who correspond with Taiwan and Japan counterparts; prioritize patching Office and PDF readers and inspecting attachments [S2][S4]. (4) Coordination: share retooling observations quickly with partners, because Mandiant and FireEye report the actor changes tools and protocols within weeks to months of disclosure [S2][S10].

provenance.importedSummary: We have observed one APT group, which we call APT5, particularly focused on telecommunications and technology companies. More than half of the organizations we have observed being targeted or breached by APT5 operate in these sectors. Several times, APT5 has targeted organizations and personnel based in Southeast Asia. APT5 has been active since at least 2007. It appears to be a large threat group that consists of several subgroups, often with distinct tactics and infrastructure. APT5 has targeted or breached organizations across multiple industries, but its focus appears to be on telecommunications and technology companies, especially information about satellite communications. APT5 targeted the network of an electronics firm that sells products for both industrial and military applications. The group subsequently stole communications related to the firm’s business relationship with a national military, including inventories and memoranda about specific products they provided. In one case in late 2014, APT5 breached the network of an international telecommunications company. The group used malware with keylogging capabilities to monitor the computer of an executive who manages the company’s relationships with other telecommunications companies

identification.summary: It was observed that a mobile network threat actor designated as ‘HiddenArt’ actively sustains a capacity to remotely access the personal devices of targeted individuals around the world on an ongoing basis. Since detecting this threat actor, periodic reconnaissance activities were observed in at least 7 target mobile networks around the world and given the wide geographic distribution of these targeted mobile operators, it is probable that the threat actor is active on a global scale.

Houken is a Chinese state-sponsored threat actor that exploits zero-day vulnerabilities in Ivanti Cloud Services Appliance devices to gain initial access to critical infrastructure networks, particularly in France. The group employs a sophisticated rootkit alongside open-source tools, primarily developed by Chinese-speaking authors, to maintain persistence and control over compromised systems. Houken is suspected to operate as an initial access broker, selling footholds in targeted networks to other threat actors for further exploitation.

Houndstooth Typhoon is Microsoft's name for a China-origin threat actor. Microsoft's public naming map links it to HASSIUM (its former Microsoft name), CrowdStrike's DRAGNET PANDA, and the labels 'isoon' and 'deepclif' [S1][S2]. The 'isoon' label points to the Chengdu-registered PRC security contractor i-Soon (Anxun Information Technology / Sichuan Anxun). Reporting describes i-Soon as an APT-for-hire contractor serving the Ministry of Public Security (MPS) [S3][S5]. A February 2024 leak exposed i-Soon's internal documents, tools and target lists [S3][S4][S5]. In March 2025 US prosecutors charged i-Soon executives and employees, together with two MPS officers [S6][S7][S10].
identification.firstObserved: CrowdStrike reports that DRAGNET PANDA has been active since at least 2015 [S9]. The 2025 US indictment covers i-Soon intrusion activity from about 2016 through 2023 [S6][S10].
identification.notes: Microsoft publishes the naming but, in the sources found, no narrative profile of Houndstooth Typhoon. Its activity therefore has to be read through what other vendors report on DRAGNET PANDA and on i-Soon. Do not assume those clusters are identical [S1][S2][S9]. Keep the cluster boundary in mind: ESET assesses that its FishMonger cluster (Earth Lusca / Aquatic Panda) is operated by I-SOON [S8], but Microsoft maps AQUATIC PANDA to Charcoal Typhoon, not to Houndstooth Typhoon [S1]. SentinelOne notes that the leak suggests i-Soon was behind activity previously attributed to several different named threat actors [S3].

attribution.sponsor: People's Republic of China. According to coverage of the March 2025 indictment, i-Soon carried out intrusions at the direction of, or for sale to, the MPS and the Ministry of State Security (MSS) [S6][S10]. In some cases it hacked first and then tried to sell the stolen data [S10].
attribution.confidence: Microsoft assigns China as the origin of Houndstooth Typhoon but publishes no confidence statement in the naming map [S1]. US prosecutors made charging allegations (not convictions) against i-Soon personnel and two MPS officers [S6][S7]. ESET assesses with high confidence that FishMonger conducted Operation FishMedley and states that it independently determined FishMonger is operated by I-SOON. That is a vendor assessment about the FishMonger cluster [S8].
attribution.basis: Microsoft's naming map [S1]; the February 2024 i-Soon document leak, whose authenticity and source were not independently confirmed although it matched prior reporting [S3][S4][S5]; press coverage of the March 2025 DOJ indictment [S6][S7][S10]; ESET research [S8]; CrowdStrike's DRAGNET PANDA profile [S9].

actors.objectives: Intelligence collection for PRC security services. Targets include dissidents, critics, religious minorities and media, alongside foreign-government espionage [S6][S9][S10]. SentinelOne describes i-Soon as a company that competes for low-value hacking contracts from many government agencies [S3]. Press coverage of the indictment says i-Soon charged MSS and MPS customers roughly $10,000 to $75,000 per compromised email inbox and worked with at least 43 MSS or MPS bureaus [S10].

sectors: Foreign government ministries, including foreign affairs ministries [S6][S10]
US federal and state government agencies [S10]
Defense / intelligence (the Defense Intelligence Agency is cited as a target) [S6]
Dissidents and critics of the PRC; Tibetan groups [S6][S9]
regions: Asia: multiple governments [S10]; India, Thailand, Vietnam and South Korea per the leaked data [S5]
targeting.notes: Victim lists come from three different evidence bases: the leak [S3][S5], the indictment [S6][S10] and the CrowdStrike DRAGNET PANDA profile [S9]. None of them is attributed by Microsoft to Houndstooth Typhoon specifically. The FishMedley victims ESET reported in 2022 (governments, NGOs, Catholic charities and think tanks in Taiwan, Thailand, Hungary, Turkey, France and the US) belong to ESET's FishMonger cluster and are kept separate here [S8].

capabilities.summary: According to the leaked i-Soon documents, the company offered: remote access trojans for Windows x64/x86 with keylogging, remote shell, registry and service management, and system reconnaissance; a Twitter/X account tool that can obtain the account email and phone number, read private messages and post as the victim; and malware with command-and-control infrastructure [S4][S5]. Some leaked records show custom hardware devices built for stealing data from victim networks [S4]. Indictment coverage stresses email-inbox compromise sold to MSS and MPS customers [S10]. ESET reports that the FishMonger cluster, which it ties to I-SOON, used ShadowPad, SodaMaster and Spyder implants [S8].

campaigns.name: DRAGNET PANDA activity begins

campaigns.summary: Per coverage of the US indictment, i-Soon hacked dissidents, a New York-based newspaper critical of the CCP, a large US religious organization, Asian foreign ministries, and US federal and state agencies. Some of this work was tasked by MPS officers.

campaigns.name: Operation FishMedley (ESET FishMonger cluster)
campaigns.summary: ESET reports that FishMonger, which it says is operated by I-SOON, compromised seven organizations in Taiwan, Thailand, Hungary, Turkey, France and the US using ShadowPad, SodaMaster and Spyder. Microsoft maps the related Aquatic Panda name to Charcoal Typhoon.

campaigns.summary: Internal i-Soon documents were posted to GitHub, exposing tools, hardware and target lists; the leaked material names governments including India, Thailand, Vietnam and South Korea, and NATO.

campaigns.name: US indictment of i-Soon personnel and MPS officers
campaigns.summary: Charges were unsealed against eight i-Soon employees, including CEO Wu Haibo and COO Chen Cheng, and against MPS officers Wang Liyu and Sheng Jing, for conspiracy to commit computer intrusions and wire fraud.

diamond.adversary: i-Soon (Anxun), a Chengdu-registered PRC contractor serving the MPS and MSS; named executives Wu Haibo (CEO) and Chen Cheng (COO); MPS officers Wang Liyu and Sheng Jing named as tasking officials [S3][S6][S10]. Microsoft tracks it as Houndstooth Typhoon [S1].
diamond.capability: Windows RATs, a social-media account takeover tool, custom hardware for data theft, and email-inbox compromise for hire [S4][S5][S10]. ShadowPad, SodaMaster and Spyder in the ESET FishMonger cluster [S8].
diamond.infrastructure: Malware command-and-control infrastructure described in the leaked documents [S4]. Specific infrastructure indicators were not obtained for this record.
diamond.victim: Dissidents, religious organizations, media, Asian foreign ministries, US federal and state agencies, and NATO and several Asian governments named in the leaked data [S3][S5][S6][S10].
diamond.socioPolitical: PRC domestic-security priorities (dissidents, Tibetan groups, religious minorities, critical media) combined with foreign-government intelligence. Delivered through a commercial contracting market that sells stolen access and data to many security-service bureaus [S3][S9][S10].
diamond.technology: Email accounts, Windows endpoints and social-media accounts are the main technical surfaces described [S4][S5][S10].

gaps: Microsoft has not published a narrative Houndstooth Typhoon profile in the sources found. The only Microsoft evidence is the naming map entry (HASSIUM, DRAGNET PANDA, isoon, deepclif) [S1].

Cluster boundary is unresolved. Microsoft maps 'isoon' to Houndstooth Typhoon but AQUATIC PANDA to Charcoal Typhoon, while ESET and the FBI tie FishMonger / Aquatic Panda to I-SOON [S1][S8]. Which i-Soon operations Microsoft counts as Houndstooth Typhoon is unknown.
No public source was found that explicitly links CrowdStrike's DRAGNET PANDA to i-Soon. The linkage rests on Microsoft's mapping [S1][S9].
The meaning and origin of the 'deepclif' label is unknown.

Primary documents were not opened: the DOJ indictment and press release, the FBI wanted notices, and the full SentinelOne, ESET and CrowdStrike pages (fetch blocked). Indictment details rely on press coverage.
The authenticity of the 2024 leak and the identity of the leaker are not confirmed [S3].
No Houndstooth Typhoon infrastructure indicators, CVEs or recent (2025-2026) activity were found.

implications.jipoe: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. STEP 1: Key terrain is email accounts, Windows endpoints and social-media accounts of government, defense-intelligence, media and diaspora-adjacent personnel, including foreign ministries of Asian partners and NATO [S3][S5][S6][S10]. STEP 2: A contractor model with many customer bureaus produces broad, opportunistic, volume-driven targeting. Sellable inbox access is the payoff [S3][S10]. STEP 3: The doctrinal template is account or endpoint compromise, then a RAT with keylogging and remote shell, then mailbox and message collection, then sale or delivery of the data to MPS or MSS customers [S5][S10]. STEP 4: MLCOA is continued mailbox compromise of partner-nation foreign ministries and US agencies for resale to security services. MDCOA is harvesting of partner or NATO communications that exposes coalition planning or personnel. Candidate indicators: anomalous mailbox access or forwarding rules on official accounts, unauthorized sign-ins to social-media accounts, and RAT behaviour (keylogging, new services or registry changes) on Windows hosts [S5][S10].
implications.jcc2: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. (1) Situational awareness: track partner-nation and NATO reporting, because the leak shows coalition partners were targeted [S3][S5]. (2) Authorities: the actor is a commercial contractor indicted by DOJ [S6], so coordinate with law-enforcement and intelligence partners before any response actions. (3) Mission assurance: prioritize identity and email hardening for personnel in intelligence-linked roles, given the reported DIA targeting [S6]. (4) Coordination: overlapping vendor names (Houndstooth Typhoon, Charcoal Typhoon, FishMonger, Aquatic Panda) can split reporting. Correlate across names in JCC2 rather than merging them [S1][S8].

Hunt3r Kill3rs is a newly emerged threat group claiming expertise in cyber operations, including ICS breaches and web application vulnerabilities exploitation. They have discussed using Java fuzzing in their exploits and have made unverified claims of joint attacks with other threat actors.

We have investigated their intrusions since 2013 and have been battling them nonstop over the last year at several large telecommunications and technology companies. The determination of this China-based adversary is truly impressive: they are like a dog with a bone. HURRICANE PANDA's preferred initial vector of compromise and persistence is a China Chopper webshell – a tiny and easily obfuscated 70 byte text file that consists of an ‘eval()’ command, which is then used to provide full command execution and file upload/download capabilities to the attackers. This script is typically uploaded to a web server via a SQL injection or WebDAV vulnerability, which is often trivial to uncover in a company with a large external web presence. Once inside, the adversary immediately moves on to execution of a credential theft tool such as Mimikatz (repacked to avoid AV detection). If they are lucky to have caught an administrator who might be logged into that web server at the time, they will have gained domain administrator credentials and can now roam your network at will via ‘net use’ and ‘wmic’ commands executed through the webshell terminal.

IcePeony is a China-nexus APT group that has been active since at least 2023, targeting government agencies, academic institutions, and political organizations in countries such as India, Mauritius, and Vietnam. They primarily employ SQL injection techniques to exploit vulnerabilities in publicly accessible web servers, subsequently installing web shells or executing malware like IceCache to facilitate credential theft. IcePeony operates under harsh work conditions, potentially adhering to the 996 working hour system, and shows a particular interest in the governments of Indian Ocean countries. Their activities suggest alignment with China's national interests, possibly related to maritime strategy.

Long-running cyber-espionage actor tracked as Inception / Inception Framework (Blue Coat, Symantec, Palo Alto Networks Unit 42) and Cloud Atlas (Kaspersky, Check Point, F.A.C.C.T., Positive Technologies) [S1][S2][S4][S5]. It relies on spear-phishing with weaponized Office documents, layered script-based implants and command and control over legitimate cloud services [S1][S3][S5]. In December 2014 Kaspersky assessed that Cloud Atlas represents a rebirth of the RedOctober operation that it exposed in 2013 [S4]. Check Point reported that after February 2022 its targeting narrowed to Russia, Belarus and conflict-affected parts of Ukraine and Moldova [S2], and Kaspersky reported that more than 80% of 2024 VBCloud targets were in Russia [S3].
identification.firstObserved: Active since at least 2014 per Unit 42 [S1] and Symantec, as reported by Security Affairs (since at least May 2014) [S6]. Kaspersky saw the first Cloud Atlas attacks in August 2014 and links the actor to RedOctober, which it exposed in 2013 [S4].
identification.notes: No Microsoft name was identified for this actor in the sources gathered. Brandefense lists the aliases Inception Framework, Blue Odin, Cloud Atlas, Clean Ursa, ATK116, G0100 and OXYGEN [S9]. MITRE tracks it as Inception (G0100) [S10]. Kaspersky's RedOctober link rests on a shared compression method, compiler setup and overlapping targets in Russia, Kazakhstan and Belarus. It is a vendor assessment, not proof of the same operator [S4]. Palo Alto Networks noted in 2014 that both the Inception and Cloud Atlas campaigns used CloudMe for command and control [S5]. Sources disagree on whether Blue Coat or Symantec coined the name 'Inception Framework' [S9].

attribution.confidence: No sponsor was identified in the open sources gathered. The Record's coverage of F.A.C.C.T.'s December 2023 reporting describes the group as state-backed but names no sponsoring country [S7]. Security Affairs, reporting on Symantec and Akamai research, describes Inception as nation-state-backed without naming the state [S6]. No government attribution was found.
attribution.basis: Vendor reporting covers tradecraft and targeting but names no sponsoring state [S1][S2][S7]. Since 2022 the targeting has centred on Russia and Belarus [S2][S3]. Kaspersky's RedOctober lineage assessment rests on code and target overlap [S4].

actors.objectives: Strategic intelligence collection against government, diplomatic and strategic-industry targets [S4][S5][S9]. The tooling is built for reconnaissance, system profiling and document theft [S1][S3]. Brandefense characterizes the goal as collection of diplomatic communications, government documents and related research [S9].

sectors: Executives in oil, finance and engineering; military officers; government officials [S5][S9]
Agro-industrial enterprises and state-owned research organizations [S7]
Defense sector (Russia, 2025, per Positive Technologies coverage) [S8]
Energy, defense, aerospace, research and media organizations [S9]
regions: Russia-controlled or contested areas of Ukraine and Moldova (2022) [S2]
Smaller 2024 VBCloud victim sets in Belarus, Canada, Moldova, Israel, Kyrgyzstan, Turkey and Vietnam [S3]
Africa, Europe and the Middle East (Brandefense profile) [S9]
targeting.notes: The 2014 lures referenced diplomatic car sales [S4]. Unit 42 saw the group in 2017 against government targets in Europe, Russia and Central Asia [S1]. Check Point says the post-2022 shift narrowed its scope but did not change its tactics [S2]. The 2023 lures appealed for support to Russian soldiers in the 'special military operation' [S7]. The cross-regional sector list comes from secondary profiles and is not tied to dated campaigns [S9].

capabilities.summary: Initial access is spear-phishing with Word documents. Kaspersky saw a CVE-2012-0158 variant in 2014 [S4]. Later campaigns used remote-template retrieval with Equation Editor exploits CVE-2017-11882 and CVE-2018-0802 [S1][S3][S7]. In 2014 the documents dropped a Visual Basic script that installed the loader and payload rather than writing a PE backdoor to disk [S4]. Command and control ran over CloudMe WebDAV storage [S5]. In 2018 Symantec reported that the group hid its origin behind chains of hijacked UPnP home routers, which needed no custom malware on the routers [S6]. In 2018 Unit 42 named POWERSHOWER, a PowerShell reconnaissance backdoor that cleans up after itself [S1]. Check Point reported a DLL in 2022 that proxies connections through victim machines [S2]. Kaspersky's 2024 reporting describes an HTA-to-VBShower chain that deploys PowerShower (network probing and payload download) and VBCloud (system information and file theft) [S3]. In 2025 Positive Technologies observed several new TLS certificates issued in a single day for fresh infrastructure [S8].

diamond.adversary: Unattributed espionage actor tracked as Inception / Cloud Atlas since 2014. Kaspersky assesses lineage from RedOctober [S1][S4][S7].
diamond.capability: Weaponized Office documents using remote templates and Equation Editor exploits; VBS/HTA loaders; the VBShower, PowerShower/POWERSHOWER and VBCloud implants; a victim-side proxy DLL [S1][S2][S3][S4].
diamond.infrastructure: Cloud storage used for C2 (CloudMe WebDAV) [S5]; chains of hijacked UPnP home routers used as proxies [S6]; regularly refreshed domains and TLS certificates [S8].
diamond.victim: Diplomatic, government, defense, research and agro-industrial organizations, now mainly in Russia and Belarus [S2][S3][S4][S7][S8].
diamond.socioPolitical: Targeting narrowed to Russia, Belarus and contested areas of Ukraine and Moldova after Russia's 2022 invasion of Ukraine, which suggests intelligence requirements tied to that conflict [S2]. No sponsoring state is named [S7].
diamond.technology: Windows endpoints running Microsoft Office with unpatched Equation Editor; consumer routers exposing UPnP; legitimate cloud storage services [S1][S3][S5][S6].

gaps: No sponsoring state is named in open sources. Neither a government attribution nor a Microsoft name was found.

The primary Kaspersky Securelist reports could not be opened: securelist.com was blocked by the session proxy. Details of the VBCloud report and of the 2025 to early-2026 reports (including the PowerCloud tool) rest on search summaries and secondary coverage.
The original Blue Coat (2014), Symantec (2018) and F.A.C.C.T. (2023) reports were not opened. They are cited through secondary coverage.
Positive Technologies research (2024-2025) on Google Sheets C2 and Yandex.Disk-hosted modules was seen only in Russian-language summaries and has no confirmed date. It is not included as a campaign.
The Akamai 65,000-router UPnProxy botnet is only 'related' to Inception per coverage. Do not attribute the whole botnet to this actor.
Kaspersky's Cloud Atlas-RedOctober linkage and the merging of the Inception and Cloud Atlas vendor clusters are vendor assessments.
Brandefense's sector and region list (Africa, Middle East, aerospace, media) is not tied to dated primary campaign reporting.

implications.jipoe: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. STEP 1: The operational environment includes diplomatic, government and defense networks and the cloud-storage and consumer-router infrastructure that the actor abuses for C2 and anonymization [S1][S5][S6]. STEP 2: Legacy Office Equation Editor flaws (CVE-2017-11882, CVE-2018-0802) remain usable years after patching. This shows that unpatched Office clients are the decisive terrain [S1][S3]. STEP 3: The doctrinal template runs from a themed spear-phish to a remote template or Equation Editor exploit, then an HTA/VBS loader (VBShower), then PowerShell reconnaissance (PowerShower), then file theft (VBCloud) over cloud or proxied C2 [S1][S3][S6]. STEP 4: MLCOA is continued espionage against Russian and Belarusian government, defense and research targets; US and allied equities face spillover risk through the smaller victim sets in other countries [S2][S3][S8]. MDCOA is retasking against diplomatic or coalition entities with geopolitical lures, using residential-router proxy chains to frustrate attribution and blocking [S4][S6]. Candidate indicators: Word documents that fetch remote templates over HTTP; EQNEDT32 spawning mshta or wscript; VBS files with randomized names in user profile directories; outbound WebDAV to cloud storage; PowerShell reconnaissance followed by self-cleanup [S1][S3][S5].
implications.jcc2: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. (1) Situational awareness: the current focus is on Russia and Belarus [S2][S3], so this actor is lower priority for DoDIN defense. Track it for retargeting signs, such as lures themed on coalition or diplomatic issues [S4]. (2) Authorities: no sponsoring state is named [S7], so any response beyond network defense needs careful attribution coordination; do not treat vendor lineage claims as government attribution [S4]. (3) Mission assurance: verify that Equation Editor is removed or disabled and that remote-template loading is restricted on mission systems, since the actor reuses years-old exploits [S1][S3]. (4) Coordination: its anonymization relies on consumer UPnP routers and legitimate cloud storage [S5][S6], so takedown or blocking requires coordination with cloud providers and partners rather than simple IP blocking.

identification.summary: IndigoZebra is a suspected Chinese-speaking cyber-espionage group that has targeted Central Asian governments since at least 2014 [S1][S8]. Kaspersky first named it in its Q2 2017 APT Trends report, describing activity against former Soviet republics using Meterpreter, Poison Ivy, xDown and a previously unknown backdoor it called xCaon [S6][S5]. In July 2021 Check Point Research reported a spear-phishing campaign against the Afghan National Security Council that delivered BoxCaon, a new xCaon variant that uses Dropbox for command and control [S1][S2][S3].
identification.firstObserved: Activity since at least 2014: Check Point found about 30 xCaon samples, the earliest from 2014 [S1][S4]. First public naming was Kaspersky's Q2 2017 APT Trends report (dated 2017-08-08 per Malpedia) [S6][S7].
identification.notes: No Microsoft name for IndigoZebra was found in the searches run for this record (Microsoft's naming mapping could not be opened); the encyclopedia keeps the vendor name IndigoZebra. MITRE tracks the group as G0136 [S8]. Check Point described the 2021 Afghan activity as only 'believed' to be IndigoZebra, based on malware links to the earlier xCaon cluster [S2][S4].

attribution.sponsor: Suspected China-linked. Kaspersky listed IndigoZebra among Chinese-speaking actors [S5][S6], and Check Point called it a Chinese-speaking group [S2]. Check Point named no government sponsor [S2][S4].
attribution.confidence: Vendor assessment only. Kaspersky made no definitive attribution in 2017 [S5]. Check Point's language is 'Chinese-speaking' and 'believed to be' IndigoZebra [S2][S4]. Malpedia's 'Chinese state-sponsored' label is stronger than the primary vendors' wording [S7]. No government attribution was found in the sources gathered.
attribution.basis: Malware lineage (xCaon to BoxCaon) and code overlap linking the 2021 Afghan intrusions to earlier Central Asian activity [S1][S4]. Kaspersky noted ties to other Chinese-speaking actors in 2017 [S5].

actors.objectives: Political and government espionage against Central Asian states, including Afghanistan's National Security Council and political entities in Kyrgyzstan and Uzbekistan [S1][S3][S4].

targeting.notes: Check Point telemetry showed the HTTP-based xCaon variants mainly targeted political entities in Kyrgyzstan and Uzbekistan [S3]. Check Point said the campaign may extend beyond the three named countries; these were the ones it could confidently tie to the victim list [S2].

capabilities.summary: Kaspersky's 2017 report described a toolset of Meterpreter, Poison Ivy, xDown and the custom xCaon backdoor [S5][S6]. The xCaon family (about 30 samples since 2014) used HTTP for C2 [S1]. BoxCaon, the 2021 variant, uses an attacker-controlled Dropbox account as C2. It creates a unique folder per victim, reads commands from a sub-folder named 'd', and writes results back to Dropbox, so its traffic blends with legitimate HTTPS cloud-storage use [S1][S5]. BoxCaon's features are narrow: file download and upload, command execution, and returning results. That is enough to stage further reconnaissance and lateral-movement tools [S1]. Initial access in 2021 was by spear-phishing that impersonated the Administrative Office of the President of Afghanistan, with a password-protected RAR archive leading to a backdoor dropped as 'spools.exe' [S3][S4]. MITRE lists Poison Ivy, xCaon and BoxCaon as associated software [S8].

campaigns.summary: NSC officials received lure emails claiming to come from the Administrative Office of the President of Afghanistan. They carried a password-protected RAR archive that installed a backdoor.

campaigns.name: Check Point BoxCaon report
campaigns.summary: Check Point Research published its analysis of BoxCaon (Dropbox C2) and linked the Afghan intrusions to the long-running IndigoZebra activity against Kyrgyzstan and Uzbekistan.

diamond.adversary: Suspected Chinese-speaking espionage operators; government sponsorship not confirmed by the reporting vendors [S2][S4][S5].
diamond.capability: Spear-phishing with government-impersonation lures and password-protected RAR archives; custom xCaon/BoxCaon backdoors; commodity Poison Ivy, Meterpreter and xDown [S1][S3][S5].
diamond.infrastructure: HTTP C2 for older xCaon variants; attacker-controlled Dropbox account with a per-victim folder structure for BoxCaon [S1][S5].
diamond.victim: Afghan National Security Council; government and political entities in Kyrgyzstan and Uzbekistan; former Soviet republics more broadly [S1][S2][S6].
diamond.socioPolitical: Intelligence collection on Central Asian governments [S1][S4].
diamond.technology: Abuse of trusted cloud storage (Dropbox) as C2, and trust in inter-agency email from senior government offices [S1][S3].

gaps: The Check Point Research report, Check Point blog, Kaspersky Securelist report and MITRE page could not be fetched in this session (network errors). Facts are drawn from search-result excerpts and secondary coverage of those documents and should be verified against the originals.
No Microsoft name was confirmed; Microsoft's MicrosoftMapping.json could not be accessed.
No public reporting after 2021 was found; current activity status is unknown.
No government attribution or indictment was found. Malpedia's 'state-sponsored' label goes beyond what Kaspersky and Check Point state.
Whether the 2021 intrusions succeeded in exfiltrating data, and the full victim set beyond Afghanistan, Kyrgyzstan and Uzbekistan, are not public in the sources gathered.
Specific IOCs (Dropbox tokens, domains, hashes) were not retrieved; secondary claims about a hardcoded bearer token were not verified against Check Point.

implications.jipoe: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. STEP 1: Relevant terrain is the email and cloud-storage traffic of Central Asian partner governments' national security and presidential offices, plus coalition personnel who exchange mail with them [S1][S4]. STEP 2: Allowed cloud-storage services (Dropbox) give the actor C2 that blends into normal HTTPS. Long-running custom tooling since 2014 shows patience and persistence [S1]. STEP 3: The doctrinal template is a spear-phish impersonating a senior government office, then a password-protected RAR, then the xCaon/BoxCaon backdoor, then Dropbox-based tasking, then follow-on reconnaissance tools [S1][S3]. STEP 4: MLCOA is continued collection on Central Asian government policy and security deliberations through impersonation phishing. MDCOA is use of a compromised partner-government mailbox to phish US or coalition personnel working regional security issues, giving access to shared planning data; this is an extrapolation, not observed. Candidate indicators: password-protected RAR attachments claiming senior-office origin, endpoints making Dropbox API calls with no sanctioned Dropbox use, and a new 'spools.exe' or similar look-alike system binary [S1][S3][S4].
implications.jcc2: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. (1) Situational awareness: flag Dropbox and other cloud-storage API traffic from mission and partner-liaison enclaves, because BoxCaon C2 resembles legitimate use [S1]. (2) Authorities: activity is vendor-attributed only, so treat it as a suspected PRC-linked espionage threat and avoid overstating government attribution in products [S2][S4]. (3) Mission assurance: harden email trust paths with Central Asian partner governments, since lures impersonated a presidential office [S3]. (4) Coordination: share indicators with partner-nation CERTs in Kyrgyzstan, Uzbekistan and the region, and with commercial vendors, because public reporting has been sparse since 2021.

provenance.importedSummary: IndigoZebra is a Chinese state-sponsored actor mentioned for the first time by Kaspersky in its APT Trends report Q2 2017, targeting, at the time of its discovery, former Soviet Republics with multiple malware strains including Meterpreter, Poison Ivy, xDown, and a previously unknown backdoor called “xCaon.”

identification.summary: Dark Engine has emerged as a significant threat actor targeting industrial control systems and SCADA systems in sectors such as metallurgy and food processing. The group has conducted multiple ICS-targeted incidents, with a pronounced operational surge in June 2025. Additionally, Dark Engine is involved in a campaign that embeds fraudulent CAPTCHA prompts into legitimate WordPress sites, utilizing SEO poisoning to harvest login credentials. Reports also indicate a data leak from Dark Engine that exposed sensitive phone data in the U.S.

Infy is a group of suspected Iranian origin. Since early 2013, we have observed activity from a unique threat actor group, which we began to investigate based on increased activities against human right activists in the beginning of 2015. In line5with other research on the campaign, released prior to publication of this document, we have adopted the name “Infy”, which is based on labels used in the infrastructure and its two families of malware agents. Thanks to information we have been able to collect during the course of our research, such as characteristics of the group’s malware and development cycle, our research strongly supports the claim that the Infy group is of Iranian origin and potentially connected to the Iranian state. Amongst a backdrop of other incidents, Infy became one of the most frequently observed agents for attempted malware attacks against Iranian civil society beginning in late 2014, growing in use up to the February 2016 parliamentary election in Iran. After the conclusion of the parliamentary election, the rate of attempted intrusions and new compromises through the Infy agent slowed, but did not end. The trends witnessed in reports from recipients are reinforced through telemetry provided by design failures in more recent versions of the Infy malware.

IronHusky is a Chinese-based threat actor first attributed in July 2017 targeting Russian and Mongolian governments, as well as aviation companies and research institutes. Since their initial attacks ceased in 2018, they have been working on a new remote access trojan dubbed MysterySnail.

North Korean state-sponsored actor focused on stealing cryptocurrency, usually by socially engineering developers and staff at blockchain firms and their vendors [S1][S3]. US government advisories track the same activity as TraderTraitor [S1][S3][S5]. In July 2023 GitHub, which Microsoft owns, named Jade Sleet as the actor behind a social-engineering campaign that used repository invitations and malicious npm dependencies [S1][S2]. The FBI has tied TraderTraitor to the theft of about $308 million from DMM Bitcoin in 2024 and about $1.5 billion from Bybit in February 2025 [S5][S6]. Reporting in 2026 links the actor to the KelpDAO/LayerZero bridge exploit and to an intrusion at an India-based IT services firm that used macOS backdoors [S9][S10][S12].
identification.firstObserved: US advisory AA22-108A (April 2022) describes TraderTraitor activity since at least 2020 [S3]. The Microsoft/GitHub public naming of Jade Sleet dates to July 2023 [S1].
identification.notes: Microsoft name: Jade Sleet (in-development name Storm-0954). Microsoft's naming map lists LABYRINTH CHOLLIMA (CrowdStrike) as an alias [S13]. GitHub equated Jade Sleet with CISA's TraderTraitor [S1]. FBI statements on the DMM Bitcoin and Bybit thefts list Jade Sleet, UNC4899 and Slow Pisces as other names for TraderTraitor [S5][S6]. Mandiant says UNC4899 likely corresponds to TraderTraitor [S4]. Palo Alto Networks Unit 42 tracks the activity as Slow Pisces [S8]. AA22-108A groups TraderTraitor under the broader Lazarus Group / APT38 / BlueNoroff umbrella [S3]. Keep that umbrella separate from this specific cluster. MITRE ATT&CK has no Group ID assigned in this record.

attribution.sponsor: Democratic People's Republic of Korea. Mandiant assesses UNC4899 as a cryptocurrency-focused element within the DPRK Reconnaissance General Bureau (RGB) [S4].
attribution.confidence: The FBI publicly attributed the Bybit theft (2025-02-26 PSA) and the DMM Bitcoin theft (December 2024, with DC3 and Japan's National Police Agency) to TraderTraitor, i.e. to North Korea [S5][S6]. Mandiant assesses with high confidence that UNC4899 is an RGB element, and assesses that UNC4899 'likely' corresponds to TraderTraitor [S4]. In coverage of the LayerZero incident report, Mandiant and CrowdStrike attribute the KelpDAO operation to TraderTraitor/UNC4899 [S10]. GitHub attributed the July 2023 campaign to Jade Sleet [S1].
attribution.basis: Joint FBI/CISA/Treasury advisory AA22-108A [S3]. FBI attributions of specific thefts [S5][S6]. Mandiant incident response, including an OPSEC slip in which UNC4899 connected directly from a Pyongyang netblock during the JumpCloud intrusion [S4]. GitHub/Microsoft telemetry [S1]. Vendor reporting from Unit 42, Safe{Wallet}/Mandiant and LayerZero [S7][S8][S10].

actors.objectives: Revenue generation for the DPRK state through theft of cryptocurrency from exchanges, DeFi protocols, wallet and custody providers, and individuals [S3][S5][S6]. The actor also gains access to software and service providers so it can compromise their downstream cryptocurrency customers [S4][S7].

sectors: Cryptocurrency wallet and custody software providers [S5][S7]
Play-to-earn gaming and crypto-focused venture capital [S3]
Identity/SaaS service providers used as supply-chain pivots [S4]
IT services, DevOps and fintech personnel [S12]
targeting.notes: The actor targets people more than perimeter devices. Developers, DevOps engineers and executives at crypto firms or their suppliers are approached through fake recruiter or developer personas on LinkedIn, GitHub, Slack and Telegram [S1][S2][S5][S8][S12]. GitHub said most targets were connected to blockchain, cryptocurrency or online gambling, with a few in cybersecurity [S1].

capabilities.summary: Social engineering through fake recruiters and developers, using job-interview 'coding challenges' and repository invitations. These lead victims to clone and run trojanized projects or malicious npm dependencies [S1][S2][S5][S8]. AA22-108A describes trojanized cryptocurrency applications for Windows and macOS [S3]. The actor runs supply-chain operations: it compromised JumpCloud's commands framework to reach downstream customers [S4], and it compromised a Safe{Wallet} developer laptop, hijacking AWS session tokens to bypass MFA and tamper with front-end JavaScript that Bybit signers used [S7]. Unit 42 documents gated, in-memory payload delivery (RN Loader, RN Stealer) that steals SSH keys and AWS, Kubernetes and Google Cloud configuration files from macOS hosts [S8]. Mandiant observed macOS keychain theft and persistence through backdoors and plist files within 24 hours of access [S4]. In 2026 the actor used a booby-trapped Terraform project with typosquatted provider registries, plus Rust macOS backdoors: FLATROOF (Telegram exfiltration) and ROOFDECK (Nostr-relay C2) [S12]. It also manipulated RPC responses and ran DDoS against healthy nodes to defeat a bridge verifier [S10]. After thefts, the actor quickly launders funds across thousands of addresses and multiple blockchains [S6].

campaigns.name: DMM Bitcoin theft (~$308M)

campaigns.name: Bybit theft (~$1.5B)
campaigns.summary: A compromised Safe{Wallet} developer machine and tampered front-end code let the actor alter a multisig transaction signed by Bybit. The FBI attributed the theft to TraderTraitor on 2025-02-26.

campaigns.name: Slow Pisces coding-challenge campaign
campaigns.summary: Unit 42 reports LinkedIn recruiter lures that lead to GitHub 'coding challenges' delivering RN Loader and RN Stealer to crypto developers.

campaigns.name: KelpDAO rsETH / LayerZero exploit (~$292M)
campaigns.summary: A LayerZero Labs developer is socially engineered from 6 March 2026. RPC responses are later poisoned to drain about 116,500 rsETH. Mandiant and CrowdStrike attribute the operation to UNC4899.

campaigns.name: India IT services firm compromise (FLATROOF/ROOFDECK)
campaigns.summary: A fake job interview delivers a trojanized Terraform project to a DevOps engineer. Rust macOS backdoors trigger when the project is opened in the Cursor AI editor.

diamond.adversary: DPRK RGB-linked crypto-theft cluster (Jade Sleet / TraderTraitor / UNC4899 / Slow Pisces) [S1][S4][S5][S8].
diamond.capability: Recruiter and coding-challenge lures; trojanized repositories and npm packages; supply-chain compromise of SaaS and wallet providers; macOS stealers and backdoors (RN Loader, RN Stealer, FLATROOF, ROOFDECK); cloud session-token theft [S1][S4][S7][S8][S12].
diamond.infrastructure: Fake personas on LinkedIn, GitHub, Slack and Telegram; GitHub-hosted repositories; ORB proxy infrastructure (one direct connection from Pyongyang observed); typosquatted HashiCorp registries; Telegram and Nostr relays for C2 and exfiltration [S1][S4][S8][S12].
diamond.victim: Developers, DevOps staff and executives at crypto exchanges, DeFi/bridge protocols, wallet providers, and their IT and SaaS suppliers in the US, Japan, India and elsewhere [S1][S4][S5][S6][S12].
diamond.socioPolitical: Sanctions-evading revenue generation for the DPRK regime [S3][S6].
diamond.technology: Developer workstations (often macOS), package managers, CI/IaC tooling, cloud consoles and multisig signing front ends [S4][S7][S8][S12].

gaps: No Microsoft Threat Intelligence profile of Jade Sleet was found in the searches. The Microsoft-side description comes from GitHub's July 2023 post, and that post was not fetched directly (github.blog was unreachable); content comes from search summaries and SecurityWeek coverage [S1][S2].

Primary US government documents (AA22-108A, the FBI PSA on Bybit, the FBI/NPA statement on DMM Bitcoin) could not be opened. Their content here comes from search summaries and press coverage [S3][S5][S6].

The Microsoft naming map links LABYRINTH CHOLLIMA (CrowdStrike) to Jade Sleet [S13], but no CrowdStrike source was found confirming this mapping or naming the CrowdStrike designation used for Bybit or KelpDAO. Treat the CrowdStrike alias as unverified.

Mandiant hedges the UNC4899 = TraderTraitor equivalence as 'likely' [S4]. FBI statements treat Jade Sleet, UNC4899 and Slow Pisces as the same cluster [S5][S6]. Cluster boundaries may still differ between vendors.
Relationship to the broader Lazarus/APT38/BlueNoroff umbrella and to other Microsoft Sleet actors (e.g., Sapphire Sleet, Citrine Sleet, Moonstone Sleet) is not resolved in the sources gathered.

SentinelOne's original 2026 report on FLATROOF/ROOFDECK and LayerZero's primary incident report were not opened. Details come from the CSA research note and The Defiant [S10][S12]; the FLATROOF/ROOFDECK details were not corroborated in fact-check searches.
No MITRE ATT&CK Group ID is recorded for this cluster.

implications.jipoe: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. STEP 1 (operational environment): The relevant cyberspace terrain is the people layer (developers, DevOps engineers, executives) and the developer toolchain: GitHub, npm, Terraform/IaC registries, cloud session tokens and SaaS administration frameworks. Perimeter devices matter less [S1][S4][S7][S12]. STEP 2 (effects): Any DoD or DIB element with cryptocurrency, fintech, or third-party SaaS and identity dependencies inherits risk from supplier compromise. JumpCloud and Safe{Wallet} show one supplier compromise reaching many downstream victims [S4][S7]. STEP 3 (threat evaluation): The template is recruiter or developer persona, then trojanized repository or coding challenge, then macOS stealer or backdoor, then theft of cloud and SSH credentials, then supply-chain pivot or direct asset theft, then rapid multi-chain laundering [S4][S6][S8][S12]. STEP 4 (COAs): MLCOA is continued job-lure targeting of crypto, fintech and DevOps staff to fund the DPRK [S8]. MDCOA is applying the same developer-workstation and SaaS supply-chain tradecraft to an identity or IT provider serving defense customers; JumpCloud is the precedent [S4]. Candidate indicators: unsolicited 'coding test' repositories run on corporate hosts; unexpected npm or Terraform provider sources and typosquatted registries; Telegram or Nostr-relay traffic from developer Macs; anomalous use of cloud session tokens; SaaS command or agent frameworks executing unfamiliar scripts [S1][S4][S8][S12].
implications.jcc2: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. (1) Situational awareness: Track supplier and SaaS compromise reporting, plus FBI attributions of crypto thefts, as early warning of the actor's current tradecraft. Its supply-chain intrusions reach downstream customers within days [S4][S6]. (2) Authorities: The activity sits largely in private-sector and FBI law-enforcement lanes [S5][S6]. DoD roles are mostly defending its own networks and supporting partners, so coordinate through the appropriate interagency channels. (3) Mission assurance: Developer and DevOps workstations, IaC pipelines and identity platforms should be treated as mission-relevant terrain. Brief cleared personnel on fake recruiter and coding-test lures [S8][S12]. (4) Coordination: Share indicators with DC3 and DIB partners; DC3 joined the DMM Bitcoin attribution [S5]. Expect vendor names (Jade Sleet, TraderTraitor, UNC4899, Slow Pisces) to differ across reports [S5][S6].

identification.summary: Jasper Sleet is Microsoft's name for North Korea's remote IT worker activity. Microsoft says the workers are mainly focused on making money for the North Korean government [S1]. Operatives use stolen, rented or fabricated identities to get hired into remote IT, software and web development roles. Once hired, they collect salaries that are laundered back to the DPRK and at times steal data or extort their employers [S1]. Microsoft says the workers have used AI since 2024 to scale the operation, and it describes AI use at every stage: getting hired, staying hired and misusing access [S1][S4].
identification.firstObserved: Microsoft says it has tracked this global operation since at least early 2020 [S1]. The January 2025 DOJ indictment that Microsoft cites describes fraudulent work from 2018 to 2024 [S1][S6].
identification.notes: Microsoft name: Jasper Sleet, formerly tracked as Storm-0287 [S1][S2]. Microsoft tracks other North Korean clusters that use similar fraudulent-employment techniques separately, including Storm-1877 and Moonstone Sleet [S1]. Microsoft has since renamed Storm-1877 to Coral Sleet [S2][S4]. Microsoft's naming mapping lists no other-vendor aliases for Jasper Sleet [S2]. US DOJ actions against the DPRK IT worker scheme do not use Microsoft's cluster names [S5][S6][S7].

attribution.sponsor: Democratic People's Republic of Korea (North Korea). Microsoft says the remote IT workers generate revenue for the North Korean government and likely fall under a particular leadership structure in North Korea [S1].
attribution.confidence: Microsoft attributes the activity to North Korea and attributed at least one 2025 incident response case to Jasper Sleet [S1][S3]. The US government attributes the broader remote IT worker scheme to the DPRK through indictments and guilty pleas, but it does not use the name Jasper Sleet [S5][S6][S7].
attribution.basis: Microsoft telemetry and machine-learning detection of suspect accounts. Microsoft also found a public repository in October 2024 that held suspected workers' photos, resumes, accounts and payment-tracking records [S1]. Microsoft's Incident Response team (DART) investigated a case involving PiKVM devices [S3]. Microsoft also cites DOJ indictments [S1][S6].

actors.objectives: The primary objective is to generate revenue for the DPRK, which Microsoft says violates international sanctions [S1]. Secondary objectives are stealing intellectual property, source code and trade secrets, and extorting employers by threatening to release stolen data [S1]. Microsoft's incident response reporting also cites deploying malicious tools and sending profits to state programs [S3]. In a related DOJ case, workers in the scheme reached ITAR-controlled data at a California defense contractor [S8].

sectors: Information technology and software development (remote roles)
Fortune 500 companies (via staffing and contracting firms)
Defense industrial base (ITAR data exposure in a DOJ case)
regions: Global; Microsoft says targeting has broadened to various industries worldwide [S1]
targeting.notes: The historic focus on US technology, critical manufacturing and transportation companies, and the shift to global targeting, come from Microsoft [S1]. The targeted roles are IT, software development, web development and administrator jobs [S1]. Microsoft says the workers are most often located in North Korea, China and Russia [S1]. The defense-contractor ITAR exposure comes from DOJ case reporting that does not name Jasper Sleet [S8].

capabilities.summary: Identity fraud: personas are stolen, rented from willing people or bought from fraud services, then matched to the target's location. The workers back them with email, GitHub, LinkedIn and freelance-site profiles [S1]. AI: Faceswap is used to place operatives' faces onto stolen ID documents and headshots, and voice-changing software is used in interviews [S1][S4]. Generative AI is used to analyze job postings, build culturally fitting names, polish resumes and keep up job performance [S4]. Facilitators validate identities, open accounts, receive company laptops and run laptop farms [S1]. Remote access: IP-based KVM devices (PiKVM, TinyPilot) and RMM tools (JumpConnect, RustDesk, TeamViewer, AnyViewer, AnyDesk) [S1]. Microsoft DART observed PiKVM used as an out-of-band channel that bypassed EDR and exfiltrated data [S3]. Evasion: VPNs (notably Astrill VPN), VPSs and proxies; workers also avoid turning on cameras [S1].

campaigns.summary: Two North Korean nationals and three facilitators were charged over work obtained from at least 64 US companies between 2018 and 2024. Payments from ten of those companies totaled at least $866,255. Microsoft cites this case in its Jasper Sleet reporting.

campaigns.name: Microsoft disruption and DOJ coordinated nationwide actions
campaigns.summary: Microsoft published its Jasper Sleet profile and suspended 3,000 known Outlook/Hotmail accounts created by North Korean IT workers. The same day, DOJ announced an arrest, two indictments, searches of 29 suspected laptop farms in 16 states, and seizures of 29 financial accounts and 21 websites. DOJ says the schemes involved more than 100 US companies. The DOJ materials do not use the Jasper Sleet name.
