implications.jipoe: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. STEP 1: The operational environment includes allied Japanese government, political, think-tank and defense-industrial networks, Taiwanese government institutions, and diplomatic bodies that engage on Japan [S1][S3][S7]. Internet-facing VPN appliances and personal or cloud email are key terrain [S4][S5]. STEP 2: Patches to edge devices (Array, Fortinet, Citrix) and controls on Windows Sandbox, VS Code tunnels and DoH egress shape the actor's access [S3][S4][S7]. STEP 3: The model runs from a tailored spear-phish (OneDrive ZIP, macro document, event-themed lure) or an edge-device exploit, to DLL side-loaded ANEL, LODEINFO or NOOPDOOR, to credential theft and file exfiltration [S3][S5][S6][S7]. STEP 4: MLCOA is continued spear-phishing of individuals in Japan- and Taiwan-related policy, research and diplomatic communities to collect security and technology information [S1][S5][S7]. MDCOA is exploitation of edge devices at defense-industrial or coalition partners, establishing durable NOOPDOOR access that harvests alliance planning or advanced-technology data during a regional crisis [S4][S6]. Candidate indicators: unexpected VS Code tunnel processes or code.exe network sessions; Windows Sandbox (.wsb) launched on non-developer hosts; signed binaries side-loading unknown DLLs; encrypted blobs in the registry; DoH traffic from endpoints; OneDrive-delivered ZIPs with macro-enabled Excel files [S3][S6][S7].
implications.jcc2: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. (1) Situational awareness: track Japanese government (NPA) and JPCERT/CC advisories alongside vendor reporting, because allied disclosures preceded or complemented vendor reporting [S1][S6]. (2) Authorities: the actor targets allied and partner networks (Japan, Taiwan, European diplomatic bodies), so most response actions sit with host nations; DoD action centers on its own networks and information sharing [S1][S3][S7]. (3) Mission assurance: harden and monitor internet-facing VPN appliances on DODIN and Defense Industrial Base enclaves that support Indo-Pacific operations, and restrict VS Code tunnels and Windows Sandbox where not required [S3][S4]. (4) Coordination: share indicators with Japanese counterparts, USINDOPACOM components and DC3/DIB partners, and deconflict naming (MirrorFace, Earth Kasha, APT10/Purple Typhoon) in shared reporting [S1][S3][S7].

identification.summary: Moafee is a China-based cyber espionage group named by FireEye in September 2014 research that described it as operating from Guangdong Province and targeting military and government organizations involved in the South China Sea dispute [S1][S2][S3]. FireEye reported targets that included organizations within the US defense industrial base [S3]. FireEye described Moafee alongside a second group, DragonOK, which shares custom backdoors, RATs and the HTRAN proxy tool but was assessed as a distinct group with a different mission and location [S1][S3]. MITRE ATT&CK tracks Moafee as G0002 [S4].
identification.firstObserved: Publicly named by FireEye in September 2014 [S1][S2][S3]. The start date of its activity is not stated in the sources gathered.
identification.notes: Microsoft name: none found in the sources gathered. Cluster boundary: FireEye treats Moafee (Guangdong) and DragonOK (Jiangsu) as separate groups that may be subgroups with their own mission focus [S1][S3]. This encyclopedia's imported record merges DragonOK, BRONZE OVERBROOK and Shallow Taurus into Moafee; the sources gathered here describe DragonOK as a related but separate cluster, and no gathered source mapped BRONZE OVERBROOK or Shallow Taurus to either name. Post-2014 campaigns below are DragonOK reporting and are labeled as such. Press coverage spells the name variously as Moafee, Moafree and Moafe [S3].

attribution.confidence: FireEye assessed Moafee as a China-based group operating from Guangdong Province [S1][S2][S3]. No government attribution or named state sponsor appears in the sources gathered.
attribution.basis: FireEye research released in September 2014 ahead of its full 'Operation Quantum Entanglement' report, as covered by trade press [S1][S2][S3]; MITRE ATT&CK group entry G0002 [S4].

actors.objectives: Political and military espionage against government and military organizations with interests in the South China Sea dispute, per FireEye reporting [S2][S3]. FireEye contrasted this with DragonOK's economic espionage against high-tech and manufacturing companies [S1][S3].

targeting.notes: FireEye reported Moafee targets as military and government organizations involved in the South China Sea dispute, including organizations within the US defense industry [S2][S3]. Related cluster DragonOK targeted high-tech and manufacturing companies in Japan and Taiwan [S1][S2], and later Japan with possible targeting of Taiwan, Tibet and Russia [S6]. Specific Moafee victim countries are not named in the sources gathered.

capabilities.summary: FireEye reported that Moafee and DragonOK used similar TTPs, including custom-built backdoors and remote-administration tools, shared malware implants and social-engineering approaches, and the HTRAN proxy tool [S1][S2][S3]. MITRE ATT&CK notes binary padding for defense evasion and lists PoisonIvy among associated software [S4]. FireEye said the shared tooling may reflect collaboration, common training, a common toolkit supply chain, or a combination, and noted a possible third group using the same TTPs [S1][S3].

campaigns.name: Operation Quantum Entanglement (FireEye)
campaigns.summary: FireEye reported two China-based groups operating in parallel: Moafee, from Guangdong, targeting government and military organizations tied to the South China Sea dispute, including US defense industry targets, and DragonOK, from Jiangsu, targeting high-tech and manufacturing firms in Japan and Taiwan. Both used shared custom backdoors, RATs and HTRAN.

diamond.capability: Custom backdoors and RATs shared with DragonOK, the HTRAN proxy tool, PoisonIvy, and binary padding for evasion [S1][S3][S4].
diamond.infrastructure: Proxied C2 using HTRAN [S2][S3]. No specific domains or IPs appear in the sources gathered.
diamond.victim: Government and military organizations involved in the South China Sea dispute, and US defense industrial base organizations [S2][S3].
diamond.socioPolitical: Intelligence on the South China Sea territorial dispute in support of Chinese interests, per FireEye's targeting description [S2][S3].
diamond.technology: Users' susceptibility to social engineering, and Windows hosts that run custom implants [S1][S4].

implications.jipoe: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. STEP 1: The relevant environment includes government, military and defense-industrial networks of South China Sea stakeholders, including US DIB contractors [S2][S3]. STEP 2: Spearphishing and custom RATs mean user mailboxes and endpoints are the primary avenues of approach [S1][S5]. STEP 3: The doctrinal template is socially engineered delivery, then a custom backdoor or PoisonIvy, with C2 relayed through HTRAN proxies [S1][S3][S4]. STEP 4: MLCOA is persistent collection of policy and military planning information related to South China Sea issues from government and DIB targets. MDCOA is coordinated collection across allied and partner networks during a maritime crisis, using shared toolkits that blur attribution between related clusters [S1][S3]. Candidate indicators: HTRAN proxy activity, PoisonIvy or NewCT-family implants, binary-padded executables, and themed phishing to personnel working on the South China Sea [S3][S4][S5].
implications.jcc2: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. (1) Situational awareness: shared tooling across Moafee, DragonOK and a possible third group means detections of these malware families should be correlated across clusters rather than assigned to one actor [S1][S3]. (2) Authorities: DIB targeting implies coordination with contractors under DIB cybersecurity information-sharing mechanisms [S3]. (3) Mission assurance: protect planning data on South China Sea and Indo-Pacific operations held on mission-partner networks [S2][S3]. (4) Coordination: regional partners named as DragonOK targets (Japan, Taiwan) may hold telemetry relevant to the shared toolkit [S1][S6].

identification.summary: Mofang is a cyber-espionage group that Dutch security firm Fox-IT named and publicly exposed in June 2016. Fox-IT assesses it as almost certainly operating out of China and probably government-affiliated [S1][S2]. MITRE ATT&CK describes it as a likely China-based group that has run focused attacks on government and critical infrastructure in Myanmar and other countries, and says the name comes from its frequent practice of imitating a victim's infrastructure [S4]. The group relies on social engineering rather than exploits, delivering its custom ShimRat and ShimRatReporter tools [S1][S2][S4].
identification.firstObserved: Fox-IT reporting (via SecurityWeek): active since at least February 2012 [S2]. MITRE ATT&CK: observed since at least May 2012 [S4]. Fox-IT published its report on 2016-06-15 [S1].
identification.notes: MITRE ATT&CK group ID G0103 [S4]. The imported record lists BRONZE WALKER (Secureworks CTU) and Superman as aliases, but no cited source in this file confirms either name, so neither is added to aliasesAdd. Start dates differ: February 2012 in Fox-IT-derived press coverage [S2] versus May 2012 in MITRE [S4].

attribution.sponsor: Suspected People's Republic of China government affiliation (vendor assessment only) [S1][S2].
attribution.confidence: Fox-IT says the actor almost certainly operates out of China and is probably government-affiliated [S1][S2]. MITRE describes it as a likely China-based group [S4]. These are vendor and knowledge-base assessments, not government attribution; no US or allied government attribution was found.
attribution.basis: Fox-IT's analysis of tooling, infrastructure and target selection, which it links to investments or technological advances that could threaten the Chinese sphere of influence [S1][S2]. Press coverage reports that targeting of the Myanmar Kyaukphyu special economic zone lined up in time with a tender later won by China's CITIC group [S2].

actors.objectives: Politically and economically motivated information theft. Fox-IT links Mofang's target selection to investments or technological advances that could be perceived as a threat to China's sphere of influence [S1]. Press reporting says experts believe information taken from Myanmar government organizations and the Singapore firm CPG Corporation could have helped a Chinese company win the Kyaukphyu infrastructure tender. This is an expert inference, not a confirmed outcome [S2].

sectors: Engineering and consulting firms involved in Myanmar infrastructure (CPG Corporation) [S2]
targeting.notes: Fox-IT suspects there are more victims than the countries it lists [S1]. In 2015-2016 the reported targeting centers on Myanmar and on organizations with interests in Myanmar's Kyaukphyu special economic zone [S2].

capabilities.summary: Mofang does not use exploits for initial infection. It relies on social engineering, usually email inviting targets to open attached files or follow links [S1][S2]. The only exploits reported in its toolset are previously known privilege-escalation exploits built into the malware [S2]. Its custom tools ShimRat (a remote access trojan) and ShimRatReporter (used for automated initial discovery) date back to at least 2012 [S2][S4]. MITRE lists two software entries for the group, ShimRat (S0444) and ShimRatReporter (S0445). It also lists spearphishing attachments and links, user execution, and encrypted or compressed payloads among the group's techniques [S4]. The group's name comes from its practice of imitating victim infrastructure, such as lookalike domains [S4].

campaigns.name: Early ShimRat operations
campaigns.summary: Mofang has been active since at least February 2012 (MITRE: May 2012), targeting government, military, critical infrastructure, automotive and weapons organizations in several countries including India, Germany, Canada, the United States, Singapore and South Korea [S2][S4].

campaigns.name: Kyaukphyu special economic zone targeting
campaigns.summary: In mid-2015 Mofang attacked Myanmar government organizations and the Singapore-based firm CPG Corporation, which had won a 2014 consulting tender for the Kyaukphyu SEZ. CITIC was later declared winner of an infrastructure tender in early 2016. Experts believe stolen information could have helped the Chinese bidder, though this is not confirmed [S2].

campaigns.name: Fox-IT public exposure
campaigns.summary: Fox-IT published its Mofang threat report, describing the group as almost certainly China-based and probably government-affiliated [S1][S3].

diamond.adversary: A likely China-based espionage group that Fox-IT assesses as probably government-affiliated [S1][S4].
diamond.capability: Social-engineering lures carrying the custom ShimRat RAT and ShimRatReporter discovery tool. The malware has built-in, previously known privilege-escalation exploits, and payloads are encrypted or compressed [S2][S4].
diamond.infrastructure: Infrastructure that imitates the victim's own, which is the source of the 'Mofang' name [S4]. Specific domains and IP addresses are in the Fox-IT report, which was not opened for this file.
diamond.victim: Myanmar government and organizations tied to the Kyaukphyu SEZ (for example CPG Corporation), plus government, military, critical infrastructure, automotive and weapons organizations in India, Germany, the United States, Canada, Singapore and South Korea [S1][S2].
diamond.socioPolitical: Targeting tracks Chinese strategic and economic interests, such as Myanmar's Kyaukphyu SEZ, where China's CNPC had invested and CITIC won an infrastructure tender [S1][S2].
diamond.technology: Windows endpoints reached through email and user execution of attachments or links [S2][S4].

Specific indicators (domains, C2 IPs, hashes) and details of ShimRat's application-shimming persistence were not verified from primary sources.

implications.jipoe: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. Step 1 (operational environment): concern centers on organizations tied to Chinese strategic investments and infrastructure projects, especially in Myanmar and South/Southeast Asia, and on defense and weapons-industry partners in allied nations [S1][S2]. Step 2 (effects): exposure is mainly loss of confidentiality of negotiating positions, tender data and defense-industrial information. No destructive activity is reported [S1][S2]. Step 3 (threat evaluation): low-sophistication initial access through social engineering, with no exploit-based entry; custom ShimRat tooling; and infrastructure that imitates victims [S2][S4]. Step 4: MLCOA is spearphishing with attachments or links aimed at government and partner organizations involved in China-linked economic projects, followed by ShimRat discovery and data theft [S2][S4]. MDCOA is long-term access to defense-industrial or military networks in partner nations, exposing weapons or program data [S2]. Candidate indicators include lookalike domains that mimic the victim organization [S4], email attachments that drop compressed or encrypted payloads [S4], and unexpected shim database installation (inferred from the ShimRat name; validate).
implications.jcc2: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. Situational awareness: Mofang's reported activity is from 2012-2016, with no recent public reporting, so treat it as a historical case study of economically motivated PRC-linked espionage rather than a current tracked threat [S1][S2][S4]. Authorities: attribution is vendor-only (Fox-IT, MITRE), so any defensive action should rest on observed indicators rather than government attribution [S1][S4]. Mission assurance: the threat to deployed or partner-nation networks comes mainly from user-targeted phishing, so user awareness and email and attachment controls are the main mitigations [S1][S2]. Coordination: the targeting of partner governments (for example Myanmar) and defense industry in allied countries [S2] suggests information sharing with partners and the defense industrial base.

identification.summary: North Korean threat actor that Microsoft named in May 2024 (formerly Storm-1789). Microsoft says it runs both financially motivated and espionage operations against software and IT, education and defense industrial base targets [S1]. Its signature tradecraft is social engineering through fake companies, fake job offers and personas on LinkedIn, Telegram and freelancing platforms. Through those channels it delivers trojanized PuTTY, malicious npm packages and a fully functional malicious tank game [S1]. It deployed its own FakePenny ransomware in April 2024 [S1]. In February 2025 it began deploying Qilin ransomware-as-a-service payloads, its first use of ransomware not built in-house [S2].
identification.firstObserved: Microsoft: earliest dated activity is trojanized PuTTY delivery in early August 2023 [S1].
identification.notes: Microsoft name: Moonstone Sleet (formerly Storm-1789) [S1]. Microsoft reports that early activity strongly overlapped with Diamond Sleet, including reuse of Comebacker code. The group later moved to its own infrastructure and attacks, and the two groups have since run concurrent operations [S1]. Microsoft's mapping file lists CrowdStrike's LABYRINTH CHOLLIMA as a related name [S9], but CrowdStrike's LABYRINTH CHOLLIMA is a broader, older cluster (see gaps) [S8]. Checkmarx initially attributed the group's npm packages to Jade Sleet before separating them out by code style [S3][S4]. Datadog tracks an npm cluster called Stressed Pungsan that overlaps with Moonstone Sleet [S5]. MITRE tracks the group as G1036 [S10].

attribution.sponsor: Democratic People's Republic of Korea (North Korea). Microsoft describes Moonstone Sleet as a North Korean threat actor [S1] and later as 'a North Korean state actor' [S2].
attribution.confidence: Attribution to North Korea is Microsoft's assessment [S1][S2]. No government attribution of Moonstone Sleet by name was found in the sources gathered. Bitdefender describes Moonstone Sleet's role in the 2025 'Korean Leaks' campaign as only 'potential' involvement [S6][S7].
attribution.basis: Microsoft telemetry, code overlap with Diamond Sleet (Comebacker) and infrastructure analysis [S1]. Checkmarx found indicators linking npm packages to Moonstone Sleet [S3][S4].

actors.objectives: Microsoft assesses dual goals: intelligence collection, such as credential and intellectual-property theft from defense and aerospace firms, and revenue generation through ransomware, possibly also remote IT-worker employment [S1]. Microsoft says the move to Qilin RaaS continues the financially motivated line of effort [S2].

sectors: Defense industrial base and aerospace, including defense technology, drone technology and aircraft parts makers [S1]
Individual software developers and job seekers [S1][S3]
Financial services, potentially, via an MSP compromise in South Korea [S6][S7]

targeting.notes: Microsoft lists aerospace and defense intrusions in December 2023, April 2024 and May 2024 [S1]. The public npm registry gives the group access to an open-ended pool of developers [S3][S4]. Microsoft has not identified a Moonstone Sleet supply-chain attack, but warns that its access to software companies would pose a high risk [S1].

capabilities.summary: Social engineering with fake companies (StarGlow Ventures, C.C. Waterfall, DeTankZone) and fake recruiters or job applicants on LinkedIn, Telegram, freelancing sites and email [S1][S2]. Trojanized PuTTY delivered with the SplitLoader multi-stage dropper [S1]. npm packages disguised as skills tests, which Checkmarx says use a 'single-package approach' that runs at install time [S1][S3][S4]. A fully playable blockchain tank game (DeTankWar/DeTankZone) that delivers the custom YouieLoad loader [S1]. LSASS credential theft with Procdump and Mimikatz [S1]. Custom FakePenny ransomware, with one $6.6M Bitcoin ransom demand [S1]. Qilin RaaS ransomware deployed at a limited number of organizations since late February 2025 [S2].

diamond.adversary: North Korean state actor per Microsoft (formerly Storm-1789), with early overlap with Diamond Sleet [S1][S2].
diamond.capability: SplitLoader, YouieLoad, FakePenny, malicious npm packages, Mimikatz and Procdump against LSASS, and Qilin RaaS [S1][S2][S3].
diamond.infrastructure: Fake company websites and domains such as starglowventures[.]com, ccwaterfall[.]com and detankwar[.]com; C2 domains such as mingeloem[.]com and matrixane[.]com; and the public npm registry [S1][S3].

diamond.technology: Developer trust in open-source packages, freelance and recruiting platforms, and shared tools such as PuTTY; MSP remote-management trust relationships [S1][S3][S6].

gaps: Microsoft's mapping links Moonstone Sleet to LABYRINTH CHOLLIMA [S9]. CrowdStrike's LABYRINTH CHOLLIMA is an older cluster (also UNC4034/Temp.Hermit) that CrowdStrike split into three adversaries in January 2026 [S8]. Which CrowdStrike sub-cluster, if any, corresponds to Moonstone Sleet is not stated in the sources gathered. Do not import LABYRINTH CHOLLIMA or Bureau 121 facts wholesale.
No government attribution or indictment naming Moonstone Sleet was found. The DPRK organizational sponsor (for example, which RGB element) is unverified.

Moonstone Sleet's role in Korean Leaks is described only as 'potential' [S6][S7]. The Bitdefender primary report and the CrowdStrike blog could not be fetched (host unreachable); details come from search summaries and secondary coverage.
BleepingComputer's coverage of Microsoft's March 2025 Qilin statement could not be fetched. The exact publication day and the victims are unknown.
No sources from 2026 describe new Moonstone Sleet operations, so current activity is unverified.
Overlap boundaries with Datadog's Stressed Pungsan and with Diamond Sleet and Jade Sleet npm activity are not fully resolved [S1][S3][S5].
The scale and placements of Moonstone Sleet's IT-worker job seeking are undocumented [S1].

implications.jipoe: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. STEP 1: Key terrain is the developer and contractor workforce: personal devices used for job hunting, npm and other package registries, and MSP management channels into DIB and aerospace suppliers [S1][S3][S6]. STEP 2: Recruiting platforms (LinkedIn, Telegram, freelance sites) and open package registries put the first contact outside DoD-controlled networks, which limits visibility before compromise [S1][S2]. STEP 3: The template is a persona and fake-company lure, then a trojanized tool, skills-test package or game, then a loader (SplitLoader or YouieLoad), then LSASS credential theft and IP theft, with ransomware optional (FakePenny or Qilin) [S1][S2]. STEP 4: The MLCOA is continued job-lure and npm-package intrusions against defense and aerospace contractors and developers to steal credentials and IP. The MDCOA is turning access at a software vendor or MSP into a supply-chain compromise or ransomware against DIB suppliers that support Air Force programs, a risk Microsoft flags [S1][S6]. Candidate indicators: Procdump run against LSASS; connections to known Moonstone Sleet domains; unsolicited job or skills tests that require running PuTTY or npm code; Defender detections such as SplitLoader, YouieLoad or PennyCrypt [S1].
implications.jcc2: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. (1) Situational awareness: fuse Microsoft and vendor npm and package-registry reporting into the JCC2 common operational picture for DIB and aerospace partners, because the first intrusion step happens off-network [S1][S3]. (2) Authorities: the activity mixes espionage with criminal ransomware (FakePenny, Qilin), so incidents may fall under law-enforcement as well as DoD and DC3 lanes. Classify carefully and coordinate early [S1][S2]. (3) Mission assurance: treat contractor developer workstations, build pipelines and MSP connections as mission-relevant terrain; ransomware against a key supplier could degrade sustainment [S1][S6]. (4) Coordination: work with the DIB CS program and industry partners on fake-recruiter and fake-company indicators; brief personnel about job and game lures [S1].

provenance.importedSummary: Moonstone Sleet is a North Korean-linked threat actor executing both financially motivated attacks and espionage operations. The group previously overlapped significantly with another North Korean-linked entity, Lazarus Group, but has differentiated its tradecraft since 2023. Moonstone Sleet is notable for creating fake companies and personas to interact with victim entities, as well as developing unique malware such as a variant delivered via a fully functioning game.

identification.summary: Mora_001 is a threat actor exhibiting a distinct operational signature that combines opportunistic attacks with ties to the LockBit ecosystem. The actor has been observed exploiting CVE-2024-55591 and CVE-2025-24472 vulnerabilities affecting Fortinet devices. The ransom note associated with Mora_001 includes the same TOX ID used by LockBit, indicating a potential affiliation or shared communication channels. Their post-exploitation patterns suggest a structured playbook that differentiates them from other ransomware operators, including LockBit affiliates.

Moshen Dragon is a Chinese-aligned cyberespionage threat actor operating in Central Asia. They have been observed deploying multiple malware triads and utilizing DLL search order hijacking to sideload ShadowPad and PlugX variants. The threat actor also employs various tools, including an LSA notification package and a passive backdoor known as GUNTERS. Their activities involve targeting the telecommunication sector and leveraging Impacket for lateral movement and data exfiltration.

China-based espionage actor that Microsoft tracks as Mulberry Typhoon (formerly MANGANESE) and that Mandiant and MITRE track as APT5 [S1][S8][S9]. MITRE says it primarily targets the telecommunications, aerospace and defense industries in the U.S., Europe and Asia and has a strong interest in compromising networking devices and their software, including with zero-day exploits [S8]. Microsoft reported in 2023 that Mulberry Typhoon targeted the US defense industrial base, most notably with a zero-day exploit against devices (CVE-2022-27518) [S1]. In December 2022 NSA published threat-hunting guidance on APT5's exploitation of Citrix ADC [S4][S5].
identification.firstObserved: MITRE: active since at least 2007 [S8]. 2019 press coverage of FireEye reporting also says the group has been active since 2007 [S7].
identification.notes: Microsoft name: Mulberry Typhoon (formerly MANGANESE) [S1][S9]. MITRE associates Mulberry Typhoon, MANGANESE, BRONZE FLEETWOOD, Keyhole Panda and UNC2630 with APT5 [S8]. NSA-related coverage calls APT5 also UNC2630 and MANGANESE [S4][S6]. Mandiant itself only assessed UNC2630 as possibly tied to APT5, based on a trusted third party's evidence that it could not independently confirm [S2]. 2019 coverage of FireEye reporting describes APT5 as several subgroups with distinct tactics and infrastructure [S7].

attribution.sponsor: People's Republic of China (suspected). Mandiant suspected UNC2630 operates on behalf of the Chinese government [S2]. Its May 2021 update says UNC2630 and UNC2717 are believed to be affiliated with the Chinese government [S3]. Coverage of the NSA guidance calls APT5 a Chinese state-sponsored group [S5][S6].
attribution.confidence: Microsoft describes Mulberry Typhoon as China-based [S1]. NSA publicly attributed the CVE-2022-27518 exploitation to APT5 in December 2022, according to press coverage of the advisory [S4][S5]. Mandiant held the UNC2630 to APT5 link at low-to-moderate confidence ('may have ties'; 'not able to definitively connect') [S2]. 2019 coverage notes that FireEye had not formally attributed APT5 to a nation-state [S7].
attribution.basis: Microsoft telemetry and reporting [S1]; Mandiant incident response at Pulse Secure victims, plus third-party linkage to historic APT5 campaigns [S2][S3]; NSA threat-hunting guidance, which this record relies on through press reporting [S4][S5][S6]; MITRE ATT&CK group entry [S8].

actors.objectives: Espionage aimed at defense, aerospace and telecommunications targets [S1][S8]. Mandiant judged that Pulse Secure-era activity sought to steal credentials, keep long-term persistent access to victim networks and access or exfiltrate sensitive data, in support of key Chinese government priorities [S3]. Earlier VPN-exploitation coverage reported spying on pricing and bidding information [S7].

sectors: Government, high tech, education, transportation and financial (broader Pulse Secure campaign, not UNC2630 alone) [S3]
targeting.notes: Microsoft groups Mulberry Typhoon with Circle Typhoon and Volt Typhoon as China-based groups targeting the US DIB. It says their targets occasionally overlap but they are distinct actors with different infrastructure and capabilities [S1]. Mandiant's May 2021 sector list covers the whole Pulse Secure campaign (UNC2630 and UNC2717) [S3].

capabilities.summary: Exploits edge and network appliances, including zero-days: Pulse Secure CVE-2021-22893 alongside older flaws [S2], Citrix ADC/Gateway CVE-2022-27518 [S1][S4], and, per 2019 coverage, Pulse Secure CVE-2019-11510 and Fortinet CVE-2018-13379 [S7]. CVE-2022-27518 allowed unauthenticated remote code execution on appliances configured as a SAML SP or IdP [S4]. UNC2630 deployed purpose-built Pulse Secure implants: SLOWPULSE, which modifies legitimate Pulse Secure files to bypass or log credentials in authentication flows, including some 2FA, plus RADIALPULSE, THINBLOOD, ATRIUM, PACEMAKER, SLIGHTPULSE and PULSECHECK [S2]. Later families include BLOODMINE, BLOODBANK, CLEANPULSE and RAPIDPULSE [S3]. Operators patched devices for persistence that survived upgrades, removed webshells to evade detection and cleared logs [S3]. MITRE also lists Mimikatz, Skeleton Key, PoisonIvy, gh0st RAT and PcShare [S8].

diamond.capability: Zero-day and n-day exploits for VPN and application-delivery appliances; trojanized appliance binaries (SLOWPULSE family); webshells; credential theft; log tampering [S2][S3][S4][S7].

gaps: The NSA advisory 'APT5: Citrix ADC Threat Hunting Guidance' (December 2022) could not be opened; its content is cited through press coverage [S4][S5][S6].
No Microsoft report dedicated to Mulberry Typhoon was found. Microsoft's public description is limited to the 2023 East Asia report [S1].
Original FireEye reporting on APT5's 2007 origins and subgroups was not retrieved; it is cited through 2019 press coverage [S7].
The UNC2630 to APT5 link rests on an unnamed third party per Mandiant [S2]. Some press coverage overstates it as confirmed; treat Pulse Secure-era facts as UNC2630, not as definitively APT5.

The vendor sources gathered here do not substantiate the CrowdStrike (Keyhole Panda) and Secureworks (BRONZE FLEETWOOD) alias mappings beyond MITRE's listing [S8].
No sponsoring organization (MSS, PLA or contractor) is named in the sources gathered.

implications.jipoe: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. STEP 1: Key terrain is the edge: SSL VPN concentrators, Citrix ADC/Gateway and SAML-integrated access appliances on DIB, aerospace and telecom networks that connect to DoD programs [S1][S2][S4]. STEP 2: These appliances often fall outside EDR coverage and retain few logs. The actor patches appliance binaries and clears logs, so absence of evidence is weak [S2][S3]. STEP 3: The doctrinal template is appliance exploit (zero-day or fresh n-day), then trojanized authentication components or a webshell, then credential harvest, then internal access and data staging [S2][S3]. STEP 4: MLCOA is quiet, long-term credential theft and data collection from DIB and telecom networks via edge devices [S3]. MDCOA is a rapid mass-exploitation wave against a newly discovered appliance zero-day across DoD-adjacent contractors, with implants that survive vendor patching and upgrades, giving persistent access to program data during a crisis [S1][S3]. Candidate indicators: modified Pulse Secure or Citrix system files and integrity-check failures, unexpected webshells on appliances, gaps or truncation in appliance logs, and authentication successes that bypass MFA [S2][S3][S4].
implications.jcc2: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. (1) Situational awareness: JCC2 should track edge-appliance inventory and patch state, plus vendor integrity-check results, for DoD and mission-partner networks, because this actor's entry point is the appliance [S2][S4]. (2) Authorities: most observed victims are DIB companies [S1][S2]. Response depends on DC3/DIB CS sharing, CISA and NSA advisories and contractor cooperation rather than DoD-owned terrain. (3) Mission assurance: an appliance patch alone does not remove a persistence patcher [S3]. Plan for rebuild or replacement and credential resets on systems behind compromised appliances. (4) Coordination: Mulberry, Circle and Volt Typhoon target the same DIB sector but are distinct actors [S1]. Deconflict hunts and reporting by actor, and avoid merging indicators across clusters.

identification.summary: Russian covert influence operation that Microsoft's Threat Analysis Center (MTAC) tracked as Storm-1516 and described as Kremlin-aligned [S1][S2]. Its signature is a fabricated video, often with a paid actor posing as a whistleblower or citizen journalist, laundered through newly created websites that imitate local or well-known media outlets and then amplified by influencers [S1][S2][S9]. France's VIGINUM analyzed 77 Storm-1516 operations documented from the operation's emergence through 5 March 2025 [S8]. NewsGuard assessed in December 2025 that Storm-1516 had overtaken Russian state media (RT and Sputnik) as the leading source of false Russia-Ukraine claims it tracks, based on roughly 400 debunked narratives [S6][S7].
identification.firstObserved: VIGINUM dates the operation's start to March 2023 [S8].
identification.notes: Microsoft name: Neva Flood (formerly Storm-1516), per the encyclopedia's imported Microsoft naming mapping; not re-verified in this research pass. Recorded Future tracks a closely related network as CopyCop, which it links to John Mark Dougan, the Moscow-based Center for Geopolitical Expertise (CGE) and the GRU [S4][S5]. VIGINUM treats Storm-1516 and CopyCop as overlapping rather than identical, and links Storm-1516 to sub-clusters including former Prigozhin troll-farm staff and Dougan's fake-news sites [S8]. Keep CopyCop website counts and Storm-1516 operation counts separate.

attribution.sponsor: Russian Federation. VIGINUM attributes central coordination to Yury Khoroshenky, whom it describes as a suspected officer of Russian military intelligence (GRU) [S8]. The US Treasury said the GRU directed and funded the CGE and US-based facilitators who built an AI server and at least 100 imitation news websites for 2024 US election interference [S10]. The EU sanctioned Dougan in December 2025 as responsible for the Storm-1516 campaign, and the German government publicly blamed Russia for using Storm-1516 against its federal election [S11].
attribution.confidence: Microsoft (MTAC) labels Storm-1516 Kremlin-aligned [S1][S2]. VIGINUM (French government) states its investigations confirm involvement of individuals and organizations close to the Russian state, including Dougan [S8]. Recorded Future assesses CopyCop is very likely operated by Dougan with CGE and GRU support [S4][S5]. Treasury's December 2024 designation of the CGE describes a GRU-funded website network but, in the coverage reviewed, does not name Storm-1516 or Dougan [S10]. Dougan denies working for the Russian government [S3].
attribution.basis: Microsoft MTAC election reporting [S1][S2]; VIGINUM technical report (via secondary coverage) [S8]; Recorded Future Insikt Group CopyCop reporting [S4][S5]; US Treasury OFAC sanctions on CGE and Valery Korovin (via press coverage) [S10]; EU sanctions and German government statement (via CORRECTIV) [S11]; investigative reporting by CORRECTIV [S3].

actors.objectives: Undermine Western support for Ukraine and shape elections in target countries in Russia's favor [S1][S9]. Bloomberg's 2026 analysis of Storm-1516 videos found more than 40% aimed at undermining support for Ukraine and about one-third targeted elections in countries other than the US [S9]. NewsGuard found false narratives aimed at France closely followed French expressions of support for Ukraine [S7].

sectors: News media (impersonation of outlets and real journalists) [S1][S4]
regions: Ukraine (narratives about Ukraine and its leadership) [S6][S9]
targeting.notes: Targets track Russian foreign-policy priorities: the US election in 2024, then Germany ahead of its February 2025 election, and France following its support for Ukraine [S1][S3][S7]. Canada and Moldova targeting is from Recorded Future's CopyCop reporting, an overlapping cluster [S4].

capabilities.summary: Production of staged or AI-manipulated videos featuring actors posing as whistleblowers or citizen journalists [S1][S9]. Rapid creation of fake news websites that imitate local outlets, sometimes registered only days before use, with large reserves of dormant sites prepared in advance (more than 100 German-named sites before the 2025 election) [S1][S2][S3]. Generative AI used to rewrite the same story for each site [S3]; Recorded Future reports self-hosted, uncensored Llama 3 models, likely GRU-financed, and over 300 inauthentic CopyCop websites in 2025 [S4]. Impersonation of media outlets, political parties, fact-checkers and real journalists [S4]. Amplification through pro-Russian influencers, Telegram channels and hashtags on X [S2][S3].

The Insider and Gnida Project report 2025 Storm-1516 fabrications aimed at Moldova, Armenia and France that used real journalists' identities; not included as cited events because publication dates were not confirmed.
Secondary coverage of the VIGINUM report says Khoroshenky is possibly assigned to GRU Unit 29155; this was not confirmed in the primary report.
No MITRE ATT&CK group entry exists; the actor is an influence operation, not an intrusion set, so cyber-intrusion TTPs are not documented.
Measured effects on voter behavior or policy outcomes are not documented; reach figures (views) are vendor and media estimates.
Secondary coverage states Clemson University's Media Forensics Hub first identified the operation in December 2023, before MTAC named it; the Clemson report was not located.

implications.jipoe: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. STEP 1 (operational environment): The relevant terrain is the information environment of the US and allies that support Ukraine. This includes local-news brand trust, social platforms (X, Telegram), and AI chatbots that repeat narratives [S3][S7]. STEP 2 (effects): Pre-positioned dormant domain reserves let the actor surge within days of a political trigger, such as a coalition collapse or an election [S3]. STEP 3 (threat model): The template is fabricated video with an actor, then laundering through a fake local outlet created days earlier, then amplification by influencers and Telegram [S1][S2][S3]. STEP 4 (COAs): MLCOA is continued fabrications against leaders of pro-Ukraine states timed to aid decisions and elections [S7][S9]. MDCOA is a fabricated whistleblower video alleging misconduct by US or allied military personnel or units during a crisis, aimed at splitting coalition support. Candidate indicators: bursts of newly registered domains with local-news names, sites that share templates or AI-rewritten copy, and actor-led 'whistleblower' videos first posted on new channels [S1][S3][S4].
implications.jcc2: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. (1) Situational awareness: track public reporting from VIGINUM, Microsoft MTAC, Recorded Future and NewsGuard, and monitor new domain registrations that imitate news outlets near allied elections [S3][S4][S8]. (2) Authorities: this is foreign malign influence aimed at civilian audiences. Response, including attribution and sanctions, has come through Treasury, the EU and allied governments, not military cyber channels [S10][S11]. DoD roles are mainly support and force protection. (3) Mission assurance: prepare rapid public-affairs and command responses to fabricated claims about personnel or operations, because fabricated videos gain millions of views quickly [S1][S2]. (4) Coordination: share indicators with allied agencies (e.g., VIGINUM) and interagency partners. Recognize vendor cluster differences (Storm-1516 vs CopyCop) when fusing reporting [S5][S8].

provenance.importedSummary: CopyCop is a Russian covert influence network that has established over 300 fictional media websites targeting the US, France, Canada, and other countries, primarily to disseminate pro-Russian and anti-Ukrainian narratives. The network employs TTPs such as deepfakes, fake interviews, and self-hosted LLMs for content generation, while also impersonating local media outlets and fact-checking organizations. Its operations are supported by the Moscow-based Center for Geopolitical Expertise and the GRU, aiming to undermine support for Ukraine and exacerbate political fragmentation in Western nations. CopyCop's influence content is amplified by a network of pro-Russian social media influencers and other Russian influence networks.

identification.summary: NICKEL ALLEY is a North Korean threat group that targets technology professionals through fake job opportunities, employing social engineering tactics such as creating fraudulent LinkedIn pages and GitHub repositories for malware delivery. They utilize the ClickFix tactic to deploy the PyLangGhost RAT, which supports file exfiltration and system profiling, particularly focusing on Chrome cryptocurrency wallet data. The group has also leveraged Visual Studio Code tasks to execute commands for malware retrieval based on the victim's operating system. Their operations indicate a dual focus on cryptocurrency theft and potential supply chain compromise or corporate espionage.

identification.summary: These attackers were the subject of an extensive report by Symantec in 2011, which termed the attackers Nitro and stated: 'The goal of the attackers appears to be to collect intellectual property such as design documents, formulas, and manufacturing processes. In addition, the same attackers appear to have a lengthy operation history including attacks on other industries and organizations. Attacks on the chemical industry are merely their latest attack wave. As part of our investigations, we were also able to identify and contact one of the attackers to try and gain insights into the motivations behind these attacks.' Palo Alto Networks reported on continued activity by the attackers in 2014.

Russian-speaking cyber-espionage group that MITRE ATT&CK says has mainly targeted Central Asia, including local governments, diplomatic missions and individuals, since at least 2014, using Android and Windows malware written largely in Delphi [S1]. ESET named it Nomadic Octopus and presented it at Virus Bulletin 2018 as a previously undocumented group focused on diplomatic missions in the region [S4][S5]. Kaspersky tracks the same actor as DustSquad and documented its Delphi 'Octopus' Windows Trojan disguised as a Russian-interface Telegram client [S2][S3]. In April 2023 PRODAFT reported 'Paperbug', a surveillance campaign against high-ranking Tajik officials, telecom services and public service infrastructure, ongoing since 2020 [S8][S9].
identification.firstObserved: Kaspersky: campaign dating back to 2014 [S2][S6]. ESET: active since at least 2015 [S4][S6]. MITRE ATT&CK: since at least 2014 [S1].
identification.notes: Vendor names: Nomadic Octopus (ESET) and DustSquad (Kaspersky) [S1][S6]. Kaspersky says the name 'Octopus' was coined by ESET in 2017 after the 0ct0pus3.php script found on the actor's old C2 servers [S2]. MITRE tracks the group as G0133 and its Windows backdoor as Octopus (S0340) [S1]. No Microsoft (weather-taxonomy) name was found in the sources gathered. Scope differs between vendors: in 2018 ESET reported only one malware family, while Kaspersky reported Windows and Android malware [S6].

attribution.confidence: No government attribution found. Vendors describe the operators as Russian-speaking [S1][S2]. ESET's Anton Cherepanov told SecurityWeek the Russian-language inference rests on spear-phishing emails and Russian malware filenames [S6]. Kaspersky linked the Octopus Trojan to DustSquad with its similarity-based Attribution Engine and found no strong similarities tying Octopus to Zebrocy/Sofacy, even though some victims were infected with both [S2]. For Paperbug, coverage reports PRODAFT said the observed TTPs align with patterns associated with Russia-linked actors such as Sofacy, while also stating the ultimate motive is unknown [S8][S9].
attribution.basis: Language artifacts in lures and filenames [S6]; code-similarity analysis by Kaspersky [S2]; PRODAFT victim data and access to a C2 backend panel during the Paperbug investigation [S8].

actors.objectives: Political and diplomatic intelligence collection in Central Asia: ESET describes cyber espionage against diplomatic missions as the main goal and noted a campaign against a local political blogger, suggesting surveillance beyond high-value targets [S4][S5]. In Paperbug, operators periodically stole emails, documents and chat histories and took real-time screenshots of victims writing emails and contracts [S8][S9]. PRODAFT reportedly left the ultimate sponsor open, citing domestic opposition forces or intelligence gathering by Russia or China as possibilities [S9].

sectors: Public service infrastructure, including OT such as gas station systems [S8]
targeting.notes: In Paperbug, initial access to victims came through the compromised network of a Tajikistan-based telecom company; further access came from stolen documents, client contracts and credentials, weak network configurations and unpatched software [S8].

capabilities.summary: Custom Delphi malware: the Octopus Windows Trojan, delivered as a fake Russian-interface Telegram client in a ZIP lure, gives remote access, command execution, file upload and download, screenshots and searches for RAR archives, using third-party Delphi libraries for JSON-based C2 traffic and compression [S2][S3]. ESET's slides describe a documents collector and about 280 exfiltrated archives, mostly documents [S5]. Kaspersky also found Android malware [S6]. In Paperbug the group used an updated Octopus variant plus mostly public offensive tools, disguised tools as 'Google Update' and 'Java Update', sometimes deployed tools carelessly during victims' active hours, and ran several C2 servers [S8][S9]. MITRE lists the group's techniques separately [S1].

gaps: No primary document could be opened directly: Securelist, PRODAFT, Virus Bulletin, SecurityWeek, Security Affairs, The Hacker News and Malpedia all failed to fetch (DNS errors). Facts come from search-result excerpts of these pages and should be checked against the originals.
The Paperbug report PDF (prodaft.com/m/reports/PAPERBUG_TLPWHITE-1.pdf, in the actor record) was not reviewed. Its IOCs, victim counts and C2 details are unverified.
A secondary search summary claimed Nomadic Octopus compromised 499 systems since January 2022. The source of this figure could not be identified, so it is excluded.

Sponsor is unknown. 'Russian-speaking' is a linguistic assessment. PRODAFT's comparison to Sofacy-like TTPs conflicts with Kaspersky's finding of no strong Octopus-Zebrocy/Sofacy ties; neither is government attribution.
No Microsoft name for this actor was found.
Some aggregator pages show an alias 'Golden Falcon' alongside DustSquad; no cited vendor source confirms it, so it was not added.
No public reporting after the April 2023 Paperbug disclosure was found; current activity status is unknown.
Exact publication dates for several 2018 and 2023 articles are given to month precision only.

implications.jipoe: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. STEP 1: The operational environment is Central Asian government, diplomatic and telecom networks, including the networks of partner nations and of US and coalition diplomatic or liaison elements in the region [S1][S8]. Regional telecom carriers are key terrain because Paperbug used one as an access point to downstream victims [S8]. STEP 2: Local mobile carriers and weak network configurations can expose traffic and endpoints of personnel who rely on host-nation services [S8]. STEP 3: The doctrinal template is a socially engineered lure (fake messaging app, political-themed ZIP) or carrier-network pivot, then a Delphi backdoor or public tooling disguised as updaters, then document and screenshot collection [S2][S8]. STEP 4: MLCOA is quiet, long-running political surveillance of officials and diplomats, with collection of email, documents and chats [S8][S9]. MDCOA is use of telecom access to monitor coalition or partner communications, or misuse of the OT access shown in Paperbug (gas station systems) [S8]. Candidate indicators: unsigned Telegram-lookalike installers; processes named Google Update or Java Update in non-standard paths; periodic screenshot capture; outbound JSON-over-HTTP beacons from Delphi binaries; staging of RAR archives [S2][S8].
implications.jcc2: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. (1) Situational awareness: tag Central Asian partner-nation telecom and government networks as possible compromised transit, and treat host-nation carrier paths as untrusted [S8]. (2) Authorities: the actor targets foreign government and partner networks rather than the DODIN directly, so response options rely on information sharing with partners and the State Department rather than DoD defensive action on those networks. (3) Mission assurance: personnel deployed or traveling in Central Asia should use enterprise-managed messaging and avoid sideloaded apps, given the fake-Telegram lure [S2][S3]. (4) Coordination: report suspected indicators through CTI channels, and ask vendors (ESET, Kaspersky, PRODAFT) for updated reporting, since public data ends in 2023.

provenance.importedSummary: Prodaft researchers have published a report on Paperbug, a cyber-espionage campaign carried out by suspected Russian-speaking group Nomadic Octopus and which targeted entities in Tajikistan. According to Prodaft, known compromised victims included high-ranking government officials, telcos, and public service infrastructures. Compromised devices also included OT devices, besides your typical computers, servers, and mobile devices. identification.summary: Nylon Typhoon (formerly NICKEL) is a China-based espionage actor that Microsoft says uses exploits against unpatched systems to compromise remote access services and appliances, targeting government agencies, diplomatic organizations and NGOs in Central and South America, the Caribbean, Europe and North America [S1][S11]. MITRE ATT&CK tracks the same group as Ke3chang (G0004), attributed to actors operating out of China, which has targeted oil, government, diplomatic, military and NGO organizations since at least 2010 [S3]. Microsoft reports that the actor achieved long-term access to several victims and ran regularly scheduled data exfiltration [S1]. Symantec reported the group, which it tracks as Flea, still attacking foreign ministries in the Americas in late 2022 and early 2023 with a new Microsoft Graph-based backdoor, Graphican [S12][S13].
identification.firstObserved: MITRE: targeting since at least 2010 [S3]. Microsoft has tracked NICKEL since 2016 and tracked the operations it disclosed in 2021 since September 2019 [S1]. Latest dated public campaign found: late 2022 to early 2023 (Symantec, Flea) [S12][S13].
identification.notes: Microsoft name: Nylon Typhoon (formerly NICKEL). Microsoft maps NICKEL, VIXEN PANDA, Playful Dragon, RedRiver, ke3chang, APT15 and Mirage to it [S4]. In 2021 Microsoft wrote that it 'observed some common activity' with actors known as APT15, APT25 and KeChang, which is an overlap statement rather than a one-to-one equivalence [S1]. Microsoft's Security Insider profile (dated 2024-01-25) lists APT15 and Vixen Panda as other names [S11]. Symantec's Flea is linked to APT15/Nickel in coverage of its 2023 report [S13]. MITRE lists Ke3chang, APT15, Mirage, Vixen Panda, GREF, Playful Dragon, RoyalAPT, NICKEL and Nylon Typhoon as associated names [S3]. The imported summary on this record described ESET's 'GREF' cluster (active since March 2017, Android BadBazaar campaigns against Uyghurs). That summary was not carried forward because no source gathered here ties that ESET cluster to Microsoft's Nylon Typhoon (see gaps).

attribution.sponsor: People's Republic of China (state nexus). Microsoft describes NICKEL as a China-based threat actor [S1][S4], and MITRE attributes Ke3chang to actors operating out of China [S3]. None of the sources gathered names a specific PRC agency or unit.
attribution.confidence: Microsoft attributes the activity to NICKEL / Nylon Typhoon by name and assesses that China-based actors will keep targeting government, diplomatic and NGO sectors, likely for economic espionage or traditional intelligence collection [S1]. Microsoft did not publish a numeric or worded confidence level for state sponsorship. The December 2021 domain seizure was a civil action by Microsoft's Digital Crimes Unit under a US District Court order, not a US government attribution [S1][S2]. Symantec assesses Flea as China-linked [S13]; that is a vendor assessment, not government attribution.
attribution.basis: Microsoft MSTIC telemetry and customer notifications, plus the DCU seizure of NICKEL-operated websites [S1][S2]; sign-in activity concentrated Monday to Friday, 08:00 to 17:00 China Standard Time [S1]; long-running vendor reporting summarized by MITRE ATT&CK (Mandiant, NCC Group, Intezer, ESET) [S3][S6][S7][S8][S9]; Symantec reporting on Flea/Graphican, as covered by the press [S12][S13]; Mandiant reporting on shared China-nexus ORB infrastructure [S5].

actors.objectives: Intelligence collection against foreign ministries, diplomatic entities, other government bodies and NGOs. Microsoft assesses this is likely in pursuit of economic espionage or traditional intelligence collection as China expands bilateral relations and Belt and Road partnerships [S1]. Mandiant's 2014 Operation Ke3chang report focused on attacks against Ministries of Foreign Affairs [S3][S9]. Symantec's 2022-2023 Flea victims were mainly foreign affairs ministries in the Americas, plus a government finance department, consistent with continued diplomatic intelligence collection [S12][S13].

sectors: Government, including ministries of foreign affairs and a finance department [S1][S9][S12][S13]
Private corporation in Central and South America (2022-2023) [S13]
regions: Central and South America, with a large share of activity against Central and South American governments [S1]
North America, including the United States [S1][S3]
Africa: Mali appears among the 29 countries Microsoft listed [S1]
Middle East: Mandiant lists it among regions historically targeted by APT15 and APT5 [S5]
targeting.notes: Microsoft's December 2021 list of 29 targeted countries: Argentina, Barbados, Bosnia and Herzegovina, Brazil, Bulgaria, Chile, Colombia, Croatia, Czech Republic, Dominican Republic, Ecuador, El Salvador, France, Guatemala, Honduras, Hungary, Italy, Jamaica, Mali, Mexico, Montenegro, Panama, Peru, Portugal, Switzerland, Trinidad and Tobago, United Kingdom, United States and Venezuela [S1]. In its 2021 Digital Defense Report summary, Microsoft names NICKEL among the four nation-state groups most active against the government sector from July 2020 to June 2021, mostly against government entities involved in international affairs [S10]. Symantec's 2022-2023 activity hit foreign ministries in the Americas, a corporation in Central and South America and one European victim [S12][S13].

capabilities.summary: Initial access through exploits against unpatched internet-facing Microsoft Exchange and SharePoint servers and remote-access appliances such as VPNs, including a Pulse Secure VPN vulnerability [S1]. MITRE also records VPN access using compromised accounts and stolen VPN certificates [S3][S6]. Credential theft uses keyloggers, Mimikatz, WDigest abuse and NTDSDump [S1]. Custom backdoors include Neoichor, Leeson, NumbIdea, NullItch and Rokum; several use the Internet Explorer COM interface for C2 hidden in legitimate-looking web pages, and implants are dropped into existing application paths to blend in [S1]. Stolen credentials are used for routine Microsoft 365 email collection through browser sign-ins and legacy Exchange Web Services, routed through commercial VPNs and actor infrastructure [S1]. Scheduled, incremental file collection is staged and archived with renamed RAR or 7-Zip [S1]. Earlier tooling includes RoyalCLI and RoyalDNS (DNS C2) and the SharePoint dumping tool spwebmember [S3][S6], the MirageFox RAT, an upgraded Mirage [S3][S7], and the Okrum backdoor, in use since December 2016 [S3][S8]. Mandiant reports that APT15 has used the provisioned ORB network SPACEHOP for reconnaissance scanning and vulnerability exploitation [S5]. In 2022-2023 the group (as Symantec's Flea) used Graphican, an evolution of the Ketrican backdoor (itself based on BS2005), which uses the Microsoft Graph API and OneDrive to retrieve encrypted C2 addresses and supports an interactive shell, file transfer, hidden process creation and hidden PowerShell execution [S12][S13]. The same campaign used the EWSTEW Exchange email-extraction backdoor, the Zerologon flaw CVE-2020-1472, Mimikatz, Pypykatz, Safetykatz and the public K8Tools toolkit [S12][S13].

implications.jipoe: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. STEP 1 (define the OE): Key cyber terrain is internet-facing Exchange, SharePoint and VPN appliances, plus Microsoft 365 tenants that still allow legacy authentication (EWS). It matters most for foreign-affairs, diplomatic and partner-nation government networks in Latin America, the Caribbean, Europe and North America [S1]. STEP 2 (describe effects): Exposed and unpatched remote-access edges are the entry point. Shared ORB relay networks such as SPACEHOP spread source infrastructure across commercial VPS providers, which weakens IP-based blocking and attribution [S1][S5]. STEP 3 (adversary template): Exploit edge service or VPN, then dump credentials (Mimikatz, NTDSDump, WDigest, keylogger), then deploy an IE-COM backdoor in a legitimate software path, then collect mailboxes through M365/EWS sign-ins over commercial VPNs, then run recurring, date-filtered file collection archived with renamed RAR or 7-Zip [S1]. STEP 4 (COAs): MLCOA is quiet, long-term diplomatic and government intelligence collection with scheduled exfiltration from partner-nation ministries [S1]. MDCOA is persistent access to partner-nation foreign-affairs and military networks, or to shared coalition email, exposing coalition planning or negotiating positions (analyst extrapolation from the targeting [S1][S3]). Graphican shows the actor moving C2 into Microsoft Graph/OneDrive traffic, which blends with normal M365 use [S12][S13]. Candidate indicators: unexpected Graph API or OneDrive access by non-browser processes on servers; Zerologon (CVE-2020-1472) exploitation attempts against domain controllers [S12][S13]; EWS or legacy-auth sign-ins from commercial VPN ranges during 00:00-09:00 UTC on weekdays; WDigest UseLogonCredential being enabled; executables such as AcroRd64.exe or FoxitRdr64.exe in unexpected application folders; IE registry changes (IEHarden=0, ClearBrowsingHistoryOnExit=1); renamed rar.exe or 7z.exe with keyboard-walk passwords [S1].
implications.jcc2: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. Situational awareness: Fuse identity telemetry (legacy-auth and EWS sign-ins, VPN-sourced logons) with edge-device patch status. The actor relies on valid credentials after initial exploitation, so host-only sensing will miss mailbox collection [S1]. Track ORB/SPACEHOP-linked infrastructure as shared China-nexus terrain rather than as a single-actor indicator [S5]. Authorities: The 2021 disruption came through a private civil seizure (Microsoft DCU under a US District Court order), not government action [S1][S2]. Planners should not count such actions as DoD effects, and they should coordinate deconfliction with private-sector disruption efforts. Situational awareness should also cover cloud API telemetry, because Graph/OneDrive C2 bypasses traditional C2 domain blocking [S12][S13]. Mission assurance: Block legacy authentication, enforce MFA, apply the ASR rule against LSASS credential theft, and prioritize patching of Exchange, SharePoint and VPN appliances on DODIN and mission-partner enclaves [S1]. Coordination: Many victims are partner-nation and Western Hemisphere foreign ministries [S1]. Information sharing with partner nations and combatant commands, especially SOUTHCOM-area partners, is an analyst-inferred coordination need for protecting shared diplomatic and military communications.

provenance.importedSummary: GREF is a China-aligned APT group that has been active since at least March 2017. identification.summary:
Scattered Spider is a native English-speaking cybercriminal group active since at least 2022.   The group initially targeted customer relationship management (CRM) providers, business process outsourcing (BPO) firms, and telecommunications and technology companies before expanding in 2023 to gaming, hospitality, retail, managed service provider (MSP), manufacturing, and financial sectors. 
Scattered Spider relies heavily on social engineering, including impersonating IT and help-desk staff, to gain initial access, bypass multi-factor authentication (MFA), and compromise enterprise networks. The group has adapted its tooling to evade endpoint detection and response (EDR) defenses and used ransomware for financial gain.   
Scattered Spider had expanded into hybrid cloud and identity environments, using help-desk impersonation and MFA bypass to obtain administrator access in Okta, AWS, and Office 365.

identification.summary: Oka Flood is Microsoft's name for a Russia-based influence-operations actor that Microsoft previously tracked as Storm-1679 [S4]. Microsoft calls Storm-1679 a prolific Russian influence actor whose main tactic is spoofed content that imitates reputable media outlets [S1]. Microsoft says the Paris 2024 Olympics were a primary objective since at least summer 2023, when the actor released the fake documentary 'Olympics Has Fallen' with AI-generated audio imitating Tom Cruise's voice [S1][S2]. In September 2024 Microsoft reported that Storm-1679 shifted from the French election and the Olympics to content targeting Kamala Harris [S3].
identification.firstObserved: Microsoft: Olympics-focused activity since at least summer 2023, with the fake documentary released on Telegram in June 2023 [S1][S2]. CheckFirst's related 'Operation Overload' reporting begins in 2023 [S5].
identification.notes: Microsoft name: Oka Flood (formerly Storm-1679), listed as a Russian influence-operations actor [S4]. Researchers outside Microsoft (ISD, as relayed by the AI Incident Database) treat Operation Overload, Matryoshka and Storm-1679 as one campaign [S8]. CheckFirst names the newsroom-flooding campaign Operation Overload [S5][S6]. These are separate analytic clusters whose equivalence Microsoft has not confirmed in the sources gathered. Microsoft reports Storm-1679 alongside Storm-1099 (Doppelganger) and Storm-1516, but tracks them as separate actors [S1][S3].

attribution.sponsor: Russia (Microsoft: Russia-affiliated influence actor) [S1][S4]. No sourced attribution to a specific Russian government organization.
attribution.confidence: Microsoft describes Storm-1679 as a Russian influence actor but does not name a state sponsor in the sources reviewed [S1][S3]. CheckFirst found that some email accounts used in Operation Overload were accessed from Russian residential IP addresses [S6][S9]. CheckFirst's CEO, Guillaume Kuster, called this 'a red flag' but 'not proof of anything', and said it was unclear who was behind the campaign or whether it was state-backed [S9]. No US government attribution was found.
attribution.basis: Microsoft Threat Analysis Center (MTAC) observation of content and amplification [S1][S2][S3]; Microsoft naming taxonomy [S4]; CheckFirst/Reset.Tech technical analysis of email infrastructure (Operation Overload cluster) [S5][S6].

actors.objectives: Microsoft says the actor's goals were to damage the International Olympic Committee's reputation, create expectations of violence at the Paris 2024 Games, and discourage spectators from attending [S1][S2]. Earlier Russia-aligned celebrity-video content pushed the false narrative that President Zelensky abuses drugs [S1][S7]. In 2024 the actor turned to US election narratives that disparaged Kamala Harris [S3]. CheckFirst says the related Operation Overload campaign aims to drain fact-checker and newsroom resources and to push Kremlin narratives through trusted information channels [S5].

sectors: National governments and political leaders (France/Macron; US presidential campaign) [S1][S3]
Media, newsrooms and fact-checkers (impersonated or flooded) [S1][S5]
regions: Ukraine and Ukrainian refugee communities (earlier campaigns) [S1]
Germany (2025 federal election, per AI Incident Database reporting on Matryoshka/Operation Overload) [S8]
targeting.notes: Before spring 2024, content was mostly in English with some French, German and other European languages. French-language content increased in spring 2024 [S1]. Germany targeting comes from the Matryoshka/Operation Overload cluster, not from Microsoft reporting [S8].

capabilities.summary: Influence-operations tradecraft rather than network intrusion. Documented techniques include: AI-generated voice imitation of celebrities (Tom Cruise) in a feature-length fake documentary with spoofed Netflix branding and fake reviews attributed to the New York Times, Washington Post and BBC [S1][S2]; doctored Cameo videos bought from US celebrities and re-edited with anti-Ukraine messaging [S1][S7]; fake news clips and video 'press releases' impersonating Euronews, France 24, the CIA and France's DGSI [S1]; likely digitally generated graffiti images and false-flag impersonation of militant groups [S1]; and bot-amplified accounts and Telegram channels [S1]. In the September 2024 Harris content, Microsoft found the actor used actors and conventional editing rather than generative AI [S3]. The related Operation Overload cluster sends mass email to newsrooms (at least 71,000 emails reported by September 2024, with the volume having trebled since June) and uses 'content amalgamation' across X, Telegram and Russia-aligned sites [S5][S6][S9].

implications.jipoe: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. STEP 1 (operational environment): The information environment counts as key terrain. That includes Telegram, X, short-form video platforms, the brands of trusted Western media and agencies (CIA, DGSI, BBC, France 24), and fact-checking organizations [S1][S5]. STEP 2 (effects): The actor imitates trusted brands and celebrity voices cheaply, so audiences and newsrooms face content that looks authoritative. Verification capacity is the friendly vulnerability the actor exploits [S1][S5]. STEP 3 (adversary model): Pick a high-visibility event (Olympics, election). Produce spoofed media or a fake press release that hints at violence or scandal. Seed it on Telegram and amplify it with bots. Then email newsrooms asking them to 'verify' it [S1][S3][S5]. STEP 4 (COAs): The most likely COA (MLCOA) is fabricated news clips or fake official statements around major Western events and elections that discredit leaders and support for Ukraine [S1][S3]. The most dangerous COA (MDCOA) is a fabricated 'official' threat warning (for example, a spoofed CIA or allied intelligence press release) released during a real crisis or a major event with a US military presence, which would trigger panic, force-protection confusion or misdirected public affairs responses [S1]. Candidate indicators: content carrying spoofed logos of agencies or outlets that is absent from their official channels; new Telegram channels pushing event-specific fear narratives; bursts of verification-request emails to press and public affairs offices [S1][S5].
implications.jcc2: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. (1) Situational awareness: Track impersonation of US government and DoD brands alongside media spoofing, since the actor has faked CIA press releases [S1]. Give public affairs and IO cells a shared picture of active fabricated narratives. (2) Authorities: This is an influence actor with no sourced network-intrusion activity. Responses fall mainly under IO, public affairs and interagency (State GEC successor functions, FBI FITF) lanes rather than DCO. Confirm authorities before any cyberspace response. (3) Mission assurance: Expect fabricated threat content around large events and exercises with a US presence. Prepare rapid authoritative messaging to prevent operational disruption [S1]. (4) Coordination: Share indicators with platform operators and allied counterparts (France, Germany) that are dealing with the same campaigns. Do not merge vendor clusters (Storm-1679, Operation Overload, Matryoshka) in reporting without noting the source of each [S5][S8].

provenance.importedSummary: Storm-1679 is a Russian disinformation group believed to be a spinoff of the Internet Research Agency, actively engaged in influence operations targeting the International Olympic Committee and the 2024 Olympic Games. The group has employed AI-generated content, including deepfake videos and fabricated narratives about violence, to discredit the IOC and instill fear among potential attendees. Their campaigns have been identified across multiple languages and platforms, utilizing techniques such as impersonation of media outlets and the creation of disinformation websites. Microsoft attributes significant disinformation activities related to the Olympics to Storm-1679, highlighting their focus on spreading falsehoods and promoting anti-Olympics messaging.

identification.summary: OldGremlin is a Russian-speaking ransomware group that has been active for several years. They primarily target organizations in Russia, including banks, logistics, industrial, insurance, retail, and IT companies. OldGremlin is known for using phishing emails as an initial infection vector and has developed custom malware for both Windows and Linux systems. They have conducted multiple malicious email campaigns and demand large ransoms from their victims, with some reaching millions of dollars.
This threat actor targets the South Korean government, transportation, and energy sectors.

implications.jipoe: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. STEP 1: The OE includes DIB contractors, military installations' IT and healthcare systems supporting military communities. This actor targets all three. STEP 2: Ransomware against hospitals near installations can degrade medical support to forces and families. STEP 3: The template is exploitation of internet-facing systems, then custom RATs for espionage, and in some cases ransomware deployment for revenue. STEP 4: MLCOA is persistent espionage against defense and aerospace technology to support weapons programs. MDCOA is ransomware against healthcare or installation-support providers during a Korean Peninsula crisis, combining revenue with disruption. Candidate indicators: TigerRAT or SmallTiger detections, ransomware staging in healthcare networks, and intrusions at aerospace and defense suppliers [S1][S2].
implications.jcc2: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. (1) Coordinate with USFK and INDOPACOM, and with South Korean partners, since South Korea is the primary target. (2) Include Defense Health Agency and community hospital partners in situational awareness for ransomware threats. (3) Financial disruption (seizures, sanctions) is a DOJ and Treasury lead but affects the actor's resources; track it as part of campaign assessment. provenance.importedSummary:
Andariel is a North Korean state-sponsored threat group that has been active since at least 2009. Andariel has primarily focused its operations--which have included destructive attacks--against South Korean government agencies, military organizations, and a variety of domestic companies; they have also conducted cyber financial operations against ATMs, banks, and cryptocurrency exchanges. Andariel's notable activity includes Operation Black Mine, Operation GoldenAxe, and Campaign Rifle.

Andariel is considered a sub-set of Lazarus Group, and has been attributed to North Korea's Reconnaissance General Bureau.

North Korean group definitions are known to have significant overlap, and some security researchers report all North Korean state-sponsored cyber activity under the name Lazarus Group instead of tracking clusters or subgroups.

identification.summary: North Korea-linked espionage actor that Microsoft calls Opal Sleet (formerly OSMIUM) and that other vendors track as Konni and TA406 [S1][S4]. Microsoft reported that in March 2023 an attacker account attributed to Opal Sleet sent phishing emails to Russian diplomatic government entities [S2]. Proofpoint reported that from February 2025 the group, which it calls TA406, phished Ukrainian government entities with both credential-harvesting and malware lures [S4]. Later Konni reporting describes abuse of Google Find Hub to wipe South Korean victims' Android phones (activity from September 2025, reported November 2025) and an AI-assisted PowerShell backdoor aimed at blockchain developers (January 2026) [S11][S9].
identification.notes: Microsoft name: Opal Sleet. Microsoft's mapping lists OSMIUM, VELVET CHOLLIMA, Planedown, Konni and APT43 as other names [S1]. Proofpoint says TA406 activity overlaps with what third parties track as Opal Sleet and Konni [S4]. Press coverage also gives Vedalia as an alias [S10]. Coverage of Genians' reporting describes KONNI as sharing targets and infrastructure with Kimsuky and APT37 [S11]. These are vendor cluster overlaps, not proof that the groups are identical.

attribution.sponsor: Democratic People's Republic of Korea (North Korea), per vendor assessments [S2][S4].
attribution.confidence: Microsoft attributes the March 2023 phishing of Russian diplomatic entities to Opal Sleet by name [S2]. Proofpoint calls TA406 a North Korean state-sponsored actor, but says it could not confirm with full certainty that every observed operation was TA406's. Its attribution rests on technical overlaps and the choice of targets [S4]. No government attribution of Opal Sleet or Konni was found in the sources gathered.
attribution.basis: Microsoft telemetry and threat-intelligence reporting [S2]; Proofpoint technical overlaps and targeting [S4]; Genians and Check Point reporting on Konni malware and infrastructure, via secondary coverage [S9][S10][S11].

actors.objectives: Strategic and political intelligence collection. Microsoft assessed that North Korean groups targeting Russia in 2023 were likely gathering intelligence [S2]. Proofpoint assessed that the 2025 Ukraine campaigns aimed to gather intelligence on how the Russian invasion was progressing, possibly to help North Korean leadership judge the risk to its own forces in the theater [S4]. The January 2026 targeting of blockchain and cryptocurrency developers suggests interest in that sector as well [S9].

sectors: Think tanks and policy experts, impersonated as lure personas [S4]
Individuals reached via KakaoTalk, including North Korea human-rights contexts [S11][S10]
Blockchain/cryptocurrency software developers and engineering teams [S9]
regions: Asia-Pacific: Japan, Australia, India (2026 developer campaign) [S9]
targeting.notes: Coverage of Check Point's reporting says Konni historically focused on South Korean government and academic targets [S9]. Proofpoint describes the move to Ukraine as a change from the group's earlier focus on Russia [S4].

capabilities.summary: Spear-phishing is the core access method. Lures include fictitious think-tank personas sending links to password-protected archives on external file hosts. Those archives hold HTML and CHM files with embedded PowerShell that profiles the host. The group also sends spoofed Microsoft security alerts to harvest credentials [S4]. Konni operators used KakaoTalk lures and stolen Google credentials to locate victims' Android devices and factory-reset them through Google Find Hub. They then used the victim's still-active KakaoTalk PC session to send malware to the victim's contacts [S11]. In January 2026 Check Point reported a heavily obfuscated, in-memory PowerShell backdoor that it assessed as AI-assisted. It persisted through a scheduled task disguised as OneDrive and dropped the legitimate SimpleHelp remote-management tool [S9][S10]. Genians' 'Operation Poseidon' reporting describes Google and Naver ad-redirect URLs that delivered LNK files, an AutoIt loader and EndRAT, with payloads and C2 hosted on compromised WordPress sites [S10].

campaigns.summary: Check Point reported phishing with fake project documentation that delivered an obfuscated PowerShell backdoor and SimpleHelp. Samples were linked to Japan, Australia and India.
