campaigns.summary: Genians-attributed Konni spear-phishing impersonated North Korean human-rights groups and South Korean financial institutions. It used Google and Naver ad-redirect URLs to deliver EndRAT.

diamond.adversary: North Korea-linked operators that Microsoft tracks as Opal Sleet and Proofpoint as TA406, also called Konni [S1][S2][S4].
diamond.capability: Spear-phishing with HTML/CHM/LNK payloads and embedded PowerShell; credential-harvesting pages; RATs including EndRAT; an AI-assisted PowerShell backdoor; abuse of the SimpleHelp RMM tool [S4][S11][S9][S10].
diamond.infrastructure: Freemail and Proton Mail sender accounts; external file-hosting services; compromised WordPress sites for payloads and C2; ad-redirect URLs; hijacked Google and KakaoTalk accounts [S4][S11][S10].
diamond.victim: Russian diplomatic entities; Ukrainian government entities; South Korean individuals and organizations; APAC blockchain developers [S2][S4][S11][S9].
diamond.socioPolitical: Collection on the Russia-Ukraine war and on Korean Peninsula issues in support of North Korean leadership [S2][S4].
diamond.technology: Windows endpoints running PowerShell and CHM; Google accounts linked to Android devices; KakaoTalk desktop sessions; developer workstations [S4][S11][S9].

gaps: Microsoft has published no stand-alone Opal Sleet profile in the sources gathered. The only Microsoft-sourced campaign found is the March 2023 Russia phishing, known from press coverage of Microsoft's 2023 East Asia report; the report itself was not retrieved [S2].
Proofpoint's original blog could not be fetched. Its details come from search excerpts and secondary coverage, and the exact publication day (around 2025-05-13/14) is unconfirmed [S4].
The BleepingComputer article's exact date (late August or early September 2023) is unconfirmed.

Cluster boundaries: Microsoft's mapping lists VELVET CHOLLIMA and APT43 under Opal Sleet [S1], while other vendors commonly associate those names with Kimsuky. Coverage of Genians' reporting says KONNI overlaps with Kimsuky and APT37 [S11]. It is unresolved whether the 2025-2026 Konni campaigns from Genians and Check Point fall inside Microsoft's Opal Sleet boundary.
First-observed date is unverified. Secondary sources give different start years for Konni (2014 vs. about 2016), and no primary source was found.
No MITRE ATT&CK group ID is confirmed for Opal Sleet/Konni.
No US government attribution or advisory naming Opal Sleet, Konni or TA406 was found.
Which North Korean organization (for example, an RGB element) sponsors the group is not established in the cited sources.

implications.jipoe: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. STEP 1 (operational environment): The relevant cyberspace includes diplomatic and government email, personal cloud identities (Google/Naver) tied to mobile devices, messaging apps such as KakaoTalk, and developer workstations [S4][S11][S9]. STEP 2 (effects): The actor relies on social engineering rather than exploits of perimeter devices, so the decisive terrain is user identity and email/messaging trust [S4][S11]. STEP 3 (threat model): Think-tank or official persona -> link to archive or file host -> HTML/CHM/LNK running PowerShell -> reconnaissance and RAT or backdoor -> credential theft, sometimes followed by device wipe and contact-chain spread [S4][S11][S9][S10]. STEP 4 (COAs): MLCOA is continued credential and intelligence collection against government, diplomatic and policy targets on the Russia-Ukraine war and Korean issues [S2][S4]. MDCOA is the use of stolen cloud credentials to wipe devices and blind victims during operations, as seen in the Find Hub campaign [S11]. Candidate indicators: unsolicited think-tank 'senior fellow' outreach; password-protected archives holding CHM/HTML files; scheduled tasks posing as OneDrive; unexpected SimpleHelp installs; Google/Naver ad-redirect links leading to LNK downloads; unexpected Find Hub remote-reset events [S4][S9][S10][S11].
implications.jcc2: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. Situational awareness: Fuse vendor reporting under all aliases (Opal Sleet, Konni, TA406, OSMIUM) while keeping cluster caveats visible [S1][S4][S11]. Authorities: The reported activity is espionage against government and diplomatic targets, so defensive responses fall mainly under DODIN/DCO and partner information-sharing channels, and the cited sources contain no government attribution [S2][S4]. Mission assurance: Personnel who deal with the Korean Peninsula, Ukraine or Russia policy face phishing aimed at personal and official accounts. Protecting cloud identities and device-management features such as Find Hub reduces the risk of losing data and devices [S4][S11]. Coordination: Coordinate with allied and partner CERTs (for example Ukraine and South Korea) and with commercial vendors whose telemetry covers the actor's lures [S4][S11][S9].

identification.summary: This threat actor targets critical infrastructure entities in the oil and gas sector, primarily in Ukraine. The threat actors deploy the BugDrop malware to remotely access the microphones in their targets' computers to eavesdrop on conversations.

Operation DRBControl is a cyberespionage campaign targeting gambling companies in Southeast Asia, first identified in 2019. The operation involves the use of HyperBro malware and SysUpdate variants, with evidence of customer database and source code exfiltration. The threat actor has employed domain spoofing for command and control and has shown a consistent interest in the gambling industry. Trend Micro's analysis linked multiple tools and malware families to this campaign, indicating a sophisticated and evolving threat landscape.

Operation Emmental, also known as the Retefe gang, is a threat actor group that has been active since at least 2012. They primarily target customers of banks in countries such as Austria, Sweden, Switzerland, and Japan. The group has developed sophisticated malware, including a Mac alternative called Dok, to bypass two-factor authentication and hijack network traffic. They have also been observed using phishing emails to spread their malware. The group is believed to be Russian-speaking and has continuously improved their malicious codes over the years.

The threat actors compromised the update server of a remote support solutions provider to deliver a remote access tool called 9002 RAT to their targets of interest through the update process. They carried this out by first stealing the company’s certificate then using it to sign the malware. They also configured the update server to only deliver malicious files if the client is located in the range of IP addresses of their target organisations.

Operation Shadow Force is a group of malware that is representative of Shadow Force and Wgdrop from 2013 to 2020, and is a group activity that attacks Korean companies and organizations. The group's first confirmed attack was in March 2013, but considering the date of malware creation, it is likely to have been active before 2012. Since the malware used mainly by them is Shadow Force, it was named Operation Shadow Force, and it has not been confirmed whether the attacker is associated with a known group.

The PassCV group continues to be one of the most successful and active threat groups that leverage a wide array of stolen Authenticode-signing certificates. Snorre Fagerland of Blue Coat Systems first coined the term PassCV in a blog post. His post provides a good introduction to the group and covers some of the older infrastructure, stolen code-signing certificate reuse, and other connections associated with the PassCV malware. There are several clues alluding to the possibility that multiple groups may be utilizing the same stolen signing certificates, but at this time SPEAR believes the current attacks are more likely being perpetrated by a single group employing multiple publicly available Remote Administration Tools (RATs). The PassCV group has been operating with continued success and has already started to expand their malware repertoire into different off-the-shelf RATs and custom code. SPEAR identified eighteen previously undisclosed stolen Authenticode certificates. These certificates were originally issued to companies and individuals scattered across China, Taiwan, Korea, Europe, the United States and Russia. In this post we expand the usage of the term ‘PassCV’ to encompass the malware mentioned in the Blue Coat Systems report, as well as the APT group behind the larger C2 infrastructure and stolen Authenticode certificates. We’d like to share some of our findings as they pertain to the stolen certificates, command and control infrastructure, and some of the newer custom RATs they’ve begun development on.

identification.summary: Iranian nation-state threat actor that Microsoft tracks as Peach Sandstorm (formerly HOLMIUM), whose activity overlaps with public reporting on APT33, Elfin and Refined Kitten [S1]. Microsoft assesses that it operates on behalf of the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) and runs long-term intelligence-gathering operations [S2]. Since 2023 its typical tradecraft has been large-scale password spraying followed by cloud-focused post-compromise activity in Microsoft Entra ID and Azure, including command and control (C2) hosted in fraudulent Azure subscriptions [S1][S2]. Earlier Mandiant (FireEye) reporting describes a group focused on aviation and on energy and petrochemical targets in Saudi Arabia, the United States and South Korea [S3].
identification.firstObserved: Mandiant: cyber espionage since at least 2013, with the earliest TURNEDUP compile timestamp dated April 2013 [S3]. Microsoft cites a 2019 password-spray wave and spraying since at least February 2023 [S1][S2].
identification.notes: Microsoft name: Peach Sandstorm (formerly HOLMIUM). Microsoft states overlap, not identity, with APT33 (Mandiant), Elfin (Symantec) and Refined Kitten (CrowdStrike) [S1]. MITRE tracks the group as APT33 (G0064) [S7]. Facts from APT33/Elfin-era reporting (2013-2019) stay attributed to their original vendors and are not merged into Microsoft's Peach Sandstorm findings. Microsoft notes that other Iranian groups, including Smoke Sandstorm, have used similar techniques, so tradecraft alone does not identify this actor [S2].

attribution.sponsor: Islamic Republic of Iran. Microsoft assesses that Peach Sandstorm operates on behalf of the IRGC [S2]. Mandiant (2017) assessed that APT33 works at the behest of the Iranian government [S3].
attribution.confidence: These are vendor assessments only. Microsoft bases its IRGC assessment on victimology and operational focus and states no confidence level [S2]. Its 2023 report says the spray campaign is 'likely' used for intelligence collection in support of Iranian state interests [S1]. Mandiant uses hedged language and calls APT33 'most likely government sponsored' [S3]. Press coverage of FalseFont says Microsoft did not tie that activity to a specific Iranian government entity [S6]. This pass found no US government attribution naming Peach Sandstorm or APT33.
attribution.basis: Victimology and operational focus [S2]. Activity in late May and June 2023 fell almost entirely within 09:00-17:00 Iran Standard Time [S1]. Mandiant also cited activity in a UTC+04:30 time zone and on Iran's Saturday-Wednesday workweek, use of Iranian hacker tools and hosting providers, Farsi artifacts in DROPSHOT/SHAPESHIFT, and the persona 'xman_1365_x', which open sources linked to the Nasr Institute [S3].

actors.objectives: Intelligence collection in support of Iranian state interests [S1][S2]. Targeting of satellite, defense, government and oil-and-gas organizations shows interest in military, space and energy information [S1][S2]. Mandiant judged the aviation focus may serve Iran's interest in military and commercial aviation, and the petrochemical focus its energy-sector interests [S3]. Earlier reporting also shows possible preparation for disruption. Mandiant found the SHAPESHIFT wiper in APT33's toolset but had not seen it used destructively [S3]. Microsoft in 2019 (as reported) suggested that targeting industrial control system (ICS) suppliers might be aimed at physically disruptive access, though it said motive remained unclear [S5].

sectors: Oil and gas, energy and petrochemical [S2][S3]
regions: Global (2023 spraying of thousands of organizations) [S1]
targeting.notes: Microsoft lists earlier targeting across aviation, construction, education, energy, financial services, healthcare, government and telecommunications [S1]. Peach Sandstorm used compromised education-sector accounts to buy Azure infrastructure, so universities are both victims and enablers [S2].

capabilities.summary: Microsoft-reported (2023-2024) capabilities: high-volume password spraying from TOR IPs with a 'go-http-client' user agent, and exploitation of public proof-of-concept exploits for Zoho ManageEngine (CVE-2022-47966) and Confluence (CVE-2022-26134) [S1]. Post-compromise, Microsoft reported Entra ID reconnaissance with AzureHound and ROADtools, and persistence through Azure Arc, new or abused Azure subscriptions and AnyDesk [S1]. It also reported the custom tunneling tool EagleRelay, a Golden SAML attack in March 2023, and DLL search-order hijacking [S1]. The custom multi-stage backdoor Tickler (2024) used Azure C2 nodes under azurewebsites.net in fraudulent subscriptions, Run-key persistence and SMB lateral movement [S2]. LinkedIn personas have been used for reconnaissance and possible social engineering since at least November 2021 [S2]. The FalseFont backdoor (late 2023) offers remote access, file execution and data exfiltration to C2 (as reported) [S6]. Mandiant-reported (2017) tooling includes the DROPSHOT dropper, TURNEDUP backdoor, SHAPESHIFT wiper, NANOCORE, NETWIRE and ALFA Shell, plus recruitment-themed spear-phishing with .hta files and domains impersonating Boeing, Alsalam Aircraft, Northrop Grumman Aviation Arabia and Vinnell Arabia [S3].

campaigns.name: Aviation and petrochemical espionage (Mandiant APT33)
campaigns.summary: A US aerospace organization was compromised from mid-2016 to early 2017. A Saudi conglomerate with aviation holdings and a South Korean petrochemical company were targeted with job-recruitment spear-phishing that delivered TURNEDUP. Domains impersonated defense and aviation firms.

campaigns.name: Narrowed password spraying against ICS suppliers (Microsoft, CYBERWARCON)
campaigns.summary: Microsoft (as reported) said the group narrowed spraying to about 2,000 organizations a month. About half of its top 25 targets were makers, suppliers or maintainers of ICS equipment.

campaigns.name: LinkedIn persona operations
campaigns.summary: Fake LinkedIn profiles posing as students, developers and recruiters targeted higher education and satellite sectors from at least November 2021 to mid-2024.

campaigns.name: Global password spray campaign
campaigns.summary: From February to July 2023, password spraying hit thousands of organizations. Follow-on activity included Entra ID reconnaissance, Azure Arc persistence and EagleRelay, a March 2023 Golden SAML intrusion, and data exfiltration in a small number of cases.

campaigns.name: FalseFont backdoor against defense industrial base
campaigns.summary: Microsoft (as reported) saw Peach Sandstorm attempting to deliver the new FalseFont backdoor to individuals at defense industrial base organizations. First use was observed in early November 2023.

campaigns.name: Tickler backdoor and Azure C2 operations
campaigns.summary: From April to July 2024, Tickler was deployed against satellite, communications equipment, oil and gas, and government targets in the US and UAE. Password spraying hit defense, space, education and government organizations in the US and Australia. Microsoft disrupted the fraudulent Azure subscriptions.

diamond.adversary: IRGC-aligned Iranian operators, per Microsoft's assessment [S2]. Mandiant linked the persona 'xman_1365_x' to the tooling [S3].
diamond.capability: Password spraying, public N-day exploits, Entra ID and Azure abuse (Golden SAML, Azure Arc) and custom backdoors (Tickler, FalseFont, TURNEDUP), plus the SHAPESHIFT wiper [S1][S2][S3][S6].
diamond.infrastructure: TOR exit IPs for spraying [S1]. Fraudulent Azure subscriptions bought with compromised education accounts and used for C2 [S2]. Earlier, dynamic-DNS domains impersonating aviation and defense firms [S3].
diamond.victim: Satellite, defense/DIB, government, oil and gas, aviation and pharmaceutical organizations in the US, Gulf states, Australia, Europe and South Korea [S1][S2][S3][S6].
diamond.socioPolitical: Intelligence collection for Iranian state interests [S1]. Microsoft tied a 2019 spray wave to rising US-Iran tensions [S1]. Mandiant linked the aviation focus to Iran's interest in military aviation capability [S3].
diamond.technology: Internet-facing cloud identity (Microsoft 365 and Entra ID) with weak passwords and no MFA, unpatched ManageEngine and Confluence servers, and cloud tenant trust relationships [S1][S2].

gaps: No US government attribution or advisory naming Peach Sandstorm or APT33 was located; IRGC sponsorship rests on Microsoft's assessment [S2].
FalseFont details come from press coverage of Microsoft's December 2023 social-media disclosure, which did not disclose the delivery method; no Microsoft blog post was opened [S6].
The Microsoft 2019 CYBERWARCON findings come from Axios coverage; no Microsoft primary document was found [S5].

A 2026 CloudSEK advisory (seen only in search excerpts; fetch failed) claims APT33 deployed a 'Shamoon 4.0' wiper against about 15,000 Saudi energy workstations in January 2026. It is single-source, unverified and NOT included as fact.
No Microsoft or Mandiant primary reporting on Peach Sandstorm activity in 2025-2026 was found. A November 2025 Brandefense forecast was seen but not used.
Mandiant's link between the persona and the Nasr Institute, and any ties to Shamoon/StoneDrill, remain unproven. Mandiant said it had not directly seen APT33 carry out destructive operations [S3].
Trend Micro (2019 narrow-targeting botnets) and Recorded Future (2019, more than 1,200 domains) reports were not opened in this pass.
It is unclear whether any ICS supplier targeted in 2019 was breached, or whether any damage resulted [S5].

implications.jipoe: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. STEP 1 (operational environment): Key terrain is cloud identity (Entra ID and Microsoft 365 tenants) at satellite, space, defense-industrial-base and government organizations, along with Azure subscriptions and internet-facing ManageEngine and Confluence servers [S1][S2]. STEP 2 (effects): Weak passwords and missing MFA on DIB and space contractor tenants offer an indirect path to DoD program data. Compromised university accounts let the adversary stand up infrastructure on trusted cloud domains that blend with normal traffic [S2]. STEP 3 (adversary model): The pattern runs from LinkedIn persona reconnaissance, to low-and-slow password spraying from TOR, to Entra ID reconnaissance (AzureHound/ROADtools), to persistence (Azure Arc, AnyDesk, Golden SAML), to a custom backdoor (Tickler or FalseFont) with Azure-hosted C2, to SMB lateral movement and exfiltration [S1][S2][S6]. STEP 4 (COAs): MLCOA is continued credential-based intelligence collection against DIB, satellite and government tenants that rises with US-Iran tension [S1][S2]. MDCOA is using ICS-supplier and energy footholds for disruptive or wiper operations, given SHAPESHIFT in the toolset and 2019 ICS-supplier targeting [S3][S5]. Candidate indicators: bursts of failed sign-ins from TOR with 'go-http-client' user agents; unexpected Azure Arc enrollment or new Azure subscriptions; outbound traffic to newly created azurewebsites.net hosts; new SharePoint.exe Run-key entries; and AnyDesk installs on servers [S1][S2].
implications.jcc2: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. (1) Situational awareness: identity telemetry (sign-in logs, conditional access failures, federation/SAML changes) from DIB and space-sector partners should be fused with DoD network sensing, because this actor's primary access vector is cloud identity, not the DODIN perimeter [S1][S2]. (2) Authorities: most targets are contractor- or university-owned tenants and Azure infrastructure, so response depends on partners and cloud providers (Microsoft disrupted the fraudulent subscriptions), not on DoD action [S2]. (3) Mission assurance: Prioritize MFA and password-spray detection for satellite, space and weapons-program contractors, and track defended-asset dependence on vendors such as ICS suppliers [S2][S5][S6]. (4) Coordination: Coordinate with DC3/DIB CS and cloud-provider threat intelligence, and raise the watch level during periods of US-Iran tension, which Microsoft linked to earlier spray waves [S1].

identification.summary: Microsoft tracks Pepper Typhoon as a China-origin actor and maps it to CrowdStrike's LIMINAL PANDA and Palo Alto Networks Unit 42's CL-STA-0969 [S1]. CrowdStrike describes LIMINAL PANDA as an actor that has targeted telecommunications entities since at least 2020, using custom tools for covert access, command and control (C2) and data exfiltration [S2][S4]. The actor uses telecom-specific protocols (GSM, SIGTRAN) and has used compromised telecom servers to start intrusions into further providers in other regions [S2][S4]. Unit 42 reported a February-November 2024 campaign by CL-STA-0969 against telecom operators, which it says heavily overlaps with Liminal Panda [S6][S7][S8].
identification.firstObserved: CrowdStrike: active since at least 2020 [S2][S4]. CrowdStrike says some activity it now attributes to LIMINAL PANDA was earlier attributed to LightBasin [S2][S3]. First public naming as LIMINAL PANDA: 2024-11-19 [S2][S5].
identification.notes: Microsoft name: Pepper Typhoon, origin China, other names LIMINAL PANDA and CL-STA-0969 [S1]. Microsoft has published no Pepper Typhoon reporting in the sources gathered, so the substance of this profile comes from CrowdStrike (LIMINAL PANDA) and Unit 42 (CL-STA-0969) [S2][S6]. Cluster boundaries differ: CrowdStrike split LIMINAL PANDA out of activity it had earlier called LightBasin, and Unit 42 reports tooling overlaps between CL-STA-0969 and LightBasin, UNC3886, UNC2891 and UNC1945 without merging those clusters [S2][S7]. Axios reports CrowdStrike saw no evidence of coordination between LIMINAL PANDA and Salt Typhoon [S5].

attribution.sponsor: China nexus (vendor assessment, not government attribution). Microsoft lists the origin of Pepper Typhoon as China [S1].
attribution.confidence: CrowdStrike assesses with low confidence that LIMINAL PANDA activity aligns with China-nexus cyber operations [S4]. CrowdStrike assesses with high confidence that the activity supports intelligence collection, based on target profile, likely mission objectives and observed TTPs [S2]. Unit 42 assesses with high confidence that CL-STA-0969 has a nation-state nexus and says the cluster heavily overlaps with Liminal Panda based on activity and victimology [S6][S7]. CrowdStrike linked the SIGweaver tool to LIMINAL PANDA with moderate confidence [S9]. No US government attribution was found in the sources gathered.
attribution.basis: CrowdStrike incident-response and intelligence reporting [S2][S3][S4]; Unit 42 incident reporting on CL-STA-0969 [S6][S7][S8]; Microsoft's alias mapping [S1]; Singapore IMDA advisory relaying CrowdStrike's SIGweaver reporting [S9].

actors.objectives: Signals-intelligence-style collection from mobile networks, such as subscriber information, call metadata and device location, rather than financial gain [S2][S4][S6]. Unit 42 notes that use of Cordscan suggests that collecting victim location data was a likely objective [S6][S8].

sectors: Telecommunications (mobile network operators and GPRS/roaming providers) [S2][S6]
Telecom core network elements such as HSS, VLR, SGSN and NMS (SIGweaver reporting) [S9]
regions: Southeast Asia or Southwest Asia (Unit 42 CL-STA-0969; sources differ on wording) [S6][S8]
targeting.notes: CrowdStrike reports that the actor used compromised telecom servers to start intrusions into providers in other regions, so targeting can spread through inter-operator trust relationships [S2]. Unit 42 says the actors abused interconnected mobile roaming networks [S6]. Unit 42's executive summary says Southwest Asia, while Security Affairs coverage says Southeast Asia [S6][S8].

capabilities.summary: Telecom-specialist tradecraft. CrowdStrike reports public tools (TinyShell, ProxyChains), custom telecom tools (CordScan, SIGTRANslator), and use of mobile protocols such as GSM for C2 [S4]. Unit 42 reports likely initial access through SSH brute-forcing with credential lists built for telecom equipment [S8]. Its custom implants include AuthDoor (a malicious PAM module that captures credentials and allows access with a hard-coded password), GTPDoor (malware for hosts next to GPRS roaming exchanges), EchoBackdoor, ChronosRAT and NoDepDNS, plus a Serving GPRS Support Node emulator [S7][S8]. In January 2026, CrowdStrike linked SIGweaver to LIMINAL PANDA with moderate confidence. SIGweaver is a Linux kernel-level driver that injects malicious messages into live telecom traffic over SS7 (2G/3G) and Diameter (4G LTE) without opening new network connections. IMDA calls it the actor's first confirmed capability to operate natively in 4G infrastructure [S9].

diamond.adversary: Pepper Typhoon / LIMINAL PANDA / CL-STA-0969. CrowdStrike assesses with low confidence that it is China-nexus, and Unit 42 assesses with high confidence that it has a nation-state nexus [S1][S4][S6].
diamond.capability: Telecom-specific tools (CordScan, SIGTRANslator, SIGweaver), Linux implants (AuthDoor PAM backdoor, GTPDoor, EchoBackdoor, ChronosRAT, NoDepDNS), and public tools (TinyShell, ProxyChains) [S4][S7][S9].
diamond.infrastructure: Compromised telecom servers used to pivot to other providers; GSM, GTP, DNS, ICMP and SSH channels for C2 [S2][S4][S7].
diamond.victim: Mobile network operators and their core and roaming elements (HSS, VLR, SGSN, NMS, GPRS roaming exchanges) in South Asia, Africa and Southeast/Southwest Asia [S6][S7][S9].
diamond.socioPolitical: Intelligence collection on mobile subscribers, call metadata and device location, consistent with SIGINT goals rather than profit [S2][S4][S6].
diamond.technology: Trust between operators in roaming networks, legacy SS7/SIGTRAN and GTP signaling, Diameter in 4G, and internet-exposed Linux and telecom management hosts reachable by SSH [S6][S8][S9].

gaps: Microsoft has published no Pepper Typhoon reporting in the sources gathered; the Microsoft name comes only from the alias mapping [S1].

Primary documents could not be opened (fetch blocked): CrowdStrike blogs [S2][S3], the Unit 42 report [S6] and the IMDA advisories [S9]. Facts are drawn from search excerpts and secondary coverage, and confidence wording should be checked against the originals.

Unclear confidence wording: coverage says CrowdStrike's China-nexus assessment is low confidence and its intelligence-collection assessment is high confidence. Confirm the exact statements in the CrowdStrike blog.
Region discrepancy for CL-STA-0969: Unit 42 says Southwest Asia, while coverage says Southeast Asia [S6][S8].
Not verified: a claim in secondary coverage that targets cluster in Belt and Road Initiative countries, and a claim that the 2024 disclosure came in US Senate testimony. Neither is included as fact.
Boundaries between LIMINAL PANDA, LightBasin (UNC1945), UNC2891 and UNC3886 are unresolved across vendors. Tooling overlaps do not prove a single operator [S2][S7].
No specific victims, sponsoring organization (MSS, PLA or contractor), or confirmed exfiltration volumes are public in the sources gathered.
Whether SIGweaver has been seen deployed in live victim networks, rather than only analyzed, is unclear [S9].
No MITRE ATT&CK group entry was identified for this actor.

implications.jipoe: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. STEP 1 (operational environment): Key cyber terrain is commercial mobile-network core and roaming infrastructure (HSS, VLR, SGSN, GPRS roaming exchanges, signaling gateways) that carries location and metadata for deployed personnel and partner-nation officials using host-nation carriers [S6][S9]. STEP 2 (effects): Because operators trust each other on roaming links, a compromise in one partner-nation carrier can expose traffic from another, so collection risk reaches beyond the directly compromised carrier [S2][S6]. STEP 3 (adversary model): Access through SSH brute force or a compromised peer operator, then PAM backdoors and GTP/DNS/ICMP covert channels, then telecom-protocol tools (CordScan, SIGTRANslator, SIGweaver) for subscriber, metadata and location collection [S4][S7][S8][S9]. STEP 4 (COAs): MLCOA is persistent, low-noise collection of subscriber location and call metadata from carriers in South Asia, Africa and Southeast/Southwest Asia [S2][S6]. MDCOA is use of 4G-capable signaling injection (SIGweaver) during a crisis for location tracking, denial of service against subscribers, or covert C2 inside partner carriers that support US forces [S9]. Candidate indicators: unexpected PAM modules or changes on telecom Linux hosts; brute-force SSH against carrier management interfaces; anomalous GTP or DNS traffic near GPRS roaming exchanges; unsolicited SS7/Diameter location queries; unknown kernel modules on signaling nodes [S7][S8][S9].
implications.jcc2: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. (1) Situational awareness: telecom carriers in host and partner nations are outside the DODIN, so visibility depends on partner and vendor reporting; track carrier advisories (for example IMDA) and vendor reporting on this cluster [S6][S9]. (2) Authorities: defending a foreign commercial carrier is not a DoD action by default; any hunt-forward or partner support requires host-nation consent and coordination through the appropriate CCMD and interagency channels. (3) Mission assurance: assume mobile metadata and location on commercial networks in affected regions may be collected; enforce COMSEC and emissions discipline and prefer DoD-controlled transport for C2 [S2][S6]. (4) Coordination: fuse CrowdStrike, Unit 42 and Microsoft naming (LIMINAL PANDA / CL-STA-0969 / Pepper Typhoon) in common operational picture products, and keep LightBasin/UNC-cluster overlaps flagged as unresolved, to avoid double-counting or false merging [S1][S7].

provenance.importedSummary: LIMINAL PANDA is a China-nexus APT that targets telecommunications entities, employing custom malware and publicly available tools for covert access, C2, and data exfiltration. The adversary demonstrates extensive knowledge of telecom networks, utilizing GSM protocols to retrieve mobile subscriber information and call metadata. LIMINAL PANDA exploits trust relationships and security gaps between providers to access core infrastructure, indicating a focus on SIGINT collection rather than financial gain. Their intrusion activity has primarily affected telecom providers in southern Asia and Africa, with potential for broader targeting based on network configurations.

identification.summary: Periwinkle Tempest (formerly DEV-0193) is what Microsoft calls a financially motivated cybercriminal group. It develops, distributes and manages several payloads, including Trickbot, BazaLoader and AnchorDNS [S1][S2]. Microsoft describes it as the most prolific ransomware-associated cybercriminal activity group it tracked. It managed the Ryuk ransomware-as-a-service program until Ryuk shut down in June 2021 and also managed Ryuk's successor, Conti, as well as Diavol [S1][S2]. As other malware operations shut down, the group hired developers from Emotet, Qakbot and IcedID [S1][S2]. Microsoft also tracks DEV-0365, which provides Cobalt Strike Beacon infrastructure as a service to other cybercriminals, as a subgroup of DEV-0193 [S2].
identification.firstObserved: Microsoft has tracked DEV-0193 since October 2020 [S1][S2]. Per DOJ charges reported by TRM Labs, the Trickbot conspiracy began in November 2015 [S7].
identification.notes: Microsoft also associates the name 'Trickbot LLC' with this group [S1][S2]. Microsoft said DEV-0193 overlaps with activity Mandiant tracks as UNC1878 [S3]. Mandiant later promoted UNC1878 to FIN12, a Ryuk-deploying intrusion actor that 'worked closely with TrickBot-affiliated actors' [S10]. FIN12 is therefore best treated as a closely linked affiliate cluster, not a synonym for the Trickbot developers. German BKA reporting refers to the Trickbot group as 'Wizard Spider' [S9]. Microsoft's mapping places some Wizard Spider and Conti names under separate entries (Storm-0230, Conti Team 1, and Pistachio Tempest/DEV-0237, a Ryuk and Conti affiliate) [S2], so these boundaries should not be merged.

attribution.sponsor: No state sponsor is assessed. Microsoft classifies Periwinkle Tempest as financially motivated [S1]. The US and UK governments describe the Trickbot group as Russia-based [S7].
attribution.confidence: Microsoft attributes the Trickbot, BazaLoader, AnchorDNS, Ryuk, Conti and Diavol management roles to DEV-0193/Periwinkle Tempest based on its telemetry and says leaked Conti chats from February 2022 confirmed the scale of the activity [S2]. The US and UK sanctioned alleged members in February and September 2023, and DOJ unsealed indictments of nine Russian nationals in September 2023 [S7]. In 2025 Germany's BKA publicly named a suspected founder and leader known as 'Stern' [S9].
attribution.basis: Microsoft telemetry and the Conti chat leak [S1][S2]; Microsoft's 2020 civil and technical action against Trickbot infrastructure [S4]; US Treasury and UK sanctions and DOJ indictments (via secondary coverage) [S7]; and the BKA's Operation Endgame identification (via secondary coverage) [S9].

actors.objectives: Financial gain. The group runs malware and ransomware services that enable ransomware extortion of large organizations, and earlier ran banking and credential theft [S1][S2][S7]. According to DOJ charges as reported by TRM Labs, Trickbot was used to steal money and personal information [S7].

sectors: National government institutions, e.g. Costa Rica's finance and customs systems (Conti) [S8]
regions: Global, opportunistic (inferred from RaaS and botnet model; not region-limited in Microsoft reporting) [S1][S2]
targeting.notes: Microsoft's profile lists education and healthcare [S1]. Treasury said the group targeted many US critical infrastructure and health care providers during the COVID-19 pandemic [S7]. A joint CISA/FBI/HHS advisory warned of an imminent Trickbot and Ryuk threat to US hospitals in October 2020 [S5]. Mandiant found that nearly 20% of directly observed FIN12 victims were in healthcare [S10], but FIN12 is a separate, affiliated cluster.

capabilities.summary: The group develops and operates modular malware and loaders (Trickbot, BazaLoader, AnchorDNS) and manages ransomware programs (Ryuk, Conti, Diavol) [S1][S2]. Its DEV-0365 subgroup provides Cobalt Strike Beacon command-and-control as a service [S2]. In the typical Trickbot/Ryuk chain described by CISA, FBI and HHS, a malicious email installs Emotet and/or Trickbot, Trickbot moves laterally, disables protections and steals data, and Ryuk then encrypts systems [S5]. In 2021 its infrastructure hosted BazaLoader and Trickbot payloads alongside oleObjects used in CVE-2021-40444 (MSHTML) exploitation [S3]. The group recruits talent from other malware operations (Emotet, Qakbot, IcedID) [S1][S2], and the BKA said the group had more than 100 members at times [S9]. MITRE ATT&CK tracks the broader Wizard Spider cluster as G0102 [S11].

implications.jipoe: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. Step 1 (operational environment): Treat the defense industrial base, base hospitals and medical treatment facilities, and education and training enclaves on commercial or DODIN-adjacent networks as in scope, since the group has hit healthcare, education and critical infrastructure [S1][S5][S7]. Step 2 (effects): Ransomware encryption of Windows enterprise systems can degrade medical, logistics and administrative mission support, and the Costa Rica case shows national government services can be disrupted [S5][S8]. Step 3 (adversary model): Email-delivered loaders (Emotet/Trickbot/BazaLoader) lead to Cobalt Strike, then lateral movement, then data theft, then Ryuk/Conti-family encryption. Access is often shared or sold to affiliates [S2][S5]. Step 4 (courses of action): The most likely course of action is opportunistic loader infection of a mission-partner or support network, followed by affiliate ransomware within days. The most dangerous is a time-sensitive ransomware event against healthcare or a critical-infrastructure dependency (power, water, comms supporting an installation) during a crisis or surge, timed for maximum leverage, as with the 2020 hospital threat [S5][S7]. Candidate indicators: Trickbot/BazaLoader/AnchorDNS artifacts; Cobalt Strike Beacon C2 matching DEV-0365 patterns; malicious Office documents exploiting MSHTML; and protection tampering before encryption [S2][S3][S5].
implications.jcc2: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. Situational awareness: Fuse Microsoft, CISA/FBI and vendor indicators for Trickbot-lineage loaders and Cobalt Strike-as-a-service infrastructure into DODIN and mission-partner monitoring [S2][S3][S5]. Authorities: This is a criminal actor, so the primary responses are law enforcement (DOJ indictments, BKA/Operation Endgame), sanctions (OFAC/UK) and private civil action (Microsoft's 2020 court order) [S4][S7][S9]. Any DoD role should be coordinated through those lanes and existing defense-support authorities. Mission assurance: Prioritize backup integrity and recovery for medical and logistics systems and plan for loss of supporting civilian infrastructure, given healthcare and critical-infrastructure targeting [S5][S7]. Coordination: Coordinate with CISA, FBI, HHS (for medical facilities) and allied partners such as the UK and Germany, who have acted jointly against the group [S5][S7][S9].

provenance.importedSummary: GRIM SPIDER is a sophisticated eCrime group that has been operating the Ryuk ransomware since August 2018, targeting large organizations for a high-ransom return. This methodology, known as “big game hunting,” signals a shift in operations for WIZARD SPIDER, a criminal enterprise of which GRIM SPIDER appears to be a cell. The WIZARD SPIDER threat group, known as the Russia-based operator of the TrickBot banking malware, had focused primarily on wire fraud in the past. Similar to Samas and BitPaymer, Ryuk is specifically used to target enterprise environments. Code comparison between versions of Ryuk and Hermes ransomware indicates that Ryuk was derived from the Hermes source code and has been under steady development since its release. Hermes is commodity ransomware that has been observed for sale on forums and used by multiple threat actors. However, Ryuk is only used by GRIM SPIDER and, unlike Hermes, Ryuk has only been used to target enterprise environments. Since Ryuk’s appearance in August, the threat actors operating it have netted over 705.80 BTC across 52 transactions for a total current value of $3,701,893.98 USD. Grim Spider is reportedly associated with Lunar Spider and Wizard Spider.

identification.summary: Iranian threat actor that Microsoft tracks as Pink Sandstorm (also known as Agrius) [S2]; public reporting has linked it to Iran's Ministry of Intelligence and Security (MOIS) [S3]. It is known for destructive wiper and fake-ransomware operations focused on Israeli targets since 2020 [S3][S4]. Over time its operations moved from wipers disguised as ransomware (DEADWOOD, Apostle) to supply-chain wiper deployment (Fantasy, 2022), new ransomware (Moneybird, 2023), and data theft followed by wiping in Israeli higher education and technology (2023) [S4][S6][S7][S9]. In December 2023 Israel's National Cyber Directorate named Agrius, working with Hezbollah's Lebanese Cedar, in a late-November 2023 attack on Ziv Medical Center [S10].
identification.firstObserved: SentinelLabs observed Agrius operating in Israel starting in 2020 [S4]. MITRE also dates the group's activity to 2020 [S3].
identification.notes: Microsoft name: Pink Sandstorm (formerly AMERICIUM). Microsoft lists SPECTRAL KITTEN, Agrius, Deadwood, BlackShadow, SharpBoys, FireAnt and Justice Blade as other names [S2]. Palo Alto Unit 42 tracks the group as Agonizing Serpens and equates it with Agrius, BlackShadow, Pink Sandstorm and DEV-0022 [S9]. MITRE tracks it as Agrius (G1030) [S3]. Check Point says the group has operated under multiple aliases and leaked Moneybird victim data through one of its previous personas [S7][S8]. BlackShadow is the persona that extorted Israeli insurer Shirbit in 2020 [S8].

attribution.sponsor: Iran, Ministry of Intelligence and Security (MOIS). MITRE notes that public reporting has linked Agrius to MOIS [S3]. Israel's National Cyber Directorate (INCD), as reported by the press, described Agrius as affiliated with the Iranian Ministry of Intelligence [S10].
attribution.confidence: SentinelLabs (2021) assessed with medium confidence that Agrius is of Iranian origin [S4]. Check Point (2023) said the group's affiliation was not fully clear [S8]. The INCD attribution of the Ziv Medical Center attack is an Israeli government statement reported by the press [S10]; no US government attribution was found in the sources gathered.
attribution.basis: Vendor incident response and malware analysis (SentinelLabs, ESET, Check Point, Unit 42) [S4][S6][S7][S9]; INCD statement on the Ziv Medical Center incident, based on a joint investigation with the IDF and Shin Bet [S10].

actors.objectives: Disruption and destruction against Israeli organizations, with ransomware used as cover rather than for profit; SentinelLabs judged it unlikely that Agrius is financially motivated [S4]. Espionage and data theft come before destructive operations [S4][S9].

sectors: HR consulting and IT support services [S6]
targeting.notes: Israel is the consistent focus across all vendor reporting [S3][S4][S9]. Victims outside Israel came through the 2022 supply-chain compromise of an Israeli software developer [S6]. Check Point did not specify which sectors Moneybird hit [S8].

capabilities.summary: Initial access usually comes through internet-facing web servers and known vulnerabilities, including FortiOS CVE-2018-13379, and is followed by ASPXSpy web shells [S5][S7]. After access the group uses public tools for lateral movement, credential harvesting and exfiltration [S7]. Its custom destructive tooling has evolved over time: the DEADWOOD wiper; the .NET Apostle wiper, which later gained working ransomware encryption; and the IPsec Helper .NET backdoor [S4]. Fantasy, a wiper built from Apostle code, was pushed through a compromised Israeli software vendor's updates; the campaign lasted under three hours [S6]. Moneybird is C++ ransomware using AES-256 GCM [S7][S8]. In 2023 the group used the MultiLayer, PartialWasher and BFG Agonizer wipers and the Sqlextractor database-theft tool. It also switched between public proof-of-concept tools and custom code to evade EDR [S9].

diamond.adversary: MOIS-linked Iranian operators (Pink Sandstorm/Agrius) using rotating personas such as BlackShadow [S3][S8]. The INCD reported Agrius working with Hezbollah's Lebanese Cedar [S10].

gaps: No Microsoft reporting on Pink Sandstorm operations was verified during fact-check; Microsoft detail here is limited to the naming page [S2].

Attribution of the Ziv Medical Center incident: the INCD named Agrius with Lebanese Cedar, while a separate 'Malek Team' persona claimed a data leak; press reporting does not settle whether these are one operation [S10].
No 2024-2026 Pink Sandstorm operational reporting (for example during the 2025 Israel-Iran conflict) was found in the searches run.
The SentinelLabs confidence assessment is medium, and Check Point in 2023 called the affiliation not fully clear; no US government attribution was located [S4][S8].
The Unit 42 alias DEV-0022 and the Malpedia aliases DEV-0227 are not confirmed against Microsoft's current mapping [S2][S9].
Vendor profiles of UAE targeting were seen in search results but not verified from primary reporting, so the UAE is excluded from regions.

implications.jipoe: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. STEP 1 (operational environment): Key terrain includes internet-facing web servers and VPN appliances, software vendors' update channels and database servers at Israeli and partner organizations [S5][S6][S7][S9]. The environment also includes the information space, where leak personas publish stolen data [S8]. STEP 2 (effects): Unpatched public-facing applications and trusted update paths let the actor turn one intrusion into many victims within hours [S6]. Ransomware branding hides state intent and complicates attribution and response priorities [S4]. STEP 3 (threat model): web-server exploit, then ASPXSpy web shell, then credential harvesting and lateral movement with public tools, then data theft (including Sqlextractor), then wiper or ransomware deployment and a leak via a persona [S7][S9]. STEP 4 (COAs): MLCOA is continued data theft followed by wiping or fake ransomware against Israeli education, technology and healthcare targets, amplified through hack-and-leak during periods of Israel-Iran tension [S9][S10]. MDCOA is a supply-chain wiper push through a trusted vendor, or a joint operation with Hezbollah-linked cyber actors such as Lebanese Cedar, hitting healthcare or partner-nation organizations at scale, including entities outside Israel [S6][S10]. Candidate indicators: ASPXSpy web shells on IIS servers; exploitation of known FortiOS or web-application CVEs; credential harvesting tools appearing weeks before a destructive event [S6]; new ransomware families with no payment infrastructure; and leak-persona claims after intrusions [S5][S7][S8].
implications.jcc2: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. Situational awareness: Track Israeli INCD and vendor reporting (Unit 42, Check Point, ESET), because the group's operations are usually first exposed through incident response [S6][S7][S9][S10]. Treat a 'ransomware' event at an Israel-linked or partner organization as possibly state-directed destruction [S4]. Authorities: The 'ransomware' framing can steer cases toward criminal channels. Coordinating early with intelligence and partner-nation cyber authorities supports a correct attribution and response posture [S4][S10]. Mission assurance: Prioritize patching internet-facing servers, monitoring for web shells, verifying the integrity of third-party software updates and maintaining offline backups for mission-relevant databases [S6][S7][S9]. Coordination: The INCD attributed the Ziv Medical Center attack to Agrius working with Hezbollah's Lebanese Cedar, so combined Iran-proxy activity needs coordination across CCMD and partner-nation boundaries, with information sharing with Israeli partners [S10].

identification.summary: PlushDaemon is a China-aligned APT group that has conducted cyberespionage operations against targets in China, Taiwan, Hong Kong, South Korea, the United States, and New Zealand. They executed a supply chain attack on the South Korean VPN provider IPany, compromising its installer to deploy the SlowStepper backdoor, which features a toolkit of over 30 components. PlushDaemon primarily gains initial access by hijacking legitimate updates of Chinese applications and has also exploited vulnerabilities in legitimate web servers. Additionally, they have utilized the Visual Studio command line utility regcap.exe to side-load a malicious DLL named lregdll.dll.

Pumpkin Sandstorm is a Microsoft threat actor name whose origin/threat category is listed as Iran, with DEV-0146 listed as another name in Microsoft's published mapping [S1]. In Microsoft's 2023 weather-based taxonomy, the 'Sandstorm' family denotes Iranian actors and DEV-#### designations are temporary names for emerging or developing clusters [S3]. No Microsoft blog, report, or vendor write-up describing Pumpkin Sandstorm's activity was found in open sources during this research.
identification.notes: Microsoft's MSTIC mapping file lists 'DEV-0146' as another name [S1]. The MISP Galaxy 'Microsoft Activity Group' cluster lists 'DEV-0146' and 'ZeroCleare' as synonyms for Pumpkin Sandstorm, citing Microsoft's naming page and the MSTIC mapping file as references [S2]. ZeroCleare is a wiper malware family, not an actor name: IBM X-Force linked it to ITG13 (APT34/OilRig) plus a second Iran-based group [S5], and Microsoft described it as shared among a small number of affiliated Iranian actors, including actors with links to MOIS [S4]. Do not merge ZeroCleare, APT34, or Albania-attack actors (DEV-0842, DEV-0861, DEV-0166, Europium) into this record without a Microsoft statement linking them [S4].

identification.summary: puNK-003 is a North Korean APT group known for deploying the Lilith RAT, a sophisticated C++ remote access trojan, and its AutoIt variant, CURKON, which functions as a downloader. The group primarily distributes malware through targeted phishing attacks using malicious LNK files. Analysis indicates that puNK-003 shares similarities with the KONNI group, particularly in the use of AutoIt scripts and specific coding functions. Key indicators of infection include unusual network activity and system slowdowns, with removal methods involving specialized antivirus software and manual techniques.

China-based cyber-espionage actor that Microsoft tracks as Purple Typhoon (formerly POTASSIUM), mapped to APT10, menuPass, Stone Panda and Red Apollo [S1]. US prosecutors allege APT10 intrusions from about 2006 through 2018 aimed at intellectual property and confidential business information, including against managed service providers (MSPs), more than 45 technology companies and US government agencies [S2]. The group is best known for Operation Cloud Hopper, a sustained campaign against global MSPs and their clients [S4][S3], and has repeatedly targeted Japanese organizations [S5][S6][S7].
identification.firstObserved: DOJ indictment alleges activity from about 2006 [S2]; FireEye stated it had tracked APT10 since 2009 [S6]; Unit 42 reported Japanese targeting since at least 2014 [S5].
identification.notes: Microsoft name: Purple Typhoon (formerly POTASSIUM); Microsoft's mapping lists POTASSIUM, STONE PANDA, GOLEM, Evilgrab, AEON, LIVESAFE, ChChes, APT10, Haymaker, Webmonder, Foxtrot, Foxmail, MenuPass and Red Apollo [S1]. Symantec tracks the actor as Cicada [S7][S8]. Several mapped names (ChChes, Evilgrab, Haymaker) are malware family names rather than vendor cluster names [S1][S5]. MirrorFace / Earth Kasha is assessed by Japan's NPA as a sub-group within the APT10 umbrella [S9]; it is kept as a related cluster here, not merged.

attribution.sponsor: People's Republic of China, Ministry of State Security (MSS). The December 2018 DOJ indictment alleges that two APT10 members, Zhu Hua and Zhang Shilong, worked for Huaying Haitai Science and Technology Development Company in Tianjin and acted in association with the MSS Tianjin State Security Bureau [S2].
attribution.confidence: UK NCSC assessed 'with the highest level of probability' that APT10 was responsible for the MSP campaign and that it is 'highly likely' APT10 has an enduring relationship with the MSS and operates to meet Chinese State requirements [S3]. The US indicted two alleged members [S2], and Canada, Australia, New Zealand and the UK also publicly attributed the activity to the MSS [S10]. Japan's NPA assesses MirrorFace as an APT10 sub-group [S9].
attribution.basis: DOJ indictment (SDNY, December 2018) [S2]; coordinated UK and allied government attribution [S3][S10]; vendor reporting from PwC/BAE (Cloud Hopper) [S4], Palo Alto Unit 42 [S5], FireEye [S6] and Symantec [S7][S8].

actors.objectives: Theft of intellectual property and confidential business information [S2], achieved at scale by compromising MSPs that hold direct access to client networks [S4][S3]. Later campaigns collected information from government, legal, religious and NGO organizations [S8]; the MirrorFace sub-group is assessed to target Japanese national-security and advanced-technology information [S9].

sectors: Managed IT service providers (MSPs) and their clients [S3][S4]
regions: Global; MSP campaign reached providers in at least 14 countries [S4]
United States (at least a dozen states) [S2]
Japan and Japanese subsidiaries in as many as 17 regions [S7][S5][S6]
Europe, Asia and North America (2021-2022 campaign) [S8]
targeting.notes: Japan is a persistent focus across vendor reporting [S5][S6][S7]. MSP compromise expanded the scale and scope of targeting across multiple sectors [S4].

capabilities.summary: Spear-phishing with malicious, sometimes password-protected Word documents carrying VBA macros [S6]; custom and shared malware including PlugX and Poison Ivy [S4][S5], ChChes signed with a certificate leaked from HackingTeam [S5], UPPERCUT/ANEL with per-C2 encryption keys and anti-analysis changes [S6], and Backdoor.Hartip [S7]. Exploitation of the Zerologon vulnerability (2019-2020) [S7] and of Microsoft Exchange servers for initial access [S8]. DLL side-loading through a legitimate VLC Media Player and remote control with WinVNC [S8]. Abuse of trusted MSP access to pivot into client networks [S4][S3]. The MirrorFace sub-group used a revived ANEL backdoor, a customized AsyncRAT run inside Windows Sandbox, and VS Code remote tunnels [S11].

Symantec's original 2020 and 2022 Cicada blogs, the ESET AkaiRyu blog and the Japanese NPA report could not be fetched (host resolution errors); details come from coverage and vendor press releases [S7][S8][S9][S11].
Activity attributed specifically to Purple Typhoon after 2022 (outside the MirrorFace sub-group) is not documented in the sources gathered.

implications.jipoe: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. STEP 1: Key cyber terrain includes MSP and IT-outsourcing remote-administration channels, domain controllers and Exchange/mail servers supporting defense and DIB networks [S4][S7][S8]. STEP 2: Trust relationships with service providers bypass perimeter defenses; unpatched Zerologon and Exchange exposure shorten time-to-compromise [S4][S7][S8]. STEP 3: Doctrinal template is spear-phishing or public-facing exploit, then DLL side-loaded RAT (PlugX, ANEL, Hartip), credential theft, lateral movement via MSP access, and staged exfiltration of IP and policy documents [S4][S5][S6][S7][S8]. STEP 4: MLCOA is long-dwell espionage against contractors and allied (especially Japanese) partners through MSP and mail-server access to collect technology and national-security information [S2][S7][S9]. MDCOA is simultaneous compromise of multiple shared service providers to gain persistent access across many DoD-adjacent customers before a crisis [S4][S3]. Candidate indicators: anomalous MSP admin-account logons outside maintenance windows, legitimate binaries (e.g., VLC) loading unsigned DLLs from user paths, Zerologon exploitation events on domain controllers, password-protected macro documents with diplomatic or maritime lures, and VS Code tunnel traffic from servers [S6][S7][S8][S11].
implications.jcc2: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. (1) Situational awareness: map which mission systems depend on third-party MSPs and track their compromise reporting, since victims in Cloud Hopper were reached through providers [S4]. (2) Authorities: activity against contractor and MSP networks falls outside DODIN boundaries; coordinate via DC3/DIB CS, FBI and partner-nation agencies (NCSC, NPA) that have attributed this actor [S2][S3][S9]. (3) Mission assurance: prioritize patching and monitoring of domain controllers and Exchange servers, the observed entry points [S7][S8]. (4) Coordination: Japan-focused targeting makes combined information sharing with Japanese partners relevant for INDOPACOM-supporting networks [S7][S9][S11].

Individual members of menuPass are known to have acted in association with the Chinese Ministry of State Security's (MSS) Tianjin State Security Bureau and worked for the Huaying Haitai Science and Technology Development Company.

identification.summary: PurpleHaze is a China-nexus threat actor tracked by SentinelLABS, linked to APT15, known for targeting critical infrastructure sectors such as telecommunications and government organizations. The actor has been associated with reconnaissance attempts against SentinelOne and has utilized ShadowPad, a modular backdoor platform, for cyberespionage and potential ransomware deployment. Investigations are ongoing to determine overlaps between ShadowPad intrusions and PurpleHaze activity, highlighting the extensive sharing of malware and operational practices among Chinese threat groups. The targeting of third-party service providers has raised significant concerns regarding operational security and supply chain monitoring.

China-based cyber-espionage group that CrowdStrike publicly attributed in June 2014 to People's Liberation Army (PLA) Unit 61486, part of the 12th Bureau of the PLA Third General Staff Department (3PLA), based in Shanghai [S1][S2]. CrowdStrike reported the group has operated since at least 2007 and focused on US defense and European satellite and aerospace targets [S1]. Coverage of the 62-page report describes targeting of the US space, aerospace and communications sectors through targeted email carrying exploits for productivity software and custom malware [S2][S3]. MITRE ATT&CK tracks the group as Putter Panda (G0024) with associated names APT2 and MSUpdater [S6].
identification.firstObserved: CrowdStrike: activity since at least 2007 [S1][S2]. Public disclosure: 2014-06-09 [S1][S3].
identification.notes: No Microsoft weather-taxonomy name was found: the group does not appear in Microsoft's published threat actor naming mapping as retrieved on 2026-10-15 [S7]. The CrowdStrike name 'Putter' reflects phishing aimed at golf-playing victims [S8]. MITRE lists APT2 and MSUpdater as associated names [S6]. Other aliases in this record (4HCrew, SearchFire, SULPHUR, TG-6952) came from imported galaxy data and were not confirmed in the sources gathered. Putter Panda (Unit 61486) is a separate cluster from Comment Panda/APT1 (Unit 61398), although CrowdStrike reported infrastructure overlap between the two [S4][S9].

attribution.sponsor: People's Republic of China, PLA Unit 61486 (3PLA 12th Bureau, Shanghai), per CrowdStrike [S1][S2]. MITRE ATT&CK repeats this attribution [S6].
attribution.confidence: This is a vendor attribution by CrowdStrike, not a US government attribution, and no indictment of Unit 61486 personnel appears in the sources gathered [S1][S2]. Some security experts questioned the findings and whether they would help defenders [S5]. China has denied similar accusations and asked for evidence [S2].
attribution.basis: CrowdStrike tied the actor handle 'cpyy', reported as Chen Ping, to Unit 61486. The links were registration of command-and-control domains and background details in personal photos that placed him at a Shanghai facility associated with the 3PLA 12th Bureau, a method CrowdStrike called 'hat-tribution' [S1][S4]. CrowdStrike also reported infrastructure overlap with Comment Panda (PLA Unit 61398 / APT1) and interaction between actors tied to both groups [S4][S9]. CrowdStrike said its intelligence partners had had the information for months before release [S2].

actors.objectives: Theft of trade and military secrets for the PRC. Collection focused on space, satellite, aerospace and communications technology from Western government agencies and defense contractors [S1][S2][S8].

targeting.notes: CrowdStrike described US defense and European satellite and aerospace targets [S1]. Reuters coverage describes Western government agencies and defense contractors as targets since 2007 [S2]. Named victims were not disclosed in the sources gathered.

capabilities.summary: Spear-phishing, including golf-themed lures, delivering exploits for Adobe Reader and Microsoft Office, followed by custom malware [S3][S8]. MITRE attributes four software families to the group: 4H RAT, 3PARA RAT, pngdowner and httpclient [S6]. MITRE also describes droppers that hide payloads with RC4 or a 16-byte XOR key, persist through a Run-key value named 'McUpdate', inject DLLs into network-facing processes such as Outlook and Firefox, and try to terminate Sophos antivirus components [S6]. Command-and-control domains were procured by an individual CrowdStrike tied to the unit [S4].

diamond.capability: Spear-phishing with Adobe Reader and Microsoft Office exploits; 4H RAT, 3PARA RAT, pngdowner and httpclient; RC4/XOR-obfuscated droppers; Run-key persistence; DLL injection; antivirus termination [S6][S8].

gaps: The primary CrowdStrike PDF report (imported reference URL on vox-cdn) and the CrowdStrike blog could not be opened. Details here come from search-result coverage, so technical claims should be checked against the original report.
No public reporting after 2014 attributed to Putter Panda or Unit 61486 was found. Current status after the 2015 PLA reorganization (Strategic Support Force, later Cyberspace Force) is unknown.
Microsoft has no published name for this group in its naming mapping (retrieved 2026-10-15). The 'SULPHUR' alias in imported data is unconfirmed and should not be read as a Microsoft attribution.
Aliases 4HCrew, SearchFire, TG-6952 and the APT2 equivalence come from imported galaxy data or MITRE; the original Mandiant and Secureworks documents asserting them were not reviewed.
Some third-party profiles mention targeting of Japan and research organizations; these claims were not confirmed in a dated primary source.
MITRE ATT&CK pages, Wikipedia, Threatpost and Infosecurity Magazine could not be fetched directly. MITRE details rely on search snippets of the G0024 entry (version 1.2, modified 2024-11).
The yoga-themed lures sometimes associated with this group could not be confirmed in the sources found.

implications.jipoe: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. STEP 1: Space, satellite, aerospace and communications program data held by government agencies and defense contractors is the relevant key terrain. This includes contractor email systems and the Windows endpoints of engineers and program staff [S1][S2][S3]. STEP 2: Initial access depended on users opening documents that exploit Adobe Reader and Microsoft Office. Patch currency for document readers and email filtering therefore shapes the threat's freedom of action [S8]. STEP 3: The doctrinal template is a tailored phishing email, sometimes keyed to personal interests such as golf, then a document exploit, a dropper with obfuscated payload, Run-key persistence ('McUpdate'), DLL injection into Outlook or Firefox, and RAT command and control over HTTP to actor-registered domains [S6][S8]. STEP 4: MLCOA is quiet, long-duration theft of space and satellite technical data from the defense industrial base. MDCOA is persistent access to satellite and communications program networks being used to support counterspace or targeting decisions during a crisis. That MDCOA is an extrapolation, not reported activity. Candidate indicators: Run-key values named McUpdate, unexpected termination of antivirus processes, injected DLLs in Outlook or Firefox, and connectivity checks to legitimate sites followed by outbound HTTP to unfamiliar domains [S6].
implications.jcc2: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. (1) Situational awareness: the cluster's last public reporting dates to 2014, so JCC2 tracking should treat it as a historical PLA space- and aerospace-espionage template rather than a current named threat until new reporting appears [S1][S6]. (2) Authorities: the attribution is a vendor (CrowdStrike) assessment, contested by some experts and not backed by a US indictment of this unit in the sources gathered. Products should label it as vendor attribution [S1][S5]. (3) Mission assurance: space and satellite programs depend on contractor networks, so defense-industrial-base email and endpoint hygiene is a mission-assurance concern [S2][S3]. (4) Coordination: overlap with APT1 infrastructure argues for joint analysis with teams tracking other 3PLA-linked clusters, without merging the clusters [S4][S9].

identification.summary: RaHDit is a pro-Kremlin hacktivist group known for orchestrating hack-and-leak operations, including the publication of personal information about Ukrainian military intelligence personnel and their associates. The group has been linked to Russian intelligence and has claimed to provide actionable intelligence to the Russian army. RaHDit operates a website called NemeZida, where they disclose sensitive data, and has been involved in disinformation campaigns supporting Russian narratives. Their activities include collaboration with other hacktivist groups and targeting Ukrainian cyberdefense efforts.

Rancor is a cyber espionage group that Palo Alto Networks Unit 42 first described on 26 June 2018. Unit 42 found it through attacks in Southeast Asia during 2017 and 2018, work that grew out of its research into the KHRAT Trojan [S1][S2]. Unit 42 said the group used two main malware families, DDKONG and PLAINTEE, against targets in countries including Singapore and Cambodia. Because the decoy documents drew on political news, Unit 42 judged that the group was targeting political entities [S1]. Check Point later tracked a seven-month Rancor spear-phishing campaign against Southeast Asian government entities, and Unit 42 reported repeated attempts against a Cambodian government organization using new custom malware called Dudell [S3][S6][S7].
identification.firstObserved: 2017. Unit 42 observed DDKONG in use from February 2017, and the earliest known PLAINTEE sample dates to October 2017 [S1][S2]. Check Point describes the group as active since at least 2017 [S3][S4].
identification.notes: No Microsoft (Typhoon) name for Rancor appears in the sources gathered. Palo Alto Networks tracks the group as Rancor Taurus, and the ETDA threat encyclopedia also lists the names Rancor Group and Rancor Taurus [S10]. MITRE ATT&CK tracks it as Rancor (G0075) and describes it as operating in Southeast Asia with politically themed lures [S9]. Secondary coverage reports Kaspersky-identified links between Rancor and DragonOK, and a link to the KHRAT operators, whom Unit 42 has associated with DragonOK. These are overlaps between clusters, not evidence that Rancor and DragonOK are the same group [S2][S10].

attribution.sponsor: Suspected China-nexus. ETDA lists the country as China [S10], and CFR's Cyber Operations Tracker describes Rancor as a China-linked group [S8]. Check Point said its 2019 report contained insights that 'might indicate' a Chinese origin [S3][S4]. No government attribution appears in the sources gathered.
attribution.confidence: Low to moderate, vendor-only. Check Point's wording is hedged ('might indicate') [S3]. Unit 42 notes that Derusbi, which Rancor used, is believed to be unique to a small subset of Chinese cyber espionage groups [S6]. A Unit 42 analyst quoted by CyberScoop said Rancor's tools are all custom, either unique to Rancor or shared with a small cluster of Chinese espionage groups [S7].
attribution.basis: Malware overlap with a small set of China-associated groups (Derusbi; links to KHRAT and DragonOK) [S6][S7][S2]; Check Point's origin indicators [S3]; and consistent targeting of Southeast Asian governments and political entities [S1][S3].

actors.objectives: Espionage against Southeast Asian governments and political entities [S1][S3][S10]. Unit 42 inferred the political focus from decoys built on public political news, including material linked to the opposition Cambodia National Rescue Party [S1]. ETDA lists the group's motivation as information theft and espionage [S10].

targeting.notes: Cambodia appears in every major reporting window: decoys hosted on a Cambodian government website in 2018 [S1], and persistent attempts against a Cambodian government organization from December 2018 to January 2019 and again in mid-2019 [S6][S7]. Check Point reported five unnamed government targets in the region, according to secondary coverage [S4]. Unit 42 said the attempts against the Cambodian organization appear to have failed [S7].

capabilities.summary: Spear phishing is the main way in. Unit 42 did not see the original 2018 emails and inferred them from the decoy documents found on infected systems [S1]. In 2018, delivery used HTA files and DLL loaders that downloaded further malware and displayed decoy images or PDFs hosted on legitimate sites, including a Cambodian government website and, at least once, Facebook [S1]. The payloads were DDKONG and PLAINTEE, and PLAINTEE communicates over a custom UDP protocol [S1][S2]. In the 2018-2019 campaigns, the group sent Excel and other Office documents with macros, exploited known vulnerabilities, and sent lures from real government email accounts [S3][S4][S5]. It also used DLL side-loading through trusted signed executables [S3]. Unit 42 reported a new custom macro-based malware, Dudell, and attempts to install Derusbi or KHRAT [S6]. MITRE also records msiexec use to fetch installers over HTTP, certutil for tool transfer, scheduled-task persistence, and HTTP C2 [S9].

campaigns.name: DDKONG / PLAINTEE operations (Clusters A and B)
campaigns.summary: DDKONG was in use from February 2017, and PLAINTEE samples appeared from October 2017. Unit 42 linked two activity clusters through PLAINTEE. They targeted political entities in Singapore and Cambodia with HTA and DLL-loader lures.

campaigns.name: Unit 42 public disclosure of RANCOR
campaigns.summary: Unit 42 named the previously unidentified group RANCOR and published details on DDKONG, PLAINTEE, and decoys hosted on a Cambodian government website.

campaigns.name: Southeast Asian government spear-phishing campaign
campaigns.summary: From December 2018 to June 2019, Check Point tracked lures sent to government departments and embassies. The lures were updated over time, sent from real government email accounts, and used macros and known exploits to install backdoors.

campaigns.name: Attempts against a Cambodian government organization (Dudell)
campaigns.summary: From December 2018 to January 2019, the group sent weaponized Excel documents (Dudell) and tried to install Derusbi or KHRAT. A further script-based attempt followed in July 2019. Unit 42 said none of the attempts appear to have succeeded.

diamond.adversary: Rancor (Unit 42: Rancor Taurus), a suspected China-nexus espionage group. Vendor-only attribution [S1][S3][S10].
diamond.capability: Custom malware: DDKONG, PLAINTEE (custom UDP C2) and Dudell. Shared families: Derusbi and KHRAT. Delivery and execution via HTA, DLL loaders, side-loading, Office macros, known exploits, msiexec and certutil [S1][S3][S6][S9].
diamond.infrastructure: Decoys hosted on legitimate sites, including a Cambodian government website and Facebook [S1]. Compromised or abused real government email accounts used as senders [S5]. HTTP-based C2 [S9].
diamond.victim: Government departments, embassies and political entities in Cambodia, Singapore and the wider Southeast Asia region [S1][S3][S4].
diamond.socioPolitical: Lures built from regional political news, including Cambodian opposition (CNRP) themes, around a period of Cambodian political tension. This points to collection of political intelligence on Southeast Asian governments [S1].
diamond.technology: Windows endpoints running Microsoft Office with macros enabled or unpatched against known vulnerabilities. Trust in signed executables, which enables side-loading [S3][S9].

gaps: Primary documents could not be opened: WebFetch failed to resolve unit42.paloaltonetworks.com, research.checkpoint.com, cfr.org, thehackernews.com, cyberscoop.com and securityaffairs.com. Report details come from search-result excerpts of those pages.
The publication date of the Unit 42 Dudell report (S6) is listed as 2019-12-17 in search-result metadata; the exact date of the CyberScoop article (S7) was not confirmed beyond December 2019.
No Microsoft threat actor name for Rancor was found. Mapping to the Microsoft taxonomy is unverified.
No activity reported after 2019 was found in reliable sources. A secondary blog's claim that Dudell was 'discovered in 2024' conflicts with Unit 42 and was not used.
The Rancor/DragonOK/KHRAT relationship is stated only in secondary coverage of Kaspersky and Unit 42 research. The Kaspersky source itself was not located.
No government (USG or allied) attribution or sponsoring-agency identification (e.g., MSS or PLA unit) was found.
Thailand and Vietnam come from secondary sources (Security Affairs, ETDA) and are not confirmed in a primary vendor report reviewed here.

implications.jipoe: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. STEP 1 (operational environment): The relevant terrain is Southeast Asian partner-nation government networks, embassies and political-party systems, especially Cambodia and Singapore, plus the legitimate government websites and email accounts the actor abuses for staging and delivery [S1][S3][S5]. STEP 2 (effects): Partner ministries' trust in mail from real government accounts weakens email-based defenses. This affects US engagement and coalition planning that runs through these partners [S3][S5]. STEP 3 (threat model): The template is a politically themed spear-phishing document (HTA, macro Excel or exploit document), then a loader or DLL side-load, then a custom backdoor (DDKONG, PLAINTEE, Dudell, Derusbi or KHRAT) with HTTP or custom UDP C2 and scheduled-task persistence [S1][S3][S6][S9]. STEP 4 (COAs): MLCOA is sustained, iterative phishing of partner ministries and embassies to collect political intelligence, retargeting after failed attempts [S3][S7]. MDCOA is compromising partner-government mail accounts and websites to send lures to US or coalition personnel engaged in the region. That second scenario is extrapolated from observed account and website abuse, not from reported targeting [S1][S5]. Candidate indicators: Office documents spawning msiexec or certutil downloads over HTTP; new schtasks /create entries; signed binaries loading DLLs from user-writable paths; unusual outbound UDP from workstations; decoys pulled from government or Facebook URLs [S1][S3][S9].
implications.jcc2: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. (1) Situational awareness: Track partner-nation reporting and vendor feeds on Southeast Asian government phishing. Rancor reporting is sparse after 2019, so lack of reporting does not mean the group is inactive [S3][S6]. (2) Authorities: The victims are mainly foreign partner governments [S1][S3]. Defensive support is a matter for partner-engagement and information-sharing arrangements rather than DODIN authorities, except where DoD personnel or systems receive lures. (3) Mission assurance: Mission-partner and embassy-adjacent DoD users should treat mail from partner-government accounts as possibly compromised, and macro and HTA execution controls should be enforced [S3][S5]. (4) Coordination: Coordinate with interagency and partner CERTs (for example, Cambodian and Singaporean) to share decoy hashes and abused legitimate URLs. Attribution remains vendor-only and hedged, so products should describe it that way [S3][S10].

provenance.importedSummary: The Rancor group’s attacks use two primary malware families which are naming DDKONG and PLAINTEE. DDKONG is used throughout the campaign and PLAINTEE appears to be new addition to these attackers’ toolkit.
