identification.summary: China-based nation-state activity group that Microsoft tracks as the primary threat group targeting nations that ring the South China Sea [S1][S2]. Microsoft reports that it consistently targets government ministries, military entities, and corporate entities connected to critical infrastructure, particularly telecoms, and that it has been particularly persistent since January 2023 [S1]. In June 2023 it successfully targeted military and executive entities in Indonesia and a Malaysian maritime system [S2]. Microsoft maps APT30, LotusBlossom and LOTUS PANDA to Raspberry Typhoon [S3]; vendor reporting under those names describes Southeast Asia-focused espionage going back to at least 2005 (FireEye, APT30) [S5] and continuing into 2025-2026 (Cisco Talos, Symantec and Rapid7 reporting on Lotus Blossom / Lotus Panda) [S8][S9][S10].
identification.firstObserved: Microsoft does not state a first-observed date [S1][S2]. FireEye said APT30 had been conducting cyber espionage since at least 2005 [S5]. Cisco Talos said Lotus Blossom has conducted espionage since at least 2012 [S8]; coverage of the Rapid7 reporting says Lotus Blossom has been active since 2009 [S10].
identification.notes: Microsoft name: Raspberry Typhoon (formerly RADIUM) [S1][S3]. Microsoft's public naming map lists RADIUM, LOTUS PANDA, LotusBlossom and APT30 as other names for Raspberry Typhoon without naming the vendor for each [S3]. Microsoft does not map Naikon, Spring Dragon, Billbug/Thrip or PLA Unit 78020 to Raspberry Typhoon [S3]; Symantec, however, treats Billbug, Lotus Blossom and Thrip as one group [S7], and press coverage of Talos lists Lotus Panda, Billbug, Spring Dragon and Thrip as Lotus Blossom aliases [S8]. MITRE tracks APT30 (G0013), Naikon (G0019), Lotus Blossom (G0030) and Thrip (G0076) as separate groups [S4]. Facts below are labelled by the reporting vendor's cluster name; do not assume every event is inside Microsoft's Raspberry Typhoon boundary.

attribution.sponsor: China. Microsoft describes Raspberry Typhoon as a nation-state activity group based out of China [S2]. FireEye assessed APT30 activity as state sponsored, most likely by the Chinese government [S5]. Talos describes Lotus Blossom as China-backed [S8]. No specific sponsoring organization (MSS or PLA) is named for the Microsoft cluster in the sources reviewed.
attribution.confidence: Microsoft attributes activity to Raspberry Typhoon by name without a stated confidence level [S1][S2]. FireEye: 'most likely' Chinese government (2015) [S5]. Unit 42: likely nation-state sponsored, country not named (2015) [S6]. Talos: high confidence that the 2025-reported campaigns are Lotus Blossom, based on exclusive use of Sagerunex [S8]. Symantec (2025): Chinese actors, with attribution to a single actor not determined, though indicators linked to Billbug [S9]. Rapid7: medium confidence that Lotus Blossom compromised Notepad++ update infrastructure [S10]. No government attribution of the Microsoft-defined cluster was found.
attribution.basis: Microsoft telemetry in its East Asia reports [S1][S2] and naming map [S3]; vendor malware and infrastructure analysis by FireEye [S5], Palo Alto Unit 42 [S6], Symantec [S7][S9], Cisco Talos [S8] and Rapid7 [S10], mostly reviewed through press coverage.

actors.objectives: Long-term intelligence collection on governments, militaries and critical-infrastructure entities in South China Sea littoral and wider Southeast Asian states, consistent with Chinese strategic goals in the South China Sea [S1][S2]. FireEye described APT30 as focused on targets holding key political, economic and military information about the region, with activity spikes around ASEAN meetings [S5]. Microsoft's 2024 report places June 2023 Indonesia and Malaysia activity in the weeks before a rare multilateral naval exercise involving Indonesia, China and the United States [S2]. Symantec raised the concern that a compromised certificate authority could let the group sign malware with valid certificates [S7].

sectors: Government ministries, including defense, intelligence, economic and trade ministries [S1][S9]
Aviation: air traffic control and air freight [S9]
Manufacturing, media and news agencies, construction [S8][S9]
Journalists and commercial organizations with regional information [S5]
regions: Nations ringing the South China Sea [S1]
Unnamed Southeast Asian countries (2024-2025 Symantec reporting) [S9]
India and wider Southeast Asia (APT30 coverage) [S5]
Central America (per coverage of Rapid7 reporting) [S10]
targeting.notes: Microsoft's 2024 report lists Raspberry Typhoon with Flax Typhoon and Granite Typhoon as actors behind observed events in or around the South China Sea [S2]. Regions and sectors beyond S1-S2 come from vendor clusters that Microsoft maps (APT30, LotusBlossom, LOTUS PANDA) [S3] or that Symantec equates with Lotus Blossom (Billbug) [S7].

capabilities.summary: Microsoft says Raspberry Typhoon typically conducts intelligence collection and malware execution against government and infrastructure targets [S1]. APT30 used a sustained, planned malware development effort, including tools able to reach air-gapped networks, according to FireEye coverage [S5]; MITRE's G0013 software list includes BACKSPACE, NETEAGLE, SHIPSHAPE, SPACESHIP and FLASHFLOOD [S4]. Lotus Blossom used spearphishing with decoy documents (reportedly CVE-2012-0158) to deliver the Elise backdoor [S6]. Symantec tied the 2022 activity to the Hannotog and Sagerunex backdoors [S7]. Talos reports Sagerunex variants that use Dropbox, Twitter and Zimbra webmail as C2 tunnels instead of VPS servers [S8]. Symantec's 2025 reporting describes DLL sideloading through legitimate Trend Micro and Bitdefender binaries, ChromeKatz and CredentialKatz browser credential stealers, a reverse SSH tool, and a timestamp-altering utility (datechanger.exe) [S9]. Rapid7 reports a hijacked Notepad++ update path delivering a trojanized NSIS installer that sideloaded via a renamed Bitdefender binary to launch the Chrysalis backdoor [S10].

campaigns.name: Operation Lotus Blossom (Unit 42)

campaigns.name: Billbug targeting of an Asian certificate authority

campaigns.name: Sustained South China Sea targeting
campaigns.summary: Microsoft reports Raspberry Typhoon has been particularly persistent since January 2023 against government, military and telecom-linked critical-infrastructure targets around the South China Sea.

campaigns.name: Indonesia and Malaysia targeting before multilateral naval exercise
campaigns.summary: Raspberry Typhoon successfully targeted military and executive entities in Indonesia and a Malaysian maritime system in the weeks before a rare naval exercise involving Indonesia, China and the United States.

campaigns.name: Southeast Asia government, aviation and telecom intrusions (Symantec, Lotus Panda)
campaigns.summary: From August 2024 to February 2025, intrusions hit a government ministry, an air traffic control organization, a telecom operator and a construction company in one Southeast Asian country, plus a news agency and an air freight organization elsewhere in the region, using sideloading and Chrome credential stealers.

campaigns.name: Sagerunex campaigns in the Philippines, Vietnam, Hong Kong and Taiwan (Talos)
campaigns.summary: Talos reported Lotus Blossom campaigns against government, manufacturing, telecommunications and media organizations using Sagerunex variants with cloud-service C2.

campaigns.name: Notepad++ update infrastructure hijack (Chrysalis)
campaigns.summary: Rapid7 attributed, with medium confidence, a June-December 2025 compromise of Notepad++ hosting/update traffic to Lotus Blossom, used to deliver the Chrysalis backdoor to selected users; publicly reported February 2026.

diamond.adversary: China-based nation-state activity group (Microsoft: Raspberry Typhoon, formerly RADIUM) [S1][S2][S3]; overlapping vendor clusters APT30, Lotus Blossom/Lotus Panda and Billbug [S3][S5][S7][S8].
diamond.capability: Spearphishing with decoy documents and Elise [S6]; APT30 malware families [S4][S5]; Sagerunex and Hannotog backdoors [S7][S8]; DLL sideloading, Chrome credential stealers and reverse SSH [S9]; software-update hijacking delivering Chrysalis [S10].
diamond.infrastructure: Sagerunex C2 tunnelled through Dropbox, Twitter and Zimbra webmail instead of the earlier VPS servers [S8]; compromised Notepad++ hosting used to redirect update traffic to attacker-controlled downloads [S10].
diamond.victim: Government ministries, military, executive and defense entities, telecoms, maritime systems, aviation, certificate authorities and media in South China Sea and Southeast Asian states [S1][S2][S6][S7][S8][S9]; Notepad++ users selected for redirection [S10].
diamond.socioPolitical: Collection that mirrors Chinese strategic goals in the South China Sea, timed around ASEAN meetings and a multilateral naval exercise involving the United States [S1][S2][S5].
diamond.technology: Government and military Windows networks, telecom and aviation infrastructure, PKI/certificate services, cloud services abused for C2, and software update mechanisms [S2][S7][S8][S9][S10].

gaps: Primary documents could not be opened: FireEye APT30 report (2015), Unit 42 Operation Lotus Blossom, Symantec Billbug (2022) and Lotus Panda (2025) blogs, Cisco Talos Lotus Blossom blog, Rapid7 Chrysalis report, Kaspersky Naikon/Spring Dragon and MITRE pages; content is drawn from search-result summaries and press coverage.

Cluster boundaries are unresolved. Microsoft maps only RADIUM, LOTUS PANDA, LotusBlossom and APT30 [S3]; MITRE keeps APT30, Naikon, Lotus Blossom and Thrip separate [S4]. Symantec merges Billbug/Thrip with Lotus Blossom [S7]. Naikon (and its PLA Unit 78020 attribution) is not verified as part of Raspberry Typhoon.

Microsoft has not publicly tied the 2025 Sagerunex, 2024-2025 Symantec or Notepad++ activity to Raspberry Typhoon by name; those links rest on Microsoft's alias mapping plus vendor attributions of differing confidence (Symantec could not pin the 2025 activity to a single actor; Rapid7 medium confidence).
Exact publication dates for the Talos (2025-03) and Rapid7 (2026-02) reports were taken from coverage, not the primary pages.
No sponsoring organization (MSS vs PLA) is named for the Microsoft cluster; no government attribution found.
Victims of the Notepad++ redirection and specific Raspberry Typhoon victim organizations after 2023 are not public in reviewed sources.
The claim of Central America targeting appears only in secondary coverage [S10] and is unverified.

implications.jipoe: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. STEP 1 (Operational environment): Key terrain includes partner-nation government ministries, military and executive networks, telecom carriers, maritime and aviation systems, PKI providers, and software update channels in South China Sea littoral states [S1][S2][S7][S9][S10]. STEP 2 (Effects): Coalition and exercise planning shared with these partners is exposed through partner networks, and activity has been timed before multilateral naval exercises and ASEAN meetings [S2][S5]. STEP 3 (Threat model): spearphishing or trusted-software update hijack, DLL sideloading of signed security-vendor binaries, Sagerunex/Chrysalis-class backdoors with C2 over Dropbox, Twitter or Zimbra, browser credential theft and timestamp tampering [S6][S8][S9][S10]. STEP 4 (COAs): MLCOA is persistent, quiet collection from partner defense and foreign ministries and telecoms ahead of regional exercises and diplomatic events [S1][S2][S5]. MDCOA is use of a compromised certificate authority or software update channel to sign or push implants into many networks, including those connected to US forces [S7][S10]. Candidate indicators: unexpected Trend Micro or Bitdefender binaries loading DLLs from unusual paths; workstation traffic to Dropbox/Twitter/Zimbra APIs from non-browser processes; GUP.exe or updater processes fetching installers from non-vendor IPs; ChromeKatz/CredentialKatz artifacts; file timestamp anomalies [S8][S9][S10].
implications.jcc2: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. Situational awareness: fuse partner-nation and vendor reporting on Lotus Blossom/Lotus Panda/APT30 under the Raspberry Typhoon name while keeping vendor cluster labels visible, since attributions vary in confidence [S3][S8][S9][S10]. Authorities: most victims are partner-nation government and telecom networks [S1][S2][S9], so response depends on partner agreements and defend-forward or hunt-forward authorities rather than DODIN-only actions. Mission assurance: exercise and coalition planning data shared with Southeast Asian partners, and software update and PKI trust used by mission systems, are at risk [S2][S7][S10]; validate update integrity for third-party tools on mission networks. Coordination: synchronize with partner CERTs, and with the security vendors whose binaries are abused for sideloading, before and during regional exercises [S2][S9].

provenance.importedSummary: Microsoft has tracked Raspberry Typhoon (RADIUM) as the primary threat group targeting nations that ring the South China Sea. Raspberry Typhoon consistently targets government ministries, military entities, and corporate entities connected to critical infrastructure, particularly telecoms. identification.summary: In 2021, PwC started tracking a series of intrusions under the moniker of Red Dev 17 that they assess were highly likely conducted by a China-based threat actor. Their analysis suggests Red Dev 17 has been active since at least 2017. Red Dev 17's observed targets are mainly in India, and include the Indian military, a multinational India-based technology company, and a state energy company. They assess that it is highly probable that the threat actor behind intrusions associated with Red Dev 17 is also responsible for the campaign known in open source as Operation NightScout. Red Dev 17 is a user of the 8.t document weaponisation framework (also known as RoyalRoad), and abuses benign utilities such as Logitech or Windows Defender binaries to sideload and execute Chinoxy or PoisonIvy variants on victim systems. They identified capability and infrastructure links between Red Dev 17 and the threat actor they call Red Hariasa (aka FunnyDream APT), as well as infrastructure overlaps with Red Wendigo (aka Icefog, RedFoxtrot), and with ShadowPad C2 servers. At this time, they do not have sufficient evidence to directly link Red Dev 17 to any of these threat actors. However, They assess with realistic probability that Red Dev 17 operates within a cluster of threat actors that share tools and infrastructure, as well as a strong targeting focus on Southeast Asia and Central Asia.

Since 2021, Red Menshen, a China based threat actor, which has been observed targeting telecommunications providers across the Middle East and Asia, as well as entities in the government, education, and logistics sectors using a custom backdoor referred as BPFDoor. This threat actor uses a variety of tools in its post-exploitation phase. This includes custom variants of the shared tool Mangzamel (including Golang variants), custom variants of Gh0st, and open source tools like Mimikatz and Metasploit to aid in its lateral movement across Windows systems. Also, They have been seen sending commands to BPFDoor victims via Virtual Privat Servers (VPSs) hosted at a well-known provider, and that these VPSs, in turn, are administered via compromised routers based in Taiwan, which the threat actor uses as VPN tunnels. Most Red Menshen activity that has been observed took place between Monday to Friday (with none observed on the weekends), with most communication taking place between 01:00 and 10:00 UTC.131 This pattern suggests a consistent 8 to 9-hour activity window for the threat actor, with realistic probability of it aligning to local working hours.

Red Nue, active since at least 2017, is known for its use of the multi-platform LootRAt backdoor, also known as ReverseWindow. LootRAT has variants for Windows and Macintosh (reported in open source as Demsty), as well as an Android variant known as SpyDealer. Red Nue has also used another Windows backdoor known as WinDealer since at least 2019, when it deployed it to targets as part of a watering hole campaign on a Chinese news website for the Chinese diaspora community. Parts of Asia feature heavily in Red Nue's victimology.

Iranian destructive cyber actor that Microsoft tracked as DEV-0842 (now Storm-0842), the cluster that deployed ransomware and a wiper against the Albanian government on 15 July 2022 [S1]. Check Point tracks the activity as Void Manticore, a MOIS-affiliated group that runs the 'Homeland Justice' persona against Albania and the 'Karma' persona against Israel and uses custom wipers [S4]. Later vendor reporting ties the 'Handala' hack-and-leak persona to the same cluster, including the March 2026 Intune-based mass wipe at Stryker [S7][S8].
identification.firstObserved: Destructive deployment by DEV-0842 against Albania on 2022-07-15. Microsoft says other Iranian clusters held access from May 2021 [S1]. Mandiant saw a ROADSWEEP ransomware sample from Albania on 2022-07-22 [S3].
identification.notes: Microsoft name in this record: Red Sandstorm. The Microsoft sources gathered here use DEV-0842/Storm-0842 [S1], and secondary 2026 reporting says Microsoft tracks the Handala cluster as Storm-0842 [S7][S8]. Microsoft splits the 2022 Albania operation across several clusters: DEV-0861 (initial access, mail exfiltration), DEV-0166 (mail exfiltration), DEV-0133 (probing) and DEV-0842 (ransomware and wiper) [S1]. Only the DEV-0842 role belongs to this record. Check Point describes a handoff in which Scarred Manticore gains access and then passes targets to Void Manticore [S4]. CrowdStrike's name is Banished Kitten [S7].

attribution.sponsor: Iran, Ministry of Intelligence and Security (MOIS), per Check Point's assessment of Void Manticore [S4]. FBI and CISA attribute the 2022 Albania attacks to 'Iranian state cyber actors' [S2].
attribution.confidence: Microsoft has high confidence that Iranian government-sponsored actors carried out the 15 July 2022 destructive attack [S1]. Microsoft has moderate confidence that the initial-access and exfiltration actors are linked to EUROPIUM, which is publicly tied to MOIS [S1]. Mandiant made a moderate-confidence assessment that one or more actors operating in support of Iranian goals were involved, but tied the activity to no named group [S3]. Check Point links Void Manticore to MOIS [S4]. The Handala-to-Void Manticore link is a vendor assessment that secondary sources credit to Check Point in May 2024 [S7][S8].
attribution.basis: Microsoft incident response and telemetry [S1]; FBI investigation summarized in Joint Cybersecurity Advisory AA22-264A [S2]; Mandiant malware and persona analysis [S3]; Check Point research on overlaps in wipers and personas [S4]; secondary vendor analyses of the 2026 Stryker incident [S7][S8].

actors.objectives: Disruptive and destructive attacks combined with hack-and-leak influence operations that punish and intimidate states and organizations opposed to Iranian policy. These include Albania for hosting the MEK [S1][S3] and Israeli organizations [S4]. Microsoft assessed the 2022 Albania attack as retaliation for cyberattacks on Iran that Tehran blamed on Israel and the MEK [S1]. Handala claimed the 2026 Stryker attack as retaliation for a reported US strike [S8].

regions: United States-headquartered multinationals with global device fleets (Stryker, 2026) [S7][S8]
targeting.notes: Reporting says the Karma persona claimed attacks on more than 40 Israeli organizations [S4].

capabilities.summary: In Albania (July 2022), DEV-0842 deployed GoXml.exe ransomware and the cl.exe wiper, which uses the RawDisk driver rwdsk.sys. It also used a Defender-disabling tool and the Mellona.exe SMB distributor. Web shells, Mimikatz and Impacket were seen in the wider intrusion [S1]. FBI/CISA report that the actors deployed a ZeroCleare variant after defenders responded to the ransomware [S2]. Check Point-based reporting names custom wipers: CI Wiper and No-Justice/LowEraser in Albania, and an updated BiBi wiper with partition-table deletion in Israel [S4]. In 2026 the cluster shifted to abusing living-off-the-cloud administration. Reporting describes AiTM phishing and infostealer-derived session tokens used to compromise an Intune administrator, the creation of a new Global Administrator, and Microsoft Graph API calls that issued mass factory resets without custom malware [S7]. Hack-and-leak through Telegram personas and websites is a constant feature [S3][S4].

campaigns.name: Stryker Intune mass-wipe (Handala)
campaigns.summary: On 11 March 2026, attackers using the Handala persona reportedly compromised Stryker's Intune administration and factory-reset a large device fleet. Device counts reach about 200,000 in some reports, and Stryker said no malware was found.

diamond.adversary: Iranian MOIS-affiliated destructive unit (Microsoft DEV-0842/Storm-0842; Check Point Void Manticore; CrowdStrike Banished Kitten) operating the Homeland Justice, Karma and Handala personas [S1][S4][S7].
diamond.capability: Custom wipers and ransomware (cl.exe, GoXml, ZeroCleare variant, CI Wiper, No-Justice/LowEraser, BiBi) [S1][S2][S4]; credential tools and web shells [S1]; in 2026, Intune and Graph API remote wipe through a compromised administrator identity [S7].
diamond.infrastructure: Telegram channels and persona websites used for leaks and claims [S3][S4]; access handed off from partner MOIS clusters (Scarred Manticore; EUROPIUM-linked actors in Albania) [S1][S4]; victim cloud management planes used as the delivery mechanism [S7].
diamond.victim: Albanian government and public services [S1][S2]; Israeli organizations [S4]; the global medtech firm Stryker [S7][S8].
diamond.socioPolitical: Retaliation tied to Albania hosting the MEK and to Israel/US conflict with Iran, amplified through influence messaging [S1][S3][S8].
diamond.technology: Windows domain environments, on-premises SharePoint (initial access by partner clusters), and cloud endpoint management (Microsoft Intune/Entra ID) [S1][S7].

gaps: Could not confirm in any source that Microsoft uses the name 'Red Sandstorm'. learn.microsoft.com could not be fetched. The cited Microsoft and secondary sources use DEV-0842/Storm-0842. A Wikipedia article (Handala Hack Team) surfaced in search with the alias 'Red Sandstorm' and attributes it to Iran International reporting, but the article could not be opened or dated.

Primary documents not opened: CISA/FBI AA22-264A (cisa.gov blocked), the Check Point Void Manticore and 'Bad Karma, No Justice' reports (fetch failed), the Mandiant ROADSWEEP blog, Unit 42's Handala wiper report, and Microsoft's March 2026 Intune hardening guidance. Details come from search-result coverage.
Microsoft assigns initial access in Albania to other clusters (DEV-0861, EUROPIUM-linked). Do not credit access-phase TTPs to Storm-0842 without checking.
Mandiant did not confirm that ROADSWEEP was the ransomware used in the government attack, and tied the activity to no named group [S3].

Stryker impact figures (device counts, 61 vs 79 countries, a 50 TB exfiltration claim) conflict across secondary sources and are unverified. One vendor claims MuddyWater pre-positioned access before the wipe; this is single-source.

Reported link between the unit and sanctioned MOIS deputy minister Yahya Hosseini Panjaki (and his reported 2026 death) comes only from Wikipedia citing Iran International. Treasury's September 2024 designation, as summarized in search results, concerns transnational repression, not cyber.
Sources disagree on whether the Karma persona was retired and replaced by Handala, or whether both were active at once.
First-activity date of the cluster before July 2022 is not established in public sources.

implications.jipoe: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. STEP 1 (operational environment): Key terrain is identity and management planes, meaning domain controllers, Entra ID Global Administrator roles and Intune or other MDM consoles, which can be turned into fleet-wide wipe mechanisms [S7]. It also includes internet-facing collaboration servers that partner MOIS clusters exploit for initial access [S1]. STEP 2 (effects): Destruction is timed to political events (MEK conference, diplomatic disputes, kinetic conflict), and hack-and-leak amplifies the psychological effect [S1][S2][S3]. STEP 3 (threat model): A partner cluster gains long-dwell access (about 14 months in Albania) and exfiltrates mail; this unit then deploys ransomware-styled wipers or abuses MDM remote wipe, and a persona claims the attack on Telegram [S1][S2][S4][S7]. STEP 4 (COAs): MLCOA is a hack-and-leak plus wiper attack against government or regional partner-nation networks during periods of Iran-Israel/US tension [S4]. MDCOA is an identity-plane compromise of a defense contractor or mission partner leading to mass MDM wipe of endpoints that support operations, as at Stryker [S7]. Candidate indicators: creation of new Global Administrator accounts; bulk Intune wipe or retire actions through Graph API; RawDisk driver (rwdsk.sys) loading; Defender-disable tooling; Telegram persona claims naming the organization [S1][S7].
implications.jcc2: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. Situational awareness: Track Handala, Homeland Justice and Karma persona channels as early warning, since claims and leaks accompany or follow attacks [S3][S4]. Watch for joint advisories on Iranian destructive activity [S2]. Authorities: Activity hits partner nations (Albania is a NATO member) and US companies, so response may require DCO coordination with mission partners and DIB/CISA/FBI channels rather than DoDIN-only actions [S2][S7]. Mission assurance: Enforce multi-admin approval and phishing-resistant MFA for MDM and identity admins, keep offline recovery for endpoints, and harden SharePoint and VPN edges used by access-broker clusters [S1][S7]. Coordination: Because access and destruction are split across MOIS clusters, hunt across the handoff boundary, so that detecting a partner's long-dwell access becomes a pre-strike warning for Storm-0842 effects [S1][S4].

provenance.importedSummary: Void Manticore is an Iranian APT group affiliated with MOIS, known for conducting destructive wiping attacks and influence operations. They collaborate with Scarred Manticore, sharing targets and conducting disruptive operations using custom wipers. Void Manticore's TTPs involve manual file deletion, lateral movement via RDP, and the deployment of custom wipers like the BiBi wiper. The group utilizes online personas like 'Karma' and 'Homeland Justice' to leak information and amplify the impact of their attacks.

identification.summary: Recorded Future’s Insikt Group has identified a large cluster of new operational infrastructure associated with use of the custom Windows and Linux backdoor KEYPLUG. We attribute this activity to a threat activity group tracked as RedGolf, which is highly likely to be a Chinese state-sponsored group. RedGolf closely overlaps with threat activity reported in open sources under the aliases APT41/BARIUM and has likely carried out state-sponsored espionage activity in parallel with financially motivated operations for personal gain from at least 2014 onward.

RedJuliett is a likely Chinese state-sponsored threat actor targeting government, academic, technology, and diplomatic organizations in Taiwan. They exploit vulnerabilities in network edge devices for initial access and use SQL injection and directory traversal exploits against web and SQL applications. The group operates from Fuzhou, China, and aims to support Beijing's intelligence collection on Taiwan's economic and diplomatic relations. RedJuliett has also expanded its operations to compromise organizations in other countries such as Hong Kong, Malaysia, and the United States.

relatedRecords.note: Lumen Black Lotus Labs lists RedJuliett (Recorded Future) as overlapping Flax Typhoon in its Sept 2024 Raptor Train reporting. Microsoft's mapping does not list RedJuliett under Flax Typhoon. Kept as separate records.

identification.summary: A group monitored as REF2924 by Elastic Security Labs is wielding novel data-stealing malware — an HTTP listener written in C# dubbed Naplistener by the researchers — in attacks against victims operating in southern and southeast Asia.According to a blog post by Elastic senior security research engineer Remco Sprooten, in that region of the world, network-based detection and prevention technologies are the de facto method for securing many environments.

REF7707 is a cyber campaign targeting government entities, particularly a foreign ministry in South America, utilizing malware families such as FinalDraft, GuidLoader, and PathLoader for persistence and lateral movement. The threat actor employs the Microsoft Graph API for C2 communication, blending malicious traffic with legitimate activity to evade detection. Despite their technical sophistication, REF7707 operators exhibited poor operational security, leading to the exposure of their infrastructure and malware. Their tactics enable the extraction of sensitive data, including passwords and Active Directory information, facilitating ongoing espionage activities.

identification.summary: Microsoft Threat Intelligence tracks Ruby Sleet (formerly CERIUM) as a North Korea-linked threat actor and says it has tracked the actor since 2020 and that its phishing operations have grown significantly more sophisticated over the past several years [S1][S2]. Microsoft reports it compromising aerospace and defense-related organizations, signing malware with legitimate but compromised certificates taken from victims, and distributing backdoored VPN clients and other legitimate software [S1].
identification.firstObserved: Microsoft: tracked since 2020 [S1].
identification.notes: Microsoft name: Ruby Sleet (formerly CERIUM) [S2]. The Microsoft naming mapping used by this encyclopedia also lists VELVET CHOLLIMA as an alias [S8]. NAMING CONFLICT: several secondary sources and vendors list Ruby Sleet as an alias of APT37/ScarCruft (also InkySquid, Reaper, Ricochet Chollima, RedEyes) [S5][S6], while CrowdStrike's Velvet Chollima profile is the name usually associated with Kimsuky-related activity and lists Cerium and Ruby Sleet among community identifiers [S9]. Cluster boundaries across Microsoft, MITRE and CrowdStrike are not reconciled here; facts below are attributed only to the vendor that stated them. The 2023-2024 Microsoft reports cited do not themselves state a mapping to APT37 or Kimsuky [S1][S2].

attribution.sponsor: North Korea (DPRK). Microsoft's September 2023 East Asia report groups Ruby Sleet with other North Korean actors and says the North Korean government appears to assign multiple threat actor groups at once to meet high-priority collection requirements [S2]. Malpedia describes it as linked to North Korea's Ministry of State Security [S7]; that is a third-party catalog statement, not a Microsoft or government finding.
attribution.confidence: No explicit Microsoft confidence statement for Ruby Sleet was found in the sources reviewed [S1][S2]. No government attribution located.
attribution.basis: Microsoft telemetry and incident observation (victim compromises, supply-chain incident, infrastructure) [S1][S2]; Microsoft's interpretation of overlapping targeting across North Korean actors [S2].

actors.objectives: Collection of defense, aerospace and maritime-sector information. Microsoft says stolen aerospace and defense technology may be used by North Korea to increase its understanding of missiles, drones and related technologies [S1]. Microsoft assessed the 2022-2023 maritime and shipbuilding targeting as occurring shortly before North Korean maritime military tests in March and April 2023, which included underwater attack drones [S2].

sectors: Construction (Korean company used as a supply-chain entry point)
regions: Russia (aerospace research institute, March 2023, with Onyx Sleet) [S2]
Germany and Israel (two arms manufacturing companies, with Diamond Sleet, November 2022 to January 2023) [S2]
targeting.notes: Maritime and shipbuilding targeting November 2022 to January 2023 was conducted alongside Diamond Sleet and Sapphire Sleet [S2][S3]. Microsoft's regions beyond those listed are not stated in the sources reviewed.

capabilities.summary: Social-engineering and phishing operations that Microsoft says have become significantly more sophisticated; reconnaissance to identify the software a target uses and custom capabilities built for specific targets; malware signed with legitimate but compromised certificates obtained from victims; distribution of backdoored VPN clients, installers and other legitimate software [S1]. In December 2023 Microsoft observed the actor compromise a Korean construction company and replace a legitimate Wizvera VeraPort software version with one that communicated with known Ruby Sleet infrastructure [S1]. No named malware families are given in the Microsoft sources reviewed [S1][S2]. If Ruby Sleet is treated as APT37, Zscaler's 2026 reporting on the 'Ruby Jumper' campaign describes RESTLEAF (Zoho WorkDrive C2), SNAKEDROPPER, THUMBSBD (USB-based air-gap bridging), VIRUSTASK and FOOTWINE [S4]; that mapping is a secondary-source alias claim and not confirmed by Microsoft here [S5].

diamond.adversary: North Korea-linked actor tracked by Microsoft as Ruby Sleet (formerly CERIUM) [S1][S2]. Third parties variously equate it with APT37/ScarCruft or place it near Kimsuky-associated names; unresolved [S5][S9].
diamond.capability: Phishing, stolen-certificate code signing, backdoored VPN clients and installers, and software supply-chain replacement (VeraPort) [S1].
diamond.infrastructure: Microsoft refers to 'known Ruby Sleet infrastructure' contacted by the trojanized VeraPort package; specifics are not published in the sources reviewed [S1]. Compromised victim certificates serve as signing infrastructure [S1].
diamond.victim: Aerospace and defense organizations, maritime and shipbuilding firms, arms manufacturers in Germany and Israel, a Russian aerospace research institute, and a Korean construction company [S1][S2].
diamond.socioPolitical: Collection supporting North Korean missile, drone and maritime-military development, as assessed by Microsoft [S1][S2].
diamond.technology: Software trust relationships (VPN clients, VeraPort-style identity/plug-in delivery, code-signing certificates) and defense-contractor email and software supply chains [S1].

gaps: Cluster mapping is unresolved: sources equate Ruby Sleet with APT37/ScarCruft [S5][S6], CrowdStrike lists Cerium and Ruby Sleet as community identifiers under Velvet Chollima [S9], and the Microsoft reports cited do not state a mapping. The Microsoft naming mapping file was retrieved by the encyclopedia but its entry text was not re-verified here [S8].

Whether Zscaler's Ruby Jumper campaign (2025-2026) belongs to Microsoft's Ruby Sleet cluster is unverified; Zscaler's own blog could not be opened (host blocked) and it was read only through secondary coverage [S4].
Malpedia's Ministry of State Security statement was read only through search results and its basis is not given [S7].
No named malware families, hashes, domains or IP indicators for Ruby Sleet are published in the Microsoft sources reviewed.
Microsoft's CYBERWARCON article gives no explicit confidence level or victim count; the December 2023 construction-company incident rests on that single source [S1].
Microsoft's September 2023 full report PDF and the Register article were read via summary and search snippets, not in full [S2][S3].
No US government (CISA, FBI, DOJ, Treasury) attribution or advisory specific to Ruby Sleet was found.

implications.jipoe: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. STEP 1: Key terrain includes defense-industrial-base and aerospace email, VPN client distribution channels, code-signing certificate stores, and software update or plug-in delivery channels (e.g. VeraPort-style) used by contractors and their suppliers [S1]. STEP 2: The actor is assessed by Microsoft as seeking missile, drone and maritime-related technology, and has coordinated with other North Korean actors against the same sector [S1][S2]. STEP 3: Observed pattern is targeted phishing and reconnaissance, then trojanized legitimate software or backdoored VPN clients signed with stolen certificates, then collection from aerospace, defense and shipbuilding victims [S1]. STEP 4: MLCOA is continued collection against allied and non-allied aerospace, defense and maritime firms, including through supplier compromise. MDCOA is use of a compromised supplier's signed software to reach defense contractors at scale during a crisis. Candidate indicators: unexpected updates to VPN clients or identity plug-ins, validly signed binaries from unusual publishers or recently compromised vendors, and beaconing from newly installed client software [S1].
implications.jcc2: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. (1) Situational awareness: track Microsoft and vendor reporting on North Korean clusters together, since Microsoft observed multiple groups on the same targets and naming across vendors does not align [S2][S9]. (2) Authorities and coordination: supply-chain incidents at contractors are best routed through DC3 and DIB cybersecurity channels with the affected company and, for foreign partners, through established allied intelligence-sharing arrangements. (3) Mission assurance: verify code-signing trust, third-party VPN client provenance and software-update integrity for mission-relevant systems; treat valid signatures as insufficient evidence of legitimacy [S1]. (4) Avoid attributing incidents to Ruby Sleet by alias alone until the cluster mapping is resolved.

identification.summary: RuskiNet is a pro-Russian hacktivist collective associated with disruptive operations including DDoS attacks, website defacements, phishing, and data leaks against government, infrastructure, financial, and civil targets.

Ruthless Rabbit has been running investment scam campaigns since November 2022, primarily targeting users in Russia, Poland, Romania, and Kazakhstan. The actor utilizes RDGA patterns to create over 2,600 domains, hosted on multiple dedicated IPs, and employs a cloaking service for validation checks on user leads. Their campaigns have included themes such as Baltic Pipe financial scams and spoofing well-known platforms like WhatsApp and Google Finance. The most prevalent campaign theme involves a spoofed news article from "Channel One" promoting the "GazInvest" platform with promises of high returns.

Ruza Flood is Microsoft's name for a Russia-affiliated influence operation that Microsoft also labels Doppelganger [S1]. The Doppelganger campaign was publicly named by EU DisinfoLab in September 2022 as a network using clones of at least 17 media outlets (including Bild, 20minutes, ANSA, The Guardian and RBC Ukraine) with fake articles, videos and polls [S5]. This is an influence operation, not an intrusion set.
identification.firstObserved: Doppelganger cloned-media activity was publicly documented by EU DisinfoLab in 2022-09 [S5]. Meta's Q3 2022 threat report (2022-11) covers a Russia-origin network but does not use the name Doppelganger in the sources gathered [S6]. The date Microsoft first assigned the name Ruza Flood is not established.
identification.notes: Microsoft equates Ruza Flood with Doppelganger [S1]. Microsoft tracks Storm-1516 and Storm-1679 as separate actors that it says synchronized messaging with Ruza Flood [S1]; do not merge them. Facts about Doppelganger from non-Microsoft sources (EU DisinfoLab, Meta, DOJ, UK) are assumed to describe the same operation because Microsoft equates the names; Microsoft's own tracking boundaries are not published in the sources gathered.

attribution.sponsor: Meta linked a Russia-origin network to two Russian companies, Structura National Technologies and Social Design Agency, in a December 2022 update to its Q3 2022 report [S6]. US DOJ (as reported) attributed Doppelganger to Social Design Agency, Structura and ANO Dialog acting under the direction of the Russian Presidential Administration [S2]. The UK sanctioned all three firms on 2024-10-28 [S4]. Microsoft's own sponsor attribution is not established in the sources gathered.
attribution.confidence: DOJ statements are government allegations reported second-hand, not Microsoft findings [S2]. Microsoft's confidence statements on Ruza Flood could not be verified from the sources gathered.
attribution.basis: US DOJ announcement as reported [S2]; Meta company attribution [S6]; UK sanctions as reported [S4]; Microsoft reporting via press coverage [S1].

actors.objectives: Per Microsoft (via press coverage), in the 2024 US election cycle Ruza Flood, Storm-1516 and Storm-1679 made a synchronized shift from targeting President Biden to undermining Vice President Harris [S1]. DOJ (as reported) said the domains aimed to influence voters in US and foreign elections [S2].

sectors: Voters and general public (US 2024 election audience)
regions: Europe: Germany, France, Italy, Ukraine media brands cloned [S5]
targeting.notes: Spoofed outlets named by EU DisinfoLab include Bild, 20minutes, ANSA, The Guardian and RBC Ukraine [S5]. UK describes the operation as cloning legitimate websites and social media pages [S4].

capabilities.summary: Cloned news websites on look-alike domains with fake articles, videos and polls [S5]. DOJ (as reported) cited cybersquatting, fabricated influencers and fake profiles promoting AI-generated narratives [S2]. Press coverage of Microsoft's report ties Ruza Flood and Storm-1516 to fake videos, including one pushed via a fabricated San Francisco news outlet [S1].

implications.jipoe: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. STEP 1: Key terrain is the information environment, specifically look-alike news domains, paid social advertising and influencer channels reaching US audiences. STEP 2: DOJ alleges the adversary uses commercial PR and IT firms under Russian Presidential Administration direction [S2]. STEP 3: Template is domain cloning, AI-generated narratives and fake personas, shifting themes with the news cycle [S2][S5]. STEP 4: MLCOA is continued election- and Ukraine-themed content on replacement domains after seizures. Candidate indicators: newly registered domains imitating major outlets, coordinated persona networks, and synchronized theme shifts across Russian-affiliated actors [S1][S5].
implications.jcc2: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. Situational awareness: track Microsoft and DOJ domain-seizure disclosures for IW indicators. Authorities: influence operations are largely outside DoD network defense and require coordination with interagency partners such as DOJ, Treasury and FBI. Mission assurance: brief personnel on spoofed media and social ads. Coordination: share indicators with public affairs, cyber and intelligence staffs and with platform providers.

identification.summary: Salmon Typhoon is Microsoft's name for what it calls a sophisticated Chinese state-affiliated threat actor with a long operational history, which has historically targeted US defense contractors, government agencies and organizations in the cryptographic technology sector [S1]. Microsoft says its operations span more than a decade with intermittent periods of dormancy and resurgence, and that it has recently shown renewed activity [S1]. Microsoft states that other researchers track the same group as APT4 and Maverick Panda [S1]. CrowdStrike describes Maverick Panda as a China-nexus targeted intrusion adversary associated with the Sykipot (aka Wkysol) implant [S2].
identification.firstObserved: CrowdStrike states Maverick Panda was active from at least 2007 until November 2015 [S2]. Microsoft says only that operations span more than a decade [S1]. A CFR page says the actor has targeted US defense and aerospace firms since at least 2006 [S7]. Vendor start and end dates differ.
identification.notes: Microsoft name: Salmon Typhoon (formerly SODIUM) [S1][S2]. Names listed by CrowdStrike for the same adversary: APT4, Getkys, Sykipot Group, Wkysol [S2]. A threat-actor encyclopedia card (ETDA) lists APT 4 as the FireEye/Mandiant name, Wisp Team as Symantec's and TG-0623 as SecureWorks', but the card could not be opened directly and is known only through search-result summaries [S8]. Not to be confused with Salt Typhoon (separate Microsoft-named telecom-focused cluster). Malpedia attributes the Sykipot family to Samurai Panda rather than Maverick Panda, which is a vendor-boundary discrepancy to resolve [S8].

attribution.sponsor: Microsoft describes the actor as Chinese state-affiliated [S1]. CrowdStrike describes it as China-nexus [S2]. No specific PRC agency (MSS, PLA, MPS or contractor) is named in the sources gathered.
attribution.confidence: Confidence level is not stated in the sources gathered. These are vendor assessments (Microsoft, CrowdStrike); no government attribution was found and none should be inferred.
attribution.basis: Microsoft telemetry and its joint investigation with OpenAI of the actor's AI-service accounts [S1][S3]. For the earlier Sykipot activity, AlienVault cited Chinese characters in malware code and China-based command-and-control servers [S4]. Those code and C2 indicators are vendor-reported and not independently confirmed in the sources gathered.

actors.objectives: Microsoft's description of targets (defense contractors, government agencies, cryptographic technology) is consistent with intelligence collection [S1]. CrowdStrike lists intellectual property theft and intelligence gathering as the adversary's objectives [S2]. Microsoft assessed the actor's 2023 LLM use as exploratory research on sensitive topics, prominent individuals, regional politics, US influence and internal affairs [S1].

targeting.notes: Defense contractors, government agencies and cryptographic technology are from Microsoft [S1]. CrowdStrike says the adversary was most active against the US aerospace sector [S2]. In January 2012 AlienVault reported a Sykipot variant aimed at stealing DoD smart-card credentials [S4][S6], and in July 2012 PCWorld reported Sykipot email attacks including aerospace-industry targets [S5]. Linking this earlier Sykipot activity to the Salmon Typhoon cluster relies on CrowdStrike's Sykipot/Wkysol association [S2]; Microsoft itself names Wkysol [S1].

capabilities.summary: Microsoft names Win32/Wkysol as malware this actor used to maintain remote access to compromised systems [S1]. CrowdStrike associates the cluster with the Sykipot implant (aka Wkysol) [S2]. Sykipot has been used in spearphishing campaigns since about 2007 against primarily US victims, and one variant hijacks smart cards [S2]. AlienVault's January 2012 variant logged keystrokes to capture smart-card PINs and could act as the authenticated user when a card was inserted in an infected reader (a smart-card proxy attack) [S4]. In 2023 the actor used LLMs for public-domain reconnaissance on intelligence agencies, individuals, cybersecurity topics and threat actors, for finding and fixing code errors, for researching file types and methods to conceal activity in operating systems, and for translating technical papers; Microsoft says the model declined requests for apparently malicious code [S1]. OpenAI's account is similar [S3]. Microsoft saw no uniquely novel LLM-enabled techniques [S1][S3].

campaigns.name: Sykipot smart-card proxy variant (approximate start)
campaigns.summary: AlienVault reported that code in a new Sykipot variant contained a March 2011 date, suggesting use since then, and that it targeted DoD smart-card credentials by keylogging PINs (ActivClient involvement was reported by some outlets and disputed by ActivIdentity). It was reported in mid-January 2012. Attribution of Sykipot to the Salmon Typhoon cluster rests on CrowdStrike's mapping [S2][S4][S6].

campaigns.name: Sykipot email campaigns against aerospace
campaigns.summary: PCWorld reported AlienVault findings of email-based attacks distributing new Sykipot variants, some aimed at the aerospace industry, including one using the 2013 IEEE Aerospace Conference as a lure [S5].

campaigns.name: End of CrowdStrike-tracked activity window
campaigns.summary: CrowdStrike states Maverick Panda was active from at least 2007 until November 2015, mostly against the US aerospace sector. Microsoft later described intermittent dormancy and resurgence [S1][S2].

campaigns.name: Exploratory LLM use
campaigns.summary: Throughout 2023 Salmon Typhoon interacted with LLMs for reconnaissance, scripting help, concealment research and technical translation. Microsoft assessed this as exploratory [S1].

campaigns.name: Joint Microsoft and OpenAI disruption
campaigns.summary: Microsoft and OpenAI reported disabling accounts and assets associated with Salmon Typhoon, one of five state-affiliated actors named [S1][S3].

diamond.adversary: Chinese state-affiliated actor per Microsoft; China-nexus per CrowdStrike; the sponsoring organization is not named in the sources gathered [S1][S2].
diamond.capability: Win32/Wkysol (Sykipot) remote-access malware, spearphishing, a DoD smart-card proxy variant, and exploratory LLM use for reconnaissance, scripting and translation [S1][S2][S4].
diamond.infrastructure: Earlier Sykipot strains used command-and-control servers in China per AlienVault [S4]. Current infrastructure is not described in the sources gathered. Actor-held AI-service accounts were disabled in 2024 [S1][S3].
diamond.victim: US defense contractors, government agencies, cryptographic technology firms and aerospace organizations [S1][S2]; DoD smart-card users in the 2011-2012 Sykipot reporting [S4].
diamond.socioPolitical: Microsoft's wording on LLM queries (US influence, internal affairs, regional politics, intelligence agencies) indicates interest in understanding foreign intelligence and policy landscapes [S1]. No explicit PRC tasking is documented in the sources gathered.
diamond.technology: Smart-card and PKI-based authentication (CAC-style deployments) was the target of the 2011-2012 Sykipot variant [S4]. Email-borne delivery into defense and aerospace environments [S5]. Cloud AI services were used as a research aid [S1].

gaps: No Microsoft-published detail on recent (2023 onward) intrusions by Salmon Typhoon was found beyond the LLM activity and the statement of renewed activity [S1].
Specific PRC sponsor (agency or contractor) is not named in any source gathered.
Names of victims and campaign dates between 2015 and 2023 are not documented in the sources gathered; the dormancy and resurgence pattern is Microsoft's claim only [S1].

Vendor boundary issues: CrowdStrike maps Sykipot/Wkysol to Maverick Panda [S2], while Malpedia attributes the Sykipot family to Samurai Panda per a search summary [S8]. Date ranges differ (CrowdStrike 2007-2015, CFR since 2006, ETDA 2007-2018 per search summary) [S2][S7][S8].
The CrowdStrike profile and the ETDA card could not be opened by WebFetch; their content is taken from search-result summaries of the pages [S2][S8].
The primary OpenAI post could not be located in search results; OpenAI's account is known through secondary coverage [S3].
No Mandiant/Google primary APT4 report was found; Mandiant naming is known only via the ETDA card summary [S8].
MITRE ATT&CK group id is not confirmed in this research; the existing record has none.
Microsoft Digital Defense Report content on Salmon Typhoon was not verified.

implications.jipoe: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. STEP 1: Defense contractor networks, government agencies, cryptographic technology firms and aerospace organizations form the relevant environment [S1][S2]. DoD smart-card authentication infrastructure was a stated target in 2011-2012 [S4]. STEP 2: The actor shows intermittent dormancy and resurgence, so absence of reporting is not evidence of absence [S1]. STEP 3: Known elements are spearphishing delivery of Sykipot/Wkysol, a keylogger and smart-card proxy capability, and 2023 LLM-assisted research and scripting [S1][S4][S5]. STEP 4: MLCOA is continued low-visibility collection against US defense contractors and cryptography-related firms, with LLM and public-source research supporting target selection and tradecraft. MDCOA is resurgence of Sykipot-style credential and smart-card abuse against DoD-connected users to gain authenticated access. Candidate indicators: Wkysol/Sykipot detections, spearphishing using aerospace or conference lures, anomalous smart-card authentications from workstations with PIN-capture malware, and use of consumer AI services for reconnaissance [S1][S4][S5].
implications.jcc2: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. (1) Situational awareness: track Microsoft and vendor updates on Salmon Typhoon; Microsoft's public record is thin and recent activity is unspecified, so treat reporting as incomplete [S1]. (2) Authorities and coordination: contractor-hosted incidents should be coordinated with DC3 and the DIB cybersecurity program, and defensive cooperation with service providers (Microsoft and OpenAI disabled the actor's accounts in 2024) is a precedent for provider-led disruption [S1][S3]. (3) Mission assurance: smart-card and PIN-entry endpoints are sensitive terrain given the 2012 smart-card proxy variant; prioritize endpoint monitoring for keylogging on workstations used with card readers [S4]. (4) Do not merge this cluster with Salt Typhoon or Samurai Panda reporting without further evidence [S8].

identification.summary: PRC state-sponsored cyber-espionage cluster targeting the core of telecommunications networks: provider-edge and customer-edge routers, network management and authentication infrastructure. Publicly exposed from September 2024 after intrusions into multiple US telecommunications providers, with collection against lawful-intercept systems and the communications of senior US political figures. US agencies and partners describe overlapping commercial designations and state the activity continues worldwide [S1][S2][S4][S5].
identification.firstObserved: Activity under overlapping designations (GhostEmperor, FamousSparrow) publicly reported from 2021 [S9]. Cisco Talos observed persistence in one victim environment for over three years as of February 2025 [S3].
identification.notes: Microsoft name: Salt Typhoon. Microsoft maps OPERATOR PANDA, GhostEmperor and FamousSparrow to it [S8]. AA25-239A lists overlapping designations including RedMike, UNC5807 and GhostEmperor [S1]; Trend Micro tracks overlapping activity as Earth Estries. Overlap is not identity: vendors draw cluster boundaries differently.

attribution.sponsor: People's Republic of China. OFAC designated Sichuan Juxinhe Network Technology Co., Ltd. for 'direct involvement' in Salt Typhoon intrusions and described it as part of a contractor pool used by the Ministry of State Security (MSS) [S2]. AA25-239A names Sichuan Juxinhe, Beijing Huanyu Tianqiong Information Technology Co. and Sichuan Zhixin Ruijie Network Technology Co. as firms providing cyber products and services to PRC intelligence and military units [S1].
attribution.confidence: Formal US government attribution: FBI/CISA joint statement (Nov 2024) [S4], OFAC designation (Jan 2025) [S2], and a multinational joint advisory (Aug 2025) [S1]. The underlying technical attribution evidence has not been published.
attribution.basis: Incident response across US telecommunications victims, vendor forensics (Cisco Talos) [S3], sanctions findings [S2], and the joint advisory's TTP and infrastructure reporting [S1].

actors.objectives: Strategic intelligence collection through telecommunications infrastructure. Reported effects include theft of customer call-record metadata, collection of call and text content from a limited number of individuals in government and political activity, and copying of information subject to US law-enforcement requests under court order [S4]. Joint reporting describes the intent as giving PRC intelligence the ability to identify and track targets' communications and movements worldwide [S1]. Exfiltration of network configuration files supports follow-on intrusions elsewhere [S6].

sectors: Military infrastructure networks, including a US state Army National Guard network (Mar–Dec 2024)
regions: United States (FBI: at least 200 US organizations affected)
Global: organizations in more than 80 countries (FBI, Aug 2025)
targeting.notes: Sector list as reported from AA25-239A coverage [S1][S5]. National Guard compromise from a DHS I&A memo dated 11 Jun 2025, reported Jul 2025 [S6]. The Singapore telecommunications intrusions disclosed in 2025–2026 were attributed by Singapore to UNC3886, not Salt Typhoon [S10].

capabilities.summary: Credential-led access to network infrastructure: in nearly all cases Talos investigated, initial access to Cisco devices used legitimate stolen credentials, with one case of likely CVE-2018-0171 (Cisco Smart Install) exploitation [S3]. Post-access, the actor harvests further credentials from device configurations and captured SNMP, TACACS and RADIUS traffic, modifies router configurations, clears logs, and persists across multi-vendor equipment for years [S3]. Custom tooling includes JumbledPath, a Go-based ELF that runs packet capture on Cisco devices through actor-defined jump hosts [S3][S7]. Vulnerabilities cited across the broader campaign include Cisco IOS XE CVE-2023-20198/20273, Ivanti CVE-2023-46805/CVE-2024-21887 and Palo Alto CVE-2024-3400 [S1].

campaigns.name: Cisco Talos technical findings
campaigns.summary: Credential-led access, one likely CVE-2018-0171 case, JumbledPath packet capture, log clearing, persistence above three years in one environment; no new Cisco vulnerabilities found.

campaigns.name: AA25-239A multinational advisory
campaigns.summary: CISA, NSA, FBI and international partners publish router-focused TTPs and name three PRC contractor firms. FBI states at least 200 US organizations and organizations in more than 80 countries were affected.

diamond.adversary: PRC state-sponsored operators working through contractor firms (Sichuan Juxinhe, Beijing Huanyu Tianqiong, Sichuan Zhixin Ruijie) that serve MSS and PLA customers [S1][S2].
diamond.capability: Stolen valid credentials; n-day edge-device exploits (CVE-2018-0171, CVE-2023-20198/20273, CVE-2023-46805, CVE-2024-21887, CVE-2024-3400); router configuration tampering; SNMP/TACACS/RADIUS capture; JumbledPath; log clearing; Demodex rootkit in earlier overlapping activity [S1][S3][S9].
diamond.infrastructure: Compromised network devices used as relays, including pivots from one telecommunications provider's device to another's; actor-controlled jump-host chains for packet-capture tasking and exfiltration [S3].
diamond.victim: Telecommunications backbone and edge, lawful-intercept systems, government, military (state Army National Guard), transportation and lodging networks across the US and 80+ countries [S1][S4][S5][S6].
diamond.socioPolitical: Collection on US government and political leadership communications and on US lawful-intercept targeting, serving PRC intelligence requirements [S4].
diamond.technology: Exploits the trust and low monitoring of network infrastructure devices; configuration files double as intelligence and as enablers for the next intrusion [S3][S6].

gaps: Full victim list and current eviction status at US and allied carriers are not public; FBI statements describe the activity as ongoing [S5].
Technical basis for the MSS link has not been published; attribution rests on sanctions findings and joint-advisory judgments [S1][S2].

Cluster boundaries: overlap among Salt Typhoon, Earth Estries, GhostEmperor, FamousSparrow, UNC2286 and UNC5807 is asserted by different vendors on different evidence. Confirm per-designation before merging reporting.
Your imported record cited the Mandiant UNC4841 (Barracuda ESG) blog as a Salt Typhoon reference. UNC4841 is a separate cluster; that reference was dropped from this profile.
Your salt_typhoon_research_brief lists 'Singapore — all four national telecommunications providers' under Salt Typhoon. Singapore attributed that campaign to UNC3886 [S10]. Correct the brief.
AA25-239A primary text could not be fetched from this environment (cisa.gov blocked). The alias list (UNC5807) and CVE list should be checked against the PDF.
Possible relationship between Salt Typhoon's configuration-file theft and Volt Typhoon's pre-positioning is not established in public reporting.

implications.jipoe: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. STEP 1: Treat commercial telecommunications backbone, including leased circuits carrying DoD traffic, as part of the cyberspace OE and as assumed-compromised terrain. STEP 2: Communications terrain is not neutral. Adversary collection may be reading metadata and selected content on unencrypted commercial paths, which affects OPSEC, deception and force-protection estimates. STEP 3: The doctrinal template is valid credentials, then router configuration changes, then credential capture from AAA protocols, then packet capture and config exfiltration, with multi-year dwell. STEP 4: MLCOA is continued quiet collection on government and military communications and on lawful-intercept targeting. MDCOA is using collected configurations and credentials to support disruption or to enable another PRC cluster's pre-positioning during a crisis. Candidate indicators: unexpected ACL or loopback changes, new GRE/IPsec tunnels, Guest Shell activation, non-standard SSH ports, and AAA traffic anomalies [S1][S3].
implications.jcc2: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. (1) Assume degraded confidentiality on commercial paths in C2 planning; prioritize end-to-end encryption and authenticated identity for operational traffic. (2) Network-device telemetry such as config diffs, AAA logs and NetFlow is the primary detection layer. JCC2 data integration should ingest it from DODIN and, by agreement, from carrier partners. (3) Authorities: carriers are private critical infrastructure. Response leads are CISA, the FBI and the FCC, with DoD supporting through DISA and service providers. Command relationships should not assume DoD access to carrier networks. (4) Counterintelligence integration: compromise of lawful-intercept systems is a CI equity, so fuse CI reporting into the threat picture used by Cyber Protection Team (CPT) and Mission Defense Team (MDT) planners.

provenance.importedSummary: GhostEmperor is a Chinese-speaking threat actor that targets government entities and telecom companies in Southeast Asia. They employ a Windows kernel-mode rootkit called Demodex to gain remote control over their targeted servers. The actor demonstrates a high level of sophistication and uses various anti-forensic and anti-analysis techniques to evade detection. They have been active for a significant period of time and continue to pose a threat to their targets.

identification.summary: First disclosed in 2023, the Sandman APT is likely associated with suspected China-based threat clusters known for using the KEYPLUG backdoor, specifically STORM-0866/Red Dev 40. Sandman is tracked as a distinct cluster, pending additional conclusive information. A notable characteristic is its use of the LuaDream backdoor. LuaDream is based on the Lua platform, a relatively rare occurrence in the cyberespionage domain, historically associated with APTs considered Western or Western-aligned.

Sangria Tempest (formerly ELBRUS) is Microsoft's name for a financially motivated cybercriminal group also tracked as Carbon Spider and FIN7 [S1]. Microsoft says it conducts intrusions that often end in data theft followed by extortion or ransomware deployment such as Clop [S1]. US prosecutors charged three alleged senior FIN7 members in 2018 with attacks on more than 100 US companies and theft of more than 15 million card records [S3]. The group has persisted after those arrests, advertising an EDR-evasion tool to other criminals in 2024 and running a 4,000-plus domain phishing and malvertising network [S7][S8].
identification.firstObserved: Microsoft: the actor has used the Carbanak backdoor since 2014 [S1].
identification.notes: Microsoft name: Sangria Tempest (formerly ELBRUS); Microsoft equates it with Carbon Spider and FIN7 [S1]. MITRE ATT&CK tracks Carbanak (G0008) and FIN7 (G0046) as separate groups, while Microsoft treats Carbanak as a tool of Sangria Tempest [S1]. The 2014-2018 'Carbanak' bank-heist reporting (Kaspersky, Europol) concerns a cluster that may not be identical to FIN7; keep the two lines of reporting distinct [S5]. Microsoft tracks Lace Tempest (FIN11) separately and reports collaboration between the two [S1][S2].

attribution.sponsor: No state sponsor is claimed in the cited sources; Microsoft describes Sangria Tempest as a financially motivated cybercriminal group [S1]. The three members charged by DOJ in 2018 were Ukrainian nationals [S3]. KrebsOnSecurity describes the group as 'Russia's Fin7' [S8].
attribution.confidence: Microsoft names Sangria Tempest as the actor behind the 2023 Clop deployments and the late-2023 App Installer abuse [S1][S2]. US federal charges and convictions cover individual FIN7 members (not a state), including a 10-year sentence for Fedir Hladyr and a 7-year sentence for Andrii Kolpakov in 2021 [S3][S4].
attribution.basis: Microsoft Threat Intelligence telemetry [S1][S2]; DOJ indictment as reported by CyberScoop [S3] and sentencing as reported by The Hacker News [S4]; vendor research from Gemini Advisory, SentinelOne, Silent Push and PRODAFT as reported or published [S6][S7][S8][S9].

actors.objectives: Financial gain: theft of payment card data from US companies [S3], and in later years data theft followed by extortion or ransomware deployment [S1][S2]. The group also earns money by selling tooling, such as the AvNeutralizer EDR-evasion tool, to other ransomware operators [S7].

sectors: Enterprises reached through search-ad lures for fake software downloads (sector-agnostic) [S1]
Users of impersonated brands such as Microsoft 365, Zoom, Bloomberg, Reuters, Dropbox and Google [S8]
regions: United States (more than 100 companies, per DOJ) [S3]
targeting.notes: Early FIN7 targeting centered on US point-of-sale environments [S3]. Microsoft's 2023 reporting names no particular industries or regions [S1]. Later activity is opportunistic and driven by malvertising and impersonation of widely used brands [S1][S8]. Europol-reported Carbanak bank heists (over 100 banks in 40 countries) belong to the related Carbanak line of reporting [S5].

capabilities.summary: Long-running custom tooling: the Carbanak backdoor (in use since 2014), the obfuscated PowerShell loader POWERTRASH, and the Lizar post-exploitation kit [S1][S2]. In April 2023 Microsoft saw POWERTRASH load Lizar, followed by OpenSSH and Impacket for lateral movement and deployment of Clop ransomware [S2]. In late 2023 the actor used Google ads and malicious MSIX packages delivered through ms-appinstaller. One chain used Storm-1113's EugenLoader to drop Carbanak and Gracewire; another used POWERTRASH to load NetSupport and Gracewire [S1]. SentinelOne reports that FIN7 developed AvNeutralizer, an EDR-tampering tool sold on criminal forums with Black Basta among the first customers; a newer version abuses the Windows ProcLaunchMon.sys driver [S7]. Silent Push mapped more than 4,000 FIN7 domains and IPs used for typosquatting, malicious ads, fake browser extensions and spearphishing, with domains aged before use [S8]. In 2025 PRODAFT reported the Python-based Anubis backdoor, delivered from compromised SharePoint sites [S9]. The group has used front companies (Combi Security, Bastion Secure) to recruit IT workers who did not know they were doing intrusion work [S3][S6].

diamond.adversary: A financially motivated criminal group (Microsoft: Sangria Tempest, formerly ELBRUS; aka FIN7, Carbon Spider) [S1]. Charged members are Ukrainian nationals [S3]. The group runs a structured organization with supervisors, system administrators and front companies [S3][S4][S6].
diamond.capability: Carbanak, POWERTRASH, Lizar, Gracewire, NetSupport, AvNeutralizer, Anubis; Clop ransomware deployment; OpenSSH and Impacket for lateral movement [S1][S2][S7][S9].
diamond.infrastructure: Google search ads, more than 4,000 typosquatting and impersonation domains (some hosted at Stark Industries Solutions), compromised SharePoint sites used for payload hosting, and Storm-1113 installer and landing-page services [S1][S8][S9].
diamond.victim: US restaurant, gaming and hospitality companies (card theft) [S3]; organizations hit by data-theft extortion and Clop ransomware [S1][S2]; users searching for popular software and brands [S1][S8].
diamond.socioPolitical: Profit-driven cybercrime that cooperates with ransomware ecosystems: collaboration with Lace Tempest and sales of tooling to Black Basta and other ransomware groups [S1][S2][S7].
diamond.technology: Windows endpoints; the App Installer/MSIX protocol handler that bypassed SmartScreen; EDR products targeted for tampering; vulnerable PaperCut servers in Lace Tempest-linked activity [S1][S2][S7].

gaps: MITRE separates Carbanak (G0008) from FIN7 (G0046), while Microsoft folds both under Sangria Tempest; how much the 2014-2018 bank-heist cluster and the FIN7 card-theft and ransomware cluster overlap is unresolved in cited sources.
Primary DOJ press releases (2018 indictment, 2021 sentencings) and the Europol release could not be opened; facts here come from CyberScoop, The Hacker News and Dark Reading coverage.
The Gemini Advisory, Silent Push and PRODAFT primary reports were not read directly; secondary coverage was used.
No cited source makes any claim about Russian state sponsorship, tasking or tolerance; KrebsOnSecurity's 'Russia's Fin7' description is not a government attribution.
Microsoft's 2023 reporting names no specific victims, sectors or regions for the App Installer campaign.
The imported aliases JokerStash, Coreid, Calcium, ITG14, ATK32 and GOLD NIAGARA were not confirmed by any source cited here.
The extent of FIN7 activity after the 2025 Anubis reporting is unknown from gathered sources.

implications.jipoe: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. STEP 1 (operational environment): The relevant cyberspace includes user endpoints reached through search ads and lookalike domains, the software-installation path (App Installer/MSIX), EDR sensors, and collaboration platforms (SharePoint) used to host payloads [S1][S8][S9]. STEP 2 (effects): Malvertising and brand impersonation turn routine software downloads and brand trust into initial access, and EDR tampering degrades defensive visibility [S1][S7][S8]. STEP 3 (threat model): Template chain of malicious ad or phishing, then MSIX or loader (EugenLoader/POWERTRASH), then Carbanak, Lizar or NetSupport, then lateral movement with OpenSSH or Impacket, then data theft and Clop ransomware [S1][S2]. STEP 4: MLCOA is opportunistic access to an installation that supports defense contractors or base services through fake-software downloads, followed by data-theft extortion. MDCOA is ransomware deployment after EDR neutralization, or access handed to partner groups (Lace Tempest, Black Basta), disrupting mission-support IT [S1][S2][S7]. Candidate indicators: Defender alerts naming POWERTRASH, Carbanak or Sangria Tempest; MSIX installs launched from browser downloads; NetSupport on systems with no admin need; ProcLaunchMon.sys loading; newly registered domains impersonating Microsoft 365, Zoom or Reuters [S1][S7][S8].
implications.jcc2: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. Situational awareness: track Microsoft, SentinelOne and Silent Push reporting on Sangria Tempest tooling, and correlate it with DODIN endpoint telemetry for MSIX, POWERTRASH and EDR tamper events [S1][S7][S8]. Authorities: this is a criminal actor pursued by DOJ and Europol [S3][S5], so response coordination runs through law-enforcement and DC3 and CISA channels rather than an adversary-state framework; do not imply state attribution. Mission assurance: enforce Microsoft's ms-appinstaller handler disablement, restrict sideloading, protect EDR integrity, and keep offline backups against Clop-style extortion [S1][S2][S7]. Coordination: share brand-impersonation domain indicators with defense industrial base partners and ad platforms, and coordinate with service providers on takedown of hosting such as Stark Industries Solutions [S8].

identification.summary: Microsoft describes Sapphire Sleet as a North Korean state actor focused on the finance sector, especially cryptocurrency, venture capital and blockchain organizations, whose main motive is stealing cryptocurrency wallets to generate revenue [S2][S3][S4]. Its signature tradecraft is social engineering. Operators pose as venture capitalists or recruiters, set up fake Zoom or Teams meetings or skills assessments, and then get the victim to run a script that installs malware [S1][S3]. In 2026 Microsoft also attributed two npm software supply-chain compromises to it: Axios (March 2026) and Mastra (June 2026) [S2][S4].
identification.firstObserved: Microsoft: cryptocurrency theft and computer network exploitation since at least 2020 [S1]; 'active since at least March 2020' [S2][S3][S4]. Mandiant tracks the overlapping UNC1069 cluster as active since at least 2018 [S7][S8].
identification.notes: Microsoft name: Sapphire Sleet (legacy element name COPERNICIUM per Microsoft's mapping) [S5]. Microsoft says the actor is also tracked as UNC1069, STARDUST CHOLLIMA, Alluring Pisces, BlueNoroff, CageyChameleon and CryptoCore [S4][S5]. This record is linked to MITRE G0082 (APT38), but the Microsoft sources gathered here do not list APT38, BeagleBoyz or NICKEL GLADSTONE as Sapphire Sleet names. Keep the APT38 bank-heist history (2016 Bangladesh Bank and similar) separate from Sapphire Sleet's documented 2020+ cryptocurrency activity [S4][S6].

attribution.sponsor: Democratic People's Republic of Korea (North Korea). Microsoft calls Sapphire Sleet a North Korean state actor [S2][S4]. MITRE attributes the linked APT38 group to the Reconnaissance General Bureau [S6], but no source gathered here ties Sapphire Sleet itself to a specific DPRK organization.
attribution.confidence: Microsoft assessed with high confidence that the June 2026 Mastra npm compromise is attributable to Sapphire Sleet [S4]. Microsoft attributed the infrastructure and Axios compromise to Sapphire Sleet without stating a confidence level [S2]. Google Threat Intelligence Group separately attributed the Axios compromise to UNC1069 [S8]. All of these are vendor assessments; no government attribution of Sapphire Sleet by name was found.
attribution.basis: Microsoft telemetry and incident analysis, including C2 hosting at Hostwinds, a VPS provider Microsoft says Sapphire Sleet commonly uses [S2][S3][S4]. GTIG cited reuse of the WAVESHAPER.V2 backdoor and infrastructure overlaps with known UNC1069 activity, as reported by Security Affairs [S8]. Kaspersky's attribution of the GhostCall/GhostHire campaigns is to BlueNoroff [S9][S10].

actors.objectives: Revenue generation for the DPRK through cryptocurrency theft. Microsoft says the actor's primary motivation is stealing cryptocurrency wallets [S2][S3][S4] and estimated that more than US$10 million in cryptocurrency was stolen from multiple companies over a six-month period [S1]. Access to credentials, keychains and developer environments supports follow-on theft [S3][S4].

sectors: Web3 firms and centralized exchanges (overlapping UNC1069/BlueNoroff reporting) [S7][S9]
Software developers and open-source maintainers; npm consumers and CI/CD pipelines [S2][S4][S9]
Job seekers approached through fake recruiting [S1][S3]
regions: Global; Microsoft gives no regional restriction [S1][S2]
India, Turkey, Australia, and parts of Europe and Asia (Kaspersky, BlueNoroff GhostCall/GhostHire since April 2025) [S9]
targeting.notes: Targeting is individual-centric. Executives, investors and developers are approached through LinkedIn and Telegram [S1][S3][S7][S9]. The 2026 npm compromises extended exposure to any developer workstation or CI/CD pipeline that installed the poisoned versions, even if the package was never imported in code [S4]. Kaspersky's regional data comes from its BlueNoroff cluster and may not match Microsoft's Sapphire Sleet boundaries [S9].

capabilities.summary: Social engineering is the core capability. Lures include fake venture-capital investment meetings, where a staged connection error prompts the victim to run a .scpt (macOS) or .vbs (Windows) 'fix', and fake recruiter skills assessments hosted on actor-controlled sites [S1]. In an April 2026 macOS intrusion, a 'Zoom SDK Update.scpt' padded with thousands of blank lines launched a curl-to-osascript chain. The chain deployed backdoors (e.g., 'services', 'com.google.chromes.updaters'), a fake password prompt whose capture was exfiltrated via the Telegram Bot API, and theft of browser data, keychain, crypto wallets (Ledger Live, Exodus), Telegram sessions, SSH keys and Apple Notes. It also modified the TCC database and persisted via LaunchDaemons and LaunchAgents [S3]. A June 2026 Teams-themed variant used 'MSTeams SDK Update.scpt' [S3]. Supply-chain capability: in the Axios compromise (axios 1.14.1/0.30.4), a fake dependency, plain-crypto-js@4.2.1, used an install hook to deliver OS-specific payloads for macOS, Windows and Linux [S2]. GTIG identified that payload as the WAVESHAPER.V2 backdoor [S8]. In the Mastra compromise, a takeover of a maintainer account pushed 140+ packages that depended on the typosquat easy-day-js. Its postinstall hook disabled TLS verification and staged a Node.js implant, followed by reflective .NET injection, a PowerShell backdoor, a Defender exclusion and a SYSTEM service [S4]. Mandiant reporting on overlapping UNC1069 describes ClickFix lures, AI-generated video in fake meetings and new families SILENCELIFT, DEEPBREATH and CHROMEPUSH [S7].
