identification.summary: China-based cyber-espionage actor that Microsoft tracks as Swirl Typhoon and maps to TELLURIUM, STALKER PANDA, Tick, Bronze Butler and REDBALDKNIGHT [S1]. Unit 42 describes Tick as primarily targeting organizations in Japan and the Republic of Korea [S8]. Recent reporting covers a 2021-2022 supply-chain compromise of an East Asian data-loss-prevention (DLP) vendor [S5] and mid-2025 zero-day exploitation of Motex LANSCOPE Endpoint Manager (CVE-2025-61932) [S3][S4].
identification.firstObserved: Trend Micro says it has tracked the group since 2008 [S9].
identification.notes: Microsoft name: Swirl Typhoon; Microsoft's mapping lists TELLURIUM, STALKER PANDA, Tick, Bronze Butler and REDBALDKNIGHT as other names [S1]. Stalker Taurus (Unit 42) appears in this record's imported aliases but was not confirmed in sources gathered here. MITRE tracks the group as BRONZE BUTLER (G0060) [S12]. 'PLA Unit 61419' is a Japanese government attribution of sponsorship, not a vendor cluster name [S10][S11].

attribution.sponsor: People's Republic of China. In April 2021, Japan's Chief Cabinet Secretary Katsunobu Kato said one of the suspected attackers worked for People's Liberation Army Unit 61419, which is sometimes called Tick [S10]. The National Police Agency's Mitsuhiro Matsumoto said it was highly likely that PLA Unit 61419, a strategic support unit operating from Qingdao, Shandong, was involved [S11].
attribution.confidence: Japanese government officials named PLA Unit 61419 as highly likely involved [S10][S11]. Recorded Future's Insikt Group told The Record the unit-level attribution was most likely based on older Chinese military intelligence collected before recent PLA reforms [S11]. ESET attributed the DLP-vendor compromise to Tick with high confidence [S5]. China rejected the Japanese allegations [S11].
attribution.basis: Japanese police investigation of the 2016 JAXA intrusions, including a case filed against a Chinese national who allegedly rented servers used in the attacks while living in Japan [S10]; vendor malware and infrastructure analysis by Sophos, Unit 42, Trend Micro and ESET [S3][S5][S8][S9].

actors.objectives: Long-term espionage. Trend Micro reported attempts to steal military-related documents from defense firms [S9]. ESET judged cyberespionage the most likely aim of the DLP-vendor compromise, whose customers include government and military bodies [S5]. Sophos said the 2025 LANSCOPE targeting appeared limited to sectors aligned with the group's intelligence objectives [S3][S4].

sectors: Defense, aerospace, chemical and satellite firms [S9]
Government and military customers of a DLP software vendor (supply chain) [S5]
Air-gapped critical systems via South Korean secure USB drives [S8]
regions: East Asia (DLP vendor and its customers) [S5]
Japanese firms with subsidiaries in China [S9]
targeting.notes: Japanese investigators linked the campaign to roughly 200 Japanese companies and research bodies, but JAXA was the only victim publicly named [S10][S11]. Imported actor summary also lists Taiwan, Hong Kong and the United States; no source gathered here confirmed those regions.

capabilities.summary: Zero-day exploitation, including a 2016 zero-day in the Japanese asset-management product SKYSEA Client View [S3] and mid-2025 zero-day exploitation of LANSCOPE Endpoint Manager CVE-2025-61932, which lets unauthenticated attackers run code with SYSTEM privileges [S3][S4][S13]. Supply-chain operations: compromise of a DLP vendor's internal update servers and trojanized third-party tool installers (Q-Dir) passed to customers [S5]. Weaponized secure USB drives aimed at air-gapped systems [S8]. Use of hijacked legitimate email accounts and credentials to deliver malware [S9]. Custom malware families include Daserf [S12], Minzen, Datper, Nioupale and HomamDownloader [S8], ShadowPy, Netboy and Ghostdown [S5], and the Gokcpdoor proxy backdoor, with the Havoc C2 framework used in some 2025 intrusions [S4].

diamond.adversary: China-based operators; Japan's government names PLA Unit 61419 as highly likely involved [S10][S11].
diamond.capability: Zero-day exploitation of Japanese endpoint and asset-management software, supply-chain trojanizing, weaponized USB drives, and custom backdoors such as Datper, ShadowPy, Netboy and Gokcpdoor [S3][S4][S5][S8].
diamond.infrastructure: A compromised vendor's update servers [S5]; servers rented by a suspect while in Japan (per Japanese police) [S10]; hijacked legitimate email accounts [S9]; Gokcpdoor proxy C2 and Havoc C2 [S4].
diamond.victim: Japanese defense, aerospace, chemical and satellite firms; JAXA; South Korean organizations; government and military customers of an East Asian DLP vendor [S5][S8][S9][S10].
diamond.socioPolitical: PRC intelligence collection on its regional rival Japan and on Korean defense, including military-related documents and space-agency data [S9][S10].
diamond.technology: Trust in locally popular Japanese endpoint-management software (LANSCOPE, SKYSEA), vendor update channels, remote support tools and certified secure USB media [S3][S5][S8].

gaps: Primary vendor reports could not be opened (Sophos, ESET, Unit 42, The Register, The Record and The Hacker News were unreachable from this environment); claims rely on search-result summaries of those pages.
Exact publication dates for the Sophos LANSCOPE blog, BleepingComputer article, The Record article and the Unit 42 USB report were not confirmed in search results; month-level dates are given.
No Microsoft Threat Intelligence report naming Swirl Typhoon activity was found; Microsoft's mapping is the only Microsoft source.
The PLA Unit 61419 attribution comes from Japanese officials; Recorded Future questions whether it reflects the post-reform PLA structure. No US government attribution was located.
Initial access for the DLP-vendor compromise is unknown, per ESET coverage.
The number of compromised secure USB drives is unknown, per Unit 42.
Imported summary mentions ties to China's National University of Defense Technology and targeting of Taiwan, Hong Kong and the US; not verified in sources gathered.
ShadowPad appears in MITRE's software list for G0060 and AhnLab has linked Tick to 'Operation Triple Tiang' (Korea); neither was reviewed here.

implications.jipoe: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. STEP 1: Key terrain includes region-specific endpoint and asset-management servers (LANSCOPE, SKYSEA), software vendors' update and remote-support channels, and removable-media workflows into air-gapped networks at Japanese and Korean defense partners [S3][S5][S8]. STEP 2: Zero-day exploitation of on-premises management software and supply-chain trojanizing shrink warning time; air-gap assumptions do not hold where certified USB media is trusted [S3][S5][S8]. STEP 3: Doctrinal template: access through an exploited management agent, a trojanized installer, a spearphish from a hijacked partner mailbox; then a downloader and a custom backdoor (Gokcpdoor, Netboy, Datper), followed by collection of military-related documents [S4][S5][S9]. STEP 4: MLCOA: continued espionage against Japanese defense-industrial and government-adjacent organizations through zero-days in locally popular enterprise software. MDCOA: compromise of a security or management vendor serving the Japan Self-Defense Forces or US forces in Japan, used to push malware across many enclaves at once, including air-gapped systems. Candidate indicators: inbound traffic to LANSCOPE agent ports from untrusted hosts; Gokcpdoor listeners (Sophos noted ports 38000 and 38002); unexpected Q-Dir or utility installers delivered through vendor support sessions; Havoc C2 beacons [S3][S4][S5].
implications.jcc2: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. (1) Situational awareness: track Japanese- and Korean-specific software in partner and host-nation networks, since this actor exploits products US vulnerability feeds may cover late; CISA KEV listed CVE-2025-61932 only after Motex's October 2025 fix [S3][S13]. (2) Authorities: activity mainly affects allied and host-nation systems, so response relies on coordination with Japanese authorities (NPA, JPCERT/CC) rather than unilateral US action [S10]. (3) Mission assurance: treat removable media and vendor update/remote-support paths into mission and air-gapped systems as attack surface [S5][S8]. (4) Coordination: share indicators with DIB partners that have Japanese subsidiaries or suppliers, since Trend Micro saw targeting of Japanese firms with subsidiaries in China and of defense suppliers [S9].

provenance.importedSummary: Tick is a cyber espionage group with likely Chinese origins that has been active since at least 2008. The group appears to have close ties to the Chinese National University of Defense and Technology, which is possibly linked to the PLA. This threat actor targets organizations in the critical infrastructure, heavy industry, manufacturing, and international relations sectors for espionage purposes. The attacks appear to be centered on political, media, and engineering sectors. STALKER PANDA has been observed conducting targeted attacks against Japan, Taiwan, Hong Kong, and the United States.

identification.summary: TA406 is engaging in malware distribution, phishing, intelligence collection, and cryptocurrency theft, resulting in a wide range of criminal activities.

Proofpoint researchers have identified a targeted APT campaign that utilized malicious RTF documents to deliver custom malware to unsuspecting victims. We dubbed this campaign “Operation LagTime IT” based on entities that were targeted and the distinctive domains registered to C&C IP infrastructure. Beginning in early 2019, these threat actors targeted a number of government agencies in East Asia overseeing government information technology, domestic affairs, foreign affairs, economic development, and political processes. We determined that the infection vector observed in this campaign was spear phishing, with emails originating from both free email accounts and compromised user accounts. Attackers relied on Microsoft Equation Editor exploit CVE-2018-0798 to deliver a custom malware that Proofpoint researchers have dubbed Cotx RAT. Additionally, this APT group utilizes Poison Ivy payloads that share overlapping command and control (C&C) infrastructure with the newly identified Cotx campaigns. Based on infrastructure overlaps, post-exploitation techniques, and historic TTPs utilized in this operation, Proofpoint analysts attribute this activity to the Chinese APT group tracked internally as TA428. Researchers believe that this activity has an operational and tactical resemblance to the Maudi Surveillance Operation which was previously reported in 2013.

TA444 is a North Korea state-sponsored threat actor that primarily focuses on financially motivated operations. They have been active since at least 2017 and have recently shifted their attention to targeting cryptocurrencies. TA444 employs various infection methods and has a diverse range of malware and backdoors at their disposal. They have been attributed to stealing hundreds of millions of dollars' worth of cryptocurrency and related assets.

TA455 is an Iranian APT group targeting the aerospace industry through a campaign known as the “Iranian Dream Job Campaign,” utilizing deceptive job offers to lure victims. They employ spearphishing tactics with malicious ZIP files containing the executable “secur32[.]dll” and disguise their C2 communications within the traffic of reputable services like Cloudflare and GitHub. The group intentionally mimics the TTPs of the North Korean Lazarus group to mislead investigators and complicate attribution. Their multi-stage infection strategy enhances the likelihood of success while evading detection.

relatedRecords.note: MITRE's NIMBUS MANTICORE (G1059) lists Proofpoint's TA455 alongside UNC1549, which Microsoft maps to Smoke Sandstorm. Kept as separate records pending vendor-level confirmation.

identification.summary: TA459 is Proofpoint's name for a threat actor it believes operates out of China and that typically targets Central Asian countries, Russia, Belarus, Mongolia and others [S1][S2]. Proofpoint documented it using PlugX, NetTraveler and ZeroT through spear-phishing [S1][S3][S4].
identification.firstObserved: Proofpoint first-reported campaign began in July 2015 (possibly earlier) against telecom and military targets in Russia [S2]. A search summary of third-party reporting says activity dates to at least 2013, which this research did not verify against a primary source [S6].
identification.notes: Vendor name TA459 (Proofpoint); MITRE group G0062 [S5]. No Microsoft name mapping is recorded in the actor record. Some copies of Proofpoint text contain the typo 'TA549' for TA459 [S1]. NetTraveler malware is also tracked by Kaspersky under other actor naming; not merged here.

attribution.confidence: Proofpoint says it believes the actor operates out of China [S1][S2]. In the NetTraveler coverage, Proofpoint's Patrick Wheeler said the group was Chinese but there was 'no indication that it is state-sponsored' [S7].
attribution.basis: Proofpoint campaign analysis of lures, infrastructure and malware reuse across 2015-2017 [S1][S2][S3]. No government attribution was found in the sources gathered.

actors.objectives: Espionage-style collection against telecom, military, defense and weapons-manufacturing targets in Russia and neighbours, pro-democracy and human-rights groups, and financial analysts covering telecoms [S2][S3][S4]. Specific end-user intent is not stated by sources beyond targeting patterns.

targeting.notes: Sectors and regions from Proofpoint reporting and press coverage of it [S1][S2][S3][S4]. Financial analysts in 2015 were described as collateral to telecom targeting and in 2017 as a primary lure theme [S1][S2].

capabilities.summary: Spear-phishing with RAR self-extracting archives on lookalike domains imitating Russian military and defense sites, delivering PlugX in 2015 [S2]. In 2016, links to RAR-packed executables and Word attachments exploiting CVE-2012-0158 delivered NetTraveler [S3][S4]. In 2017, Word documents exploiting CVE-2017-0199 dropped ZeroT, which downloaded PlugX [S1]. Other malware attributed in secondary coverage: Saker, Netbot, DarkStRat and a Gh0st RAT variant [S6]. MITRE lists PlugX, gh0st RAT, NetTraveler and ZeroT for the group [S5].

identification.summary: TA4922 is a Chinese-speaking cybercrime cluster that employs localized HR, payroll, tax, and invoice lures to deliver various malware families, including Atlas RAT, RomulusLoader, and SilentRunLoader. The actor conducts targeted email campaigns, often impersonating trusted authorities, to facilitate credential phishing and fraud. TA4922's operational tempo is high, with a focus on obtaining remote access for financial gain, and it has shown a rapid evolution in its malware arsenal. The group is also noted for using social engineering to shift communications from email to messaging platforms, enhancing their phishing efforts.
TA530, who we previously examined in relation to large-scale personalized phishing campaigns
One of the most active Qbot malware affiliates, Proofpoint has tracked the large cybercrime threat actor TA570 since 2018.

TA577 is a financially motivated cybercrime actor that Proofpoint has tracked since mid-2020. It conducts broad email campaigns and has delivered Qbot, IcedID, SystemBC, SmokeLoader, Ursnif and Cobalt Strike [S3]. MITRE describes it as an initial access broker that distributed QakBot and Pikabot and was among the first groups distributing Latrodectus [S11]. It was one of the major Qbot affiliates before the Qbot disruption announced in August 2023 [S1][S2].
identification.firstObserved: Proofpoint: tracked since mid-2020 [S3].
identification.notes: Hive0118 is the IBM X-Force name carried in the existing record [S11 lists no vendor mapping; the name comes from the imported record]. A search summary of Trend Micro reporting describes Water Curupira, tied to Pikabot spam and Black Basta, as an overlapping cluster; cluster boundaries are not confirmed here [S4][S5]. TA578 (Latrodectus, contact-form lures) and TA570 (Qbot affiliate) are separate Proofpoint clusters and must not be merged with TA577 [S6][S7][S3].

attribution.confidence: No confidence statement or state sponsor is supported by the sources gathered; the encyclopedia record lists country RU from import data, unverified here.
attribution.basis: Proofpoint campaign telemetry and incident linkage [S1][S3]. Black Basta association is reported by secondary sources and a Kudelski analysis of leaked Black Basta chats, which rates TA577 links as moderate confidence [S8][S5].

actors.objectives: Financial gain: mass-distribution of loaders that provide initial access to ransomware operators [S3][S11]. In February 2024 Proofpoint assessed the goal of one campaign as capturing NTLMv2 challenge/response pairs for password cracking or pass-the-hash [S1].

targeting.notes: Proofpoint describes broad targeting across industries and geographies, with the February 2024 campaigns reaching hundreds of organizations globally in tens of thousands of messages [S1][S3]. No specific sector or country focus is stated in the sources gathered.

capabilities.summary: Primary delivery is email, notably thread hijacking where messages appear as replies to existing conversations, carrying ZIP or IMG attachments or malicious links [S4][S1]. Payload history: Qbot, IcedID, SystemBC, SmokeLoader, Ursnif and Cobalt Strike (2020-2021) [S3]; after the Qbot disruption, DarkGate in September 2023 and then Pikabot as its preferred payload [S2][S5]; Latrodectus in at least three November 2023 campaigns before reverting to Pikabot [S6][S7]. In February 2024, zipped HTML attachments forced an SMB connection to harvest NTLM hashes, with Impacket artifacts found on the SMB servers [S1][S2]. Pikabot reportedly halts if the system language is Russian or Ukrainian [S5].

campaigns.name: Pikabot spam campaigns (Water Curupira)
campaigns.summary: Trend Micro reports Pikabot spam by the cluster it tracks as Water Curupira in Q1 2023, followed by a pause from late June to early September 2023. Overlap with TA577 is not confirmed in the sources gathered.

campaigns.name: Return after Qbot disruption: DarkGate and Pikabot
campaigns.summary: After the Qbot disruption announced in August 2023, Proofpoint says TA577 was inactive slightly longer than its usual summer break, returned at the end of September with DarkGate and Pikabot campaigns, then settled on Pikabot.

campaigns.name: Latrodectus campaigns
campaigns.summary: TA577 used Latrodectus in at least three campaigns in November 2023 before reverting to Pikabot; from mid-January 2024 Latrodectus was used almost exclusively by TA578.

campaigns.name: NTLM hash theft via thread-hijacked HTML attachments
campaigns.summary: Campaigns on 26 and 27 February 2024 sent tens of thousands of messages to hundreds of organizations with zipped HTML files that triggered an SMB connection to capture NTLMv2 hashes. No malware delivery was observed from these URLs. Proofpoint recommends blocking outbound SMB and notes Outlook clients patched since July 2023 resist the direct file-URI variant.

diamond.adversary: Financially motivated cybercrime actor and initial access broker tracked by Proofpoint as TA577 since mid-2020; no individuals identified in the sources gathered [S3][S11].
diamond.capability: Thread-hijacked phishing with ZIP, IMG or HTML attachments and links; rotating loaders (Qbot, IcedID, DarkGate, Pikabot, Latrodectus); Cobalt Strike; NTLM hash capture via SMB; Impacket on attacker servers [S1][S3][S2][S4].
diamond.infrastructure: Attacker-run SMB servers for hash capture in February 2024 [S1]; payload and C2 infrastructure not enumerated in the sources gathered.
diamond.victim: Broad, opportunistic organizational targets across industries and geographies; hundreds of organizations in the February 2024 waves [S1][S3].
diamond.socioPolitical: Criminal ecosystem: loader operators supply access to ransomware affiliates; reported Black Basta links come from secondary reporting [S8].
diamond.technology: Windows endpoints with Outlook/email clients and SMB egress allowed; credential material exposed through NTLM authentication to external hosts [S1].

gaps: No 2025 or 2026 TA577 campaign reporting was found in the searches run; current status and tooling are unknown.

implications.jipoe: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. STEP 1: Email gateways, user mailboxes and outbound SMB (TCP 445) paths are the relevant terrain; the actor targets broad commercial and government-adjacent email populations without a stated sector focus [S1][S3]. STEP 2: The actor frequently rotates loaders and pauses (summer 2023), so malware-family signatures alone age quickly [S2][S4]. STEP 3: Template is thread-hijacked email, ZIP/IMG/HTML attachment or link, loader (Pikabot, Latrodectus and predecessors), Cobalt Strike, then handoff to ransomware operators [S3][S4][S6]. STEP 4: MLCOA is continued high-volume loader campaigns feeding criminal ransomware access, possibly including NTLM-capture waves [S1]. MDCOA is use of captured NTLM hashes for pass-the-hash against contractor or DoD-adjacent networks that permit outbound SMB, leading to ransomware on mission systems [S1]. Candidate indicators: inbound replies to existing threads with zipped HTML attachments, outbound SMB to external IPs, Impacket-style authentication, new loader beacons.
implications.jcc2: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. (1) Situational awareness: track vendor reporting for loader changes and feed outbound-SMB and thread-hijack indicators to network defenders. (2) Authorities: blocking outbound SMB at boundary devices and Outlook patching are configuration actions that need the owning network authority's approval; coordinate through the DODIN operating chain. (3) Mission assurance: criminal ransomware access can degrade mission systems on unclassified networks, so prioritize segmentation and backup of mission-critical enclaves. (4) Coordination: share indicators with DC3 and the DIB community; treat attribution to a named criminal cluster as vendor-assessed, not government-confirmed [S1][S3].

provenance.importedSummary: TA577 is a prolific cybercrime threat actor tracked by Proofpoint since mid-2020. This actor conducts broad targeting across various industries and geographies, and Proofpoint has observed TA577 deliver payloads including Qbot, IcedID, SystemBC, SmokeLoader, Ursnif, and Cobalt Strike.

identification.summary: TA829 is a Russia-aligned threat actor that employs the RomCom RAT for intelligence-gathering and financially motivated cyberattacks, exploiting zero-day vulnerabilities in Mozilla Firefox and Microsoft Windows. The group utilizes REM Proxy services hosted on compromised MikroTik routers to relay traffic and disguise its origin. In their operations, victims targeted by TA829 receive a strain known as SlipScreen, while their infrastructure and tactics show significant similarities to those of UNK_GreenSec. TA829's hybrid approach combines espionage with financial fraud, making it a notable player in the cyber threat landscape.

Taffeta Typhoon is Microsoft's name for a China-based espionage actor that Microsoft's public naming mapping equates with TURBINE PANDA (CrowdStrike), APT26, TECHNETIUM, TG-0055, Red Kobold, JerseyMikes and BEARCLAW [S1]. CrowdStrike describes Turbine Panda as a China-linked group that targeted aerospace, defense and manufacturing entities, with reporting centred on suppliers to China's C919 airliner [S2][S3][S9]. Google lists APT26 as targeting aerospace, defense and energy for intellectual property theft [S8].
identification.firstObserved: CrowdStrike reporting links the intrusion activity to roughly 2010-2015, starting after COMAC chose CFM International as C919 engine supplier [S2][S3]. CrowdStrike's adversary page says it tracks attacks 'primarily beginning in 2014' [S9].
identification.notes: Microsoft's mapping lists only names, not a Microsoft narrative profile; no Microsoft-authored report on Taffeta Typhoon was found [S1]. Vendor cluster boundaries differ: the Turbine Panda / JSSD narrative comes from CrowdStrike (via secondary press) [S2][S3], while APT26 malware lists come from Google [S8]. Do not merge the two without checking. The mapping equates the names, but each vendor's underlying evidence set may differ.

attribution.sponsor: CrowdStrike, as reported by Security Affairs and others, ties Turbine Panda operations to the Jiangsu Bureau of the Ministry of State Security (JSSD) of the People's Republic of China [S2][S3].
attribution.confidence: This is CrowdStrike's assessment as relayed by press coverage; the original CrowdStrike blog was not retrievable here. CrowdStrike also reportedly regards the Sakula malware as unique to Turbine Panda and JSSD [S2][S9]. No government attribution to Taffeta Typhoon by name was found.
attribution.basis: CrowdStrike reporting says JSSD officers recruited insiders at foreign aviation firms while cyber operators ran intrusions in parallel [S3][S2]. US prosecutions of JSSD officer Xu Yanjun and associated hackers are cited by the press as related to this operation [S3][S6]. Malware overlap (Sakula, PlugX, Winnti) is cited as technical basis [S4].

actors.objectives: Theft of aerospace intellectual property to help close technology gaps in components for the Chinese C919 airliner and its engine program, per CrowdStrike reporting [S3][S5]; Google summarizes APT26 as IP theft against aerospace, defense and energy [S8].

regions: United States and Europe (aerospace suppliers such as GE, Honeywell, Safran) [S4][S6]
targeting.notes: Named C919 supplier victims in press coverage of CrowdStrike's report include Safran, Capstone Turbine, Ametek, Honeywell and GE [S4]. DOJ's 2018 case against Xu Yanjun describes attempts to obtain GE Aviation composite fan module technology and a Safran laptop infection, as reported by AIN and WCPO [S6]. Whether those cases are the same cluster as Taffeta Typhoon rests on CrowdStrike's linkage in press coverage [S3].

capabilities.summary: CrowdStrike reportedly states Turbine Panda used the Sakula RAT, which it considers unique to the group and JSSD, plus PlugX and Winnti-family tools shared with other Chinese groups [S2][S4]. CrowdStrike's adversary page notes heavy use of PlugX [S9]. Google's APT26 page lists SOGU, HTRAN, POSTSIZE, TWOCHAINS and BEACON [S8]. Operations combined human sources (insider recruitment) with cyber intrusion [S3][S2].

implications.jipoe: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. STEP 1: Key terrain is the defense-aerospace industrial base: engine, avionics and composite-component suppliers and their design and engineering networks, plus overseas offices and personnel visiting China [S3][S6]. STEP 2: The actor combines insider recruitment with malware, so technical controls alone do not close the problem [S3]. STEP 3: Observed pattern is a RAT (Sakula, PlugX, Winnti-family) on engineering hosts, document collection and exfiltration [S2][S4]. STEP 4: MLCOA is continued quiet IP theft against aerospace and defense suppliers aligned to Chinese programs. MDCOA is targeting of DoD aircraft-engine or sustainment suppliers to support military rather than civil programs; this extension is not shown in the sources. Candidate indicators: PlugX or Sakula artifacts on engineering workstations, unusual copying of CAD or composite design files, and travel-linked device infections [S4][S6].
implications.jcc2: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. (1) Situational awareness: track contractor-reported intrusions in aerospace supply chains and maintain alias mapping (Taffeta Typhoon / Turbine Panda / APT26) so reports from different vendors are correlated [S1]. (2) Authorities: DIB contractor networks fall under DC3/DIB-CS and company authorities, not DAF-owned terrain; coordinate through those channels. (3) Mission assurance: protect weapon-system sustainment and engine data held by suppliers. (4) Coordination: counterintelligence and insider-threat programs must be linked, because the reported tradecraft uses recruited insiders [S3].

identification.summary: TAG-112 is a Chinese state-sponsored APT that compromised Tibetan websites, including Tibet Post and Gyudmed Tantric University, to deliver Cobalt Strike malware. The group exploited vulnerabilities in the Joomla CMS to embed malicious JavaScript that spoofed a TLS certificate error, tricking users into downloading a compromised security certificate. TAG-112's infrastructure, concealed using Cloudflare, shows notable overlap with TAG-102, but it employs less sophisticated tactics, relying on Cobalt Strike rather than custom malware. The campaign reflects ongoing cyber-espionage efforts targeting Tibetan entities, likely for information collection and surveillance.

TAG-28 is a Chinese state-sponsored threat actor that has been targeting Indian organizations, including media conglomerates and government agencies. They have been using the Winnti malware, which is commonly shared among Chinese state-sponsored groups. TAG-28's main objective is to gather intelligence on Indian targets, potentially for espionage purposes.

TAG-56 is a threat actor group that shares similarities with the APT42 group. They use tactics such as fake registration pages and spearphishing to target victims, often using encrypted chat platforms like WhatsApp or Telegram. TAG-56 is believed to be part of a broader campaign led by an Iran-nexus threat activity group. They have been observed using shared web hosts and recycled code, indicating a preference for acquiring purpose-built infrastructure rather than establishing their own.

Taizi Flood is Microsoft's name for a China-linked influence operation that other organizations track as Spamouflage (Graphika) and DRAGONBRIDGE (Google) [S1][S3][S4]. It is an influence actor, not an intrusion set; Microsoft's earlier name for the same activity was Storm-1376 [S2]. Microsoft describes the 2024 campaigns as run by a Chinese Ministry of Public Security-linked influence actor [S1].
identification.firstObserved: 2019 (first named Spamouflage Dragon by Graphika per secondary reporting) [S4]
identification.notes: Spamouflage takes its name from mixing non-political spam content with propaganda as camouflage [S4]. Vendor cluster names (Spamouflage, DRAGONBRIDGE, Storm-1376, Taizi Flood) are treated by cited reporting as the same operation, but each vendor's boundaries and counts differ and should not be merged [S2][S4][S5]. Google reports DRAGONBRIDGE content primarily targets Chinese speakers, with some English and other languages [S5].

attribution.sponsor: People's Republic of China; Ministry of Public Security (MPS) per Microsoft and Meta-linked reporting
attribution.confidence: Microsoft links Taizi Flood to the MPS [S1]. Meta confirmed that social media activity described in the April 2023 US criminal complaint is part of the Spamouflage operation it reported on [S4]. Attribution rests on vendor assessment and overlapping content; the DOJ complaint did not use the name Spamouflage [S3].
attribution.basis: April 2023: US prosecutors (EDNY) filed a criminal complaint against 34 MPS officers assigned to the '912 Special Project Working Group', alleging online harassment of dissidents; defendants are believed to reside in the PRC [S3] (reporting on the DOJ complaint). Meta and some private researchers tied that activity to Spamouflage, though the link is contested (Graphika reportedly saw only limited, low-confidence open-source connections) [S3][S4]. Microsoft's October 2024 report describes Taizi Flood as MPS-linked [S1]. China's embassy denied the allegations [S3].

actors.objectives: Promote PRC political interests and narratives, criticize the US political system and specific politicians who have denounced Chinese government policies, and harass critics [S1][S3]. Microsoft reported narratives targeting Taiwan's January 2024 election, Japan's Fukushima wastewater release, and US down-ballot Republicans in 2024 [S1][S2].

regions: Latin America (via related OpenAI-reported activity, not confirmed as Taizi Flood)
targeting.notes: In 2024 Microsoft reported campaigns from July, accelerating in September, critical of Republicans including Reps. Barry Moore and Michael McCaul and Sens. Marsha Blackburn and Marco Rubio; these lawmakers had denounced Chinese government policies [S1]. In Taiwan, Storm-1376 posted suspected AI-generated audio of Terry Gou appearing to endorse another candidate on election day [S2]. In Japan it used AI-generated memes and images against the Fukushima wastewater release, in Japanese, Korean and English [S2]. The OpenAI 'Sponsored Discontent' Latin America cluster was described as China-linked and consistent with spamouflage behavior but is not attributed to Taizi Flood in the sources reviewed [S9].

capabilities.summary: High-volume, low-sophistication social media and blog content operation using large networks of inauthentic accounts. Google disrupted over 50,000 DRAGONBRIDGE instances in 2022, over 65,000 in 2023, and over 10,000 in Q1 2024 across YouTube and Blogger, with a lifetime count over 175,000 [S5][S6]. Engagement is consistently minimal: 80 percent of the 2023 YouTube channels disabled had zero subscribers and nearly 95 percent of Blogger blogs received 10 or fewer views [S5]. Meta's August 2023 takedown removed 7,704 Facebook accounts, 954 pages, 15 groups and 15 Instagram accounts, and the operation reportedly rebuilt with new accounts including AI-generated profile pictures [S4]. Microsoft assesses Storm-1376 as the most prolific East Asian actor using AI content, including AI-generated news anchors since at least February 2023, memes and audio [S2][S7]. Microsoft judged AI efforts achieved varying resonance without a consistent formula, and the 2024 US campaigns did not achieve high engagement, though some Moore-related posts drew real-user engagement [S1][S2]. Microsoft described the 2024 posts as including antisemitic messaging and posts designed to look like students in pro-Palestinian protests [S1]. OpenAI separately reported Spamouflage using its models to generate multilingual content [S9].

implications.jipoe: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. Step 1-2: The relevant information environment is open social media and video/blog platforms, with US elections, Indo-Pacific allies (Taiwan, Japan), and diaspora communities as the audience set; the actor is MPS-linked, not a military cyber unit [S1][S3]. Step 3: Evaluated capability is high volume, low engagement, increasingly AI-enabled [S2][S5]. Step 4 MLCOA: continued reactive narratives tied to news events (elections, disasters, military or policy actions) with minimal organic reach [S1][S2][S8]. MDCOA: AI-enhanced content, including audio impersonation, gaining real-user amplification during a crisis, as partially seen with Moore-related posts [S1][S2]. Candidate indicators: bursts of low-follower accounts posting the same narrative in multiple languages, AI-generated anchors or profile images, spikes tied to named lawmakers or incidents [S2][S4].
implications.jcc2: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. Situational awareness: track platform takedown reports (Google, Meta, Microsoft, OpenAI) for narrative shifts affecting US forces, allies and Indo-Pacific partners [S2][S5]. Authorities: counter-influence action in the information environment on US platforms involves platform owners, law enforcement and State/DOJ lanes; Title 10 roles should be confirmed with legal counsel. Mission assurance: low engagement suggests limited direct operational impact, but fabricated content about US military activity (e.g., the Maui 'weather weapon' claim) can erode trust [S8]. Coordination: share indicators with platform partners and interagency counterparts; treat attribution statements as vendor assessments, not government attribution [S1][S4].

provenance.importedSummary: DRAGONBRIDGE is a Chinese state-sponsored threat actor known for engaging in information operations to promote the political interests of the People's Republic of China. They have been observed using AI-generated images and videos to spread propaganda on social media platforms. The group has targeted various countries and regions, including the US, Taiwan, and Japan, with narratives promoting pro-PRC viewpoints. DRAGONBRIDGE has been linked to campaigns discrediting the US political system, sowing division between allies, and criticizing specific companies and individuals.

identification.summary: TaskMasters is a state-sponsored Chinese APT that has been active since at least 2010, primarily targeting industrial, energy, and government sectors in Russia and the CIS. The group has been linked to the Webdav-O Trojan, which employs techniques to bypass network defenses by connecting to legitimate services. Investigations suggest that TaskMasters may have been involved in attacks against Russian federal executive authorities in 2020, potentially alongside another Chinese group, TA428. Additionally, the group has been associated with the BackDoor.RemShell.24 malware, indicating a diverse toolkit in their operations.

Researchers have uncovered a long-term cyber-espionage campaign that used a combination of legitimate software packages and commodity malware tools to target a variety of heavy industry, government intelligence agencies and political activists. Known as the TeamSpy crew because of its affinity for using the legitimate TeamViewer application as part of its toolset, the attackers may have been active for as long as 10 years, researchers say. The attack appears to be a years-long espionage campaign, but experts who have analyzed the victim profile, malware components and command-and-control infrastructure say that it’s not entirely clear what kind of data the attackers are going after. What is clear, though, is that the attackers have been at this for a long time and that they have specific people in mind as targets. Researchers at the CrySyS Lab in Hungary were alerted by the Hungarian National Security Authority to an attack against a high-profile target in the country and began looking into the campaign. They quickly discovered that some of the infrastructure being used in the attack had been in use for some time and that the target they were investigating was by no means the only one.

Teleboyi is a threat actor reportedly based in China, associated with the PlugX RAT. TeamT5 identified a custom PlugX loader used by Teleboyi that employs a similar string decryption algorithm as seen in the McUtil.dll loader from Operation Harvest. While there are weak links to the dsqurey[.]com domain, the connection remains uncertain due to the domain's registration history.

TEMP_Heretic is a threat actor that has been observed engaging in targeted spear-phishing campaigns. They exploit vulnerabilities in email platforms, such as Zimbra, to exfiltrate emails from government, military, and media organizations. They use multiple outlook.com email addresses and manually craft content for each email before sending it.

This threat actor targets organizations in the finance, defense, aerospace, technology, health-care, and automotive sectors and media organizations in East Asia for the purpose of espionage. Believed to be responsible for the targeting of South Korean actors prior to the meeting of Donald J. Trump and Kim Jong-un

TIDRONE is an unidentified threat actor linked to Chinese-speaking groups, with a focus on military-related industry chains, particularly drone manufacturers in Taiwan. The actor employs advanced malware variants such as CXCLNT and CLNTEND, which are distributed through ERP software or remote desktops. The consistency in file compilation times and operational patterns aligns with other Chinese espionage activities, indicating a likely espionage motive.
A group targeting dissident groups in China and at the boundaries.

In April 2020, Crowstrike Falcon OverWatch discovered Iran-based adversary TRACER KITTEN conducting malicious interactive activity against multiple hosts at a telecommunications company in the Europe, Middle East and Africa (EMEA) region. The actor was found operating under valid user accounts, using custom backdoors in combination with SSH tunnels for C2. The adversary leveraged their foothold to conduct a variety of reconnaissance activities, undertake credential harvesting and prepare for data exfiltration.

Tropic Trooper is a China-linked espionage group, also tracked as KeyBoy, Pirate Panda, Earth Centaur and APT23, that vendors describe as active since about 2011 and historically focused on government, healthcare, transportation and high-tech organizations in Taiwan, the Philippines and Hong Kong [S4][S7]. Trend Micro's 2015 report on Operation TropicTrooper described a campaign active since 2012 against the Taiwanese government, heavy-industry companies and Philippine military agencies [S1].
identification.firstObserved: Trend Micro (2015): active since 2012 [S1]. Later vendor reporting (Kaspersky, Trend Micro) says since at least 2011 [S4][S6].
identification.notes: Microsoft has no assigned name in this record; Microsoft naming is not established from the gathered sources. Names used by the cited vendors: Pirate Panda and Earth Centaur (Zscaler), Earth Centaur (Trend Micro), KeyBoy and Pirate Panda (Kaspersky) [S3][S4][S6][S7]. The record's imported aliases also list Red Orthrus and BRONZE HOBART, which were not confirmed in the cited sources. Check Point attributed the 2022 Nim-loader cluster to the group, citing Earth Centaur, KeyBoy and Pirate Panda as its names [S5]. Cluster boundaries between KeyBoy-labelled and Tropic Trooper-labelled activity are the vendors' own and were not independently reconciled.

attribution.confidence: Zscaler ThreatLabz attributes its March 2026 activity to Tropic Trooper with high confidence, based on observed TTPs [S3]. No source gathered attributes the group to a specific PRC government organization.
attribution.basis: Vendor tradecraft and tooling overlap: Zscaler notes a shellcode loader closely resembling the TOSHIS loader previously associated with the group, and staging infrastructure hosting Cobalt Strike Beacon and an EntryShell backdoor previously used by the group [S3]. Kaspersky links its 2024 Crowdoor sample to the SparrowDoor backdoor documented by ESET in 2021, as relayed by The Hacker News [S4]. Vendors describe the group as China-linked; Trend Micro linked USBferry to a China-based actor [S2][S7].

actors.objectives: Espionage against government, military and related organizations, with Trend Micro reporting attempts to reach internal documents such as flight schedules and financial plan documents at transportation targets [S6]. Trend Micro's USBferry work describes the aim as reaching military and government networks, including air-gapped networks, via less-protected intermediaries [S2].

sectors: Healthcare (including a military hospital used as a stepping stone)
Banking (a national bank among USBferry victims)
targeting.notes: Targeting has broadened over time from Taiwan and the Philippines to the Middle East and, in 2026, individuals in Japan and South Korea [S1][S3][S4]. The Hacker News also reported Malaysia as affected in the 2024 Kaspersky activity; Kaspersky's own release was described as a single governmental entity, so the scope differs by source [S4].

capabilities.summary: Trend Micro reported USBferry, USB-borne malware used since 2014 to run commands and pull data from air-gapped military networks, with stepping-stone access via less-protected related organizations [S2]. In 2021 Trend Micro reported compromise of vulnerable Exchange or IIS servers followed by backdoors such as ChiserClient and SmileSvr, and open-source-based customized backdoors including Lilith RAT [S6][S8]. Check Point (2022) described the Nimbda loader written in Nim, a carefully modified AES cipher, and a Yahoyah variant that harvests nearby wireless SSIDs; the loader was bundled with a Chinese-language greyware tool [S5]. Kaspersky (2024) found a China Chopper web shell variant embedded as a module in Umbraco CMS and the Crowdoor backdoor launched by DLL side-loading [S4]. Zscaler (April 2026) described military-themed ZIP lures with a trojanized SumatraPDF delivering an AdaptixC2 Beacon, Visual Studio Code tunnels for remote access, and GitHub used as C2 for a custom Beacon listener [S3]. Itochu researchers presented at Black Hat Asia 2026 a supply-chain compromise involving home routers, and Dark Reading notes the group has used rogue Wi-Fi access points [S9].

Trend Micro (2015 and 2021), Kaspersky (2024), Check Point (2022) and Itochu (Black Hat Asia 2026) primary documents could not be opened directly (fetch of vendor hosts failed); content relies on search-result summaries and secondary coverage.

implications.jipoe: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. STEP 1: Key terrain includes internet-facing Exchange, IIS and CMS servers, military-linked intermediaries such as hospitals, and any air-gapped enclaves reachable by removable media [S2][S4][S6]. STEP 2: The group adapts quickly, pairing legacy tools with open-source frameworks (AdaptixC2, Cobalt Strike) and abusing trusted services (GitHub, VS Code tunnels), which degrades signature-based detection [S3][S8]. STEP 3: Observed pattern is spear-phish or web-server exploit, then loader and backdoor (DLL side-load), then document collection, with USB and stepping-stone organizations for isolated networks [S2][S4][S5]. STEP 4: MLCOA is continued collection against Taiwan, Philippine and regional government and military targets, using military-themed lures [S1][S3]. MDCOA is use of compromised home routers or stepping-stone contractors and medical providers to reach personnel and enclaves of partner militaries during a regional crisis [S2][S9]. Candidate indicators: new web shell modules on CMS servers, unexpected Visual Studio Code tunnel processes, trojanized PDF readers from ZIP lures, outbound traffic to GitHub repositories from unusual hosts, and USB-borne installers [S2][S3][S4].
implications.jcc2: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. (1) Situational awareness: track vendor reporting on this cluster and its alias names (KeyBoy, Pirate Panda, Earth Centaur, APT23) since vendors split activity differently [S3][S4]. (2) Authorities: coverage of partner-nation and contractor networks and personal home devices of personnel falls outside owned DODIN terrain, so coordination of reporting and notification authorities must be settled in advance [S9]. (3) Mission assurance: protect air-gapped and removable-media workflows and intermediary medical or banking connections to military networks [S2]. (4) Coordination: share indicators with allies in Taiwan, Philippines, Japan and South Korea theaters and with DC3 and the DIB program where contractors are exposed [S1][S3].

identification.summary: TStark is a threat actor identified by X-Ops, associated with a cluster of devices that executed the bookmark buffer overflow exploit targeting CVE-2020-15069 (T1203). The actor exhibited odd telemetry behavior indicative of intermittent VPN usage, switching between IP addresses geolocated to Hong Kong and Chengdu. Analysis revealed malware samples for Mac OS X and iOS, as well as IFRAME injection code exploiting a WebAssembly vulnerability (T1189). Additionally, TStark was linked to the development of libsophos.so and the deployment of malicious payloads across their devices.

Tumbleweed Typhoon is a Microsoft threat actor name; Microsoft's naming page lists its origin as China and its other names as THORIUM and Karst [S1]. Palo Alto Networks Unit 42 lists Tumbleweed Typhoon and THORIUM as aliases of its China-attributed group Nuclear Taurus, alongside Bronze Vapor, Chimera, G0114 and Red Charon [S2]. The ETDA encyclopedia attributes the Chimera name to CyCraft, Bronze Vapor to SecureWorks, Red Charon to PwC, THORIUM and Tumbleweed Typhoon to Microsoft, Nuclear Taurus to Palo Alto Networks and G0114 to MITRE [S3]. The Chimera behavioural record below therefore comes from other vendors' reporting on a cluster that those aggregators map to Microsoft's name; Microsoft's own reporting on the cluster was not obtained [S2][S3].
identification.firstObserved: 2018 (Chimera activity against Taiwan semiconductor vendors, per CyCraft/NCC Group-Fox-IT reporting on the mapped cluster) [S4][S6]
identification.notes: CyCraft separates Chimera (Taiwan semiconductor focus only) from the broader cluster tracked by Fox-IT/NCC Group, which also covered EU semiconductors and aviation; the vendors' boundaries differ and should not be merged without caution [S5][S7]. The Karst alias is stated only by Microsoft's naming page and a MISP galaxy listing [S1]. Microsoft renamed element-style (THORIUM) names to weather-based names from April 2023, with Typhoon denoting China [S8].

attribution.sponsor: China (Microsoft's origin category for the Typhoon family) [S1][S8]
attribution.confidence: Microsoft's page states origin as China but gives no confidence level or named sponsoring organization [S1]. CyCraft describes Chimera as China-linked on its own assessment, and NCC Group/Fox-IT assessed with moderate confidence that a single group operating in Chinese interests carried out the intrusions they observed [S5][S7]. No government attribution was found.
attribution.basis: Vendor assessments only: Microsoft taxonomy origin label [S1]; CyCraft analysis of the Skeleton Key / Cobalt Strike / Winnti-linked toolset and targeting [S4][S5]; NCC Group/Fox-IT incident-response engagements October 2019 to April 2020 [S7].

actors.objectives: Espionage and intellectual property theft. CyCraft reported the goal against Taiwan semiconductor vendors was stealing documents, source code and SDKs of chip-related projects [S4]. NCC Group/Fox-IT reported interest in semiconductor intellectual property and, for airlines, passenger name record data [S7][S6]. These objectives belong to the Chimera/Fox-IT cluster mapped to Microsoft's name by third parties [S2][S3].

regions: European Union (semiconductor and aviation, per Fox-IT/NCC Group) [S5][S7]
targeting.notes: Targets included vendors' subsidiaries and competitors [S4]. CyCraft noted Chimera focused solely on Taiwan's semiconductor industry whereas the Fox-IT group showed a wider set of interests [S5].

capabilities.summary: Cobalt Strike was the main implant in the Chimera operation against Taiwan semiconductor vendors, with a mutated beacon replacing a Google Update binary and injecting payloads into other processes; CyCraft also reported Winnti backdoors and a Skeleton Key malware containing code from Dumpert and Mimikatz [S4][S5]. C2 servers were hosted on legitimate cloud services to complicate attribution [S4]. NCC Group/Fox-IT reported credential stuffing or password spraying with leaked credentials, access to Citrix and VPN systems, abuse of Google and Microsoft cloud services, Cobalt Strike for lateral movement, and dwell times up to three years [S7][S6].

campaigns.summary: CyCraft investigated attacks using Skeleton Key from late 2018 to late 2019 against at least seven Taiwan semiconductor vendors, with the goal of stealing chip-related documents, source code and SDKs [S4][S5].

campaigns.name: Fox-IT/NCC Group incident response engagements
campaigns.summary: NCC Group and Fox-IT observed intrusions across semiconductor and airline victims during this period, using cloud-service abuse and Cobalt Strike [S7].

campaigns.summary: Fox-IT/NCC Group published 'Abusing Cloud Services to Fly Under the Radar' in January 2021 and CyCraft published attribution analysis the same month [S5][S6][S7].

Whether Microsoft's THORIUM cluster equals CyCraft's Chimera (Taiwan only) or the broader Fox-IT cluster is asserted by Unit 42 and ETDA, not confirmed by Microsoft [S2][S3][S5].

implications.jipoe: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. Step 1-2: relevant environment is semiconductor and aviation enterprise networks and the cloud services they use [S4][S7]. Step 3: adversary tradecraft is credential abuse against remote-access services, Cobalt Strike, cloud-hosted C2 and long dwell [S7]. MLCOA: continued espionage against high-technology supply chains using valid credentials and cloud C2. MDCOA: broader aviation or defense-industrial collection (inference; not sourced). Candidate indicators: password-spray patterns against VPN/Citrix, beacon masquerading as Google Update, anomalous Google/Microsoft cloud traffic from servers [S4][S7].

Situational awareness: track vendor naming overlaps (Tumbleweed Typhoon/THORIUM/Chimera/Nuclear Taurus) so reporting is deconflicted [S2][S3]. Authorities and coordination: reporting is vendor-sourced only; coordinate with defense industrial base and transportation partners through established channels before acting. Mission assurance: prioritize credential hygiene and monitoring of remote access and cloud egress on supply-chain-relevant networks [S7].

identification.summary: The TunnelSnake campaign demonstrates the activity of a sophisticated actor that invests significant resources in designing an evasive toolset and infiltrating networks of high-profile organizations. By leveraging Windows drivers, covert communications channels and proprietary malware, the group behind it maintains a considerable level of stealth. That said, some of its TTPs, like the usage of a commodity webshell and open-source legacy code for loading unsigned drivers, may get detected and in fact were flagged by Kaspersky's product, giving them visibility into the group’s operation.

China-linked cyber-espionage actor that Microsoft tracks as Twill Typhoon and other vendors call Mustang Panda, BRONZE PRESIDENT, TA416, RedDelta, Stately Taurus and Earth Preta [S2][S5][S8]. US court documents unsealed in January 2025 describe the group as PRC-sponsored. They say the PRC government paid it to develop a USB-worming PlugX variant, which the FBI deleted from about 4,200 US computers [S3][S4]. The group focuses on government and diplomatic targets in Southeast Asia, Mongolia, Taiwan and Europe, and adjusts its lures to current geopolitical events [S5][S7][S8].
identification.firstObserved: Unit 42 assesses the group has operated since at least 2012 [S5]. Proofpoint reports continuous targeting of European diplomats since August 2020 [S8].
identification.notes: Microsoft name: Twill Typhoon. Microsoft's naming map lists TANTALUM, MUSTANG PANDA, BRONZE PRESIDENT and LuminousMoth as other names [S2]. Unit 42 lists Mustang Panda, Bronze President, Red Delta, Luminous Moth, Earth Preta and Camaro Dragon as aliases of Stately Taurus [S5]. GTIG tracks UNC6384 as a separate cluster it believes is associated with TEMP.Hex (Mustang Panda), so UNC6384 activity is kept distinct here [S1]. MITRE ATT&CK group: G0129.

attribution.sponsor: People's Republic of China. Court documents behind the January 2025 DOJ/FBI operation describe the group as PRC-sponsored and state that the PRC government paid it to develop the PlugX variant (as reported by press) [S3].
attribution.confidence: US government: court filings attribute PRC sponsorship (reported in press coverage; primary DOJ documents not opened) [S3]. Recorded Future calls RedDelta Chinese state-sponsored [S7]. Unit 42 attributes the June-August 2025 USB/PUBLOAD cluster to Stately Taurus with high confidence [S9]. GTIG says UNC6384 is 'believed to be associated with' TEMP.Hex and assesses the activity was likely in support of PRC-aligned espionage [S1].
attribution.basis: DOJ/FBI court-authorized operation and affidavits (via press) [S3][S4]; tooling, TTP, targeting and C2 overlaps reported by GTIG [S1]; long-running vendor tracking by Unit 42, Trend Micro, Recorded Future and Proofpoint [S5][S6][S7][S8].

actors.objectives: Political and diplomatic intelligence collection aligned with PRC strategic priorities. Recorded Future says targeting focuses on governments and diplomatic organizations in Southeast Asia, Mongolia and Europe [S7]. Targeting shifts with geopolitical events, such as South China Sea tensions with the Philippines [S5] and Ukrainian refugee movements after Russia's 2022 invasion [S8].

sectors: Political party organizations (Communist Party of Vietnam) [S7]
regions: Southeast Asia: Philippines, Myanmar, Vietnam, Cambodia [S5][S7]
United States: about 4,200 computers infected by the PlugX worm [S3][S4]
targeting.notes: Many US worm infections were probably collateral spread by USB rather than deliberate targeting. The sources describe the worm's spread mechanism but do not state the US victims' sectors [S3][S4].

capabilities.summary: The group's core implant is the PlugX backdoor (SOGU.SEC in GTIG's naming). It is usually loaded by DLL side-loading through legitimate signed software, such as Solid PDF Creator and SmadavProtect, and its C2 traffic has been configured to imitate legitimate Microsoft traffic [S1][S5]. A PRC-funded PlugX variant spread itself via USB drives [S3]. A separate USB tool, HIUPAN (USBFect), was used in 2025 to deliver the PUBLOAD backdoor through the CLAIMLOADER DLL [S9]. Trend Micro documents the TONEDROP, TONEINS and TONESHELL toolset and fake Google Drive download pages [S6]. Delivery has included spear-phishing with geopolitical decoy documents and web bugs used to profile targets [S8][S7]. GTIG attributes to the associated cluster UNC6384 an adversary-in-the-middle captive-portal hijack, the code-signed STATICPLUGIN downloader and the CANONSTAGER launcher, all leading to in-memory SOGU.SEC [S1].

campaigns.name: European diplomatic phishing (TA416)
campaigns.summary: Proofpoint reports sustained phishing of European diplomatic entities since August 2020. Lures were refreshed around the Russian invasion of Ukraine, and a compromised diplomat account was reportedly used against NATO-country officials on 28 February 2022.

campaigns.name: Earth Preta TONESHELL delivery
campaigns.summary: Trend Micro observed sites distributing QMAGENT and TONEDROP in April 2023 and TONESHELL in May 2023, aimed mostly at people in or working with government and telecom organizations.

campaigns.name: Philippines/South Pacific campaigns (Stately Taurus)
campaigns.summary: Unit 42 observed three campaigns against South Pacific organizations, including the Philippine government. They used DLL side-loading through legitimate software and C2 traffic disguised as Microsoft traffic.

campaigns.name: RedDelta PlugX campaigns (to 2024-12)
campaigns.summary: Recorded Future reports targeting of Mongolia, Taiwan, Myanmar, Vietnam and Cambodia. It assesses a likely compromise of the Mongolian Ministry of Defense (August 2024) and the Communist Party of Vietnam (November 2024).

campaigns.name: DOJ/FBI and French-led PlugX worm disinfection
campaigns.summary: The first of nine US warrants was obtained in August 2024, and the operation was announced on 14 January 2025. It deleted PlugX from about 4,200 US computers, using commands identified by Sekoia, alongside a French-led international disinfection effort.

campaigns.name: UNC6384 captive-portal hijack of diplomats (associated cluster)
campaigns.summary: GTIG identified a campaign against Southeast Asian diplomats. It used AitM captive-portal redirection, the signed STATICPLUGIN downloader and CANONSTAGER to deploy SOGU.SEC. GTIG attributes it to UNC6384, which it believes is associated with Mustang Panda.

campaigns.name: USB-borne PUBLOAD against SE Asian government
campaigns.summary: Unit 42 attributed, with high confidence, activity from June 1 to Aug. 15, 2025 using HIUPAN/USBFect and CLAIMLOADER to deliver PUBLOAD against a Southeast Asian government organization.

diamond.adversary: PRC-sponsored espionage group tracked by Microsoft as Twill Typhoon. US court filings say the PRC government paid it to develop PlugX tooling [S2][S3].
diamond.capability: PlugX/SOGU.SEC with a USB worm function; PUBLOAD, HIUPAN and CLAIMLOADER; TONESHELL family; DLL side-loading; signed downloaders in the associated UNC6384 cluster [S1][S3][S6][S9].
diamond.infrastructure: C2 disguised as Microsoft traffic [S5]; fake Google Drive download pages [S6]; UNC6384 used Let's Encrypt-secured lure domains and likely compromised edge devices for AitM [S1].
diamond.victim: Government, defense and diplomatic organizations in Southeast Asia, Mongolia, Taiwan and Europe; telecom-linked individuals; USB-spread infections worldwide [S3][S5][S6][S7][S8].
diamond.socioPolitical: Collection aligned with PRC strategic priorities, timed to events such as South China Sea tensions, Taiwanese elections and the war in Ukraine [S5][S7][S8].
diamond.technology: Windows endpoints, removable media and trust in signed software; browser captive-portal checks and network edge devices [S1][S3][S5].

gaps: Primary DOJ press release and unsealed affidavits (justice.gov) were not opened; PRC-funding and victim-count details come from press coverage [S3][S4].
No Microsoft blog post describing Twill Typhoon activity was found; the Microsoft name is confirmed only through Microsoft's naming map [S2].
DEV-0022, listed as an alias in this record, does not appear in Microsoft's current naming map; its Microsoft linkage is unverified [S2].
UNC6384 is a separate GTIG cluster that GTIG only 'believes' is associated with TEMP.Hex/Mustang Panda; treat its campaigns as associated, not confirmed Twill Typhoon activity [S1].
Unit 42's 2025 Southeast Asia report was cited via The Hacker News coverage; the original Unit 42 page could not be fetched [S9].
Recorded Future, Proofpoint and Unit 42 pages could not be fetched directly; details rely on search summaries of those pages.
Mapping of the group to a specific PRC agency (MSS, PLA or other) is not stated in the sources gathered.
Vendor cluster boundaries (RedDelta, Earth Preta, Stately Taurus, TA416, Camaro Dragon, LuminousMoth) vary by vendor and may not match exactly.

implications.jipoe: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. STEP 1 (operational environment): Key terrain includes diplomatic and ministry networks of partner nations in Southeast Asia and Europe, removable media crossing network boundaries, and network edge devices on partner and host-nation networks [S1][S3][S5]. STEP 2 (effects): USB-borne worms can cross air gaps and spread far beyond intended targets; one variant reached about 4,200 US computers [S3][S9]. Signed loaders and Microsoft-mimicking C2 weaken trust-based and signature-based defenses [S1][S5]. STEP 3 (threat model): The usual chain is a geopolitical lure or infected USB device, then DLL side-loading of a legitimate signed binary, then in-memory PlugX, PUBLOAD or TONESHELL, then document collection [S1][S6][S8][S9]. STEP 4 (COAs): MLCOA is continued spear-phishing and USB-borne intrusion against partner-nation ministries and diplomats, timed to regional events such as ASEAN meetings and South China Sea incidents [S5][S7][S9]. MDCOA is AitM via compromised edge devices, delivering signed malware to deployed or coalition personnel on shared or hotel networks, with USB spread into mission networks [S1][S3]. Candidate indicators: unexpected side-loaded DLLs beside legitimate signed applications; captive-portal redirects to non-portal domains; new Run keys (e.g. CanonPrinter); hidden-folder creation on USB drives [S1][S9].
implications.jcc2: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. Situational awareness: track partner-nation government and diplomatic compromises as early warning, since this actor routinely targets coalition partners in the Indo-Pacific and Europe [S5][S7][S8]. Authorities: the 2024-2025 operation shows that domestic court-authorized remote deletion, coordinated with foreign partners and a private firm (Sekoia), is a viable response model; DoD roles in such actions need authority review [S3][S4]. Mission assurance: enforce removable-media controls and treat signed binaries loading unsigned DLLs as suspicious on mission systems [S3][S5][S9]. Coordination: share indicators with FBI, CISA and partner CERTs, and with vendors tracking overlapping clusters (GTIG, Unit 42, Recorded Future), while keeping cluster boundaries clear [S1][S4][S7][S9].

provenance.importedSummary: Likely Chinese state-sponsored threat activity group RedDelta targeting organizations within Europe and Southeast Asia using a customized variant of the PlugX backdoor. Since at least 2019, RedDelta has been consistently active within Southeast Asia, particularly in Myanmar and Vietnam, but has also routinely adapted its targeting in response to global geopolitical events. This is historically evident through the group’s targeting of the Vatican and other Catholic organizations in the lead-up to 2021 talks between Chinese Communist Party (CCP) and Vatican officials, as well as throughout 2022 through the group’s shift towards increased targeting of European government and diplomatic entities following Russia’s invasion of Ukraine. During the 3-month period from September through November 2022, RedDelta has regularly used an infection chain employing malicious shortcut (LNK) files, which trigger a dynamic-link library (DLL) search-order-hijacking execution chain to load consistently updated PlugX versions. Throughout this period, the group repeatedly employed decoy documents specific to government and migration policy within Europe. Of note, we identified a European government department focused on trade communicating with RedDelta command-and-control (C2) infrastructure in early August 2022. This activity commenced on the same day that a RedDelta PlugX sample using this C2 infrastructure and featuring an EU trade-themed decoy document surfaced on public malware repositories. We also identified additional probable victim entities within Myanmar and Vietnam regularly communicating with RedDelta C2 infrastructure. RedDelta closely overlaps with public industry reporting under the aliases BRONZE PRESIDENT, Mustang Panda, TA416, Red Lich, and HoneyMyte.
